t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: Eight nunciature ciphers from Portogallo 117 that DECODE lists as partially decrypted. Lasry’s 2020 key had turned them into letters with the code words open; three leaves deciphered at the time fix 25 codes, and the rest read as Italian. The first is the nuncio’s secret account of the attempt on José I of 3 September 1758. Lisbon → Rome · two-digit homophones with a four-digit nomenclator · September 1758 – 1760 · read Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60 Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Portogallo 117, items 1–8 · DECODE R25, R195–R201, eight cipher leaves, ten pages · catalogued as partially decrypted (catalogue item 240) Lasry’s key and letter stream read as Italian · 25 code groups fixed from the three leaves deciphered at the time · about 80 rare codes still open Daniel Bourdeau · solved 19 September 2026 Summary. Portogallo 117 holds the letters of Filippo Acciaiuoli, nuncio in Lisbon, and of the abbé Testa, 1757–61. DECODE has eight of the cipher leaves, transcribed digit by digit in 2016–17. In 2020 George Lasry reconstructed the key (two-digit homophones, the digit 6 a null, four-digit code words that all begin with 2) and attached a letter-by-letter decryption of all eight, with the code groups left as numbers. No Italian text was posted, and the records stayed “partially decrypted”. Three of the leaves (10, 24 and 31 October 1758) carry the Secretariat’s decipherment in clear above the figures. Lining those up with the cipher fixes 25 code words ( Re , Regina , Spagna , tutto , molto , ministri , e che …), and with them the other five leaves read as running Italian. What they say: on 12 September 1758 the nuncio sent Rome, in cipher, what Lisbon was not saying aloud. The king had not fallen ill: coming back by night from a lady “delle prime famiglie”, he was fired on in his calesse. His valet and favourite Pedro Teixeira was wounded almost to death, the king was hit in the right arm, and a surgeon took him to the Real Barraca. The later letters follow the wound, the king’s fear of Carvalho, the Jesuits, and in 1760 the marriage of the Princess of Brazil. What stays open is about eighty code groups that occur only once or twice, and a few passages in the two long leaves where the transcription has slipped. Portogallo 117/6 (f. 106r), 24 October 1758: the decipherment made in Rome, “Benche si dica il Rè assai meglio…”, written above the figures. Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, via DECODE R199.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: The volume is “Lettere di mons. Acciaiuoli, nunzio in Portugallo, e dell’abbate Testa, 1757–1761”, ff. 2–585. DECODE dates all eight records 18 January 1757, which is the first date in the volume. The cipher leaves themselves run from 12 September 1758 to 1760: Item DECODE Folio Date Digits Clear on the leaf 117/1 R25 95r–v 12 Sept 1758 1918 no 117/2 R195 98r [Sept 1758] 860 no 117/3 R196 101r 26 Sept [1758] 492 no 117/4 R197 103r 10 Oct [1758] 190 decipherment 117/5 R198 104r 31 Oct [1758] 577 decipherment 117/6 R199 106r 24 Oct [1758] 791 decipherment 117/7 R200 115r–v 28 [Nov?] 1758 1999 no 117/8 R201 280r Lisbon, 12 [?] 1760 1499 no The key is Lasry’s reconstruction (DECODE, 24 October 2020). Letters and common syllables have fixed two-digit homophones: a 04 38 55, e 84, i 08 53, o 81, s 88, il 43 91, che 39, non 14, de 71 78, qu 70 87 90. The digit 6 is a null, scattered freely, and the code words are four digits beginning with 2. No two-digit element begins with 2 or contains a 6, so the figures cut up only one way.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
h: The attempt on the king, 12 September 1758
b: The first leaf (117/1, R25) is the longest. Code words resolved above are in plain type and open ones are given as numbers; the spelling is the cipher’s, which often drops double consonants. … e si racconta che venendo il Re da una [visita] di una dama della <2183> … Pietro Teixeira, suo assai domestico favorito … fussero sparate contro il calesse <2908> schioppettate; restò ferito malamente il cavalcante e la mula del bilancino che egli montava; il Teixeira ferito a morte, <2149> si <2981> che lo avevano sagramentato; il Re molto ferito del braccio destro … il detto chirurgo portò il Re alla Real Baracca. Non <2195> molto rumore: la materia è delicata, ma diventa <2754> in bocca di ogni popolare. Ho creduto doverne avvisare … La dama è delle prime famiglie … Si pensa che venga il colpo da di lei parenti; che venga da nemici del Teixeira … Il fatto non si mette in dubbio. … L’Infante don Manuel me ne parlò con il sospetto … né più posso per ora riferire. “…and it is said that as the King was coming back from [a visit to] a lady… Pedro Teixeira, his very intimate favourite… shots were fired at the calesse; the postilion was badly wounded, and so was the mule of the lead pair he rode; Teixeira wounded to death, so that they had given him the sacrament; the King badly wounded in the right arm… the said surgeon took the King to the Real Barraca. Little noise is made: the matter is delicate, but it is on every common man’s lips… The lady is of one of the first families… The blow is thought to come from her relatives, or from Teixeira’s enemies… The fact is not in doubt.” This is the attempt of the night of 3 September 1758, which Carvalho turned two months later into the arrest of the Távoras and the Duke of Aveiro and, in 1759, their execution at Belém.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: 117/2 (R195). The illness is the public story. The arm is said to be broken, and the fleets and merchant ships are held back “con danno del Re, de’ mercanti e de’ poveri”. 117/3 (R196, 26 Sept). “Continua la voce sulla causa del male del Re, che da nessuno più si dubitò … restò tutto il giorno a letto … nessuno vede il braccio che [è] fasciato … si vuole che il braccio resterà impedito.” 117/4 (R197, 10 Oct). Deciphered at the time: “Il Rè si è levato, ma [non esce] tutto il giorno. Vogliono i più, che sia molto guasto nel Braccio, e che almeno resterà perpetuamente impedito.” 117/6 (R199, 24 Oct) , deciphered at the time: “Benché si dica il Re assai meglio si vuole, che assolutamente il Braccio resterà impedito: parlando un suo confidente col Re sulla morte della Regina [di Spagna] il Re gli disse: è stata buona Sorella, e che sono sicuro, che il Re sposerà la mia Figlia Maria Francisca, e che lo ha promesso alla Regina avanti, che ella morisse: ciò, che il Ministro di Spagna mostra è tutto il contrario … di tutto il resto non posso io compromettermi.” Barbara of Braganza, Queen of Spain and José’s sister, had died on 27 August 1758. The widowed Ferdinand VI did not marry Maria Francisca. 117/5 (R198, 31 Oct) , deciphered at the time: the king has not had erysipelas, “ma un sacco di materia, che ha fatto la piaga”, with fever as a result. The king is very apprehensive; “il credere il male maggiore di quello, che si dice” is universal.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
h: Carvalho, November 1758, and the marriage question, 1760
b: 117/7 (R200) is the longest leaf and the most damaged by transcription slips. Its drift is clear: Carvalho is “dispotico”, “si dice che il Re ne ha paura”, and the Infantes and the court do not dare oppose him. The leaf touches on confessors and preachers, on a lay brother “cacciato nella Compagnia” and on “l’espulsione”. The nuncio notes that he himself is met with “diffidenza”. A companion “sta tutto il giorno da Carvalho”. 117/8 (R201, 1760) is about the succession. The Princess of Brazil might marry the Infante Don Luis of Spain, and there are frequent conferences between the Conde d’Oeiras (Carvalho) and others. The court of London “è molto allarmata” and fears for its trade from “uno della casa di Spagna e di Borbone sul trono di Portogallo”. The letter ends: “Il paese freme, che vorrebbe la [principessa] unita coll’Infante don Pietro.” She married her uncle Pedro on 6 June 1760. Acciaiuoli was expelled from Portugal nine days later.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: About 80 of the 107 distinct code groups that occur once or twice (2183, 2481, 2754, 2823, 2398, 2159, 2413, 2817, 2803 and others), with no crib. A fresh transcription of those two leaves from the images would recover most of them. The rest of Portogallo 117 (ff. 2–585) has more cipher than these eight leaves. It is not on DECODE and was not seen.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: Schmeh’s Top 50 lists twenty-two German radio messages of November 1918 as unsolved, but the keys were published in 2017 and the messages are garbled in transmission. The comment thread that read nine of them is tabulated for the first time, Lasry’s unpublished CHI key is rebuilt, his readers’ method re-derives the solved pages blind, and the ten never read resist every key and a key-free attack that fails its own control. Working notes · September 2026 The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys Schmeh’s Top 50 lists twenty-two German radio messages from the Eastern Front of November 1918 as unsolved. They are not unbroken ciphers. The keys were published in 2017, and what defeats these messages is loss in transmission. Nine were read in the comment thread, three partly, and ten have never been read by anyone. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 15 September 2026 · sources: Schmeh, Top 50 no. 46 and the “Unsolved ADFGVX messages” page provided by George Lasry; the 70 comments under the post (Norbert Biermann, Armin, Thomas, Max Baertl, George Lasry, 2017); Lasry, Niebel, Kopal and Wacker, Cryptologia 2017; James Rives Childs, German Military Ciphers from February to November 1918 Status 9 solved · 3 partial · 10 open The list entry should read “22 messages, 9 solved, 3 partly read, 10 open”, and the key Lasry recovered in the thread belongs alongside the published fourteen. Norbert’s method of 2017, two block edits of up to five letters against a known key, is reimplemented here with a German language model and re-derives the solved pages without a hint of their plaintext. On the ten open messages it finds nothing with any of the fifteen keys, and a key-free attack cannot recover the transposition at these lengths even on a planted control. The open ten need the Childs originals or a key that was never in the corpus.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: James Rives Childs, the American cryptanalyst attached to the French in 1918, kept a transcript of German ADFGVX traffic intercepted on the Eastern Front. In 2017 George Lasry, Ingo Niebel, Nils Kopal and Arno Wacker broke the corpus with a hill-climbing attack on the transposition and recovered 618 cryptograms under fourteen three-day keys, from September to December 1918. Lasry then gave Klaus Schmeh a list of the messages that would not decrypt under any of those keys, and Schmeh published it as “Unsolved ADFGVX messages from World War I”, with the keys attached, and later as no. 46 on his Top 50. Lasry’s own note on that page says what the problem is: the keys are “most certainly all the keys used during the period”, so “the challenge is to understand how the cryptograms were mutilated”. ADFGVX is unforgiving about length. The columnar transposition splits the letter stream by the key length, so one lost or added letter moves every column boundary after it and turns the rest of the message into noise. A message with two garbles is no longer decryptable by the key, even though the key is known. Between February and September 2017 the comment thread under the post did most of the work. Norbert Biermann, Armin, Thomas, Max Baertl and Lasry himself read message after message. Schmeh announced a consolidating article and never wrote it, so those readings existed only as scattered comments and no table of which messages are solved had been published. The first thing this write-up does is publish that table.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: Lasry’s list gives each key as a transposition permutation and a 36-character substitution square, the cells in row order of A D F G V X. Three of the fourteen squares contain runs of hyphens for cells never recovered, and the text layer of the PDF collapses those runs into en- and em-dashes, leaving squares of 34 or 35 characters. Expanding each dash back to the run length that makes 36 repairs all three. All fourteen are in keys.json . The key numbers admit two readings. Either perm[i] is the column emitted i-th, or it is the position at which column i is emitted. Both round-trip self-consistently, so an encrypt-decrypt test cannot tell them apart. Decrypting a real message can. It is the second. The key not on the list On 3 May 2017 Lasry reported in the thread that a two-part message, the FFVXV cryptogram of 13 November and the AFAFF fragment that continues it, decrypted jointly under a key that was in none of the fourteen periods: transposition word CMBLAKOHIDENFJGP, length 16. He gave the joint plaintext, 173 letters, and noted that his program had needed all 356 ciphertext letters to recover a length-16 key. The substitution square was not published. It is rebuilt here by aligning the untransposed bigrams of the two cryptograms with his plaintext, Norbert’s corrections applied: 24 of 36 cells, with the digits and the letters M, Q and Y unrecovered because the message never uses them. It is the fifteenth entry in keys.json and the repo’s notes call it the CHI key, after the header of the message it enciphered.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: Norbert stated his method in one sentence: add or remove up to five characters at two different positions, exhaustive search, an n-gram value function to rank the results. blocks.py does exactly that. For each of the fifteen keys, and each choice of up to two block edits of one to five letters, inserted or deleted at the five-letter group boundaries of the transcript, it decrypts and scores the result with a German quadgram model built from 3.6 million letters of Gutenberg German ( lm_de.py ). Windows that contain a digit or an unrecovered cell cost a floor; windows that cross an X separator cost less than junk and more than text. German prose scores about −3.3 nats per window on this model, and random letters about −7. Given no hint of the plaintext, the search re-derives pages 105, 109, 146 and 171, the “missing 10 letters” message of page 176, and the two CHI messages. On page 146 the five-letter block that Norbert inserted before group 10 comes out as (45, 5) . On the page-176 message the two five-letter blocks come out as (10, 5), (130, 5) . Page 100 falls to the same search with one two-letter insertion. The search also finds the Nov 22–24 partial of the unnumbered VGADA message. Where the printed transcription marks gaps, gaps.py restores them to their groups and anneals the residual single-letter losses; on page 132 it lands on Norbert’s text unprompted. The scores of the re-derived pages, from the run log, against the best any of the open messages achieves: page key length best score, nats per window decrypt as returned by the search 187 (CHI part 1) 16 −4.45 RUSSISCHETUNDPOLNHEERESVERKEHRVOLLERFASSENXWICHTIGESBESONDERS… 146 17 −5.25 FUNKSTELLEKERTSCHERHAE.TAB12X1.XRUFNAME.RICHARD.MILKARLX… AFAFF (CHI part 2) 16 −5.28 SOWEITFERNSCHREIBERVERBDGNITHTARBEICETXRESTSCHRIFTLICHXNACHCHEF… 100 19 −5.39 KEI.ESTOERFNGDURCHFEINDXMITTAGS2FEINDLXDIVXIMMARSCHAUFBELGRAD. 171 20 −5.50 INUKRAI.EUNDPOLEN.UBELKURSETARKSIEIGENDINFOLGEBRUCHEEZWISCHEN… 105 19 −6.02 GERMANIAATAPPEKONSTANTINOPELX6FUERMITTJLMEERDIVISIVNZUXTELXNRX62… 109 19 −6.02 OXFXMXABECDMELUNGXS4VCXUMBJRGABGLETZTEVTEILEBEEVUKTX1WEITEDE… best open message (158, 170) 20, 19 −6.89 noise The solved pages are recognisable German at a glance even where the block edit is not quite right, and the residual garbles are the single-letter losses that a second pass repairs. The 105 and 109 lines score lower than the others because the two-block search only approximates their mutilation; both texts are nevertheless readable in the raw output and both agree with Norbert’s 2017 readings.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: Two block edits, fifteen keys Every one of the ten was run against all fifteen keys with up to two block edits. The best result for each, from blocks_out.txt : page letters key length of best best score output 73 176 22 −7.12 DWR5C10WAXWBI.GWBXD1QGRA.R7OCW3Q… 152 104 22 −6.76 YPVXKTHJ7EM46PGPQ3RONDSEEUHXKTAX… 153 (both) 132, 93 20 −6.99 XWH2XBB3WATECOIFLUKTXMHK17SSY2ME… 158 240 20 −6.89 ZF2B0GEKJXII32RXRCO4LRS2DXA2RBDO… 170 106 19 −6.89 N5ADB08EKYND918UFEED92H3ELZEJ0UA… 176 (GGDAA) 220 22 −7.10 RGXCXXPPUN6RAXZK2YD8PMRX4NVX4ZYT… 189 84 22 −7.08 1AA1SLUOXO.VGXWUXUWH6LXXNHLV.9WW… 198 165 20 −6.97 LTDUUKWRA28KK61UITPUU31LEPXSIP42… 217 170 18 −7.04 YBEIEU84543EOTXT45R8K6XXGCSF4PWI… Nothing clears −6.7. The solved messages come out between −4.4 and −6.0 on the same run, and random letters at about −7.3. So none of the ten is one of the fifteen keys with two or fewer block mutilations, which is exactly the boundary the 2017 readers reached and stopped at. A digit-heavy output is the usual sign of a wrong key: real traffic here is mostly letters, and a wrong square scatters bigrams across the digit cells. The CHI key on the two page-153 messages In September 2017 Norbert suggested, without testing it, that the two page-153 messages might belong to the CHI key, since they are of the same period. Direct decryption with parity repair, and the block search, both return noise for both messages. Either a further unlisted key, or losses heavier than two blocks. A key-free attack, and why it fails If some of the open messages were enciphered under a key not in the corpus, the key would have to be recovered from the ciphertext alone. keyless.py tries: anneal the column order at each candidate length on the index of coincidence of the letter pairs the untransposition produces, since a correct untransposition pairs the bigrams of a monoalphabetic substitution, then solve the 36-symbol substitution with the German model. Before running it on the open messages it was run on a planted control: 224 letters of German enciphered under a length-19 key of the same design. candidate length 15 16 17 18 19 (true) 20 21 22 23 pair IC after annealing 0.055 0.048 0.060 0.053 0.064 0.058 0.066 0.063 0.073 The true length does not stand out: the peak at 19 is beaten by 21, 22 and 23, and the substitution stage does not converge at any length. The control is not recovered . Lasry’s own program, built for this purpose, needed 356 letters to recover a length-16 key. The ten open messages are 84 to 240 letters long. A key-free recovery is therefore out of reach at these lengths, with one exception: two or more open messages that share an unknown key could be solved jointly, as the two CHI messages were. Nothing in the ciphertext marks which those would be, and the two page-153 messages, the natural candidates, give nothing when tried together.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
h: Status, and what would change it
b: The residue is nine solved, three partly read, ten open, and the ten are open for a reason that is now measured rather than assumed. Three things would change it. what why it would matter The Childs originals Several of the ten carry explicit gap marks in the printed transcription and one is labelled “missing 10 letters”. The transcription Schmeh printed is a copy of a copy; the intercept sheets may hold the letters the search has to guess. A further key The CHI message proved the published list is not complete. A key recovered from any other source, or from a longer message in the same period that was never on this list, could be tested against all ten in seconds. A search past two edits Three block edits against fifteen keys is within reach of compute and is the natural next step; it was not run here because two edits was the standard that solved everything the 2017 readers solved, and the scores give no sign that any open message is close. Until one of those arrives, the useful products are the table above, the fifteen keys in machine-readable form with the three damaged squares repaired and the CHI square rebuilt, and a decoder that reproduces the 2017 solutions blind.

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: AGS Estado leg. 8 no. 150, catalogued as “cifrada prácticamente en su totalidad”, was deciphered by Claudio Pérez Gredilla and printed by Danvila in 1899. The ciphertext was transcribed from PARES and aligned with his text on the group xif = V. M. That rebuilds a nomenclator of three-letter code groups and homophonic signs, shows that the dead king he called “de Inglaterra” is Manuel I of Portugal, and reads or corrects about seventeen of the groups he left unread. About ten are still open. Vitoria → Charles V · nomenclator of code groups and signs · 30 December 1521 · resolved Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable of Castile to Charles V, Vitoria, 30 December 1521 Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 8 no. 150 · two leaves, “cifrada prácticamente en su totalidad” · the last letter the three governors signed together, ten days before Adrian was elected pope Deciphered in the nineteenth century by Claudio Pérez Gredilla, keeper of Simancas, and printed by Manuel Danvila in 1899. Aligned here against the ciphertext: the key rebuilt, the dead king corrected from England to Portugal, and about seventeen of the groups Gredilla left unread now read or put right. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 18 September 2026 Summary. PARES describes Estado leg. 8 no. 150 as a letter of the governors of Castile to the Emperor, Vitoria, 30 December 1521, “cifrada prácticamente en su totalidad”, and gives no decipherment. There is one, and it is in print. Claudio Pérez Gredilla, head of the Simancas archive, deciphered the letter, and Manuel Danvila printed his text in the fifth volume of his Historia crítica y documentada de las Comunidades de Castilla (Memorial Histórico Español 38, 1899, pp. 703–705), with a note that some words had resisted him and were printed as they stand in the original. The reading here is his. What this project added was the ciphertext, transcribed from the PARES images and aligned with Gredilla’s text chunk by chunk, anchored on the group xif = V. M. The alignment rebuilds a mixed nomenclator of three-letter code groups and homophonic signs, and it shows one real error in the print. Gredilla has the governors mourning “el Rey de Inglaterra”. No King of England died in 1521. The rest of the letter is about Manuel I of Portugal, who died on 13 December: his widow is Charles’s sister, his heir is “este moço”, and his house has an old alliance with France. Of the roughly twenty-five groups Gredilla printed unread, about seventeen are now read or shown to be misprints, most of them because the same group is read or spelled out elsewhere in the same letter. Status: resolved. The letter was read in the 1880s or 1890s and is corrected here. About ten groups remain open; a sibling letter in the same code would settle them. Adrian’s own ciphers of 1520–21 were checked and are different codes.

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: In 1521 Castile was governed for the absent Charles V by three men: Adrian of Utrecht, cardinal of Tortosa and Charles’s old tutor, whom he had left as regent in 1520, and the two great nobles added to him during the revolt of the Comunidades, Fadrique Enríquez, Admiral of Castile, and Íñigo de Velasco, Constable of Castile. The letter is signed by all three: Adrian in French, Votre treshumble serviteur, el Cardenal dertusense , then the Admiral and the Constable. It is dated Vitoria, 30 December 1521. On 9 January 1522 the conclave in Rome elected Adrian pope; Danvila calls this the last letter the three governors signed together. It covers two sheets, of which three sides are cipher. Only the address and the first two and a half lines are in clear; after La una es the scribe goes into the code and stays there until the dateline, De bitoria a xxx de deziembre de D.xxj . Estado leg. 8 no. 150, f. 1r, head. The clear opening runs to La vna es , and the cipher begins in the same line. The next line, log g t Len top suz lan sur nam , is the place where Gredilla read “del Rey de Inglaterra de que avemos”. Archivo General de Simancas, via PARES.

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: PARES gave the date and the place. An OCR search of the Internet Archive scan of Memorial Histórico Español 38 ( memorialhistri38realuoft ) for that date at Vitoria found the letter on p. 703, under the heading Carta cifrada de los Gobernadores de Castilla al Emperador, fecha en Vitoria á 30 de Diciembre de 1521 . Danvila’s note (3) gives the credit: Esta traducción se debe á D. Claudio Pérez Gredilla, Jefe del Archivo general de Simancas, sin que á pesar de su especial competencia haya podido descifrar algunas palabras, que se trasladan tal como resultan en el original . Note (4) gives the reference as Arch. gen. de Sim., Estado, leg. 8.°, fol. 150 , the number stamped on the leaf. Neither PARES nor the lists of unread ciphers mention the edition. Danvila, Memorial Histórico Español 38 (1899), p. 703: the beginning of Gredilla’s text. Line 4 has del Rey de Inglaterra ; the unread groups fun , suf and ral are set in italics. Internet Archive, memorialhistri38realuoft . Gredilla’s text is good. Measured against the cipher, it holds through the whole letter. What it leaves out falls into three kinds. There are about twenty-five code groups printed in italics as he found them ( fun , suf , ral , rip , pah xiu , top te , rol , xep , lag , fac , fap , fir , xin , dopca , nag , pij and others). There are a few groups dropped without a mark ( for twice; xac in “[xac] y franceses”). And there is one confident reading that is wrong, the King of England. A full transcription of his text from the page scans is adrian1521/gredilla_1880s.txt .

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
h: The cipher, and the key rebuilt by alignment
b: PARES serves these leaves at about 1,000 pixels on the long side and no larger, so the ciphertext was transcribed from upscaled line crops. The code groups, written in ordinary letters, read reliably. The signs of the spelling alphabet read less well, and several are still rough. The transcription was then cut into chunks at each xif , the group that stands for V. M. (vuestra Majestad): 19 in the cipher as transcribed, against 21 “V. M.” in Gredilla. Between anchors, cipher and Spanish were matched word by word. The alignment never has to force a reading, and every value below comes out of it. The system is a mixed nomenclator: Code groups of three letters, sometimes two, stand for words and also for syllables inside words. log is en both as a word and in s-en-tirá and fallecimi-en-to . lan is de in pier-de and de-udo . dop is ur- in urca . Inflection by suffix. A sign after a group changes the ending: mix la , mix= las ; fom cosa , fom= cosas . A homophonic alphabet of letters, figures and signs spells everything else: a = α, e4, Δ; c = a, 6, σ; d = q, z; e = ℓℓ; g = C; o = +; p = R, ff; r = nt, G; s = =; t = g, d; u/v = ≠T. These values are good enough to follow every spelled word against Gredilla’s text, but at this resolution the homophones are not all separated. The table is a reading aid, not a finished key. A triple-barred staff and the sign P4 open and close paragraphs. The code is one-part in blocks. The initial letter of a group follows the plaintext alphabet: r for words in a- (agora, al, alianza, amistad, antes, allá), f for c- (con, como, cosa, Consejo, contra), l/L for d – f (de, del, dicho, el, en, Francia, franceses), n and m for h – l , p for m – n (mar, mucha, negocios, no), s for o – r (otra, para, parece, por, que), t for r – t (Rey, razón, salvo, su, tiene), d for u- , x for v – y (V. M., voluntad, ya, yo). The order inside a block cannot be recovered from one letter. The block structure matters, because it limits which words an unread group can be. Group Reading Group Reading Group Reading xif V. M. sur que lan de Len del Loc el log en top Rey / Reina suz Portugal* te de fer con for como fom cosa som por sum para sem parece tup salvo dop ur- (urca) pex negocios rol / ral agora rum amistad lix / lux Francia / franceses xep ya tiz tiene roc al The full table, with the evidence for each value and its confidence, is in adrian1521/NOTES.md .

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: Gredilla’s first sentence of news reads la una es el fallecimiento del Rey de Inglaterra, de que avemos tenido la pena que es razón . Henry VIII was alive in December 1521 and lived until 1547. The letter itself says who died: the loss is felt by la Reina de Portugal y hermana de V. M. , that is Leonor of Austria, Charles’s sister, married to Manuel I in 1518 and widowed on 13 December 1521; the dead king was tan buen amigo y deudo de V. M. , and now there is este moço el Rey que sucede en aquel Reino : João III, nineteen, with people about him que no le dexan las orejas ociosas ; los Reyes de Portugal tienen [alianza] antigua con los de Francia , which the French will work on; Charles is asked to send someone to the new king para demostrarle el sentimiento que tiene del fallecimiento del Rey su padre , and to visit and console a la Reina . In the cipher, the dead king is Len top ( del Rey ) followed by one short group, which the notes read as suz . Gredilla left the same group unread at envié al dicho [suz] una persona , where the sense is the new King of Portugal. Inglaterra is spelled nowhere. On line 6, where Gredilla correctly reads la Reina de Portugal , Portugal is spelled out letter by letter after top , with the same signs (C = g , roc = al ) as the other spelled Portugal on line 16. The correction does not depend on reading that one group. Everything the letter says about the king fits Manuel and Portugal, and nothing fits England.

b: Most of the new readings come from the letter itself. A group Gredilla left blank in one place is often spelled out, or read by Gredilla himself, in another. The marks follow the notes: ** certain (the same group is read or spelled elsewhere in the letter), * probable (context, plus the initial-letter block the group must belong to), ? a guess. M. debe ya tener noticia los del fap Real fap los del Consejo Real** c-block; the fixed title Consejo Real , sitting at Burgos pah xiu pah xim mucha voluntad * “xiu” is a misprint for xim ; p-block and x-block tienenla antigua tiz rto rip tienen alianza * antigua rip recurs at el amor, deudo y [rip] ; a-block y ral con este moço ral agora * next to rol ; a-block top te que tiene top te a la Reina, de * que tiene top = Rey/Reina, te = de en lag= vienen; como quiera que lag= lag = ellas * d–f block; the hulks guerra fir él fir contra * c-block a su xin xin voluntad * x-block, haciendo guerra y paz a su voluntad por pij que pij manera * m–n block, por manera que ren nod sig sig procurar * o–r block; cf. para procurar de continuar en fun fun en coyuntura ? c-block, sense only en nag nag Italia ? h–l block, la guerra que se haze en [nag] los de fac fac Consejo ? c-block, beside fap Misprints in the 1899 edition , checked on the manuscript: “xiu” is xim ; “itb” is tib ; “xap” is xac ; and the numeral “40” after urcas [xub] is the code group yo , not a number. t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: Gredilla’s text, lightly normalised; bold a group now read or corrected, with its confidence mark; [brackets] still unread La una es el fallecimiento del Rey de Portugal **, de que avemos tenido la pena que es razón, para ello así por lo que pierde y sentirá la Reina de Portugal y hermana de V. M., como ** porque nos parece que el fallecimiento del dicho Rey ha acaecido en coyuntura ? que no [suf] a los negocios de V. M. … y agora * con este moço el Rey que sucede en aquel Reino, y con que diz que tiene cabe sí algunos que no le dexan las orejas ociosas, no sabemos la demostración que querrá hacer; porque como ** V. M. debe ya tener noticia, los Reyes de Portugal tienen alianza * antigua con los de Francia, y creemos que los franceses no estarán perezosos en solicitar por aquella vía lo que haze a su propósito. In English, the letter runs as follows. Since writing the general letter that goes with this one, a duplicate of one sent some days ago, two matters of substance have arisen. The King of Portugal. The governors grieve at his death, for the sake of the Queen, Charles’s sister, and because it comes at a bad moment for Charles’s affairs. With Manuel as friend and kinsman, that side was secure. Now there is a young king whose advisers do not leave his ears idle, and no one knows which way he will turn. The kings of Portugal have an old alliance with France, and the French will not be slow to use it. The governors are sending a prelate or a gentleman from Spain to visit and console the Queen. They ask Charles to do the same before the King of France takes the lead: to send a person of his household to the new king to show his sorrow at his father’s death, to ask that he succeed his father in the love, kinship and alliance between the two houses, and to promise that Charles will keep it up with great goodwill *. The same envoy should visit the Queen on Charles’s behalf. The hulks. Storms at sea have driven some urcas , the big northern cargo ships, onto the Spanish coast. One lies at San Sebastián, detained and well guarded. Two are at Laredo, and the governors are trying to hold them, but there is no force at hand to compel them. They mean to keep whatever they can seize, cargo and all, under sequestration until Charles decides. The difficulty is that the ships sail under a safe-conduct from Charles; a copy goes with this dispatch. The councillors present, and the Consejo ** Real at Burgos, hold that the safe-conduct rests only on the suspension of the marcas represalias , the letters of reprisal. Charles cannot have meant that, if [xac] were at war against * him, their hulks should go safely haciendo guerra y paz a su voluntad *. If [xac] join the French, the ships could be treated as good prize. If they stay neutral, they might be won over with [tib], or Charles might use the matter for reasons of state. In either case the French would take the hulks, by fair means or foul, for their fleet if the war between [Lag] and France goes on, and that fleet is said to be growing very large. The governors ask for orders. Postscript. After writing, they learned that the Laredo hulks had set sail, so Charles need decide only about the one at San Sebastián, which remains and will be kept under good guard until he gives other orders. F. 2r, foot: the postscript in cipher, the dateline in clear ( De bitoria a xxx de deziembre de D.xxj ), Adrian’s Votre treshumble serviteur, el Car[denal] dertusense and the signatures of the Admiral and the Constable. Archivo General de Simancas, via PARES. The full corrected text, with every change marked, is adrian1521/plaintext_corrected.txt .

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: Still unread (about ten groups): suf ( que no [suf] a los negocios ); xub and yo after urcas ; ren nod before procurar ; xac , a people ( que [xac] y franceses son a unirse , si [xac] están neutrales ); sif ; tib ; xit ; Lag , one of the belligerents with France; and ne ( la or mala fortuna ). The Scots fit xac in sense: Albany landed in Scotland with French backing in November 1521, and reprisals were a Scots–Flemish grievance. But the group sits in the x-block, which should hold words in v – z , so this is not offered as a reading. The group after Len top . In this hand r and z look much alike. The working transcription writes the group as sur , which is que , and the notes read it as suz . Que makes no sense in that place, and Gredilla printed a group suz where the new king is meant, so suz = Portugal is probable, not certain. The Portugal correction itself does not rest on this group (section 04). The spelling alphabet is good enough to follow every spelled word against Gredilla, but its homophones are not all separated at the 1,000-pixel resolution PARES serves. Several sign readings in the transcription are marked rough. The probable readings (*) come from sense plus the initial-letter block. They are not confirmed by a second occurrence, and the guesses (?) are only that. No shared key. Adrian’s own ciphered letters with decipherments were checked, in the hope that one of them would supply the key. None does. Estado 8/112 (28 July 1520) uses a sign-and-figure cipher. PTR 2/1/94, 99, 100 and 101 (October–December 1521) use Adrian’s dotted trigraph code ( leb. nud. sa. cab. ), in which V. M. , que , de and en have other groups. The joint letter is in a third code, probably the Admiral’s or the Constable’s. The Admiral’s 1521 cipher letters survive in clear copies (PTR 1/96/5, 9, 12, 13, 44, 45), but their originals were not found on PARES. A sibling in the same code, with its decipherment, is the way to close the open groups.

DECODE lists eleven of them as never solved. The Dutch codebreaker Pierre Lyonet’s decipherments of eight sibling letters are among the images, filed as ordinary clear pages. Aligned group by group with their cipher, they rebuild the code, and the code reads the letters that had no decipherment. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 19 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue listed eleven d’Affry letters of 1757–58 in the Dutch royal archives as unsolved, with DECODE’s note that the siblings’ solutions were “written on separate sheets”, not imaged. They were imaged: eight clear pages marked by the Dutch decipherer’s clerk, which read like d’Affry’s own clear letters, are Lyonet’s decipherments of the cipher beside them. Transcribed from the scans and aligned group by group (7 letters, about 3,000 groups), they give a key of 651 groups. It is one code for the whole year, to Rouillé and then to Bernis. With it nine undeciphered letters read at 60–95% each: the navy and the convoys, the Gouvernante’s tears («faut-il que ce soit moi qui favorise les moyens de faire du mal à mon père?»), Ostend and Nieuport, spies sent to England, a French loan tried in London. The reading was checked against print: Bussemaker’s 1906 extracts of 19 and 22 July and 1 April 1757 recur group for group, and Coquelle printed the Gouvernante’s words in 1904 from the Paris original. A tenth letter, R2067, had no transcription and was transcribed from the images. The eleventh, to Stainville in Vienna, is in another code and stays unread. No. 171, 26 April 1757 (DECODE R1069): the intercept copy in figures (left, 865 1028 875 1018 569 …) and Lyonet’s clear copy of the same letter, filed with it (right): J’ai l’honneur de vous addresser la copie d’une lettre que Mr de la Salle m’a écrite de Hambourg . Koninklijk Huisarchief, via DECODE.

t: The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters from The Hague, 1757–58 — the code rebuilt from Lyonet’s decipherments
b: Louis-Auguste d’Affry (1713–1793), a Swiss officer in French service, was Louis XV’s envoy and then ambassador at The Hague from 1755 to 1762. His despatches went by the Dutch post, and the stadholder’s cabinet had them opened, copied and given to Pierre Lyonet (1706–1789), the naturalist who was also the Republic’s cipher secretary. Karl de Leeuw’s history of the Dutch black chamber (2000) records that Lyonet broke d’Affry’s first code in June 1756 and then “two more French ones”. The decipherments were copied for the Princess Governess and the regents. One set is in the Nationaal Archief (Stadhouderlijke Secretarie, 1.01.50 inv. 221 and 223, “grouped by the cipher used”, not digitised). Robert Fruin excerpted it in the 1850s, and Bussemaker printed his excerpts in 1906, as Dutch summaries with some verbatim French sentences. Another set is inv. 192 of the Prins Willem V archive in the Koninklijk Huisarchief, catalogued on DECODE as nineteen records, R1052–R1076 and R2067. Each record is one letter: the intercept copy of the cipher, with the clear passages of d’Affry’s original written in. Seven are marked “solved by Dutch codebreakers, the solution written on separate sheets”, and eleven “unsolved”. The eleven are this target: DECODE Date, number To Groups R1072 6 Jan 1757, no. 123 Rouillé 556 R1076 7 Jan 1757, no. 124 Rouillé 403 R1073 25 Jan 1757, no. 133 Rouillé 312 R1064 1 Feb 1757, no. 136 Rouillé 1,249 R1065 3 Feb 1757, no. 137 Rouillé 1,082 (has a decipherment; see below) R1067 1 Apr 1757, no. 161 Rouillé 1,481 R1068 26 Apr 1757, no. 172 Rouillé 60 R1054 19 Jul 1757 “B.” (Bernis; DECODE reads Bonnac) 372 R1070 22 Jul 1757, no. 210 “B.” 400 R1071 4 Aug 1757, no. 485 Stainville (Choiseul), Vienna 760 R1074, R2067 17 Jan 1758, no. 283 “B.” / d’Usson 538 + two pages

t: The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters from The Hague, 1757–58 — the code rebuilt from Lyonet’s decipherments
h: The decipherments were in the images
b: A first pass read the DECODE note literally and treated the siblings’ solutions as lost. The attack started from cribs: Bussemaker’s verbatim sentence of 19 July placed “des précautions” (800 698) in R1054 by its repeat twelve words apart, and “le danger de la religion” turned up in the 22 July letter. That showed a word-and-syllable nomenclator, but cribs and a language-model solver got no further than a few dozen groups. The clear pages among the images then turned out to be something else. On R1066 (17 February) the clear page 5578, headed “N° 142 … D’A. à R.” with a clerk’s mark, begins with the same sentence as the intercept (“Mon courrier n’est arrivé que le 15 au soir”). It then goes on, where the intercept switches to figures, with “J’ai vu Mr de Slingerland chez moi ce matin”. It is Lyonet’s decipherment of the whole letter. The same mark heads clear copies in R1052, R1053, R1062, R1063, R1065, R1069 and R1075. Their openings fit their ciphers group for group: J’ai l’honneur de vous… = 865 1028 875 1018 569. R1066, page 5578: Lyonet’s copy of no. 142 (17 February 1757). Slingerland dictated to d’Affry the substance of Holdernesse’s letter to Yorke: Sa Majesté Britannique a évité la guerre autant que la prudence et les intérêts de sa part l’ont permis … Koninklijk Huisarchief, via DECODE. R1065, listed as unsolved, is one of them. Its cipher is cut into thirteen numbered paragraphs that alternate between two sets of pages, and its clear copy is on four others. DECODE had noted a clear letter “whose relation to the ciphered periods is unclear”.

t: The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters from The Hague, 1757–58 — the code rebuilt from Lyonet’s decipherments
b: The clear copies were transcribed from the scans and aligned with their ciphers one group at a time, each group graded H (forced by the text on both sides or repeated) or M. The seven letters were R1052, R1053, R1062, R1063, R1065, R1066 and R1069, plus the ciphered parts of R1075, about 3,300 groups. The alignments were made letter by letter and cross-checked; a vote over all of them gives the key. It is a two-part code: the numbers are not in alphabetical order. It has about 1,200 groups for letters, syllables, words and names, with homophones for the common ones ( de 219, 1018, 1138; la 583, 382, 10; que 197, 194, 31). Some examples: 13 is a full stop, and 105, 107 and 797 are usually nulls. Leurs Hautes Puissances is 399 627 261. Le Roi de Prusse is 16, Hollande 294, Reischach 488, Sa Majesté 22, religion 578. The Jan–Feb and Apr–Jul letters differ in their habits (which homophones the clerk favoured) but not in the code. The DECODE transcriptions needed correcting on the way. Two copyists wrote 8 as a looped figure that the transcribers read as 0, so 056 is really 856 and 099 is 899. This affects R1064, R1067, R1072 and R1075. Elsewhere groups are run together (58291 = 582 91) or lines dropped or repeated.

t: The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters from The Hague, 1757–58 — the code rebuilt from Lyonet’s decipherments
b: Each letter was read with the key, and the few groups missing from the key were inferred from context and recorded with their evidence. Inferred values are in braces in the working files. The full French readings are in the repository; extracts follow. 6 January 1757 (R1072, no. 123): the Italian The whole letter concerns “the Italian”, a spy who wants to be paid for earlier warnings of English designs on the French possessions in the two Indies. For a hundred louis and a pension he offers to leave at once for England and report on the English forces by land and sea, the secrets of the London cabinet, their intrigues in foreign courts, the plans for the 1757 campaign, and England’s correspondents in France. D’Affry thinks the money well spent if the man is sound. This is the weakest reading (about two thirds in sense), and Bussemaker has no entry for this date. The Italian reappears on 3 February, when d’Affry pays him the hundred louis and he leaves for Helvoet. 7 January 1757 (R1076, no. 124): convoys and herring A convoy the Dutch feared for had arrived: four ships were to escort it, and the storm kept two of them in port. D’Affry expects the navy to be enlarged sans augmentation dans les troupes de terre , and he expects the case to be pressed harder now that people see the English respect Dutch shipping only as far as it is protected. So every convoy through the Channel must be strongly escorted. In Amsterdam he talked with a regent about the herring. Bussemaker’s summary (no. 56): enlarge the navy without the army, protect trade, herring privileges for the republicans. 25 January 1757 (R1073, no. 133): a false rumour It was said that d’Affry had given the States-General a memorial calling any increase of the land forces a breach of neutrality. The rumour was quashed, but he went to see the Grand Pensionary. He told him the King neither wished to meddle nor ever had, but as a friend would regret seeing the Republic take on heavy expenses. Steyn answered that the increase would meet many difficulties. If its opponents could not stop it, he said, they could at least get a declaration made first to Versailles, Vienna and London. 1 February 1757 (R1064, no. 136): taxes and herring The States of Holland had adjourned until the 20th, when the augmentation comes up. The war funds were no larger than usual, and the means proposed (a sixth added to the house tax, a general rise in excises, interest on public funds cut to 2%) were so heavy that the augmentation looked unlikely. D’Affry then argues for a temporary favour to the Dutch herring fishery while France lacks sailors. It could be revoked when no longer deserved, and it would widen the quarrel between the Republic and England. He asks for it only if Holland blocks the augmentation. Then comes intelligence on suspects travelling through Antwerp, Breda and Liège. Bussemaker’s no. 59 gives the first part point by point and leaves out the agents, as Fruin said he did. 1 April 1757 (R1067, no. 161): the Gouvernante The Maastricht convoy crisis. D’Affry found the Pensionary “fort embarrassé”: ce qui se passe ici aujourd’hui n’est […] que pour le perdre . The same afternoon he read the King’s declaration to the Princess Governess: «… tu n’es pas ministre; faut-il que ce soit moi qui favorise les moyens de faire du mal à mon père?» Je lui ai répondu que S.A.R. savoit jusqu’à quel point le Roi mon maître a cherché à éviter la guerre … Je demande à S.A.R. d’employer non seulement ses bons offices, mais son crédit et son pouvoir pour déterminer une réponse prompte et telle que le Roi a droit de l’espérer. Coquelle quoted the Governess’s words in 1904 from the Paris original, with the day given as 5 April. The piece that Bussemaker’s no. 67 quotes about Wassenaer (“son fils cadet a actuellement un employ en Frise, dont la nomination dépend de Mme la Gouvernante”) is piece no. 7 of this letter. The numbered pieces do not follow in number order: they read in page order. 26 April 1757 (R1068, no. 172) Il a passé hier au soir un courrier de Vienne à Londres. Vous savez mieux que moi ce dont il est chargé. M. de Colloredo doit faire passer à M. d’Aremberg ce qu’on lui aura répondu. The DECODE note asked whether this note went unsolved because a different code was used. It did not: it is the same code as no. 171, which Lyonet deciphered. 19 July 1757 (R1054, to Bernis) Nobody knows the purpose of the Gouvernante’s journey to The Hague. If it is to push an augmentation of the land forces, d’Affry asks for orders at once: … il me paroit qu’il seroit essentiel aux intérêts du Roi de m’envoyer des ordres sur le champ [de demander] une confirmation de tout ce que les Etats-Généraux ont promis à Sa Majesté, et en même tems une déclaration de leur part qu’ils ne feront camper aucun corps sur leurs frontières. Je sens la dureté de cette proposition … The passage runs from group 145 to group 351, and Bussemaker’s French agrees with it word for word except in four places. The cipher has “M. le maréchal d’Estrées” where Fruin wrote “M. le Cte”. It has “de sa communication” for “de la communication du Royaume”. It spells out Leurs Hautes Puissances , and it has “des ordres” for “ordre de demander”. The page ends with an attack of gout. 22 July 1757 (R1070, no. 210, to Bernis): Ostend The Gouvernante is said to be going to the States of Holland to speak for her father George II, pointing to the danger to the Protestant religion. D’Affry doubts she will: if she proposes land troops, the other side will propose ships. Her party protested at the French occupation of Ostend and Nieuport. D’Affry notes that sensible people see the other side of it: with Ostend closed to the English, Amsterdam and Rotterdam will take over the trade England did with the Low Countries. Then Bussemaker’s sentence, group for group: Il y a quelques villes où quelques ministres hollandois ont prêché sur le danger de la religion, mais le peuple n’en paroit pas animé . If the Princess takes the Ostend affair as a pretext, he will ask her for an audience without waiting for orders. 17 January 1758 (R1074, no. 283, and R2067) The first part is an extract from a correspondent’s letter. A French loan of two millions had been tried in England by “des gens si maladroits” that the ministry heard of it and a new law followed. It could still be got round: four millions at four or four and a half per cent at most, given “un profond secret, une parfaite connoissance du pays”. D’Affry adds that a Sieur Mac[donald] of the Bulkeley regiment has passed through on his way from France to England, and he suspects him of carrying commissions for the enemy. Some Scots and Irish in French service are spies, he writes, but to act would throw suspicion on the rest. The companion letter of the same day to d’Usson (R2067) has no DECODE transcription. It was transcribed from the images and read at about 91%. It is d’Affry’s own letter of the same number, covering the extract. He thinks money operations in England useless: if found out, they would make France’s needs look greater than they are and put the English on their guard. Englishmen will still lend in France when the interest is right, and some already hold French life annuities. He adds that two or three Englishmen are at The Hague, one of them Mac…, and that two Spaniards from Paris, one a secretary of the Spanish embassy, are on their way to London.

t: The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters from The Hague, 1757–58 — the code rebuilt from Lyonet’s decipherments
b: R1071 (4 August 1757, to Stainville in Vienna) is in a different code and is not read. Per letter, 5–12% of groups stay unread (listed as [n] in each reading file). R1072 reads only about two thirds in sense: its copy is the worst transcribed. Grades: values forced by a decipherment are H; values inferred from context in the undeciphered letters are M or ? and listed with their evidence in read/R*_new.tsv . 56 groups of the key are ambiguous between two readings ( amb_M.json ). The eight decipherments themselves are Lyonet’s. The contribution here is the key and the reading of the nine letters that had none.

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: Forty-nine groups of the 1,600-element “THE = 972” diplomatic code, read in full after reconstructing 580 groups from the State Department’s own pencil decodes on NARA microfilm M34 roll 13. United States · diplomatic code · 1808 · solved Armstrong's Coded Postscript to Madison Bourbon-l'Archambault, 30 August 1808 · Library of Congress, James Madison Papers, Series 1, reel 10 · Founders Online, Madison/99-01-02-3466 Reconstruction of the “THE = 972” code from the State Department's own pencil decodes, and the reading of the postscript Daniel Bourdeau · solved 14 September 2026 · updated 18 September 2026 Summary. John Armstrong, United States Minister to France, ended a private letter to Secretary of State James Madison (Bourbon-l'Archambault, 30 August 1808) with a postscript of 49 numerical code groups. The letter is printed in Founders Online with the postscript undeciphered, and S. Tomokiyo's Unsolved Historical Ciphers lists it, with a partial reading of about a third of the groups obtained from one letter with known plaintext. The code — a 1,600-element word-and-syllable code that Armstrong used from 1804 to 1810, conventionally labelled by its group for "the", 972 — was never published. It is reconstructed here from a different source: the microfilmed State Department despatch books (NARA M34, roll 13), where a Department clerk pencilled the decode above every group of a long despatch of October 1806. Some 580 code groups are now known, enough to read the postscript in full and most of a second coded letter of 22 February 1808. The postscript reads: Russel ought to be the consul: he is an American by birth, and is much better qualified than any other candidate. In a word, he is above men in general. Next to him in fitness is O'Mealy, but he is, like Warden, an Irishman. Companion: John Quincy Adams’s St Petersburg despatches, said to be in this code, turn out to be in another, and Erving’s 1807 letter in Pinckney’s — two legation codes .

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: The letter is a "private" one, written from the spa town of Bourbon-l'Archambault where Armstrong was taking the waters. Its clear text answers Madison's private letter of 20 July: it dismisses the complaints of Fulwar Skipwith (the departing commercial agent at Paris), warns that the embargo is "not felt" in France and "forgotten" in England, and says of David Bailie Warden, secretary of the legation and candidate for the Paris consulate, only that "a letter of the same character from me to the President … will give you my opinion of the fitness of M. Warden for the consular office at Paris: to this therefore I refer." The opinion Armstrong would not put in clear follows in code, as a postscript. The postscript, Library of Congress, Madison Papers reel 10, frame 0521 (detail). Groups are separated by points; the words and , much better , In a word , in general. Next to , but are in clear. Founders Online (Early Access document 99-01-02-3466, from the forthcoming Papers of James Madison, Secretary of State Series ) prints the groups as follows; the reading of the manuscript differs in one group (§6): 1394. 1116. 1273. 250. 1165. 1405. 970. 148. 1459. 1482. 1201. 821. 130. 821. 1429. 720. 970. and 1482. much better 992. 1319. 1048. 584. 687. 249. 736. 1013. 750. 967. In a word 1459. 1482. 1202. 1561. in general. Next to 927. 1090. 1052. 832. 1482. 934. 510. 860. but 1459. 1482. 1320. 384. 1280. 1218. 1481. 1483. 555. The second line begins "972." in the manuscript (Founders' "970." is a misprint for the ).

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: Armstrong's despatches from Paris between 1804 and 1810 use a single large code in which 972 = the . Ralph Weber's survey of American diplomatic codes notes some forty letters in it among the Despatches from United States Ministers to France (DUSMF, NARA Record Group 59, microcopy M34, rolls 13–14). It is not the code of Armstrong's letter of 20 February 1808, a distinct and still unsolved system. Its structure, as recovered: Groups run from 1 to about 1600. Each stands for a whole word ( Emperor 32, Spain 326, Minister 61), a syllable ( con 470, tion 352, ness 832), or a single letter ( s 1116, n 821, d 1001). Names are spelt out in syllables: Gu-sta-va-us , Et-ru-ria , Y-ru-jo , Dan-ish , O-mea-ly . The vocabulary is laid out in many short alphabetical runs , not one alphabetical sequence. For instance 1–130 is one run of words ( circumstance, commerce, communicate, character … Minister … these, thousand, toward … week, without, yesterday ), 130–417 a second ( America, between, business, confide, contrary, country … Prince, Queen, reason, report, Russia, second, secret … which, whom, word, would, your ), and above 417 the syllables come in blocks that restart the alphabet every few dozen numbers (1201 a … 1230 c ; 1268 ed … 1298 ex ; 1302 ide … 1348 broa ; 1405 be … 1443 good ; 1500s fa … man … now ). Within a run the order is alphabetical, which is what allows unknown groups to be pinned between known neighbours. Common elements have homophones: re is 555, 561, 562, 869, 871 and 1379; on is 945 and 946; an 1210 and 1216; ing 1478 and 1594. Armstrong writes a point after each group; the clerk who decoded despatches at the Department wrote the plaintext in pencil above each group and a short dash above groups that continue a word already written out ( Et |–|–, for Etruria ).

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: 3.1 The known-plaintext letter of 4 May 1806 Tomokiyo had already exploited the one letter for which both the coded original and a clear copy survive — Armstrong to Madison, 4 May 1806 (Founders 99-01-02-0393), on the Spanish minister's discovery of the confidential Florida proposals — to assign about 230 groups, with a few marked doubtful. This gave a base of 68 firm values used here, among them the, of, to, is, he, a, and, by, in, s, n , and showed the alphabetical layout. 3.2 The Department's pencil decodes (M34 roll 13) The decisive source is the microfilm itself. NARA has digitised M34 roll 13 ("Nov 12 1804 – Dec 27 1807", catalogue ID 188671172; 393 frames). Frames 0192–0201 carry a long political despatch of October 1806 (written just after Lord Lauderdale's departure from Paris, with news of "two Russian armies now entering Silesia") whose every code group has the clerk's decode written above it. A scoring pass over the roll for faint mid-grey pixels away from ink located the annotated frames; the pairs were then read off by eye, frame by frame, and recorded with a confidence grade and their frame/line reference. M34 roll 13, frame 0200, right-hand page (p. 13 of the despatch). Ink: Armstrong's code groups; pencil above: the State Department's decode — "she wears is nearly transparent — the late meeting of the Hungarian Diet & a pleasure camp in October which is to assemble a great proportion of her army under the command of Prince Charles can deceive no body … Two Russian armies are now entering Silesia and a third is destined for Moldavia …". About 500 pairs were harvested this way, 352 of them read with confidence. Merged with the 4 May 1806 values the table stands at 580 distinct groups (§7). Ambiguities in the pencil (the roll is a 1940s microfilm of faint graphite) were resolved by requiring each reading to sit in its alphabetical slot and to recur consistently across frames. 3.3 Interpolation Twenty groups needed for the postscript and the February letter were not in either source. Each was inferred from context and then checked against its alphabetical slot; all twenty fit. Examples: 1394 between 1393 purp and 1395 Italy must open a new run — and it reads ru in three independent places ( ru-in , Et-ru-ria , Y-ru-jo ); 250 lies between 249 other and 252 own and reads ought ; 1273 between 1272 eight and 1279 Emp reads el ; 384 between 383 w and 385 was reads ward ; 1320 between 1319 li and 1325 long reads like ; 1483 between 1482 is and 1484 it reads ish . 3.4 A control text: the letter of 22 February 1808 Armstrong's private letter of 22 February 1808 (Founders 99-01-02-2733) contains about 150 code groups embedded in a clear political survey of Europe. It shares no groups of interest with the known-plaintext letter, so it serves as an independent check. With the merged table it reads, with gaps: The ruin of Gustavus is at last resolved. Russia is to seize Finland, while France & Denmark take possession of Sweden. Denmark cannot ha[ve] very willingly … independence. And it is certainly amongst the most cruel circumstances of the British attack on her Capital that it … her … of her … and [like]wise … of conduct, and thrown her completely into the arms of France, while the Danish Minister was this morning pouring out his complaints to me upon this subject, and stating the … of his government and the means taken by it to avert the introduction into Denmark of a general army … of Hamburg waited in the antichamber, with the intelligence that the Prince of Ponte Corvo had already entered Holstein … There is no one of even tolerable knowledge and sagacity who does not see this. Yet wonderful to tell Russia not only does not … but actually assists him in accomplishing one half of the object. Can Finland compensate for a state of things which shall put it in the power of France to lock up the Baltic …? The sentences that come out whole — the ru-in of Gu-sta-va-us is at last resolve-d , the Dan-ish Minister was this morning po-ur-ing out his com-plain-t-s to me upon this sub-ject , a-ve-rt the in-t-ro-duct-ion into Denmark , as-sist-s him in ac-com-pli-sh-ing one half of the object — confirm the table and fix the values ru , ish , Russia (305, which the pencil on frame 0200 also gives) used in the postscript. One group there is anomalous: 946 is on in the 4 May 1806 letter but must be Gu in Gustavus (914 = gu elsewhere) — a homophone, or a slip in the manuscript or the transcription.

Ru-s-el ought to be the consul: he is a-n America-n by bir-th , and is much better qua-li-fi(ed) than any other can-di-da-te . In a word he is above men in general. Next to him in fit-ness is O-mea-ly , but he is like Ward-en an Ir-ish-[man] . 4.1 The people Warden. David Bailie Warden (1772–1845), born in County Down, a United Irishman exiled in 1799, naturalised American, Armstrong's private secretary and then secretary of legation. He was the front-runner for the vacant Paris consulate and got it; Armstrong removed him in 1810, and when Madison reinstated him in 1811 Armstrong protested in a letter of 3 March 1811 that Warden was "without a single grain of attachment to the U.S." and asked whether "our own country furnish[es] no native citizen willing & able to fill the consulate at Paris". The postscript shows the same animus three years earlier, and its cause: Warden was not American-born. O'Mealy. Michael O'Mealy, a Baltimore merchant resident in France since 1793 and still there in 1810 (identified in the Papers of James Madison , Secretary of State Series 10:497 n. 2). The name — of obvious Irish origin — is spelt O-mea-ly . Russel. Spelt Ru-s-el . The most probable candidate is Jonathan Russell of Providence, Rhode Island (1771–1832), a merchant in the European trade whom Madison did in fact appoint chargé d'affaires at Paris when Armstrong left in 1810; the identification is inferential, since no other document places him in France in 1808.

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: Collect the ciphertext. Founders Online transcriptions of Armstrong's coded letters (4 May 1806, 22 February 1808, September 1807, 30 August 1808) were gathered, and the LOC manuscript images of the 30 August letter retrieved for collation. Locate a Rosetta stone. The NARA catalogue entry for M34 roll 13 was downloaded (393 frames). A simple image score (the proportion of mid-grey pixels not adjacent to dark ink) was used as a triage aid while browsing the roll; the annotated frames 0190 and 0192–0201 were confirmed by eye. Rerun over all 393 frames on 16 September 2026 the score does not locate them on its own: grey blank leaves outscore the annotated pages, and only the first, densest page of the October despatch ranks high (third of 392) once the score is restricted to the interlinear band near ink. See armstrong/NOTES.md. Harvest. Each annotated frame was cropped into thirds, contrast-enhanced, and read group by group; every pair was recorded with frame/line and a confidence grade (H/M). Groups seen on several frames were cross-checked. Merge and rank. A script merges the 4 May 1806 values, the harvested pairs and the inferences, ranking readings H > C > M > inferred, and renders any coded passage with unknowns and doubtful values flagged. Infer and verify. Remaining gaps were filled by context and checked against the alphabetical slot; the 22 February 1808 letter served as the independent control. Collate the manuscript. The LOC image of the postscript was enlarged to check every group against the Founders text.

h: Corrections to the printed transcription, and one residual doubt
b: Founders prints 1218 in the last line; the manuscript reads 1216 ( an ), which is also what the sentence requires. Founders prints 970. at the start of the second line where the manuscript has 972. ( the ). The fourth-line group is 1319 ( li ), as printed. A pencil s below 1116 on the Library of Congress copy shows that a reader in Washington began, and abandoned, a decode. The final group is 555 both in Founders and in the manuscript. 555 is re in the code (frame 0195: sco-re ), which makes no sense after Irish , whereas 1555 is man (frames 0195, 0200: the command of Prince Charles , man ). The reading Irishman assumes Armstrong dropped a digit; the alternative — that the postscript breaks off with "an Irish re–" — is noted for completeness. In the 22 February letter Founders' 631 ( wise ) in "his com-631-t-s" is almost certainly 651 ( plain ), and 916 ( had ) in "Denmark cannot 916 very willingly" is probably 921 ( have ); both are single-digit slips of the kind the microfilm hand invites. For the catalogues. The postscript of Armstrong to Madison, 30 August 1808 (Tomokiyo, Unsolved Historical Ciphers , "Armstrong to Madison" item 1) is read in full above; 48 of 49 groups are determined and the 49th is a probable slip for man . t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: Fourteen ciphered letters from Spain’s plenipotentiary at the Nijmegen congress to its envoy in Denmark. Ten carry a contemporary decipherment in the margin; four, of September 1677 and March 1678, carry none, and no key survives. The key was rebuilt from the ten margins by anchoring repeated words and aligning: letters and syllables in numbers, disguised letter-pair syllables, reversed vowel-first pairs and some twenty word codes. It reads all fourteen, down to the fear after the fall of Ghent. Nijmegen → Copenhagen · syllabic nomenclator · June 1677 – March 1678 · read The marqués de los Balbases to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, 1677–78 Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559 · DECODE R985–R998, fourteen letters, 47 pages · ten with a contemporary decipherment in the margin, four with none No key survives. It was rebuilt from the ten deciphered letters and reads all fourteen, including the four that had never been deciphered Daniel Bourdeau · solved 19 September 2026 Summary. Pablo Spínola Doria, third marqués de los Balbases, was one of Spain’s plenipotentiaries at the Nijmegen peace congress. DECODE catalogues fourteen of his ciphered letters to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, Spain’s envoy at Copenhagen, as “partially decrypted”. It notes that the solution is written in the margin, so the file was catalogued here as a transcription job. That turned out to be true of only ten letters. The last three, of 1, 8 and 22 March 1678, and one of 19 September 1677 have no decipherment at all. No key survives. None of the eight keys of the same Brussels series (DECODE R958–R965) fits. The key was therefore rebuilt from the cipher. Every cipher line and every margin line was transcribed afresh, because DECODE’s copies miss lines and misread the margins. Anchors came from word groups that repeat across letters. A monotone aligner, seeded with those anchors, then brought the table out of the ten margins. The system has single letters and consonant-vowel syllables in numbers, letter pairs whose consonant is disguised, reversed vowel-first pairs, some twenty word codes, and nulls. It covers 97% of the 8,150 cipher groups and reads the four unread letters. They cover the Imperial protest over the dissolution of the Bremen assembly, the Brunswick dukes’ claim to ambassadorial rank, the northern princes, and the fear after the fall of Ghent: “con la pérdida de Gante estamos temiendo la de otras importantes plazas”. Still open: a handful of rare name codes, and some homophones whose values are blurred by 4/9-type slips in the transcription. R985, 3 August 1677: the cipher block, with its contemporary decipherment in the left margin (“alegrome de la buena esperança que Mons.r d’Amerong[en]…”). The key was rebuilt from ten margins like this one.

t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: This is a syllabic nomenclator with homophones. Groups are separated by spaces. Letters. Vowels: a 21, 3+; e 2+; i 22, 67; o 18. Consonants: b 10, n; c 9; d e ; f x ; g 16; j u+; l 8, 19; n y , 24, 20; p 26; r 23, 31; s 28, B; t 27; y 25; z h. The closing consonants s, n and r are the three commonest groups. Syllables in numbers. de 46, la 55, en 76, ra 65, re 66, te 71, do 48, ta 70, lo 58, no 63, to 73, da 45, ti 72, di 47 le 56, ni 62, vi 42, ne 61, in 77, ve 41, va 40, na 60, on 78, an 75, li 57, ga 50, go 53, tu 74 vo 43, ar 80, gu 54, un 79, er 81, du 49, nu 64, ro 68, tr 188 Letter pairs: a syllable with the vowel kept and the consonant disguised. c is written x , d or l : xo , do and lo all read co; the same holds for ci, ca, ce and cu. f is written n : no fo, ni fi, ne fe, na fa, nu fu. y is written r : ro yo, ra ya. Vowel-first pairs: the syllable reversed, with the consonant disguised. s is written f : ef se, if si, af sa, of so, uf su. Also ye es, ya as, yo os. p is written d : ad pa, ed pe, od po, ud pu. m is written c : ac ma, ec me, ic mi, oc mo, uc mu. h is written q or g : aq / ag ha, eq / eg he, og ho. t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: R998, 22 March 1678: the end of the clear text and the start of the cipher. The margin is empty. This letter and the three before it were never deciphered. These are machine readings from the key: the groups are decoded one by one and the text is given here in summary. The group-by-group text is in balbases1677/read/ . 19 September 1677 (R992). Balbases has seen the protest the Imperial ministers published over the dissolution of the Bremen assembly. “De nuestra parte no nos queda que hacer sino es… temer” what the confederates will do. After Charleroi they may insist at the union that the conquests be shared out before anything positive is settled. A rumour about the Danish chancellor and the Duke of Celle. He gives it no credit, “pues V.S. no lo ha penetrado ni me lo avisa”. The claim that the duke would take his share of his father’s conquests, the duchies of Bremen and Verden. 1 March 1678 (R996). Nothing in Sweden could undo “la desconfianza que arguimos hacia nuestros aliados”. What causes it is “la miserable postura en que permanecen nuestras cosas”. The Brunswicks’ proceedings rest on solid suspicions. The ministers of the northern princes had thought of writing a protest about treaties of peace that would leave out their participation. He praises Fuenmayor’s diligence in avoiding that step. Strasbourg’s lack of constancy. A French gentleman has come back from France “satisfecho del Rey Cristianísimo”. 8 March 1678 (R997). In the business of the Brunswicks’ claim to the treatment of ambassadors, the Danes have conceded nothing. No formal act was made in writing at the first step. He comments on the Duke of Hanover and his brothers: “todo me parece muy bien pesado, pero yo creo que nada de estas intrigas llegará a fin”. “Los incesantes riesgos en que estamos”, and his growing melancholy. 22 March 1678 (R998). The dependencies between the princes of the north, “de suficiente calibre para tenernos embarazados”. The evils “que nosotros estamos padeciendo”. The loss in Flanders: “con la pérdida de Gante estamos temiendo la de otras importantes plazas”. Ghent had fallen to Louis XIV on 9 March. They are still waiting on the others’ long delays while “la enfermedad” advances.

t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: These were read at the time. The key reproduces their margins, which recover illegible margin words and confirm the doubtful ones. Their subjects: Amerongen’s hopes for a guarantee to the town of Bremen, 3 August. The dissolution of the Bremen conference, 18 June. Villahermosa, Temple’s recall and the Danish setback at Malmö. The Bishop of Strasbourg’s minister and Orange’s journey to England, 19 October. The loss of Saint-Ghislain, December. The Brunswick claim to ambassadorial rank, which runs through the winter letters of 1678. The margin text is transcribed in balbases1677/tx/ . It is summarised here, not edited.

t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: The images were fetched from DECODE. Two agents transcribed every cipher line and margin line by page into tx/ . They corrected DECODE’s transcriptions, which drop lines, confuse 46/96 and 48/98, and garble the margins. Repeated n-grams across letters were set against the margin text at the same relative position to find anchors: Brunsuic , principes , conformidad , novedad , conveniente . A hard-EM monotone aligner ( align2.py ) was seeded with those anchors and ran over the ten margined letters. Each group emits a substring of the margin text, with nulls and skips allowed. Two rounds brought out the table. A frozen key then decoded all fourteen letters.
