II pp. 295–342 · seven despatches · 12,362 groups · the decision to abandon Piedmont Decoded in full with Bazeries’ table of the Grand Chiffre; two letters he printed in clear serve as controls (98 and 99 % of characters agree); the other five, about 9,700 groups, are read here for the first time in print. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 16 September 2026 Summary. When Le Bouyer de Saint-Gervais published his great-uncle Catinat’s papers in 1819 he printed seven despatches from the court exactly as he found them, in three-figure groups, and admitted he could not read them. Étienne Bazeries reconstructed the code from these very pages in 1893 and used one sentence of the first letter, Louvois’ order to shut Bulonde up at Pignerol “avec un masque”, to name the Man in the Iron Mask. He printed that letter and the 19 August letter in clear, and the opening of a third, and stopped. The table he published reads all seven. Applied to the Bavarian State Library’s OCR of the 1819 volume, checked against the page images wherever the French breaks, it recovers 12,362 groups: two letters of Louvois (8 and 9 July) and five of Louis XIV (19, 24 and 29 August, 6 and 14 September 1691). The longest, twenty printed pages of figures dated Fontainebleau 14 September, is the King weighing the honourable course against the solid one and choosing the solid: bring the army of Piedmont back over the Alps at the end of the campaign, do not send it back in 1692, hold the passes, keep Carmagnole as long as possible to cover the negotiation with the Pope, then strip and burn it, and take Coni in the winter. Status: read. Six groups misprinted above the table’s range in 1819 and a residual OCR error rate near one group in seventy remain; the originals at Vincennes were not consulted.

II (1819), p. 320 — the end of the 6 September letter and the first lines of the King’s letter of 14 September, which runs to p. 342 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, bsb10720287, scan 354). t: Louis XIV and Louvois to Catinat — seven Grand Chiffre despatches, and the decision to abandon Piedmont
b: The Grand Chiffre de 1691 is a two-part code of 587 groups: two or three homophones for each letter, consonant-vowel syllables, word stems ( Envoi , Trouv , Expliqu ), whole words ( Sa Majesté , Pignerol , Carmagnole ), a dozen nulls that mark the ends of sentences, and one group that cancels the group before it. Bazeries rebuilt it from these letters over three years and printed his table, with 91 entries left blank, at the end of Le Masque de fer ; that table, transcribed from the Gallica scan for the Feuquières letter , is used here unchanged. The figures were taken from the Bavarian State Library’s hOCR of the volume, word by word with their boxes. Specks the OCR read as a stray “1” (which would decode as Passage ) were dropped by box size, show-through glyphs stripped, the editor’s footnote markers and running heads removed, and the letters cut at their printed headers. Each group was looked up, the units concatenated between nulls, and the result word-segmented with a lexicon drawn from the three Catinat volumes, Rousset’s Louvois , Feuquières’ memoirs and Bazeries’ book, so that sa maj este vou loit sca voi r comes out as sa majesté vouloit scavoir . The segmentation is a reading aid; the group-level decode is what is checked. Controls. Bazeries printed the 8 July and 19 August letters in clear. Our reading of the OCR’d figures matches his text at 2,640 of 2,690 characters (98.1 %) and 3,204 of 3,233 (99.1 %) after normalising accents and i/j, u/v. The residue is single groups the OCR misread (26 Vous as 24 Le ), a few places where his clear text departs from the printed figures, and his free rendering of two table entries. Every stretch the segmenter could not resolve into words, 137 in all, was then cropped from the page image and read by eye: seven OCR errors were found and corrected, six groups turned out to be misprinted above 587 in the 1819 edition itself, and the rest were seventeenth-century spelling correctly transcribed.

t: Louis XIV and Louvois to Catinat — seven Grand Chiffre despatches, and the decision to abandon Piedmont
h: What the King and Louvois wrote
b: Louvois, 9 July. The more the King reflects on Coni, the more he is touched, for the reputation of his arms and for what the place will cost the winter quarters; a siege with the whole army is no longer possible. Two tasks: fortify Carmagnole so the enemy “n’osent le regarder”, and destroy every post the enemy could hold in winter against the roads to Casale and Pignerol: Villeneuve d’Ast and Quiers “vous les devriez brusler absolument”, sparing the churches, and the castles between Turin and Asti likewise, all done “de manière qu’il ne paroisse point qu’elles vous aient esté prescrites”. Seize Bene; burn Carignan if the enemy could winter in it. Seek battle before the Germans arrive and avoid it after, to let them fall sick and desert for want of pay. Oblige the peasants to bring their grain into the King’s garrisons, with commissaries to hold the governors to it. The Duke of Savoy’s talk “mériteroit bien” two thousand bombs into Turin, and the bridge of Turin would be worth breaking, “mais ce sont des vues que Sa Majesté vous met devant les yeux et non des ordres”. Louis XIV, 24 August. Chamlay carries the King’s thoughts on every course still open in the war. Will the enemy march into Savoy, or mass by Turin to eat the forage and force Catinat back over the mountains first? The negotiation at Rome makes it very desirable to stay beyond the Alps as long as possible. Casale: palisades, money for eighteen months, grain, more cavalry, gunners. Some at court think Villefranche fortified and Saluces, Savillan and Fossano garrisoned would let the army winter in Piedmont; the King does not tire of saying so, but Catinat is not to let the King’s wish override his judgement. Pignerol is “le premier objet” in any plan. And the King would greatly wish Coni taken at the close of the campaign. Louis XIV, 29 August and 6 September. A treaty offered by the people of Mondovì is good but can only serve to sound them, since the army can no longer take quarters there. The resident at Geneva reports the enemy has asked the city for passage into Savoy and would go by the Valais into the Chablais. Larray has thrown an Irish battalion into Briançon for fear the Barbets would seize it. If Catinat crosses the Po, let it be before the enemy moves. Chamlay has arrived. Louis XIV, 14 September, Fontainebleau. Chamlay has reported, and the King has seen “avec peine” that the upshot is to withdraw the army of Piedmont over the mountains at the end of the campaign and not to bring it back. He sets out both sides at length. Against withdrawal: the enemy masters of Italy, the allies and neutral princes forced to declare against him, Casale lost from view, the reputation of his arms damaged and his enemies encouraged by an appearance of weakness “quoyque fausse dans le fonds”. For it: the impossibility of subsisting in Piedmont without Turin; a country “fort estroit et extrêmement couvert”, cut by torrents that rise in hours and cannot be bridged; the distance of Casale; the sickness of the troops every campaign, with no hospitals to hold them; the enemy’s freedom to engage or refuse behind the Doire and the Po. Then Catinat’s plan for the defensive: the cols of Provence, Dauphiné and Savoy held, the heights of Saint-Pierre by Pignerol and of Suze occupied, cheaper subsistence, fewer sick, the surplus cavalry on the Saône ready to go to Germany, and the Duke of Savoy left to choose between keeping the allied army idle in his ruined country or sending it away and seeing the French return. “J’ay comparé les inconvénients et les avantages d’un parti avec ceux de l’autre … et je me suis déterminé à préférer le parti solide à l’honorable.” The orders follow. Prolong the campaign to All Saints or even Saint-Martin, and keep Carmagnole to the last, because both cover the negotiation with the Pope and the Italian princes that might extricate him from Casale “et mesme peut-estre de la guerre de Piedmont”; the enemy must not learn that he means to quit Piedmont for good, so the works at Carmagnole go on, “avec un peu moins de vivacité et de dépense”. When the order comes, carry off what can be carried, the grain on the cavalry’s cruppers to Pignerol, throw the rest in the water, tear up the works, burn palisades, gates, hay and grain. Secure Pignerol’s magazines against a bombardment, which “me donneroit beaucoup de mortification en présence de mon armée”. Hold the valleys of Pragelas and Pérouse for the Briançon road. After recrossing, take Coni in the winter; the artillery and stores are ordered to Lyon and Grenoble. Fortify Briançon and the frontier against the valleys of Luzerne, Saint-Martin and Angrogne. Winter quarters by Catinat’s memoir. And retreat with such precaution that the enemy can attempt nothing. The full segmented readings, with the groups as printed and page breaks, are in the repository under catinat1691/letters .

The catalogue listed five ciphertexts of Barberini to Ceva as a transcription job: DECODE says “deciphered in original”, so the text was taken to have been read at the time and the work to be copying a decipherment off the leaf. That was only half right. George Lasry reconstructed the key of the whole dossier on 24 October 2020, and it is attached to all eleven of its DECODE records; he also published aligned readings of four letters, which covers three of the five this entry named. Two were left: R75 , of 25 September 1632, and R84 , of 18 December 1632. Both are read here. The system is homophonic and syllabic on two-digit figures, with every pair beginning 2 a null and the single figure 6 as word separator; because 6 occurs inside no code, word boundaries are certain and the only ambiguity is whether the next code is two digits or a three-digit nomenclator element. A position-indexed beam search resolves that under an Italian character model, interpolated with a model built from the dossier’s own clear passages; calibrated leave-one-out against Lasry’s four letters it agrees with his segmentation on 95.8% of tokens. R75 carries a contemporary interlinear decipherment which was used for nothing else, and the reading agrees with it on 77.5% of letters. Aligning the two then reads meanings off the interlinear for six of the ninety-five nomenclator elements Lasry left unsolved, among them 830 = Francia . R75 argues that the Swedish victories make an accommodation easier but the union far harder; R84, written a month after Lützen, ends on the fear that the consequences will hold France disunited and unable to help her allies. One hundred and seventeen nomenclator elements stay unread, and the names of both letters are inside them.

DECODE catalogued eleven ciphertexts from it, R74 to R84. The catalogue entry here named five — R75, R77, R78, R82, R84 — and scored them by rule from the metadata, unviewed. Opening the records changed the problem. Every one of the eleven carries, as an attachment, a key marked #KEY: reconstructed , #TRANSCRIBER NAME: George Lasry , #DATE OF TRANSCRIPTION: October 24, 2020 . Every one also carries the same 29,050-byte file of aligned decipherments, covering four letters. So the state of the dossier before this session was: DECODE Item Date Pages Before R74 346-1 7 Sept 1632 1 read by Lasry R75 346-2 25 Sept 1632 2 not read R76 346-3 1632 3 marked decrypted R77 346-4 1632 2 read by Lasry R78 346-5 1632 2 read by Lasry R79–R81, R83 346-6 to -8, -10 1632–34 7 marked decrypted R82 346-9 27 [Oct] 1632 1 read by Lasry R84 346-11 18 Dec 1632 2 not read Three of the five ciphertexts the catalogue named were therefore already read, and two were not. t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 nobody had read
b: The key is Lasry’s. It was re-derived here from his four aligned readings, parsed into 104 line pairs and 179 distinct tokens, which confirms it and settles three points the key note leaves open. Token Value 6 word separator 2x null — no pair beginning 2 ever carries plaintext XY letter or syllable, 61 codes: three homophones for each vowel, two for most consonants, and groups for al, che, chi, con, da, de, di, et, il, in, io, la, ma, mi, no, per, qu, quel, se, si, st pXY nomenclator element: one prefix digit followed by an ordinary two-digit code First, the figure 6 occurs inside no code at all — not in a key pair, not in any of the ninety-five nomenclator elements. Word boundaries in this cipher are therefore certain, which is unusual and is what makes the rest tractable. Second, the DECODE key note says the nomenclator elements “have 4 digits starting with prefix 4”. They have three . Concatenating Lasry’s own token stream for 346:1 and diffing it against the original transcription of the same leaf gives a 99.7% match with no dropped prefix; the elements are three digits as they stand. The prefix is 4 in twenty-seven of the ninety-five, but it is also 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 8 or 9. Third, in ninety-one of the ninety-five the two digits after the prefix are themselves a valid key code. The element is a prefix plus an ordinary code, which is exactly why the parse is ambiguous: at most positions a two-digit and a three-digit reading are both legal. Twenty-nine of the hundred pairs are dead ( 02 05 06 12 16 32 33 36 42 46 52 56 60–69 72 76 82 86 92 96 99 ), and meeting one forces the three-digit reading, but that is not enough on its own.

t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 nobody had read
b: The decoder is a position-indexed beam search over the digit stream. Every 6 is consumed as a separator; elsewhere the beam chooses between a two-digit code, a two-digit null and a three-digit element, scored by a character model. Scoring is incremental — the shared lang package’s dense model is a flat table of log P(c | previous four characters), so each emitted character costs one array lookup and a beam of several hundred is cheap. The model matters more than the search. it-cinquecento is Renaissance diplomatic Italian but stops around 1620 and knows nothing of this clerk’s hand: one sign for u and v, doubled letters dropped, word division his own. It was interpolated with a model built on 7,693 characters from the dossier itself — the passages the clerk wrote in clear, plus Lasry’s plaintext of whichever letters were not under test. Calibration is leave-one-document-out against Lasry’s four letters: the nomenclator inventory offered for a document is built from the other three only, which is the situation of R75 and R84. Agreement with his own segmentation: Model Tokens Nomenclator recall Precision it-cinquecento alone 0.945 0.52 0.70 interpolated, w = 0.6 0.958 0.70 0.79 Per letter, interpolated: 346:1 0.871, 346/4 0.928, 346/5 0.905, 346/9 0.951. The figure to keep in view is the nomenclator recall. Three elements in ten are still missed, and a missed element is not rendered as a gap — it comes out as two or three plausible Italian letters. Errors in the readings below are concentrated there. The one independent check is R75’s own leaf. A decipherer in 1632 wrote his reading between the cipher lines, and the DECODE transcriber copied what was legible of it. It was used for nothing — not the key, not the model, not the decoder. On the twenty-four lines where enough survives, 1,105 letters, 77.5% agreement , ignoring word division; the last line agrees at 100%. The residue is shared between this reading and the witness’s own illegibility, since the transcriber flagged much of the faded interlinear with ? and * .

t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 nobody had read
b: Two pages, 1,446 code groups. Barberini on what the Swedish victories do to the French alliance. The argument is a single one, pressed hard: the victories make l’accomodamento easier and l’unione far harder, and the nuncio is to make the French court see that the power now winning is a danger to France herself. Gaps are unresolved nomenclator elements or transcription noise; italics mark elements read here. …le vittorie di […] e quella forza renderanno per avventura più facile […] quell’accomoda mente di […], ma più difficile assai […] quell’unione… per […] interessi di Francia … è tempo che se cominci a conoscere quanto sia pericolosa alla Francia la potenza d[i …], che cominciano [hor]mai a pensar a cose [grandi] et ad indrizar la [mira] loro a […]; consideri quanto sia oportuno alli vastissimi pens[ieri] di […] natione estendere il loro dominio sino al Mediterraneo con acquisto d’una piazza , e con quanto buon fonda mente lo possono sperare in una [rivoluzione] … di Francia … hanno tanto forze marittime e terrestri; consideri… che la vittoria […] è altret anto formidabile alla Francia quanto alla […]… [non si] sarà sempre al medesimo, darà sempre orecchie a[l] torbidi, et haverà chi li suggerisca; et un successor[e]… restringer in maniera che sempre non habbi libertà di [salvarsi] in campagna… [bisogna] cercar di compor[re gli] esterni, che cagioneranno e fo[men]teranno li domestici… [è] già… arrivata a tal […] di gloria… che può con ragion temere che la […] fortuna non si rivolti; cerchi dunque d’augumentarla con l’arti… pur vuol seguitar… indrizi le cose per intraprender guerra contro… quel[li] che sola parte manca alla gloria di […]. In somma… le congiunture presenti sono più contrarie alla s[ua] […] quell’unione, tanto più deve […] pensar a ritrovar ragioni che la persuadano. The unnamed power is Sweden. The 1632 decipherer’s own interlinear supplies, where this reading has a gap, the words pensieri di goto natione — the Gothic nation — and it is the reach of that nation sino al Mediterraneo that Rome wants Paris to contemplate.

t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 nobody had read
b: Two pages, 954 code groups, written a month after Lützen (16 November 1632). The first folio is largely in clear: Barberini acknowledges Ceva’s despatch of the 8th, says he has nothing further to answer, and refers him to Mons. Bichi at court. The cipher carries the analysis, and it turns throughout on quella vittoria . ricordando a […] che si […] quella vittoria contro […] con la sua consueta prudenza , ad indur[re] […] a facilitar il […]… […] che bollivano in Francia dopo la mia partenza; pure de[…] li torbidi di […] furono cagione che li […] concludessero la […]… le gelosie [che] quella potenza di Francia cerca di […]; e li spiriti inquieti […] fanno pastura su li impegni che il […] tiene con […] potenti, e si muovono più facil mente con speranza di fo[men]to e diversione. Per stabilire et assicurar le cose […] bisogna levarsi le inimicitie esterne… nascerà l’alt[r]o in mano di Francia . Posso dire che stia […] se vo[gliono] ridur a termini ragionevoli le pretensioni… non […] entrar in […] cose, non lascierà di andar [f]acilitando le […] maniera che a lei s[i] accenna… la fuga di […] non so quanto sia a proposito con ins[o]liti rigori… [in] Francia metter in disperatione… potendo da[…] conseguenze che tengano disunita per un lungo pezzo la Francia , e sotto giogo alle esterne violenze, o almeno impotente a soccorrer li suoi alleati. That last clause is the point of the despatch and it is new. The Roman reading of Lützen, a month on, is not relief at the death of Gustavus Adolphus but apprehension about France: the danger is now a France held disunited, under external pressure, and unable to help her allies.

t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 nobody had read
b: Lasry solved none of the ninety-five elements he met. Deciphering R75 puts a placeholder at each element; aligning that reading against the 1632 interlinear shows which word of the contemporary decipherment stands at the placeholder. Twenty-two elements caught a witness fragment, and six survive checking against Lasry’s four letters, where they were not fitted: Code Reading Evidence 474 mente piena~, principal~, non sola~ per il solo proprio, malacomoda~; witness fragment met 495 quanto “e ~ al proporre arbitrare”; pairs with 498 498 tanto “che ~ in <347> quanto in <857> si sappia la cagione” 830 Francia four times out of four in Lasry’s letters, always after a feminine article: “render la ~ più poderosa”, “valere a danno quella ~”, “hoggi la ~ in a di dar legge” 854 guerra R75 interlinear, twice 149 piazza R75 interlinear, “acquisto d’una ~” Adding the six raised the control agreement on R75 from 0.737 to 0.775. That test is partly circular for 854 and 149 , which came from the witness itself; the independent evidence for 474 , 495 , 498 and 830 is that they fit the four letters Lasry read, which the witness never touched. The pairing of 498 and 495 as tanto…quanto around two unread place codes is the cleanest of them. One near miss is worth recording. 491 drew the fragment goto — the Gothic nation, Sweden — but it does not fit its four contexts in Lasry’s letters, where it stands before unione and after conferito con . It is left open rather than forced.

t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 nobody had read
b: The nomenclator, almost entirely. Eighty-nine of the ninety-five elements Lasry met are still unread, and twenty-eight more appear only in these two letters (twenty-one in R75, seven in R84) — 117 in all. The people and places of both despatches are inside them: who is to be induced, whose pretensions are to be reduced, whose flight is in question. A key for this dossier, if one survives in the Vatican archive, would close it at a stroke. The transcriptions are DECODE’s and were not re-checked against the images. R75’s transcriber flagged doubtful digits throughout. Several stretches that read badly here — quzper cavsevc , l v osts sevom — are more likely transcription than decipherment. The images are R75 I589/I590 and R84 I639/I640, behind a DECODE login. Grades. The connected passages quoted above are C (confirmed by the contemporary decipherment, for R75) and M (machine reading consistent with context, for R84 and the unchecked parts of R75). The six nomenclator values are M. Nothing here is graded H. The other six letters — R74, R76, R79, R80, R81, R83 — were read by Lasry and are not touched here.

t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
b: A two-page letter wholly in graphic cipher, addressed to Charles IX’s ambassador in Scotland and catalogued by DECODE as non-decrypted. George Lasry had already solved it and Satoshi Tomokiyo published his full-page plaintext overlays in 2022. Charles directs du Croc to shape the peace, government and council around the young James VI, prevent a marriage before France is consulted, preserve Scottish attachment to France, and stop English encroachment. The catalogue’s “1 Jan 1550” is a metadata error: Destray labels the original without place or date; it belongs to 1565–67 or 1572. French court → Scotland · homophonic nomenclator · 1565–67 or 1572 · already solved Charles IX to Philibert du Croc Archives départementales de la Nièvre, fonds du Bourg de Bozas, exact cote unreported · two pages, French, wholly ciphered · DECODE R2789, “Non-decrypted” · catalogue item 34 The images were behind DECODE’s login. Once opened, the cited edition led directly to the answer: George Lasry had already deciphered the letter and published full-page plaintext overlays in 2022. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 Summary. DECODE R2789 describes this two-page symbol cipher as non-decrypted and the catalogue consequently ranked it as an open class-C target. It is not open. Satoshi Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana page publishes George Lasry’s red plaintext overlay on both pages, dated 25 May 2022. The authenticated DECODE images, Destray’s 1924 facsimile on Gallica, and Lasry’s overlays are the same recto and verso. Charles tells his ambassador to protect the Scottish peace, shape the young James VI’s upbringing and council, prevent him from concluding a marriage before France is consulted, preserve Scottish attachment to France, and stop English encroachment. The prior reading leaves several signs and short clauses as question marks, which are retained here. The catalogue date “1 Jan 1550” is also wrong: Destray labels the letter without place or date, and Charles was not born until June 1550. The defensible date is 1565–67 or 1572, du Croc’s Scottish missions.

t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
h: The document and the date correction
b: Paul Destray printed the address as “A monsr du Croq, mon conseiller et me d’hostel ordinaire et mon ambassadeur en Escosse” and catalogued the item as document XLIII, S. l. n. d. : without place or date. He noted that the letter, its addition, and the King’s second signature were in cipher; Pinart countersigned it. The two following facsimile leaves are the same images now served by DECODE. DECODE’s structured date spans 1550–1574 but supplies day and month as 1 January; the catalogue flattened that into “1 Jan 1550.” That cannot be a document date: Charles IX was born on 27 June 1550. Cryptiana’s cautious “1565–1567 or 1572” follows the periods in which du Croc served in Scotland and is retained here. The contents fit the minority of James VI, but they do not distinguish those missions securely. The recto: the main letter in graphic cipher, followed lower on the leaf by Charles’s signature and the beginning of the ciphered postscript. Archives départementales de la Nièvre, reproduced by Destray (1924), via Gallica and DECODE R2789.

t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
b: Tomokiyo’s page “George Lasry’s Solutions of Unsolved Ciphers” has a section headed “Charles IX to Philibert du Croc (1565–1567 or 1572).” Beneath the manuscript it says “This is solved as follows” and reproduces Lasry’s plaintext in red directly over the signs on both pages. That is decisive prior art, not a conjectural match: page geometry, line breaks, signatures, and the postscript agree throughout. The system is a French homophonic nomenclator: several graphic signs can represent letters, while other signs stand for whole words or names. Lasry’s displayed key includes values such as de , et , que , par , pour , je , vous , la Royne d’Angleterre , la Royne d’Escosse , and royaulme . It is not the symbol system used in Catherine de Médicis’s separate letter to du Croc of 27 April 1567. Lasry’s published overlay on the verso, continuing the postscript about English encroachment. It reads the document in substance while honestly retaining several groups as question marks. Overlay by George Lasry, published by Satoshi Tomokiyo on Cryptiana, 25 May 2022.

t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
b: The opening tells du Croc that he knows both the man and those with whom he must deal, and that his demonstrated devotion makes further advice unnecessary. He is to follow the instructions already given and those now sent, especially “le bien de la paix du dict pais.” Charles then turns from what can presently be done for “ma seur” to the young King: Je desire que mon nepveu aussy sur toutes choses soit bien nourri, qu’il ait tousjours, à l’imitation de ses predecesseurs, à moi et aux miens sa principalle affection. Du Croc is to attend closely to the settlement of Scotland’s peace, government, and council. Without revealing that the direction comes from Charles, he must ensure that James neither marries nor concludes a marriage before Charles has been informed and can send his intention. Above all, he is to retain the hearts of the Scots so that their accustomed affection for the French kings does not diminish. The postscript is blunter: Ce que vous avez principalement affaire par delà est de donner ordre que les Anglois n’empiètent aucune chose en Escosse… Du Croc must act prudently, make the Scots recognize that France seeks their preservation, and avoid occasions that could obstruct the friendship. The closing lines mention the English ambassadors and a possible treaty, but the gaps in the overlay are too large for a responsible continuous translation. The repository preserves a line-by-line diplomatic transcription and a normalized summary.

t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
b: The original has no surviving date or place; 1565–67 or 1572 is a range, not a solved date. Destray names the Nièvre archive and the Bourg de Bozas collection but gives no exact cote. No independent sign-by-sign transcription or complete key was reconstructed here. The result is correctly classified as found already solved .

t: An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 — the “unread” two thirds were deciphered in 1586, on the next leaf and between the lines
b: A League-period letter in two-digit figures, listed with a partial key and two thirds of its first page unread. The volume holds its own decipherment: folio 168 is a clear text of the cipher down to a cross mark, and from that cross to the end the decipherer wrote the plaintext between the lines. Tomokiyo’s key agrees with the glosses ( Guienne , tres confident , Fumé ), which also give 87 = e and the King of Navarre’s sign. The letter: Fumé, vice-admiral of Guyenne and Navarre’s Catholic confidant, keeps proposing a reconciliation between Navarre and the addressee, probably Guise, while Catherine de Médicis negotiates. Angoumois → a League leader · two-digit figure cipher · 28 October 1586 · decipherment found An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 BnF Clairambault 357 ff. 167–168 · a Catholic nobleman writes to a League leader during Catherine de Médicis’s talks with Navarre · listed as “two thirds of the first page unread” The volume holds the letter’s own 1586 decipherment: a clear text on the next leaf and plaintext between the lines of the rest · Tomokiyo’s partial key checks against it · the letter is read from it Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 18 September 2026 Summary. Satoshi Tomokiyo published part of the key of this letter, a homophonic two-digit figure cipher dated 28 October 1586. He noted that about two thirds of the first page was not deciphered. The volume already holds a decipherment. Folio 168 is a clear text of folio 167r, in a secretary hand, from the first words (“Jay receu voz deux lettres en ung mesme temps”) down to a cross mark (“qui passe avant ✝”). The same cross stands in the margin of f. 167r. From that cross to the end of the verso, the decipherer wrote the plaintext between the lines , word by word over the figures. Tomokiyo’s key agrees with the interlinear words wherever it was tested, so the clear text belongs to this cipher. It is not a separate letter. The letter is from a Catholic of the Angoumois. Fumé, vice-admiral of Guyenne , a Catholic and “tres confident du Roy de Navarre”, has several times proposed through him a reconciliation between Navarre and the addressee, who is probably the duke of Guise. The letter also covers Catherine de Médicis’s negotiation, what the Queen of England could procure, and Villeroy writing about Mayenne. Status: resolved from the contemporary decipherment, not by new cryptanalysis. The transcription has uncertain words, and the verso glosses were read only in part.

t: An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 — the “unread” two thirds were deciphered in 1586, on the next leaf and between the lines
b: Clairambault 357 is volume XLVII of the Bossuet-era collection of documents on Henri III’s reign (1583–1587). On Gallica it is btv1b9001053r . Folio 167r is canvas 331, the verso with the date and the sender’s signs is canvas 332, and folio 168r is canvas 333. The letter is not solid cipher. The writer drops into clear for a word or a phrase, and in clear he names Bordeaux and writes “tres fasché du bon terme en quoy sont voz affaires”. F. 167r, the opening. After ✝ C and the dotted groups 45.31.73.65.21 come 67 14 98 43 28 18 18 24 , which is jay receu . Line 2 ends in clear, Bourdeaux , and line 3 begins in clear. F. 168r, the clear text of the same opening: Jay receu voz deux lettres en ung mesme temps, dont jay faict communication a M r de la Forest et M r de Corbet . The names are underlined where the original has them in cipher.

t: An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 — the “unread” two thirds were deciphered in 1586, on the next leaf and between the lines
h: The interlinear decipherment, and the key check
b: About thirty lines down f. 167r, a ✝ in the left margin marks the point where f. 168 stops. From there the decipherer worked between the lines. Checking the glosses against Tomokiyo’s table is a direct test of both: F. 167r. The glosses Fumé , visadmiral , de and du Roy de Navarre stand over the figures. Then the writer continues in clear: bien qu’il soit catholique et loyal a . Figures Interlinear gloss Tomokiyo’s key gives 74 24 34 28 29 72 Guienne g u i e n e 26 43 28 82 tres t r e s 18 37 19 35 34 25 28 19 26 confident c o n f i d e n t 25 24 # du Roy de Navarre d u + a nomenclator sign 35 24 64 87 Fumé f u m + 87 , which is therefore e 92 81 et que et que Above the cross, the key’s reading of the figures matches f. 168 in the runs tested. For example, 25 28 88 22 20 24 26 88 72 82 70 14 | 18 28 gives de r · autres pla|ce , where f. 168 has et autres places qui vous ont esté distraictes . The check adds a few things to the published table. 87 is e and 71 is a. 22, the commonest group, reads as a null in every word checked. 66 is a null, and so are the dotted groups 45.31.73.65.21. The double-barred # is the King of Navarre, glossed three times. D is England, and && is Mayenne, as Tomokiyo had it.

t: An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 — the “unread” two thirds were deciphered in 1586, on the next leaf and between the lines
b: From f. 168, with uncertain words marked: Jay receu voz deux lettres en ung mesme temps, dont jay faict communication a M r de la Forest et M r de Corbet … tres fasché du bon terme en quoy sont voz affaires … Indisposé d’une maladye qui m’a travaillé pres de deux moys … le commis a l’abbé de la Couronne … le voyage et negotiation qu’il entreprenoit estoit contraire a celle de l’an passé, seroit trouvé estrange non seullement de ses amys catholiques de France, mais des princes estrangers. Sur quoy il apportoit tout ce qu’il pouvoit de raisons … de la Royne mere … qui luy promettoit … de ne desirer faire la paix qu’a condition qu’il n’y auroit que la Religion catholique en France … que chascun avoit faict son affaire, et l’avoit on laissé seul abandonné. … Je croy que faisant [?] et autres places qui vous ont esté distraictes vous les pourrez avoir … la brouillerie du Roy de Navarre et de vous, que je tiens tres difficile pour la qualité que chascun de vous a prinse … qui passe avant. ✝ From the interlinear decipherment of the rest: Je vous diray que j’ay esté pressé, et la seule bonne volonté d’un que vous congnoissez … qui s’appelle Fumé, visadmiral de Guienne, tres confident du Roy de Navarre, bien qu’il soit catholique et loyal a moy … pour quelque negotiation … Il est bien adverty. Il m’a plusieurs foys proposé cette reconciliation, qu’il dict luy estre aussy aysé et facille comme je la luy fais difficille et malaisée … si vous y voullez entendre … Il m’a quasy prié de la part du Roy de Navarre … la guerre … asseurance que la Royne d’Angleterre ne pourroit procurer … and on the verso … Jay envoyé a … Villeroy, qui me manda que pour contenter Monsieur du Mayne … conclure la paix, et si l’on donne quelque advantage aux Huguenotz … The writer is a Catholic nobleman of the Angoumois or Saintonge. He mentions the abbey of La Couronne near Angoulême, M rs de la Forest and de Corbet, and Bordeaux. He writes during the autumn of 1586, while Catherine de Médicis was negotiating with Henri of Navarre (the interviews of Saint-Brice took place that December). The addressee is set against Navarre as head of the other religious party, and Mayenne is named in the third person, so the addressee is most likely Henri, duke of Guise. That identification is an inference and not a reading.

t: An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 — the “unread” two thirds were deciphered in 1586, on the next leaf and between the lines
b: F. 168 is a fast secretary hand, and several phrases are read only loosely. Examples are the words after Charry , the passage on the abbot of La Couronne, and the last sentence. That sentence seems to pair protecteur with the Catholics, the reverse of what is expected, and needs the matching cipher words decoded. Only sample runs above the cross were decoded with the key against f. 168. All of them agreed, but the page has not been checked word by word. The verso glosses were read only where they are clear. A few proper names (“Cambaronne”?, “Coride”?) and the signs R, ⊖, Ω and ✝o are not settled. The sender’s signs at the foot of f. 167v are not identified, and neither is Fumé beyond his office.

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
b: BnF fr. 3854 nos. 41–43. The two “undeciphered” mémoires of 26–27 March were read by Lasry in 2023; they are read again here from the leaves, with three small corrections. The third, whose decipherment was meant to be the crib, is a different number code, and its clerk never glossed the first twelve lines. A key rebuilt from about 3,300 glossed groups reads them: Conti to Laigue, 5 March 1649, explaining the Rueil conference away to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm. Paris → the Archduke’s camp · letter cipher and syllabic number code · March 1649 · read The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 BnF fr. 3854 nos. 41–43, the Frondeurs’ secret instructions to their envoys with Archduke Leopold Wilhelm during the Rueil conference · two mémoires “avec chiffre”, and a third “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” The two “undeciphered” mémoires turned out to be in print (Lasry 2023), and were read again from the leaves. The deciphered one was not finished: its first twelve lines had never been read Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue of new targets listed Conti’s mémoires of 26 and 27 March 1649 as two ciphers left without a decipherment. It assumed the third mémoire, which has one, would be the crib. Nos. 41 and 42 were already read. George Lasry broke them in 2023 as a “poly-homophonic” letter cipher. They were read again here, from a fresh transcription of the Gallica images with his key, and the reading adds three small corrections to his text. No. 43 is not the same cipher. It is a number code of letters and syllables, with a contemporary decipherment between the lines. That decipherment starts only at the thirteenth line. The opening — the address to Laigue and the purpose of the whole mémoire, 264 groups — had never been read. No. 43 read in full. The key was rebuilt from about 3,300 glossed groups and used to read the opening. The whole mémoire was then edited: Conti to Laigue, 5 March 1649, the day after the Rueil conference opened, explaining the conference away to the Archduke.

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
b: BnF Français 3854 (Gallica btv1b52520094g ) is a recueil of Fronde papers from the prince de Conti’s side, January to April 1649. It holds his instructions to his envoys, the marquis de Noirmoutier and Geoffroy de Laigue, the Archduke’s Spanish answers, and three pieces in cipher that Omont describes as follows: No. 41 (f. 113r–v): “Mémoire, avec chiffre, du prince de Conti. A Paris, ce 26 mars 1649”. No. 42 (f. 115r): the same, “ce 27 mars 1649”, signed Armand de Bourbon . No. 43 (ff. 117r–120r): “Mémoire, avec chiffre et déchiffrement, du prince de Conti, pour un de ses envoyés auprès de l’archiduc”, undated. The catalogue’s “verify first” was to confirm that the three share one cipher. They do not. Nos. 41 and 42 are written in lower-case letters mixed with clear words. No. 43 is written in numbers, with a clerk’s letters and syllables above most of them. No. 41, f. 113r: “A Paris ce 26 Mars 1649”, then the letter cipher inline with clear words. Jcctg nle Monsieur de nrgmtild is “Affin que Monsieur de Noirmo[u]stier”. Bibliothèque nationale de France.

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
h: Nos. 41 and 42: found already read, and read again
b: Prior art. A web search before any work found George Lasry, “Armand de Bourbon’s Poly-Homophonic Cipher – 1649”, HistoCrypt 2023 . Lasry deciphered both letters, printed their text with a translation, and described the system. How it works. Each plaintext letter is written as a cipher letter. A, L and R each have two signs. Five signs each stand for two to four letters: a = t/p/a/b, e = e/g, i = c/z, m = s/d/x, n = m/q. The key. There is no nomenclator. The key’s second row spells J’aime c’est un grand mal , a Boesset air of 1642. The catalogue entry. His paper cites the volume as “fr. 3584”, a typo, which is why the catalogue harvest did not match it. Read again here. All three pages were transcribed sign by sign from the full-resolution images. A beam search over each sign’s possible letters, scored with a French quadgram model and then a period word list, picked the readings. The text agrees with Lasry’s throughout, with three additions: f. 113r: dans lequel temps les choses ne pouvant pas . The cipher has ge = NE, which the printed text drops. No. 42: ordonne à ses députez de se joindre à ceux de son Altesse le prince de Conti pour insister à demander l’éloignement du cardinal Mazarin . The words are in the cipher ( arldtgmtmaed ) and in Lasry’s own figure, but not in his clean text. f. 113v: Bretaigne is enciphered with the L-sign in second place, a slip of the encipherer’s. “Monsieur de Tenerande ”, with whom Longueville is to treat, reads the same under the key; the person is unidentified. “Dix” or “six mil hommes” cannot be settled, because one sign serves both d and s. Depuis la lettre que je vous escrivi hier j’ay cru vous debvoir advertir qu’on a donné aujourd’huy arrest au parlement qui ordonne à ses députez de se joindre à ceux de son Altesse le prince de Conti pour insister à demander l’éloignement du cardinal Mazarin. On ne doute plus après cela de la rupture … Ne concluez rien pourtant que vous n’ayez le dernier advis, mais si elle arrive, mettez-vous en estat d’en faciliter les suittes. No. 42, 27 March 1649

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
h: No. 43: a number code, and twelve lines nobody read
b: No. 43, f. 117r. Twelve lines of numbers and clear words with nothing written above them; the clerk’s interlinear decipherment starts only at the foot ( po ur p r o cu , “pour procu[rer]”). Bibliothèque nationale de France. The clerk who deciphered no. 43 wrote a letter or syllable above almost every number from f. 117r line 13 to the end of f. 120r. He wrote nothing over the first twelve lines. Those 264 groups carry the address and the purpose of the mémoire. The key, rebuilt from his glosses. Agents transcribed number/gloss pairs page by page, and the tallies ( key43.txt ) show a regular design: Four interleaved single-letter alphabets: 3–25 run a→z, 28–50 run z→a, 51–73 run a→z again, and about 80–98 run down. Syllables in blocks of five, in vowel order: ca ce ci co cu = 256–260, and so on through the consonants, with a second, homophonic series in the gaps. Underlining a number reverses its syllable: 385 = ra , underlined 385 = ar . Code words: 451 la Reyne , 457 le cardinal , 458 le parlement , 472 l’archiduc , 482 France . The 500s are dates. Nulls: the numbers from about 99 to 250, which are never glossed. The opening, decoded. Of the 264 groups: 220 take the value the same number has in the glosses. 24 follow from the alphabets or are nulls. 20 are syllables of the second series, fixed from context. The first draft was checked against the rest of the mémoire. Nine of the context and structural values were later found glossed on ff. 117r–120r, all as predicted: 279 de , 364 la , 354 ne (underlined, en ), 443 te , 445 su , 37 o , 43 h , 86 n , and 36 p . None was contradicted. Pour Monsieur de Legue. Parce que nous ne doutons que le cardinal ne donne une mauvaise interprétation à toutes ses actions, et qu’il ne face principalement ses efforts pour mettre l’archiduc dans la défiance de nos bonnes intentions sur le sujet de la conférence que [le] parlement a accordée, j’ay jugé à propos de vous en faire instruire, afin que vous puissiés destourner les mauvais effets des artifices du cardinal, et faire comprendre à l’archiduc que ce pourparler n’a esté causé et résolu que par les retardemens que l’archiduc apporte à nous secourir, et que nous sommes tousiours dans nos mesmes desseins … No. 43, f. 117r, lines 1–12, read here for the first time

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
b: The last line of f. 120r is glossed à Paris le 5me mars 1649 . That is the day after the Rueil conference opened between the court and the parlement. Conti writes to Laigue, who is with Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, to keep the Spanish alliance alive while the Frondeurs negotiate with Mazarin’s side. Why the conference happened. The parlement laid the Archduke’s envoy’s proposals ( dom Joseph ) before the Queen. Mazarin, who saw that real peace would ruin him, proposed a conference to drag things out and to make the Archduke believe the Frondeurs were giving way. “À quoy l’on a employé Vautorte.” Conti would have refused it if the Archduke’s help had been ready and Paris not starving. What it bought. No suspension of arms. Saint-Germain lets in a hundred muids of corn a day from Corbeil for as long as the conference lasts, which buys time, “mais fort peu, en vous attendant”. Why it cannot succeed. The deputies are “tous gens de bien, dans le zèle de la paix générale et dans une haine irréconciliable pour le ministériat du cardinal”. They cannot give way on Mazarin, whom the parlement has condemned. The generals stayed away on purpose, so as to be free to break the talks at will. The promise. “Dès le moment qu’il entrera en France, cette conférence se rompra”, and a truer one will be opened with the Archduke’s own deputies. The plea. “Il n’y a plus un seul moment à perdre pour nous secourir.” Laigue is to press for help with all the Archduke’s forces. Even if the Archduke will not march without a treaty, nothing is to stand in the way of relief. The complete edited text of the mémoire is in conti1649/READING43.md . Where it fits. The three mémoires frame the Frondeurs’ double game. On 5 March, Conti promises the Archduke that the conference is only a way to buy time. On 26–27 March, he tells Noirmoutier that the talks are about to break on Normandy and Mazarin, and that he should be ready. The Peace of Rueil was signed on 11 March, in between. The parlement’s arrest of 27 March shows the generals still pressing the Mazarin article after the peace.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: Three lines found behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general, 107 characters, unsolved at the American Cryptogram Association since the 1950s. Transcribed twice, attacked in ten languages under six reading conventions; the same solver recovers matched controls at 96 to 100 percent and the note never comes close. Working notes · September 2026 The Copenhagen cryptogram Three lines of strokes, dots, carets and digits found behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum, no. 23 on Klaus Schmeh’s Top 50, attacked here as a simple substitution in ten languages under two transcriptions and six conventions, with matched controls, and not read. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 15 September 2026 · Sources: Klaus Schmeh’s Cipherbrain posts of January 2015, August 2017 and October 2021 and their comments; the 614 × 147 px scan Danish-General-Cryptogram.jpg The Copenhagen cryptogram: three lines of digits, letters and strokes. Scan published by Klaus Schmeh, Cipherbrain, 2015. Not solved — and not a simple substitution of any language tested closed from the scan Both transcriptions in circulation were attacked with a 5-gram annealer in ten languages. The best any language reached was −2.69 nats per letter , and 300 restarts did not move it. The same solver recovers twelve of fifteen random 103-letter passages enciphered the same way, and genuine text of this length scores between −1.4 and −2.1. Either the slip is not a simple substitution of a text in these languages, or both readings share a transcription error.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: The slip carries three short lines. It was found, probably in the late 1950s, behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum, and sent to the American Cryptogram Association. The ACA never solved it and never wrote it up. The museum, the general and the finder are all unrecorded. Klaus Schmeh received a scan from ACA member Kent Ramliden, a Swede living in Florida who died in 2016. He published it three times: in German in January 2015, as no. 23 of his Top 50 unsolved messages in August 2017, and as German and English “cold case” posts in October 2021. The only image in circulation is that scan, 614 by 147 pixels. Two reader contributions from the 2021 comments matter here: a 25-symbol transcription by “ShadowWolf”, and a Danish quadgram hill-climb by Matthew Brown that found nothing.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: Two readings were used. cipher.txt is this project’s, made from the scan upscaled four and six times, half a line at a time. cipher_sw.txt is ShadowWolf’s 25-symbol reading from the comments of the German post of 7 October 2021. This is the merged reading, one token per symbol, space separated: 7 N F n F B 3 A D B n o 3 D B P 6 3 B 3 P 8 D F 2 n 3 | 2 3 A W R F 0 3 A n 2 0 B n o 9 P n P 9 2 B 3 v v 3 D B | 0 A B v 3 D B P n o F 3 8 0 D B P X 0 3 B n o n F 9 n D B v n | 1 3 | n o n 3 F D B 3 F B A 1 2 3 A That is 107 tokens: 103 symbols of 20 kinds, plus 4 long vertical strokes written | and treated as sentence dividers. Digits 4 and 5 never occur. token mark on the slip count 3 digit 3 16 n plain n 13 B backslash with its trailing dot (\.) 14 F slash with its trailing dot (/.) 8 P plus sign 6 A caret or lambda (^) 6 D free-standing dot that precedes a stroke 8 o small round letter o 5 2 digit 2 5 0 tall zero 5 v as written 4 9 digit 9 3 1 digit 1 2 8 digit 8 2 7 6 X as written 1 each N n with two dots above 1 R small “or”-like glyph at the end of line 1 1 W caret with a double accent above 1 | long vertical stroke, sentence divider, not counted among the 103 4 Where the two readings differ The two readings agree symbol for symbol except that ShadowWolf splits what is merged here. He separates the backslash with a dot after it from the backslash with dots on both sides, which here is a free dot D followed by B . He separates the slash with a trailing dot from the slash with a leading dot, here D followed by F . He gives the small raised double tick after the first caret pair its own symbol. He distinguishes four caret shapes: a tall lambda-like one, which is the first caret of line 1 and the last symbol of line 3; a small one; one with a trailing dot opening line 2; and one after the zero in line 2. And he reads the second tall stroke around 1 3 in line 3 as the digit 1 rather than a divider. With those splits the symbol count is 25, which is Schmeh’s figure; merged it is 20. Both readings were attacked. Two internal regularities The letter o occurs five times and every time directly after n : no3 , no9 , +no , non and non3 , with non twice in line 3. The doubled pair vv occurs once, in line 2. Section 06 shows how far they go.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: solve.py builds character 5-gram language models from Project Gutenberg texts in ten languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, German, Dutch, French, English, Latin, Icelandic and Finnish, 0.6 to 2.4 million letters each. The corpus is not in the repository; it is fetched through the Gutendex API with the ids in the session log. The solver is simulated annealing over an injective symbol-to-letter map, 60 to 80 restarts per run, with the long strokes treated as sentence boundaries. The annealer optimises the 5-gram score alone; its top candidates are then re-ranked by dictionary coverage, which it does not optimise. Six token conventions were tested on the merged reading: the free dot as a letter, dropped, as a boundary, or fused to the following stroke; the long stroke as a letter; and the dotted n merged with plain n. The 25-symbol reading was run as it stands. A separate script, solve_sp.py , tests the hypothesis that the two dotted strokes are word separators, which would make the text 22 words averaging 3.7 letters, using a space-aware model and scoring whole-word hits. Nothing readable came out in any language under any convention. Best per-letter scores, with what the best key produced: language best score per letter, any convention what it looked like Latin −2.69 fxsisted tine togeteom scie ... Danish −2.77 junindel dige dskedesf ... / ... udstødes ... velsigne ... Norwegian −2.81 bærersag sena stjasatm ... Swedish −2.81 honensam sera stfasatv ... English −2.88 cydidsea sine stbesetf ... German −2.93 uchthien itze irbeierm ... French −2.97 chiailes lape ltbeletr ... Dutch, Icelandic, Finnish −3.07 to −3.30 The word-separator hypothesis scores −4.6 per letter under the spaced model, where real text scores about −2.3. t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: A failed search proves nothing on its own, so the solver was calibrated on texts it should solve. control.py draws passages of 103 letters with three sentence breaks at random from the same corpora, enciphers each with a random simple substitution of about 20 symbols, and attacks it with the identical solver. Three trials per language, 40 restarts each; the real cryptogram got 60 to 80, then 300. Accuracy is the share of the passage recovered. language trial letters in key accuracy score found score of true text outcome Danish 1 19 0.99 −1.99 −1.85 recovered Danish 2 19 0.99 −1.93 −1.96 recovered Danish 3 18 0.99 −1.85 −1.76 recovered German 1 22 0.96 −1.88 −1.78 recovered German 2 19 0.79 −2.64 −1.75 partial German 3 22 0.14 −3.42 −1.81 search failed English 1 20 1.00 −1.44 −1.44 recovered English 2 21 0.99 −1.99 −1.85 recovered English 3 20 1.00 −1.67 −1.67 recovered Latin 1 18 1.00 −2.09 −2.09 recovered Latin 2 18 1.00 −1.74 −1.74 recovered Latin 3 19 0.99 −1.87 −1.72 recovered Swedish 1 22 1.00 −1.95 −1.95 recovered Swedish 2 22 0.05 −3.49 −1.59 search failed Swedish 3 22 1.00 −1.99 −1.99 recovered Twelve of fifteen passages are recovered essentially completely, and the true text always scores between −1.4 and −2.1 per letter. Two trials fail outright and one partly. In each case the true key would have scored far better than what the annealer found: −1.81 against −3.42, −1.59 against −3.49, −1.75 against −2.64. These are search failures at 40 restarts, most likely tied to 22-letter keys, and they mean that a single failed run on the real text would prove nothing. That is why the strongest candidate languages were rerun with 300 restarts on both readings. Against that calibration the cryptogram never scores better than −2.7 in any language or under any reading. So either it is not a simple substitution of a text in these ten languages, or the transcription conflates or splits letters in a way that both independent readings share. Danish, the default assumption since 2015, fits no better than Latin or Norwegian. Matthew Brown’s Danish quadgram hill-climb in the 2021 comments came to the same nothing.
