t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys solved in 2023, four letters never read
b: Fr. 3083 f. 21r. Above the cipher, in clear, is the news that Aquila has been taken “par le conte de Montore et Camille Pardo”. The block opens with two nulls and MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL (Gallica btv1b90601328, view 36). Cipher in capitals, clear in lower case, spelling of the leaf kept MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL M’A CONMANDE RECHER[CHER] SON CONGE A CESTE SEIGNEVRIE, CE QV’ELLE N’A VOLV CONSENTIR, AINS A PROTESTE QVE S’IL SE DEPARTOIT QVE CE SEROIT LA TOTALLE RVINE DES EMPRINSES. ET ME SEMBLE QV’IL N’I A RAISON, VEV L’EMPRINSE DE MILLAN, LA VENVE DES ESPAIGNOLS AVEC ARGĒT POVR ICELLE SECOVRIR, ET LA PRIMEVERE APROCHER. IE CROY QV’IL NE DEPARTIRA SI LE FAICT […] sans LE CONSENTEMENT DE TOVS LES CONFEDERES, ET SI APORTEROIT […] VNG PREIVDICE IREPARABLE. Je luy ay escript AV MIEVLX QV’IL M’A ESTE POSSIBLE pour LE DIVERTIR DE CESTE OPINION, QVI EST PAR TROP DANGEREVSE. The comte de Saint-Pol commanded the French army in Lombardy from the autumn of 1528 until his defeat at Landriano on 21 June 1529. So five months before Landriano the commander wanted to leave. Venice, the league’s paymaster in the north, refused his leave on the ground that the Milan enterprise was in hand, Spanish money was coming to relieve Milan, and spring was near. The King’s ambassador tried to talk him round. The year is not on the leaf, but it is fixed by Saint-Pol’s command and by the Abruzzi news in the clear text.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys solved in 2023, four letters never read
h: Gramont, Rome, 11 October 1529: the Pope on the way to Bologna
b: Fr. 3091 f. 45r. After Monseigneur, je voy que tant par mes lettres du treziesme et du septiesme de septembre the letter is cipher for five pages. The heart on line 6 is the sign for the King (Gallica btv1b9060253s, view 49). This is the long one: 171 lines and about 7,000 signs across ff. 45r–47v, closing A Romme le xi me jour d’octobre over the signature G. de Gramont e. de Tarbe . The year is 1529. The Pope has just left Rome (Clement VII set out for Bologna on 7 October 1529), and Gramont leaves “demain” to join him at Perugia. The letter opens with the bull of the four décimes on the French clergy, raised for the princes’ ransom under the peace of Cambrai, and the prince of Orange is before Florence. In outline, modernised (the full reading, page by page, is in the repository): The council. Whatever the Emperor says or does only deepens the Pope’s distrust of that side. What won him to the King was the King’s message about the concile general , “lequel il craignoit sur toutes les choses de ce monde, combien qu’il monstrast … qu’il en ait grande envie”. Pressed, he confessed that he knew the council was being pushed to ruin him, and that he meant to grant it and then “s’arrester sur aucunes particularitez pour le differer, et que le delai lui succedast en rupture”. Into the King’s arms. He would “du tout se jecter entre ses bras et se fier en luy seul”. Because the times do not allow open trust, the King and his ministers may say publicly, whenever it helps, that they have little reason to trust the Pope, so long as the goodwill underneath stays whole. “Avec bonnes parolles vous aurez de luy ce que vous voudrez”. His one aim is to get the Emperor out of Italy. Feigning illness for the Admiral. The Emperor is bound “par ses chappitres”, the treaty of Barcelona, to bring the allies to full restitution or make war on them. Gramont has told Philippe Chabot, the Admiral, then on his embassy to Italy, to come as far forward as he can. The Pope offers to slow his journey, or to “faire le malade” in whatever town he is in, to wait for him. On 10 October he told Gramont he had already begun. Soothsayers and a dream. The Pope, though he should not believe “tout plein de gens qui se meslent de deviner”, greatly fears what they say of him. Several have foretold that he will be deposed or will die within the year, and that it will come “du costé dudict” [the Emperor]. The night before he left Rome he had a dream, which Gramont encloses, “lequel l’a mis en merveilleusement grande fantasie”, because he dreamed it at the kind of hour at which earlier dreams of his had come true. He told it to one man only, and Gramont asks that only the King, Madame and those they choose should know of it. Florence. The prince of Orange wanted to deal with [the Florentines]: restore [the Medici] to the state of Florence “comme il souloit”, in return for Pisa and Livorno being put in [the Emperor’s] hands. That is “chose grandement contraire” to what the Emperor had agreed with the Pope. Gramont’s letter adds detail to the French side of the weeks before the congress of Bologna. The council, Florence and the Venetian and Ferrarese restitutions all serve as bargaining counters in it, and the Pope keeps a private line to France through the ambassador. The enclosed dream is not in the volume.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys solved in 2023, four letters never read
h: Gramont, Rome, 21 July 1530: the princes come home
b: By July 1530 Gramont is a cardinal, and he uses a new key. The 14 cipher lines follow a clear passage on “la bonne nouvelle” and on Francisque’s coming mission: … [LE PAPE] A TROVVE BON QVE LEDICT FRANCISQVE Y AILLE … D’AVLTANT [QV’]ESTANT ICI IE POVRRAY OBVIER A TOVT CE QVE L’ON LVY POVRROIT MECTRE AVANT POVR LE DIVERTIR, A QVOY VOVS PVIS ASSEVRER QVE L’ON FAICT TOVTE LA DILLIGENCE POSSIBLE. MONSIEVR L’EVESQVE DE FAIANCE, NEPVEV DV CONTE DE CARPI, PARTIRA DEDANS TROIS OV QVATRE IOVRS POVR, DE LA PART DV [PAPE], […] CONGRATVLER AVEC LE [ROY] DE LA VENVE DE LA ROYNE ET DE MESSEIGNEVRS. The Dauphin and Henri, hostages in Spain since 1526, were handed back with Queen Eleanor on the Bidassoa on 1 July 1530. That dates the letter. The nuncio is Rodolfo Pio, bishop of Faenza, nephew of Alberto Pio, count of Carpi. Gramont had been asked to go himself, and the Pope sends “Francisque” instead because the Imperials would take Gramont’s going amiss. Two of the signs Lasry lists as unknown read out of this passage: 8Δ is pape (“de la part du 8Δ”) and the key-ring sign is roy . A third, ʃʃ on a stem at the head of a word, is a null.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys solved in 2023, four letters never read
h: Mâcon, Rome, 11 April 1537: Paul III and the Farnese marriage
b: Denonville, cardinal de Mâcon, was ambassador to Paul III during the war of 1536–38. His letter alternates clear and cipher. Its code numerals, which neither published table explains, read out of the text: 20 is the Emperor (“se precipiter a la devotion du dict 20”, “se declarer partial de 20”), 30 the Pope (a contemporary hand has written “le dict pappe” above it on f. 9r), and 40 the King . What the cipher says: Pier Luigi Farnese, the Pope’s son, has sent men to take possession of a place read as Novarre , and has approached the captain of a fortress to see whether he can be bought. (The Farnese were invested with Novara only in 1538, so the reading of the name is one of the few that needs checking.) The Pope has been offered the marriage of his granddaughter, Pier Luigi’s daughter Vittoria, with Cosimo de’ Medici. Mâcon thinks that if it goes the Pope’s way he will throw himself wholly to the Emperor. Through Latino Giovenale, the Pope sends word that if the marriages are refused “il aura occasion de se declarer partial de l’Empereur: ce qu’il vous plaira considerer”. “La confederation du Roy avec le Turc se verifie clerement.” If the Pope declares, it is “a craindre que les Venitiens le suivissent entierement”, since it is said that “le Roy avoit promis au Turc de faire passer grosse puissance en Italie, et qu’il s’amuse en Picardie”. In April 1537 François was campaigning at Hesdin. The French ambassadors at Venice, the bishops of Rodez and Lavaur, are trying to win over Alessandro Vitelli, who held the fortress of Florence and was angry with the Emperor. Mâcon holds back so as not to spoil their practique . He fears that if Cosimo marries the Pope’s granddaughter, Vitelli will follow, “car le dict pape a moyen de le contenter es terres de l’Eglise mesmes, de la ville de Castelle, dont il commance a se faire tirant”. The control. Fr. 3071 f. 9bis is a slip pasted into the volume, a contemporary decipherment of the f. 9v cipher: De quoy j’ay adverty mess rs de Rodez et de Lavaur qui m’ont escript avoir bon moyen envers luy de le practiquer … The f. 9v cipher was read glyph by glyph before the slip was compared, and the two agree almost word for word (Gallica btv1b9060315f, view 18). In the clear text, the duke of Mantua will not host the council summoned to Mantua for May 1537 without a paid guard. His brother, Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga, said so “en plain consistoire” (those three words are in cipher), and the Pope is thinking of moving the council. The dispatch goes by way of Venice to save the cost of a courier.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys solved in 2023, four letters never read
b: No cryptanalysis was needed, only reading. Each key table was checked on the first line of its letter (Langeac’s block opens MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL ; Gramont 1529’s first full line decodes d r R + W C 4 # L ● T Δ K Lo ʒ r R ● to tredecime v & avltre v ). The short letters were then read by eye from line strips. For the long ones, each glyph was given a one-character ASCII alias and a script turned the alias strings back into letters, so that every reading can be checked against the transcription and re-run. The five pages of fr. 3091 and the three parts of the Mâcon letter were read separately and in parallel, each by a model instance working from the same brief, key and crops, and then joined. The joins fall mid-sentence and agree. The things the readers found that the tables do not say: In Gramont’s 1529 hand the loose ǂǂ for a and the compact # for m cannot be told apart, so # is read as a or m by context. A is the more frequent. A triangle or ring on a stem over a foot bar looks like ♀ ( o ) but is a null, Lasry’s “4 with a flag”. It occurs about twenty times. Read as o , it produces doepesche . The heart, which Lasry lists only as a person sign, is always the King (“escript au ♡ et à vous”). Three large signs outside the table stand where the Emperor, the Florentines and the Pope or the Medici are expected. Those identifications come from context and are marked as such. In the Mâcon key a dotted r is a null in most places but must be r in partant . Its R sign is easily mistaken for its C sign.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys solved in 2023, four letters never read

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: A German recipe book of a circle of gold-makers near Passau, dated 1426 and listed on DECODE as non-decrypted, with substance names hidden in three home-made sign alphabets. The compiler wrote the key on the first leaf as one unbroken run of signs “so that no one should understand that it is an alphabet”, then struck it through. Wilhelm Wattenbach read it in 1869 and printed three facsimiles with their plaintexts. Here the struck alphabet of f. 1r and the invocation alphabet of f. 6v are recovered from the images and checked against his readings, a third set is partly fixed from the Heidelberg catalogue’s reading of f. 93r, and the book is ruled out as a record candidate. East Bavaria, near Passau · home-made sign alphabets · 1426 · found already read Alchymey teuczsch: the ciphers of an alchemists’ notebook, 1426 Heidelberg, Universitätsbibliothek, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 · paper, 95 leaves, Bavarian German · DECODE R2876, “non-decrypted” A circle of gold-makers wrote their recipes in German and hid the substance names in signs of their own. The compiler put the key on the first leaf and struck it through. Wilhelm Wattenbach read it in 1869. The alphabets are recovered here from the images and checked against his plaintexts; nothing here was deciphered that was not already in print. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 18 September 2026 Summary. The book came up as a candidate for the oldest cipher this project could read, on the strength of a DECODE record marked “non-decrypted” and a pointer to “ff. 70–71”. Neither holds. The “70–71” are Bernhard Bischoff’s item numbers in his 1954 survey of secret scripts, not folios, and those leaves are blank. The ciphers were broken in 1869 by Wilhelm Wattenbach, who printed three facsimiles with their readings and called them easy. Gerhard Eis printed more in 1957 and 1982, and the 2014 Heidelberg catalogue gives its quotations from the cipher passages resolved. What was done here: every leaf was surveyed for cipher; the compiler’s crossed-out alphabet on f. 1r and the second alphabet on f. 6v and f. 91v were recovered and checked against the printed plaintexts; and a third sign set, the one on f. 1r lines 1–2, ff. 5v–6r, 44v and 93r, was identified and partly fixed. Status: found already read. Open: a continuous transcription of the recipe passages, the f. 6r glossary and f. 44v has never been printed. It needs the doubtful signs of two keys settled first, and its value is for the history of alchemy, not for cryptography.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: A small paper book, 22.5 by 15.5 cm, written in several Bavarian hands and dated on f. 9r: Das puch ist angehaben ym [tauro] xiiii und xxvj , begun with the sun in Taurus, 1426. Most of the recipes are headed with the name of Niklas Jankowitz. Other names are Michael von Pirpach, over a list of lucky and unlucky days, and Michel Wulfing, over a fever charm. A note on f. 94r records that on the Saturday of Easter week [14]23 “we” gave “our multiplication” to one Frydryce to work, weighed at four pounds less two lot. An address formula to Leonhard, bishop of Passau from 1424, places the circle. The book is sewn into an unexecuted 1413 charter of the Landgraves of Leuchtenberg, counts of Hals, taking the Jew Salman Teublin into their service and binding him to teach them three of his best arts. The cipher is not a letter but a working notebook’s protection. Recipes are in clear German, and the substance names, quantities and some whole sentences are in signs. A survey of all 85 images, covers included, finds cipher on f. 1r, ff. 5v–7r, 9r–15v, 20r–22r, 44v, 46r–v, 54r–61r, 79ar, 91v and 93r.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 1r. Lines 1–2 in the third sign set; line 3 the alphabet, run together, then vnd ich in clear and the signs for hab es ; line 4 the rest of the sentence. Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg. Wattenbach read the leaf in 1869: Das ist ein abc vnd das haben wir selbs neus gemacht, abcdefghiklmnopqrſstuwschch vnd ich hab es darum gar an ein ander gesetzt das man nicht sul versten das es ein alfabet sei — “This is an ABC that we made ourselves, new, and I have set it all together so that no one should understand that it is an alphabet.” The alphabet is written without a break, and the whole leaf is struck through. Wattenbach thought the strike was there because the key was too easy to guess; it is still legible. With the strike line removed from the image, the run gives twenty-four signs in the order of the alphabet the text names: a b c d e f g h i k l m ▪ o 2 ∴ ⊡ 8 Y ˥ : ɓ 4 ꝝ n o p q r ſ s t u w sch ch ϙ 88 ꝗ ꝁ × F ● ◒ • T ⊙ ♣ The signs are rendered with the nearest typographic shape. Two checks in running text: Line 3 continues after the clear vnd ich with ˥ ▪ o ⊡ ●, which is hab es , as Wattenbach printed. The recipe heading on f. 11r reads ϙ : ɓ 4 ▪ ● · Y ▪ ϙ ɓ ? : 2, niklas gank?icz , with one sign unread. A modern reader had already pencilled “= Niklas Gankwiz” beside it. f. 11r, the name in the f. 1r alphabet, with a modern pencil gloss. Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg. The first eleven values, a to l, are clear on the image, and a, b, c, e, g, h, i, k, l and s are checked in running text. The last thirteen are read from the shape of the signs under the heaviest part of the strike, and only a few of them have been met in running text; they are grade C.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
h: The second alphabet: the invocation on f. 6v
b: f. 6v, the opening prayer in the second alphabet. Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg. Wattenbach printed f. 6v with its reading: In dem namen des faters vnd des suns vnd des heiligen geistes so fach ich schuldiger man dises buch an , “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost I, a guilty man, begin this book.” Segmenting the three lines and laying them against the text gives nineteen values: : i, a hooked Y n, 3 d, a trefoil on a stem e, Ω with an inner triangle m, a stroke a, a tall stroke medial s, a blob final s, a ring with a tail f, a T with a wavy top r, a ring with a dot h, T l, a looped stem g, two loops on a stem t, a ring with a 3-tail sch, an 8 with an inner loop b, a c joined to a 2 for ch, 9 o, and a cup with a 3 for the u of vnd . Every word of the prayer reads with them. f. 91v, the second alphabet written out in order and struck through. Its opening signs agree with the values from f. 6v. Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg. The same set is written out in alphabetical order on f. 91v and crossed out, like the first. Wattenbach did not reproduce that leaf, and the catalogue notes it only as an alphabet.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
h: The third set: boxes, stars and T
b: f. 5v, the preface to the glossary of cover-names, clear German with runs of the third set. Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg. Wattenbach wrote that f. 1r uses “two different systems”. Lines 1–2 of that leaf are in a third set built from boxes with and without dots, stars and T-shapes, which also carries the preface and glossary on ff. 5v–6r and the notes on ff. 44v and 93r. Two printed readings fix part of it: f. 1r line 1, Das ist ein abc : Das [✱ 中 ⊡̈] [⊡ ✱ T] [▪ o 2]. f. 93r, read in the 2014 catalogue as Nota wir haben versucht das [in dem caichen] der [iuncfrawn] , “we have tried it in the sign of the Virgin”: [✱ T] [∴ ⊡ ■] [2 ▪ ✱ 2 ⊏ ⊡ T]. f. 93r, the Virgo note. Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg. Together they give ▪ a, o b, 2 c, ∴ d, ⊡ e, ⊏ h, ✱ i, T n, a filled box m, a box on a stem s and a box with two dots t. The a, b, c, d and e are the signs of the f. 1r alphabet. The i and n are not, and T, which is w in the f. 1r alphabet, is n here. The s and t rest on one word each. The glossary on f. 6r uses further dotted-box variants and has not been read.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: The glossary on f. 5v was printed by Wattenbach in its resolved form: aqua fortis is called “the sharp water”, sal ammoniac “sal”, its oil “Nyczadar”, common salt “sal aller”, gold “the yellow earth”, silver “the white earth”, green oil “vitriol”. The cover-names were meant to spare the writers from enciphering every substance, and the recipes still mix them with signs. In the recipes (ff. 7r–22r, 46r–v, 54r–61r), the signs are mostly those of the f. 1r alphabet, as the name on f. 11r shows, with admixtures from the others; Bischoff noted that the sets are also used mixed. The runs are short, from one to a few words, and recur: the most frequent group appears about a dozen times on ff. 10v–15r. f. 79ar holds a struck table of sign groups, each over a pair of signs, which looks like a list of substances with their symbols.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: The project’s oldest read cipher is from 1497, and a list of earlier candidates was drawn up to try to beat it. This book was on it at 1426 for three reasons: DECODE lists it as non-decrypted, with 85 images; the Handschriftencensus entry cites Bischoff for “S. 12 (Nr. 70–71)”, which was read as cipher on ff. 70–71; and the key was said to be on f. 1r. The first check on any target is for a prior reading. Wattenbach’s 1869 note, with its facsimiles of f. 1r, f. 5v and f. 6v and their plaintexts, settles it. The book is ruled out as a record candidate.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)

The last thirteen signs of the f. 1r alphabet (m to ch), grade C until they are met in running text. One sign of the name on f. 11r ( o or w ). t: Hellen to Frederick II — transcription audited, decipherment sought
b: Seven intercepted letters and one supporting letter remain unread. The parser now preserves uncertain figures and marks; a repeated passage was confirmed on the manuscript. Fagel inventory 5206 lists digitized decipherments from 1752–1753, but no matching text has yet been retrieved. The Hague → Frederick II · numerical nomenclators · 1752–1763 · unsolved Hellen’s intercepted letters to Frederick II KHA, Prins Willem V, inventory 196 · seven catalogue targets and one related letter · French The transcription has been audited. An archive collection of deciphered letters offers a lead for 1752, but no matching decipherment has yet been retrieved. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 20 September 2026 Summary. These letters remain unsolved in this investigation: no cipher plaintext or key has been verified. The work so far covers existing DECODE transcriptions and images, a search for parallel texts, and an audit of the parsing used in the earlier attempt. That audit found errors which turned uncertain numbers into definite ones, lost some ciphertext, and inflated the number of unreadable groups. A repeated passage thought to be a transcription duplication is actually present twice on the manuscript. The strongest new lead is Fagel inventory 5206, catalogued as digitized copies of deciphered Hellen letters from 1752–1753. Its scans could not be retrieved during the check on 20 September 2026. This is a progress report, not a decipherment or a proof that recovery is impossible.

t: Hellen to Frederick II — transcription audited, decipherment sought
b: The previous parser removed question marks before recognizing numbers: 2 1 ? ? , for example, became the definite value 21 . It also counted empty newline fragments as unreadable groups, included the heading year 1752 as ciphertext, and discarded cipher before a cleartext tag on the same line. The revised parser retains uncertainty, source line and page references, underlining and carets, and ciphertext on both sides of cleartext tags. On R1953, image 13448, the three-line passage beginning 1426 825 963 occurs twice on the manuscript. It must not be deleted as a DECODE transcription duplication. The two versions are not identical, and neither has been established as the correct reading. The letters are provisionally grouped into 1752, 1756 and 1763 code families. Earlier frequency-density tests did not produce readable text, but that failure does not establish random codebook ordering, prove the proposed homophone clusters, or rule out a future ciphertext-only solution. Those stronger conclusions have been withdrawn.

t: Hellen to Frederick II — transcription audited, decipherment sought

A matching text for 4 January 1752 could provide known plaintext for reconstructing and checking that letter’s code. The date range alone does not establish that this particular letter is included. During the 20 September 2026 access check, the old scan link returned 404, the catalogue service timed out, and the current viewer displayed an empty content area with a maintenance notice. This is a dated access problem, not evidence that the documents are unavailable permanently. Open the current archive viewer . De Leeuw’s study points to Fagel 5177 for British decipherments with Lyonet’s additions, and Boerhaave Museum Arch 162-r for Lyonet and Croiset’s account. He reports no Prussian codes broken between April 1757 and October 1763. That makes a surviving Dutch decipherment a less secure expectation for the 1763 letters than for the earlier material; it does not prove that no parallel text survives elsewhere.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
b: The one letter marked “avec chiffre” and not “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” among some thirty of 1625–26 to the ambassador in Rome. It is not an undeciphered text: no. 26 is not a second letter but the same despatch, carrying the same cipher with the plaintext written between the lines in 1626. Identity fixed on the word-for-word clear text, the cipher runs falling at the same points and matching groups. The ciphered passages are the papal Legate and “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valteline”, the admission that France made peace with the Huguenots because “le faix d’une double guerre ne se pouvoit plus supporter”, the Dutch squadron sailing home with the Huguenot admiral, and Savoy’s attempt to engage France against Spain six weeks before Monzón. Contributed by Arya Sanketbhai Patel. Paris → Rome · nomenclator of figures and letter-forms · 13 February 1626 · resolved and read Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away BnF Français 3669 no. 25 · the one letter of some thirty catalogued “avec chiffre” without “et déchiffrement” · no. 26 is the same despatch with the plaintext written between the lines in 1626 Read from the contemporary decipherment: the Valtelline, the reason for the Huguenot peace, the Dutch ships sailing home with the Huguenot admiral, and Piedmont’s push for war with Spain Arya Sanketbhai Patel · solved 18 September 2026 Summary. Among some thirty letters of 1625–26 from Louis XIII and his secretary Raymond Phelipeaux d’Herbault to Philippe de Béthune, ambassador in Rome, bound in BnF Français 3669, the catalogue marks exactly one “avec chiffre” and not “avec chiffre et déchiffrement”: no. 25, of 13 February 1626. It looked like a one-letter gap in an otherwise readable series, and the obvious first question was whether the next piece in the volume might be its decipherment. It is. No. 26 is not a second letter but the same despatch , carrying the same cipher with the plaintext written between the lines by a contemporary decipherer. No. 25 was never an undeciphered text; its reading has been lying three folios away since 1626. What the cipher hides is worth the trip: the papal Legate’s mission and “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valt(eline)”, the reason the crown had just made peace with the Huguenots, the Dutch ships slipping away with the Huguenot admiral, and the prince of Piedmont in Paris trying to drag France into war with Spain six weeks before the Treaty of Monzón defeated him. Status: resolved and read. No cryptanalysis was required, and none would have been the right first move.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
h: A gap that was not a gap
b: Français 3669 is a recueil of originals: the King and Herbault writing to Béthune in Rome through the autumn and winter of 1625–26, most pieces catalogued “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” because the embassy’s clerk wrote the plaintext of each ciphered passage onto the sheet as he read it. One piece breaks the pattern. The volume is digitised from a black-and-white microfilm of double-page openings; canvas equals folio plus five, fixed on the foliation of ff. 70 and 73. Piece Letter Leaves Cipher 24 Herbault → Béthune, 6 February 1626 ff. 67–68 none noted 25 Herbault → Béthune, 13 February 1626 ff. 69–71 cipher, no decipherment 26 the same letter, 13 February 1626 ff. 72–74 cipher with interlinear decipherment 27 Louis XIII → Béthune f. 75– cipher and decipherment Both copies are made up for sending, each with its own address leaf, wax seal and docket. Both open on the same words under the same marginal note, “Le roy fera responce” . And their clear text runs word for word: the same paragraphs on Rambouillet’s delayed departure for Spain, the promotion of cardinals and Marquemont’s hat, the courier sent on the 6th through the Venetian ambassador Contarini, the peace with the Huguenots, the prince of Piedmont’s arrival — down to the King’s sore toe, “quelque douleur à cause d’ung ongle qui luy entre dans la chair”, which kept him in bed and delayed Herbault’s report.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
b: BnF Français 3669, f. 73r (no. 26) — cipher with the 1626 decipherment written under each line: “vray que les affaires de cet estat avoyent besoing de ce” / cipher / “relasche et que le faix d’une double guerre ne se pouvoit” / cipher / “plus supporter. J’advoue que les affections”… (Bibliothèque nationale de France). Three things establish that no. 26 reads no. 25 rather than merely resembling it. The clear text is identical , paragraph by paragraph, including incidental matter no second letter would repeat verbatim: the memoir of Cardinal Bevilacqua for Horatio Giraldi, the naturalisation letters obtained through Cardinal de la Valette, the sore toe. The cipher runs fall at the same points , after the same clear words — “en laquelle il aura laissé”, “dont nous esperons estre bientost esclaircis”, “au nom de ce prétendu comte de”, “besoing de ce”, “Vous scaurez maintenant que”, “Toutes ces propositions”, “il nous faut continuer ceste mesme routte jusques”. The groups match where checked. No. 25’s first run opens to 92 … 17 … 43 and no. 26’s opens to 92 g 17 … 43 … ; the third run ends … 68 93 … in both, with the same short group after it. The two clerks’ hands differ enough that individual figures read differently at this resolution, so no group-for-group identity is claimed here — only that the runs correspond. The cipher itself is a nomenclator of one- to three-character groups mixing Arabic figures with letter-forms. The opening run, to 92 g 17 ẓ 43 x cu 4 7 ẓ p x 3 3 6 x , stands for “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valt(eline)” — about eighteen groups for some forty-eight letters, so most groups carry a syllable or a whole word. The table is not reconstructed here because the reading does not need it, and roughly thirty further glossed letters of 1625–26 in the same cipher sit in the same volume for anyone who wants it.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
b: A secretary of state writing to his ambassador in Rome on the eve of the Treaty of Monzón, and enciphering exactly the three things that mattered. The Valtelline. Herbault waits on news of the papal Legate’s departure for Spain and of the last resolution in which he will have left “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valt(eline)” — an affair which deserves “l’envoy d’un courrier exprez” — and above all “principallement sy le Pape entroit dans la partialité” , the fear that Urban VIII would cease to mediate and take a side. Why the crown had just made peace with its Protestants. The peace “s’affermit de jour en jour” and is welcome even to those “qui ont tousjours le plus hautement conseillé le chastiment et la guerre contre les huguenots” — because, in cipher, “les affaires de cet estat avoyent besoing de ce relasche, et que le faix d’une double guerre ne se pouvoit plus supporter” , while “les affections de noz voysins qui font profession de ceste religion pretendue refformée estoyent grandement alterés” . That is the candid version: France made peace at home because it could not afford two wars, and because the Protestant powers abroad were turning. The ships. Béthune has already been told of “la conduitte des Anglois envers nous, et comme une partye des vaisseaux hollandois s’estoyent retirez” . Now he is to know that the Huguenot admiral — read as Soubise — “a suivy depuis sept ou huict jours avec le reste de sa flotte; la route des premiers par l’ordre des estatz et sans permission de Sa Ma(jes)té ny de Mons(ieu)r l’Admiral, et dans la conioncture de la conclusion de la paix” . The Dutch squadron lent to the King against La Rochelle had sailed home on its own States’ orders, at the precise moment France needed it least to be noticed. And Savoy’s push for war. The prince of Piedmont reached Paris on Monday the 9th, surprising Longueville and the maréchal de Créquy who were to have met him, and saluted the King out hunting in the warren at Saint-Germain. Once the King is back he will begin to treat, and all his propositions “tendent à engager le Roy à la guerre avec l’Espagne, (et que) la Seig(neu)rie de Venize contribue comme faict l’Angleterre et Holande” . Herbault’s answer is the whole French position in one clause: Sa Majesté “escoutera tout ce qu’il luy sera representé, et scaura bien prendre la resolution convenable au bien de ses affaires” . Six weeks later she did, settling with Spain separately at Monzón and leaving Venice and Savoy out of it. A closing practical passage, also part-ciphered, weighs keeping the ordinary courier route against going by the Grisons, rejected for “d’autres longueurs et incommoditez, outre la despense”.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
b: The key is not tabulated. It would need the groups aligned to the glossed words, which the decipherer’s placement only loosely indicates, and the volume’s thirty other glossed letters would do it better. Two proper names are read only from the gloss and are uncertain in the palaeography: the “S(ieu)r de Santriny” who made a proposition to Béthune, and the “prétendu comte de Montembelans” in whose name it was made. “L’admiral Soubise” is an identification from context — a Huguenot admiral with a fleet in February 1626 — rather than a confident reading of the gloss. Whether this letter or the series is in print was not checked. Unvalidated. Checked: the folio-to-canvas mapping on two foliated leaves, the piece list against the leaves, the word-for-word identity of the two copies’ clear text, the correspondence of the cipher runs and the matching of groups at two places, and the reading of every glossed passage quoted. Not checked: a group-by-group identity of the two ciphertexts, the key table, any printed edition. This is a reading of a contemporary decipherment, not an independent decryption.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: Rommel set the King’s ciphered passages to the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel as rows of figures he could not read, then printed the key six years later with one sample and stopped. Put together, they read all seven passages, about 4,100 groups: Bouillon and the German princes, the Gunpowder Plot and Mérargues “forgés sur mesme enclume”, two million livres for the Dutch, and on 20 May 1606 the call to the princes to take counsel together against a Spanish King of the Romans, “pour la conservation de la liberté germanique”. Contributed by Arya Sanketbhai Patel. Paris → Kassel · two-digit code with word and name lists · 1602–09 · read Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice of Hesse-Kassel, seven ciphered passages Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice-le-Savant (Rommel, 1840) · about 4,100 groups · decoded with the key Rommel printed in 1846 and never applied Arya Sanketbhai Patel · solved 17 September 2026 Summary. In 1840 Christoph von Rommel published the correspondence of Henri IV with Maurice the Learned, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, from the originals at Marburg, and printed the King’s ciphered passages as rows of two-digit figures he could not read, “dans l’espoir qu’il est possible de retrouver la clef”. Six years later he had the key, from Groen van Prinsterer and van der Kemp, printed it in a German journal with one sample letter, and stopped. Nobody put the key and the other letters together: Tomokiyo’s page lists them as undeciphered, and so does the Lettres missives . Applied to the 1840 page images, the 1846 key reads all seven of the King’s passages, about 4,100 groups, in seven letters from 22 November 1602 to 24 January 1609. Two of them are the German policy the catalogue hoped for. On 22 December 1605 the King ties the Mérargues treason and the attempt on his life to the Gunpowder Plot, “forgés sur mesme enclume”, promises the Dutch two million livres again for 1606 and asks the Landgrave and the German princes for money and troops before spring. On 20 May 1606 he writes that the Spaniards mean to have a King of the Romans elected wholly at their devotion and to turn the Diet against the United Provinces, that all kings and princes jealous of Spain must “prendre conseil ensemble” in time, and that he will do his part “pour la conservation de la liberté germanique” when the others do theirs. Status: read. A prince’s name on p. 213, seven groups on p. 307, one unlisted name-group and a line of signs the 1840 typesetter could not set remain; the Marburg originals were not seen.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: Maurice of Hesse-Kassel (1572–1632) was the most learned and the most francophile of the Calvinist princes of the Empire, and Henri IV’s regular correspondent on German affairs from the Bongars mission of 1599 to the Jülich crisis of 1610. Rommel, the Hessian archivist and historian, printed 118 pieces of the exchange from the Marburg archive in 1840 (Paris, Renouard). The Landgrave’s letters are in clear; several of the King’s carry passages in figures, which Rommel set as he found them, and some of the King’s letters he printed from a contemporary decipherment with the figures omitted. The list below is what the volume prints in figures from the King’s side; nothing else on it was ciphered by him. Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice-le-Savant (1840), p. 310 — the middle of the King’s letter of 20 May 1606: the Spanish design on the election of a King of the Romans and the call to “prendre conseil ensemble” (Internet Archive, correspondancein00henr, leaf 352). Henri IV to the Landgrave Rommel pp. In figures Read before 22 November 1602 84 13 lines no 12 January 1603 99 12 lines no; Lettres missives vi p. 12 prints the figures 3 April 1604 170–175 5 pages yes, Rommel 1846 (used here as control) 27 December 1604 211–214 3 pages no 28 April 1605 230 11 lines no; Rommel’s footnote regrets it 22 December 1605 269–272 3 pages no 20 May 1606 307–314 6 pages no 24 January 1609 391 1 line no The catalogue entry that set this target (“12 Jan 1603, 28 Dec 1603, 27 Dec 1604, pp. 12, 148–189, 388–393”) came from Tomokiyo’s page and was wrong about the pages: p. 12 is the Lettres missives reference, the 28 December 1603 letter is printed from a decipherment with no figures at all, and pp. 388–393 hold a single line. The passages of 1602, 1605 and 1606 were on no list.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
h: The key, and what the texts corrected in it
b: Rommel, “La clef des chiffres dans la Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice le Savant”, Allgemeine Zeitschrift für Geschichte V (1846), p. 403: the word lists (comma, two dots, overbar) and the symbols. The letter table is on p. 402 (Internet Archive, bub_gb_Zpc1AAAAMAAJ). The cipher is the one Tomokiyo found as an original sheet in BnF Clairambault 360 f. 168, dated October 1602, and it served the whole correspondence to 1610. Bare two-digit figures are letters, up to four homophones each; a comma after the figure sends it to a list of small words and syllables ( le, la, leur, que, qui, qu’il, pour, pro, pre, ma, me, mon, ne, ny, nous, on, où, sa, se, roy ), two dots above it to a second ( con, ca, car, don, da, di, do, de, en, eulx, faire, faict, point, elle, forces, troupes, guerre, cour impériale, diète de l’Empire ), an overbar to names and titles ( Bouillon, Comte, Conseil, Pape, Empereur, Roi d’Espagne, Roi d’Angleterre, l’Archiduc, Brandebourg, Brunswick, provinces unies, Protestant, Allemagne, Angleterre, argent, armée, alliés, ambassadeur, au, aux, afin ). A dozen drawn symbols stand for te, tion, tant, tous, tout, tre, grand, va, ville, votre, Hongrie ; one sign doubles the symbol before it, one cancels it, and a few flourishes are nulls. Rommel’s print of the key is right in every letter value, but its lists are set with fewer words than figures and its fourth row of homophones is misaligned, so the texts had to fix the rest: 70 is a fourth p missing from the table ( presse, perdra, principalement ); 85 is m and 83 is o ( maison, ensemble, favorisé ); 17, is la and 18, 19, le ; 24, lettre , 25, leur ; 65, pro ( profiter, prospèrent ), 66, pre ; 83, rompre ( cor-rompre ); 70 with dots is faict , 84 with dots forces ; 26 with overbar is Comte (Rommel’s own glossary: le comte de Solms ), which shifts the names one place so that 31 is Pape , 33 Empereur , 35 Roi d’Espagne and 37 Roi d’Angleterre , as the 24 January 1609 line “les ministres du Pape et du Roi d’Espagne” and the 1604 control both require. The group Rommel set under l’administrateur de Strasbourg as 59 is le Turc (“la paix avec [59]”, December 1605); the tall 4 is te or tion and the print does not separate them; the typesetter’s “9 +” is the doubling sign 94; and the ♀-, Ψ- and tt-like flourishes are nulls (“ayant ♀ tt sceu que le duc de Féria…”). Every one of these is recorded in key.py with the passage that fixed it. Controls. Rommel printed Groen van Prinsterer’s decipherment of the 3 April 1604 letter beside the key; the first lines of p. 171 decode here word for word to his text (“…ainsy demander la paix à leurs ennemis en leur pays, que la nécessité qui les presse est très grande…”). His footnotes to the Landgrave’s letter of 10 February 1603 gloss five groups ( diète de l’Empire, l’Archiduc, Protestants, Empereur, cour impériale ) and the key returns each; his 1840 glossary “Passages déchiffrés” agrees throughout. The strongest check is internal: every passage comes out as continuous early-seventeenth-century French that joins the clear text it interrupts.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: 22 November 1602. He holds his despatch for the advice Maurice promised on the Diet: whether it will meet, what will be treated, what proposal he should make “pour le public et le particulier de mes alliés”, and whether to send his ambassador on to Saxony and Denmark, “avec votre bon conseil sur le [mémoire] et instruction que je luy doibs donner”. 12 January 1603. Since the Emperor will not appear at the Diet nothing of weight will be treated, “et principallement de l’élection d’un roy des Romains”. Bouillon has not written a word about the Administrator of Strasbourg’s coming to France nor about the bishopric: “je ne sçay comme il aura pris ce voyage, ny de quelque sorte il embrasse la cause du dit Administrateur”. 27 December 1604. Why he has not sent the embassy to the German princes that Maurice advised: “la mauvaise intelligence que j’ay recogneue entre les [princes] protestants”, and “le mescontentement et dégoust qu’aucuns d’eulx m’ont donné … depuis qu’ils ont adjousté foy aux discours du duc de Bouillon et favorisé sa cause avec moins de respect et considération à ma personne que je n’espérois d’eulx”. The Hungarian revolt is out but “la suite et conséquence en sera grande”. James I’s courtship of Spain: “il fault qu’il en face les preuves devant qu’il le croye”. The Dutch have as much courage as ever and are provided for; a newly-visited prince has given them hope of arming for them next year, and Maurice should encourage him. The Spaniards forge new plots against him daily; the comte d’Auvergne, his father-in-law and his sister are in justice “d’avoir traité avec eulx plus avant qu’ils ne devoyent”. 28 April 1605. The lines Rommel regretted: the aid the United Provinces and Geneva continue to receive from him “justifient assez la vérité de ma conduite et volonté en tels cas, et le soin que j’ay de maintenir et soubstenir ceulx de la dite religion, pour les notables intérests que j’ay à leur conservation et de la cause publicque”. 22 December 1605. Mérargues’ treason and the attempt on the King “me sont arrivés quasi au mesme temps de la conspiration d’Angleterre. Il semble aussy qu’ils ayent esté forgés sur mesme enclume”; the Spanish ambassador’s complaint is what Spanish ministers do everywhere, “seduire et corrompre les subjects des princes auprès desquels ils résident”; James I has as much cause to complain “toutesfois il le couvre et dissimule mieulx”. He has recommended the United Provinces to James “au besoin extrême qu’elles ont à présent d’estre assistées et renforcées par leurs alliés pour relever l’année prochaine la réputation de leurs armes”, and asks Maurice, who has “notable intérest à leur conservation avec les autres princes d’Allemagne”, to see them helped “tant d’argent que de troupes” as some princes have promised. He will continue “la mesme assistance d’argent et de troupes que je leur ay départie ceste-cy; elle est très notable et non moindre de deux millions de livres; mais si avec cela ils ne sont point secourus d’ailleurs, il leur sera impossible de résister”, the enemy massing money and men “pour les assaillir plus vivement et puissamment qu’ils n’ont point faict”. Get the help to them by spring, “car celuy qui pourra prévenir sa partie en cela en sera grandement avantagé”. And what does the Emperor mean by the Diet he has summoned; the Turkish peace; the Hungarian accord; the siege of Brunswick. 20 May 1606. The Emperor “ne change point de conduite” and is ill served, above all in Hungary. “Les Espagnols feront ce qu’ils pourront pour faire eslire un roy des Romains de la maison d’Austriche qui soit entièrement à leur dévotion”, and Feria goes to the Diet to promote it and to propose the pacification of the Netherlands, failing which the Empire is to make war on the States: “deux propositions de grande conséquence et auxquelles toute la chrestienté n’a moins d’intérest que l’Allemagne mesme. C’est pourquoy j’estime estre nécessaire que tous les roys et princes qui doivent avoir jalousie de l’agrandissement et prospérité de la puissance espagnole doibvent d’heure aviser et prendre conseil ensemble de ce qu’il convient faire pour empescher que les dicts Espagnols ne fassent cadrer les affaires et résolutions de la dite diète à leur souhait. Pour mon regard, j’y contribueray tousjours très volontiers ce qui dépendra de moy et me sera bienséant de faire, principalement quand je recognoistray que les autres pourront faire le semblable … pour la conservation de la liberté germanique, sans toutesfois en attendre autre advantage que d’advancer le bien de la cause commune et la seureté publique”; Maurice is to tell those he judges worthy and to advise the King what he “puis et doibs faire maintenant”. James I will not break with Spain over Owen and Baldwin, “tant il désire vivre en neutralité et en paix”, and the Spaniards ply him with “offres et ouvertures très spécieuses”; their aim is the Netherlands, “un grand effort ceste année, principallement du costé du Rhin et de Frise”, waiting only for Spinola. The States, weaker, will be forced onto the defensive, “misérable condition … en un estat composé et gouverné par plusieurs testes”; all whose interest is joined to theirs must act “devant que leur débilité et inanition soyent plus grandes, autrement les remèdes y seront trop tardifs”. His earlier request that Maurice press the German princes has had “fort peu d’effect”. The Dutch prosper in the East Indies and off Portugal, but “je doubte que ceste bonne fortune leur dure si celle de la terre leur manque”. The Spaniards will exploit the quarrel of the Pope and Venice; he will try to compose it. 24 January 1609. “Les ministres du Pape et du Roi d’Espagne” will do everything to reconcile Matthias with the Emperor.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: Nine groups on p. 213 give the name of the prince who visited the States (“d’un nouveau …”) and do not resolve; seven groups at the top of p. 307, the unlisted name-group 98 with overbar on p. 211 (a prince whose friendship Lorraine mediated: Bavaria is a guess*), and a line of letters and signs on p. 311 that the 1840 typesetter could not set in figures. The Marburg originals would settle them. The 1840 print is a transcription, and single figures are wrong in it (a 36 for 26, an 18 for 15); the readings mark supplied words in brackets. The tall-4 symbol is te or tion by context; 55, and 56, are both used where paix or pays is wanted. Whether the Landgrave’s chancery decipherments survive at Marburg is not checked; the Lettres missives reprinted the figures without reading them.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: The Internet Archive’s hOCR of the volume located the pages with dense figures. The figures were then transcribed by eye from 900-pixel strips of the full-resolution page images, because the OCR loses exactly what matters: the comma, the two dots, the overbar and the drawn symbols. The transcriptions in hesse1603/ct/ keep Rommel’s line breaks and the clear text; key.py holds the key with each correction and its evidence; run.py decodes a transcription; the hand readings are in letters/READINGS.md . No solver was used and none was needed: with the 1846 key, the work was transcription and reading. About 4,100 groups.

t: Henrietta Maria’s household to Charles I, 1645–46 — already read by George Lasry
b: Six numerical homophonic letters in TNA SP 106/10, catalogued as undeciphered and still on Tomokiyo’s unsolved list. The DECODE records carry George Lasry’s reconstructed keys and plaintexts for the whole run, ff. 207–247 (October 2020). Only the nomenclator numbers are left open. His key, applied here to the raw transcription of f. 247, reads it at once. St Germain / Paris → Charles I · numerical homophonic with nomenclator · 1645–46 · read by others Henrietta Maria’s household to Charles I, 1645–46: already read by George Lasry The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 213–247: six letters from the queen’s circle in France to the King (DECODE R785, R787, R790, R923, R924, R929), catalogued here as undeciphered and still on Tomokiyo’s unsolved list. The keys and plaintexts have been on the DECODE records since October 2020. This page records that and one independent check. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 19 September 2026 Summary. Catalogue entry 59 grouped six numerical ciphers from SP 106/10, written from Henrietta Maria’s household at St Germain and Paris to Charles I in the last year of the first Civil War. DECODE lists them as “partially decrypted” and dates them only by the handwriting, so they looked open. Fetching the record pages shows otherwise. Every letter in the run, ff. 207–247, carries George Lasry’s reconstructed key and his plaintext, uploaded on 23 October 2020, beside Sofia Pettersson’s 2019 transcription. Lasry reconstructed four keys, one for each period of the correspondence, and dated the letters from their content (July 1645 to January 1646). The six letters of entry 59 use three of them. “Partial” refers only to the three-digit nomenclator numbers for names and some words, which stay in brackets. Applied here to the raw transcription of f. 247, without his plaintext file, his key reads the letter at once. Nothing about the text is new here. The sister entries 54 (R752), 55 (R928, Goffe from The Hague) and 60 (R789, Digby) are covered by the same work and were removed from the catalogue with this one.

t: Henrietta Maria’s household to Charles I, 1645–46 — already read by George Lasry
b: Record Folios Date and content (Lasry) Language Key R785 213–215 St Germain, 1 Sept 1645: “the Queen is perfectly recovered”; half the money already given; a letter from the Duke of Orléans; Ned Progers arrived English TNA SP 106 R787 216–217 Duplicate of 19/29 July 1645: war news from the Low Countries and Germany (Linck, Piccolomini, Enghien), perhaps Goffe’s letter sent on from France French SP106-2 R790 230–232 St Germain, 22 Sept 1645: Sir Kenelm Digby at Rome, no papal money except on terms: repeal of the penal laws against Catholics and toleration in England English TNA SP 106 R923 233–234 St Germains, 29 Sept 1645: the Duke of Lorraine’s “little remote hopes”; the writer fears a battle for a relief and wants the advantage of winter English TNA SP 106 R924 235–236 Paris, January 1646: Sir H. Compton’s embassy and the treaty for Prince Charles’s marriage English SP106-8 R929 247 Paris, 26 January [1646]: thanks for weekly news of the King’s affairs, “how bad so ever”; the embassy and the marriage English SP106-5 The systems are numerical homophonic alphabets of one- and two-digit values, with up to five signs for a vowel, and a nomenclator. Three-digit numbers stand for names and words (in Lasry’s September 1645 key, 126 the King, 127 the Queen, 279 and ). The key of January 1646 (SP106-5) writes its nomenclator as a letter and a digit (n3 the , k1 of ). Lasry notes no nulls in any of the four keys. The signatures are numbers: 120 in R785 and R923, 316 440 on f. 247.

t: Henrietta Maria’s household to Charles I, 1645–46 — already read by George Lasry
b: The plaintexts are Lasry’s and are on the DECODE records. The openings of three letters give their tone: ST GERMAIN 1 SEPT. I HAVE VERY LITTLE TO ADD TO MY LAST MORE THAN TO TELL YOU THE <295> OF THE <498>S <326> ADVANCE EXCELLENTLY, HALF THE MONEY BEING ALREADY GIVEN … A LETTRE ALSO FROM THE DUKE OF ORLEANS WRIT AS WEE COULD HAVE WISHED IS IN THE QUEEN’S HANDS (R785) I HAVE RECEIVED THIS WEEK A LARGE <330> FROM <491> K DIGBY. THE SUBSTANCE IS THAT <528> IS NO HOPE OF MONEY FROM THENCE BUT UPON NEW TERMES PROPOSED … A TOTAL TAKEING AWAY OF AL THE PENALL LAWES AGAINST PAPISTS AND TOLERATION OF RELIGION SETTLED IN ENGLAND (R790) THE DUKE OF LORRAIN PUTS US IN SOME LITTLE REMOTE HOPES BUT THAT OUGHT NOT TO BE BUILT UPON … THE RELEIF OF THE PLACE WILL GIVE US THAT WHICH WEE ONLY OUGHT NOW TO LOOK FOR AFTER SO MANY DISASTERS, THE ADVANTAGE OF WINTER (R923)

t: Henrietta Maria’s household to Charles I, 1645–46 — already read by George Lasry
b: Lasry’s SP106-5 alphabet was applied mechanically to Pettersson’s raw transcription of f. 247 (R929), without his plaintext file. It gives “…ARIS … IAN … SR … RECEIVED <425>S … DECEMB … IANVARY … THANKES … CONTINUATI[ON] … WEKLY ADVERTISEMENTS … STATE … AFFAIRES HOW BAD … EVER … DESPERATE … ABLE … SUBS[IS]T … WITHOUT FARTHER LOSSES … TILL OUR ENDEAVOURS … RELEIF … BROUGHT … EFFECT … LIKEWISE CONCERNING THE EMBASSAGE AND MARRIAGE”. The gaps are the letter-and-digit nomenclator groups, which the alphabet does not cover. The result agrees with his plaintext. The images themselves were not viewed.

t: Henrietta Maria’s household to Charles I, 1645–46 — already read by George Lasry
b: The three-digit nomenclator numbers left in brackets in Lasry’s plaintexts (for example <425>, <241> and <502>). Most look like persons, and many could be recovered from the context and the other letters of the run. Who the writers are: “120” at St Germain, probably of the queen’s secretariat (Jermyn is Lasry’s guess for the second Paris letter on ff. 245–246), and “316 440” at Paris. Tomokiyo’s unsolved list still carries these letters.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
b: Listed as “solved but specific scheme unknown”: the Japanese Foreign Ministry filed a decode nobody could read, and an encipherment nobody could name. Both recovered, and then corrected from the frames: three kana carry one character deterministically from a private code, a superfluous kana had hidden the repeats, and the vowel is not free. China / Japan · romanised kana · 1916 · scheme identified Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan Relayed through the Japanese Foreign Ministry, 25 May 1916 · Minister Ishii to Consul Ōta at Zhaoqing · JACAR B03050731500 The catalogue records it as “solved but specific scheme unknown”. Here is the filed decode, and the scheme. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 15 September 2026 Summary. In May 1916 Huang Xing asked the Japanese Foreign Ministry to pass a telegram to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan in Guangdong. It went out in a cipher of the Chinese side's own making: 139 syllables of romanised Japanese kana, packed into ten-letter telegraph words, with no voicing marks. S. Tomokiyo later found a memo recording that the Ministry had filed a decode with the telegram, so the item is listed as solved — but he could not read the handwritten Chinese, and the encryption scheme stayed unidentified. Both are settled here. The decode and its annotated Japanese reading are on frames 0247 and 0248 of the file, and the message is a short reply about the National Protection Army and a traveller's sailing date. The scheme is a kana code of a kind not previously described for this correspondence: three kana encode one character, deterministically , from a private codebook. A first analysis read the consonant row as the digit and the vowel as a free homophone; the frames, re-read at 500 dpi, overturn that (section 03). Status: scheme identified, one transmission error located, plaintext read, 42 codebook entries recovered; the kana-to-digit table and the rest of the book need a second telegram.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
b: JACAR B03050731500 is a Gaimushō volume on the anti-Yuan risings (1.6.1.75-1_015, reel 1-0955, frames 0244–0302). The covering despatch, 電送第一九八〇号, cipher, sent 25 May 1916 at 4.35 p.m. from Foreign Minister Ishii to Consul Ōta at Zhaoqing, says in plain Japanese what the enclosure is: 黄興ヨリ林虎李根源宛電報依頼アリタルニ付同人ニ伝達アリタシ 内容ハ先日来電ノ挨拶ナリ（以下支那側暗号） “Huang Xing has asked that a telegram be sent to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan; please pass it to them. The content is an acknowledgement of the telegram received the other day. (The Chinese side's cipher follows.)” Three frames matter: 0246 , the telegram on an Imperial Government Telegraphs forwarded-message form; 0247 , headed 電稿, the decoded Chinese in cursive; and 0248 , a clerk's reading of it rearranged into Japanese word order on Foreign Ministry paper, with his own glosses. Frame 0246: the telegram as handed in. Five rows of ten-letter words, ending OSOYUANIRA KISU. REKUTATA UHOYAKATE SEKANAOKU SAKEKINISE OSUKAKUCHI REUHONIUSU MAKASUSAKU FUREOHIHE YENIKIYEHI TAKASUREU SASHIKIHE WAONIAAHO SAYEHITE UHINAKUTA NEATEMUYE SUHEUHAKA YESOMIKANU TEASUUKU TSUHAKOSE KEKININAKI TEAKETASHI KONUOHIKE HIMIKANO SHIKUSAHE UHATAKASA KEKINIKA ATAREUSASU OSOYUANIRA KISU Read as kana this is 139 syllables, 36 of them distinct. There are no voiced kana at all — no ga, za, da, ba — which is normal for telegraph traffic, where the voicing marks were simply not transmitted. The syllables are Japanese (SHI, CHI, TSU, and the old YE and WA), not the consonant-vowel letters of the condenser used in the Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen six weeks earlier.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
h: What the Ministry had already read
b: Frame 0247 is the decode: a heading 電稿 and four columns of 12, 11, 12 and 11 characters — forty-six characters of message. Frame 0248 is the same text rearranged for a Japanese reader, and it is the more useful of the two, because the clerk added glosses where he was unsure. Frame 0247, 電稿 — the decoded Chinese. Frame 0248 — the clerk's reading, with his glosses. 隱印崧蕘邕行諸兄鑒：正發書翰之際，適接 哿 電，敬悉一切。護國軍能速入 湘贛 甚好。 章行嚴 何日東渡？速令出發，並望預電。興 徑 “To brothers Yin, Yin, Song, Yao and Yongxing: just as I was sending a letter, your telegram of the twentieth arrived, and I have respectfully noted it all. It would be excellent if the National Protection Army could move quickly into Hunan and Jiangxi. What day does Zhang Xingyan cross to Japan? Have him start at once, and please wire me in advance. — Xing, the twenty-fifth.” The clerk's glosses carry most of the identifications. Against the string of names at the head he wrote 林虎・李根源等ノ字ナラン , “probably the courtesy names of Lin Hu, Li Genyuan and others” — he was guessing too, and one of them is certainly 蔡鍔's 松坡. He glossed 湘贛 as 湖南江西 , Hunan and Jiangxi, and 東渡 as 日本ニ来ル , coming to Japan. 章行嚴 is Zhang Shizhao, Huang Xing's close associate. Two characters are dates in the 韻目代日 rhyme-code that Chinese telegraphy used for the day of the month: 哿 = the 20th and 徑 = the 25th — and 徑, the last character of the signature, matches the dispatch date on the covering despatch exactly. That agreement is the best single check that the decode belongs to this telegram. Correction, second session. The running text above is the clerk's paraphrase from frame 0248 (50 characters). The cursive on frame 0247, read at 500 dpi, has 46: 隱印崧誥邕行諸兄鑒正發書 · 間適接哿電敬悉一切護國 · 軍能速入湘贛甚好[章]行嚴何日 · 東渡望速啓行先電示興徑, with 章 an interlinear addition. That count matches the 46 kana triples exactly; see section 03. Several glyphs in the cursive remain uncertain and are given here on the balance of the two frames. The column lengths are 2 + 12 + 11 + 12 + 11; Tomokiyo's note gives the same figures but sums them as 68, where they add to 48.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
b: Forty-six characters against 138 usable kana is three kana to the character , with a single kana left spare at the end. That settles the rate. The question is what part of each kana does the work, and the gojūon syllabary answers it by its shape: it is a grid of ten consonant rows by five vowels. — K S T N H M Y R W A KA SA TA NA HA MA YA RA WA I KI SHI CHI NI HI MI — RI WI U KU SU TSU NU FU MU YU RU — E KE SE TE NE HE ME YE RE WE O KO SO TO NO HO MO YO RO WO If the consonant row carries a digit and the vowel is free, then a character repeated in the plaintext will repeat as a triple of rows but need not repeat as a triple of kana . That is a testable prediction, and the counts are unambiguous. Across the 46 groups: reading repeats observed expected by chance permutation test consonant row 7 1.03 p = 0.006 vowel 8 8.28 p = 0.70 literal kana 1 — — The consonant rows repeat seven times where chance predicts one. The vowels repeat eight times where chance predicts eight — they carry nothing whatever. And the surface kana, the thing an interceptor actually sees, repeats once in forty-six. The mechanism is visible in the repeated groups themselves, the same character spelled two different ways: S K N → SE - KA - NA and SHI - KO - NU R — H → RE - U - HO and RE - O - HI T — H → TA - U - HO and TE - U - HI S K H → SA - KU - FU and SHI - KI - HE That was the first reading, and the frames correct it. Re-fetched and read at 500 dpi, frame 0247 has four columns of 12, 11, 12 and 11 characters after the heading, 46 in all, the number of kana triples: 隱印崧誥邕行諸兄鑒正發書 · 間適接哿電敬悉一切護國 · 軍能速入湘贛甚好[章]行嚴何日 · 東渡望速啓行先電示興徑 The earlier 50-character plaintext above followed the clerk's Japanese paraphrase on frame 0248; the cursive has 46, and 章 is an interlinear addition. This plaintext repeats 行 three times (positions 6, 32, 41), 速 twice (26, 39) and 電 twice (17, 43). Under the grouping above only one of those pairs matched. Drop one kana at position 106 , the O of OHIKE at the start of character 36, and every triple from there on shifts by one: 行 becomes KE-KI-NI all three times, 速 HE-U-HA both times, 電 RE-U-SA both times, and the spare SU at the end completes the last character. The telegram as filed carries one superfluous kana, and the code is deterministic: the same character is always the same three kana, vowels included. The seven consonant-row collisions in the table are therefore not one character written with different vowels. After the shift they are pairs of different characters (印/護, 誥/日, 鑒/間, 書/敬, 國/嚴, 甚/何, 諸/示) that share a row triple and differ only in vowels. The vowels carry information. What survives of the first analysis is the rate, three kana to the character, and the fact that the kana's row is correlated with its code value; the excess of row collisions over chance is what that correlation looks like from outside. Three kana over a 50-kana syllabary would address 125,000 entries, far more than any private book; the natural reading is still a three-digit code with each digit written as one of a set of kana, the sets not being the rows. One test of that was run and failed. If the rows were the digits of a codebook compiled in dictionary order, some permutation of the ten rows would make the 42 distinct characters' code numbers monotone in standard telegraph-code order. Over all 3,628,800 permutations the best Spearman rho is 0.524; the same search on twelve shuffles of the plaintext gives a null of mean 0.468 and maximum 0.614. No signal.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
b: The kana-to-digit table. The row is not the digit, and 46 characters do not determine an assignment of 36 kana to ten values. The codebook beyond the 42 entries (character to kana triple) that this telegram fixes. A second telegram in the same code would settle both. What this one settles is the scheme, the plaintext, and the transmission error that hid the repeats.

t: Hyde’s ciphered superscriptions — not a cipher at all
b: The four “undeciphered addresses” on Hyde’s letters to Barwick decode to nothing under the full Hyde–Barwick key printed in 1721, because, as the 1724 editor states, they were numbers “signifying nothing … only to puzzle the Enemy”. Brussels · Restoration correspondence · 1659–60 · explained Hyde's Ciphered Superscriptions Sir Edward Hyde to Dr John Barwick, Brussels, 29 Sept and 17 Oct 1659, 14 and 16 Jan 1660 · printed in Peter Barwick, Vita Johannis Barwick (1721), pp. 358, 360, 389, 396 Not an address in cipher: dummy numbers "only to puzzle the Enemy" — on the word of the editor who had the papers, confirmed against the full key Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 15 September 2026 Summary. Four letters written by Hyde from Brussels in the months before the Restoration carry, where an address should be, a line of cipher figures. They are catalogued as undeciphered. They were never meant to be deciphered. The letters are Hyde's to John Barwick, the royalist agent in London, and were printed from the Barwick papers in 1721 together with the very key the two men used. The English edition of 1724 adds the editor's explanation: several of the letters "were superscribed with Numbers signifying nothing … only to puzzle the Enemy", and he cites exactly these pages. Applying the full Hyde–Barwick key (transcribed here from the 1721 plate) confirms it: one superscription decodes to gibberish and the other three use numbers that do not exist in the key. The item should be removed from the "unsolved" list as a non-cipher.

t: Hyde’s ciphered superscriptions — not a cipher at all
b: The 1721 plate gives the complete cipher: numbers 1–692 in eleven columns. Column 1 is the alphabet, three figures per letter (two for k, w, y; none for x, z); 64–69 are skipped; columns 2–11 (70–131, 132–193, 194–254, 255–317, 318–379, 380–440, 441–503, 504–566, 567–628, 629–692) each run A to Y down the rows, three rows per letter, so syllables and words are grouped by initial letter across the columns rather than in one alphabetical list. Several slots are deliberately empty. Entries relevant here: the = 370, for = 210, from = 211, Mr. = 536, Master = 475, Barwick = 572, Hyde, Lord Chancellor = 589; there is no entry for these , Sir or London .

t: Hyde’s ciphered superscriptions — not a cipher at all
b: The unabridged English Life of Dr. John Barwick (1724, tr. Hilkiah Bedford), working from the Barwick family papers, appends this note to the letter of 12 June 1659 that enclosed the cipher (pp. 408–409): But to render the Cypher more difficult to be found out, as each Letter in the Alphabet is represented by three several Numbers, except K, W, and Y only by two, and X and Z by none: So several of the Numbers have no Letter, Syllable, or Word over against them, because they stand for nothing, and were only us'd to perplex such as should attempt to read what was written hereby, without the Help of the Cypher. So several of the Letters were superscribed with Numbers signifying nothing, some with two or three Lines of them, only to puzzle the Enemy, if they should fall into their Hands, which I the rather mention here, because some Persons, for want of examining those Superscriptions, as printed in the Appendix to the Latin Life (p. 358, 360, 389, 396, and 417.) with the Cypher also published there, have wondered what was the meaning of them: and it was for the same Reason, that several of the Chancellor's Letters, besides the Number denoting his Name, were subscribed with other Numbers, that either had nothing in the Cypher to answer them, or nothing to the Purpose. As to the Superscriptions, B. or any Name beginning with B. seems to have signified Barwick. The pages he names are the four in question. The same puzzle, it turns out, had already been raised and answered in 1724.

h: The Voynich manuscript is probably elaborate nonsense
b: It is a real book from the early 1400s, but the text is not a language in disguise. Every simple cipher of every European language we could test is ruled out: the writing is far too predictable, letter to letter, for any of them. Two explanations are left standing, a rigid glyph-by-glyph encoding with something behind it, or carefully made meaningless text, and the numbers lean toward meaningless. The write-up names the five tests that would settle it. 2.2–2.9 bits of conditional entropy, against 3.3 for language 1.7–2.3× more rigid word grammar than any language tested 0.09 bits H(language | scribe): Currier A/B is almost the hand Read the adjudication → ★ Solved · 1644

t: Unsolved Historical Ciphers
b: Newest first. One line each — the evidence is in the write-up linked, or in the tracker in the repository. The date on each line, and on every write-up, is the day the finding landed in the public repository, taken from the commit history. 20 Sept 2026 Vatican Challenge Part 5, the Farnese letter of April 1542 — solved by Simon Klee; reviewed here and accepted by MysteryTwister. Klee recovered the same eighteen letter codes and null from either half independently, validated the search on synthetic and shuffled controls, corrected the public transcription against the manuscript, and published the key, edited Italian and token alignment. The earlier classification here is retracted: 4 is o , 9 is the null, and the core key uses mixed one- and two-digit letter codes. review and credit 20 Sept 2026 Pallotto to Barberini, 4 August – 29 November 1629 — twenty-eight “non-decrypted” ciphers of the nuncio at Vienna whose contents have been in print since 1897 : Kiewning’s Nuntiaturberichte volume prints the despatches from the Roman office’s own decipherments, and the register’s clear pages confirm it — the Mantuan succession, Sabran, Eggenberg, Susa and the Grisons. The cipher itself is not broken, and a run-length control rules out the obvious hypothesis: the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36 to 39, where a synthetic cipher at the same noise reaches 207. write-up 20 Sept 2026 Throckmorton to Cecil and the Queen, 1560–63 — archived key and printed plaintext verified : two samples, 42 tokens; twenty-record source concordance. write-up 20 Sept 2026 Charles IX to Philibert du Croc, undated (1565–67 or 1572) — the “non-decrypted” Scottish cipher was already solved by George Lasry in 2022 : preserve James VI’s attachment to France, prevent a marriage before France is consulted, and ensure “que les Anglois n’empiètent aucune chose en Escosse.” The catalogue’s 1 January 1550 date is a metadata error; Destray says the letter is undated. write-up 20 Sept 2026 Hellen to Frederick II, 1752–1763 — Unsolved; transcription audited and an archival lead identified. The repeated passage is on the manuscript; Fagel 5206 may supply a parallel decipherment for 1752. No plaintext verified. Progress report 20 Sept 2026 Beatrice d’Aragona, 1482–1505 — four earlier readings and one plain letter. Cipher readings in editions of 1877–78; R1154 is dated 1505 and says the queen has no cipher. The March edition’s markers remain unexplained. Evidence and limits 20 Sept 2026 Catherine de Médicis to the bishop of Rennes, 31 July 1563 — the passage La Ferrière printed as an empty bracket, read in part . The standard edition of Catherine’s letters gives this folio in full except for thirteen lines, set as [ ] and footnoted « Partie chiffrée »; Tomokiyo, who reconstructed the Bishop of Rennes’ cipher, lists it undeciphered. His key is a table of shapes and does not fit this scribe glyph for glyph — but the sibling letter two folios on carries a line-by-line decipherment down its margin , and its first ciphered line reads que les princes . That calibrates the hand, and about three fifths of f. 55 now reads: sceu ce que vous avez descouvert , du mariage , l’avancement du concile, à ce que , avoir l’utilité qui en sortira . What Catherine enciphered was the Council of Trent and the Habsburg marriage — while the fall of Le Havre, in the same letter, went in clear. write-up 19 Sept 2026 Spanish despatches of 1593: Miranda, Sessa and Ibarra — the Spanish office’s own key survives, with the nomenclature no published table has , in the Nevers cipher book BnF fr. 3995 f. 97 — found by following the catalogue’s own instruction to check DECODE, whose only two hits for these correspondents turn out to be keys rather than letters. It confirms Tomokiyo’s syllable table against the original and reads the leaves. write-up 19 Sept 2026 Henri IV to Maisse at Venice, 3 November 1592 – 27 April 1593 — four leaves listed as undeciphered; two different ciphers, and Tomokiyo had already published a key for each — as images , invisible in a text dump of his page and never applied to these leaves. The 1592 key decodes f. 370 letter-for-letter, 81 of 81 characters , against a clear copy found independently in Brienne 13; it adds an omega-shaped sign for d missing from the table. f. 406 is the duplicate of f. 404. write-up 20 Sept 2026 A Jacobean codebreaker’s file of Italian intercepts, TNA SP 106/10, c. 1623–24 — seven anonymous ciphertexts shown to be one case, dated, and the cipher explained; the letters read in fragments : DECODE lists them undated, “1558/1625”, sender and recipient unknown. The key the codebreaker himself reconstructed sits three records away, catalogued as a key and so outside the target list; it sets out two-figure groups read as a letter, or as a word of one list, or of a second, according to a bar or a tick — “there are numbers of woordes expressed by this difference of — over the figures”. Its vocabulary — Marques Inichiosa , Palatinato , C. Barberino , Il Principe — dates the whole file to 1623–24. The file holds three ciphers, not one, and about forty-five values of the three-figure code are rebuilt from the codebreaker’s own syllables: della loro sicurezza — write-up 20 Sept 2026 Lope Hurtado de Mendoza (Rome) to Charles V, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read : nine records catalogued as part of Sánchez’s Venice correspondence turn out to be in a different key that nobody had published. The crib was bound with it — two of them carry the clerk’s own clear version — and the rebuilt key reads el papa unaided in a letter with no crib at all.
