Read in order: 帝制取消 on 25 March, 600 gold wired via Taiwan, 250,000 asked for a Wuhan rising, then 英士昨下午在山田家被兇[轟?]斃 on 19 May. A week later Tokyo passed Sun the Foreign Ministry’s own advice not to go to Qingdao, on a wire the Ministry was copied and could not read. Write-up . 18 Sept 2026 Robert Yard to the Earl of Manchester, Whitehall, 12 and 16 October 1699 — read; two letters catalogued “almost entirely in cipher, undeciphered”, and the key was in the same papers at Yale. The HMC calendared both letters in 1881 and noted that no key to the ciphers of the period was known. The Manchester papers at the Beinecke also hold a printed one-part code sheet with handwritten numbers, endorsed “Copy of the E. of Manchester’s Cypher”, in which 454 is the ; Tomokiyo had said the two letters go with a THE = 454 code and had decoded their first groups. The sheet was transcribed (1,456 slots) and checked against the decipherment written at the time on the sibling letter of 5 October; it then reads all 368 groups of the two letters, apart from five slips of Yard’s pen. Messengers wait at Dover for Mills and Lord Drummond’s priest , the Lords Justices of Ireland report many disaffected persons return dayly into that Kingdom , and all is said to be carryed on very privately at Saint Germains . Write-up . 18 Sept 2026 Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, Vitoria, 30 December 1521 — resolved; the letter was deciphered in the nineteenth century by Claudio Pérez Gredilla and printed by Danvila (Memorial Histórico Español 38, 1899), and his reading is now checked against the cipher and corrected. AGS Estado leg. 8 no. 150 was transcribed from PARES and aligned with the print on xif = V. M., which rebuilds the key. The dead king is Manuel I of Portugal, not the “Rey de Inglaterra” of the print. About seventeen unread groups are read or shown to be misprints ( rol agora, xep in cuya , dopca urcas, for como; “40” is the group yo ); about ten stay open. Write-up . 18 Sept 2026 Erving at Madrid, 24 March 1807, and John Quincy Adams at St Petersburg, No. 88, 25 June 1812 — two American legation codes: every hole in Madison’s decode of Erving closed, and Adams’s “nine lines not decyphered” read. The Madison editors say Armstrong’s code ( the = 972) was also Adams’s at St Petersburg. His despatches are not in it: every coded despatch checked on NARA M35 reel 3 has 1385 = the and 1576 = of . His own code is rebuilt to some 370 groups from the clerk’s interlinear decodes, and with it the passage of No. 88 that Ford prints as “[Nine lines of this paragraph not decyphered.]” reads, 124 of 134 groups: Rumyantsev’s apoplectic stroke soon after reaching Wilna, a second and worse one before 25 June, and a false report of his death in the German gazettes. Erving’s letter of 24 March 1807, printed from Madison’s decode with the key “not found”, closes from both received copies and Pinckney’s decoded despatches: Haweder is Hanover, “to the se al e” is in the scale , and the holes are Madison’s slips. Write-up . 17 Sept 2026 Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, Ferrara, February 1529 — read; the catalogue’s top row, three letters in a symbol cipher whose key had been published and never applied to them. BnF fr. 3096 nos. 65 and 66 are the same despatch of 23 February written twice (no. 66 is docketed duplicata ) and no. 63 the sequel; the two glossed siblings in the volume gave Lasry his key in 2023. Applied at glyph level — 18,273 signs segmented from the scans, clustered, classified, then every line read on a review sheet — it reads nos. 65 and 66 end to end and no. 63 as far as its leaves go, and the leaves add a null, a double-circle nomenclator for duca and the crossbarred long-s as e . The pair enciphers different stretches, so each is the other’s crib. Alfonso d’Este, asked to lead the French army on Naples and offered the kingdom, risolutamente concluse per cosa dil mondo non voler per sé alcunamente accettare il regno et manco far l’impresa a suo nome ; Sormano writes that this confirmed quello che io sempre dubitai . Write-up . 17 Sept 2026 BnF Espagnol 318, the Catholic Monarchs’ ciphered letters, 1497–1504 — the catalogue’s oldest entry has five ciphered letters, not four, and four different answers: one solved in print in 2020, one keyed here and proved on its own glosses, one read in part, two named and blocked on a key. No. 5 was never open — Ivan Parisi printed the whole text in 2020, having found that Federico of Naples had his secret letter enciphered in the Spanish ambassador’s own cipher, by the ambassador’s hand; a Spanish speaker’s failure to use the double- s sign in possano and promesso gives him away. No. 92 , the Great Captain to Lorenzo Suárez of 17 August 1500, which nobody has read, is in the Cifra general de los Reyes Católicos that Galende Díaz printed in 1994. Tomokiyo proposed that from the look of the code groups; it is proved here against the partial decipherment a later hand wrote between the lines of f. 116r — yuy Lo, boy Tiempo, zez Por, xiz + 7 Estar, xuy En, baz Tanto, xix zol El negocio, zik No, eight hits and no misses — and a gloss-anchored line reads straight through, …y tiempo, por estar en tanto… . The key is transcribed, 683 groups. No. 95 has George Lasry’s 2022 alphabet and no published text; segmenting its 963 signs, clustering the shapes and labelling the clusters against his key reads about two thirds, with letter frequencies that come out Spanish before any decipherment ( e 9 %, a 7 %, q about 1 %). The leaf is about the French: emos franceses … que puedan merced … de Francia … señoría … muy grandes cosas … no creo que … quieren go|uernar … por obra creo que … amigo … escreuir a … dificultad . Two of Lasry’s signs corrected. Nos. 93 and 94 stay unread but are no longer “unidentified”: both are ordinary secretariat ciphers, a homophonic sign alphabet with a one-part CVC nomenclator, and their code initials exclude both printed keys and fall inside the band of the Gran cifra of 1501–04 ( lnq against Bergenroth’s LUQ = capitán ). The alternative that they were runs of letter-shaped signs was tested and rejected: 1,016 signs of f. 118r anneal to −3.5 nats a token where real Spanish scores −1.8, and 66 % of the p signs sit inside pie . What blocks them is one Madrid manuscript, BNE MSS 20.211/52, bot-checked at every endpoint and absent from Europeana and Hispana. Write-up . 17 Sept 2026 Nicolas Raince to Montmorency, Rome, 13 May and 20 November 1526 — about 106 lines that exist in no edition, read; the published key had been read off by one column. BnF fr. 2984 keeps eight of the embassy secretary’s ciphered despatches. Tomokiyo published the key in 2020 and no plaintext, but reading which glyph sits under which letter in his table by eye slips a place: l is the 9 , not the round s ; m is the round s , not the long f ; n is the long f ; and H is an s . Measured off the image instead — every ink blob within 15 px of a header column — the table resolves a control line with nothing left over, s [null] qui estoit en la court de Savoye [null] est party pour venir icy , and 86 of the 106 lines then read by hand off the microfilm against numbered-token images. Nine days before the League of Cognac: the Castilians and the Bourguignons, delibéré prendre le chemin de Valence , a capitulation for which ilz seront cause de la destruction … de la part d’avoir faict capituler , mondict seigneur l’Admiral luy avoit dict que seroit celuy qui y tiendroit , la peste qui est au logis , des advis qui viennent aux imperiaulx par leurs , and a man taken un jour, en plaine place pres du palais, un nommé Pietro Anthonio . Two months after the Colonna raid, the 20 November letter turns on a pontificate that seroit la cause de la totale ruine de sa maison . The clear close of 13 May, transcribed here, expects Andrea Doria at Civitavecchia within a day with six galleys and two brigantins. The Gallica leaf numbers run two apart, which looked like half the volume missing and is only pagination on odd pages. Write-up . 17 Sept 2026 Jean du Bellay to Montmorency, London, 1528–29 — the catalogue’s five “undeciphered” letters have all been in print in clear since 1688 and 1905; the leaf that has never been read is the one the catalogue did not list, 16 June 1529. BnF fr. 3077 and 3078 are bound by day and month without years; Le Grand’s Histoire du divorce (1688) prints the Court’s readings of the four 1529 letters, and the fifth (fr. 3077 no. 23) is the 28 October 1528 letter that Bourrilly and de Vaissière deciphered in 1905 with a key they recovered. The 22 June 1529 leaf (fr. 3078 pp. 25–27) carries the decipherer’s interlinear reading over every sign, and aligning it re-derives the key Tomokiyo published as “Bayonne’s Cipher (1529)”, with additions ( B = o; word signs for bien , fault , paix ; a boxed cross for Wolsey), and that key reads the 17 October letter on Wolsey’s fall straight from its four cipher pages, j’ay esté veoir le Cardinal en ses ennuis , as Le Grand printed it. The 16 June leaf (p. 21, DECODE “non-decrypted”) then reads in stretches: semblant [que] madame ne fust … pour conclure … la [name] luy ayt par[lé] … [il] fault envoyé querir pouvoir, il ne fauldroyt oublyer a le faire . Scheurer (1969) not checked. Notes . 17 Sept 2026 Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two of the three read, and a measured ceiling on the third. BnF fr. 3484 nos. 7, 8 and 12 are catalogued “avec chiffre” without decipherment. F. 36, four leaves on, is the minute of the 10 November letter in clear, and aligning it with the cipher recovers a Villeroy-office key of the design Bazeries printed for Béthune’s brother in 1599: dix mil escuz par l’entremise du sieur de Sillery … sans avoir esgard à l’arrest obtenu par lad. duchesse de Nemours. The 22 November letter, thought to be forty lines of cipher in blocks, is nothing of the kind — it interleaves clear French with eighty short ciphered runs inside the same lines, so it reads without breaking them, and all four pages are now transcribed: the Camaiano pension paid to “relever le party françois a Rome”, Barberini’s coming, and the courier sent to invite the Pope to the dauphin’s baptism, lequel se faict tres bien nourrir et se fortifie a veue d’oeil. The 9 November letter, a solid page of cipher with neither minute nor gloss, stops at about six words in ten, and an oracle bound says why as a number: the decoder already scores above the ceiling its own transcription allows, so some 29 % of the letter’s letters cannot be produced by its glyphs at all. Ten further attempts, each measured, failed to move it; two careful readers of the same ink agree on 69 % of its tokens. What would finish it is archival — Cinq cents de Colbert 346, copies of the Béthune despatches from August 1601, made from the minutes and not digitised. Write-up . 17 Sept 2026 Nevers to Pisany, 8 September and 14 October 1593 — two of the catalogue’s seven Nevers letters read; the set is two keys, not one. Tomokiyo’s Nevers cipher no. 46, read from the full-resolution table in fr. 3995 f. 87 and checked against the office’s interlinear decipherment of a Gondi letter in the same key, resolves every figure of the two letters to Pisany (fr. 3985 f. 209, fr. 3986 f. 168). L’on dissuadoit [le Roy] de rechercher [que le Pape] luy donnast l’absolution … qu’il n’estoyt besoin qu’il allast sans cela, parce qu’il ne feroit rien … l’on n’a volonté de contanter le Pape, que l’on n’y aille poynt. The five letters to Revol are in the Court’s symbol cipher no. 60: the 27 August copy is in clear, the 9 October copy carries about ninety symbols, three were not reached on the image. Write-up . 17 Sept 2026 Lanssac’s Polish election letters, April–May 1573 — read; the first class-A item of the new catalogue, and with it the three election letters whose “déchiffrement” was only a gutter-cut gloss. BnF fr. 4735 f. 124 (26 April) is catalogued “avec chiffre” with no decipherment. One surviving gloss line on the sibling f. 154v, “car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”, fixes eleven signs; the fragments on f. 124 fix the rest; a pinned annealer fills in the remainder against shuffled and blind controls. The same key then reads 1 May to the King ( ceste nation est autant vénale et sujette à se laisser gaigner par argent comme sont les Allemans ), 1 May to Anjou ( l’Empereur en y a despendu plus de trois cens mil … faisant le pis qu’il peult contre vous ) and 9 May from Płock, the election carried contre la volunté et menées du Grand Seigneur, de l’Empereur, des princes de l’Empire, du Roy d’Espaigne, du Moscovite et du Roy de Suède, qui tous estoient bandez contre vostre Majesté . Tomokiyo’s table for this cipher is off by one letter from m . Write-up . 17 Sept 2026 Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — resolved; the catalogue’s “second undeciphered letter” is the 1589 decipherer’s copy of the first, and the general cipher Cg.13 is partly rebuilt from the pairs. BnF fr. 3641 holds both letters of that day twice, as Cg.13 originals (ff. 10, 12) and as fair copies with the unread code words in the margin (ff. 14, 76). Aligning them gives some seventy syllables and fifty code groups, reads pur respeto, mes vuestro, san negocio, and shows the copyist’s “Francia” to be England. Fourteen groups still open. Write-up . 16 Sept 2026 Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich, 1652 — read in full, without the plaintext the August 2026 AI claim published; the distich claim not reproduced. The k-th number indexes physical page k of Urquhart’s own Jewel , and he took the first word of the initial he needed, a property of number and page alone. The public transcription was thirteen numbers short; the 1983 edition’s photographs on the HCPortal record give 285, which decode straight against the TCP text with 238 of 284 first-occurrence hits against 0.43 for shuffled and random-page controls: a prayer for Charles II, Great Lord, mantaine that regal familie … Our Emperour, King, Monarch and Protector. Amen, so be it. Ten letters of line 5 stay unread. The distich rule gives 34 of 64, chance, and no English. Full write-up → 16 Sept 2026 Louis XIV and Louvois to Catinat, July–September 1691 — read; seven Grand Chiffre despatches, five of them never printed in clear, including the King’s decision to abandon Piedmont. The 1819 Mémoires de Catinat print 12,362 groups the editor could not read; Bazeries built his table from them in 1893 and printed only the two letters that served the Man in the Iron Mask. His table reads all seven from the library’s OCR, checked against the page images; the two controls agree at 98 and 99 %. The 14 September letter, twenty pages of figures, weighs the honourable course against the solid one and chooses the solid: over the Alps at the end of the campaign, hold the passes, keep Carmagnole while the Pope negotiates, then burn it, and take Coni in the winter. Full write-up → 15 Sept 2026 Feuquières to Catinat, 1691 — read; a Louis XIV war plan, the first reading since Bazeries’ unpublished one of 1893. The code is the petit chiffre of the Pignerol governors, and a second letter in it, Louvois to d’Herleville of 6 September 1690, is printed with its translation in vol. I of the same 1819 edition. Every aligner and annealer failed; hand anchoring carried between the two letters reads 586 of 601 tokens. Feuquières is ready, names the two roads into Avigliana, cannot see how to pass the eighty horse to Saint-Ambroise, and will keep the dragoons from escaping into the castle. Full write-up → 16 Sept 2026 Colbert passages, 1674–75 — two “unsolved ciphers” are one key, and it is Maulevrier’s; not read. Read from the Gallica images: the duc de Charost’s letter from Calais is 3 July 1675, not 1673, and its 55 figures share thirteen groups, a four-group phrase and a sentence-final trigram with the abbé de Gravel’s 51 figures to Maulevrier of 1674; Charost says he is sending Maulevrier “la mesme nouvelle” that morning. La Roncière’s printed catalogue then gave every Charost and Maulevrier letter by folio: all 24 online are in clear. A monotone annealer reads matched 106-token controls of both strict alphabetical designs this office used and fails the target under each; looser designs fail their controls. Probably a word nomenclator; needs the key or a clear copy of the news. Notes → 16 Sept 2026 Roosevelt cryptogram, 1935 — explained; the numbers 1 to 52 written once each, not a cipher. Ernst’s 2017 doodle claim confirmed at glyph level from the NSA book scan; the permutation drifts upward and falls into sixteen rising chains where a shuffle gives 26, and the testable ordered-key readings fail while seven of eight matched controls are read. Full write-up → 16 Sept 2026 Henry of Navarre to Ségur, 1585–86 — read; an alphabetical syllabary cipher, and the sender was not Henry III. Three of the four “Henry III” letters in BnF 500 de Colbert 401 (ff. 233, 239, 288v) are Navarre’s, to his envoy raising a German army. The upper figures fall into blocks of five (mod-5 test), a syllable table ba be bi bo bu … in alphabetical order; an annealer built on that structure, with the letters’ own clear French as context, returned a key that is alphabetical by itself (a 4–6 … u 45–47, x y z 48–51, doubles ée ll ss) and reads a matched control at 97%. Conclude with Duke Casimir, raise the largest levy and march it; Clervant’s two thousand reiters; the Vivarais or Dauphiné road; “la plus grande levée qui ayt esté faite”. A dozen word-signs glossed or open; f. 143 (1583) is another key. Write-up . 16 Sept 2026 From Warsaw, 24 December 1627 — read; the alphabet was in plain order. DECODE R1408, listed as non-decrypted with only a dateline in clear. The stray letters a and m are nulls, the letter pairs stand for consonants, the rare groups for syllables; a 5-gram-plus-dictionary annealer converges from random and seeded starts where shuffles fail, and the key it returns puts a – m on the odd figures 13–33 and n – z on the even ones. The writer, back from Nikolsburg, presses for a promised canonry of Olmütz for one of the sons of “this Most Serene [Queen]”. Word codes glossed only. Full write-up → 16 Sept 2026 Bordeaux to Brienne, 1653 — a Brienne-office cipher, identified but not read. Thurloe’s intercept, 810 tokens over 156 symbols. The design is the 1651–54 family in which consecutive numbers run through the syllabary alphabetically across the diacritic series; a solver with that order as a prior reads matched 810-token controls to 99%, and the letter never leaves the failed-seed band. One misread diacritic in ten drops the control to 52% and 9%, and the transcription is provisional. The 1654 companion letter was solved by Lasry in 2025 and is closed. Notes → 16 Sept 2026 Armstrong to Madison, 20 February 1808 — the 2025 contest solution does not hold. Its 56-entry key covers 36% of the groups, leaves 93 of its own 133 mapped occurrences unread, and uses five numbers absent from the letter; keys built by the same procedure on a shuffled ciphertext fit the claimed sentence better. Madison said in 1808 that no such cipher was in the office, and the roll-13 decodes are all THE = 972. The letter stays unsolved. Notes → 16 Sept 2026 Richard Forster, 1644 — found already read; Tomokiyo’s page still says unsolved. Deciphered by Lasry, by Biermann, and again by Pitt in September 2026. Verified here at z = 8.8 against 20,000 permuted keys, and 31 of 34 symbols recovered blind once word edges are used and the French model writes u for v ; six matched controls read. A mixed homophonic alphabet, not a regular Stuart key. Full write-up → 16 Sept 2026 Birago to Nevers, 1571 — structure fixed, not read. Re-transcribed glyph by glyph from Gallica: two-digit letters with heavy vowel homophony, marked one- or two-digit code groups, six nulls. Variable-length, polyphonic and syllabic designs excluded with methods that read their controls; at 228 letter tokens over 62 symbols the annealer fails its own matched controls, so the target’s negative is the method’s limit. No sibling letter in the volume. Notes → 15 Sept 2026 BLUME SALAMANCA telegram, 1937 — a transposition of telegraphic Spanish; attempted, not solved. A lag scan excludes every single columnar and every reversed-direction double columnar (controls z 11–22, telegram 3.3); exhaustive enumeration of the second key, proven on plants up to 41 × 8 and 30 × 10, excludes forward double columnar and both mixed conventions with a second key of ten or fewer letters. Local search on long second keys fails on plants at this length. What is left is the German-practice region, two keys of 15–25 letters, and that needs the second telegram. Notes → 16 Sept 2026 Fra Giovanni di Lucca to the Emperor, 1644 — read; a polyphonic figure cipher. DECODE R2159, listed as non-decrypted and left at Al principe di… on Tomokiyo’s page because the crib puts i and n on the same figure. Fixing the eight consistent crib letters and annealing the rest, every seed gives one Italian reading and five shuffled controls give none; 17 is i or n , 19 is t or s , and the 231 figures read end to end: keep the Turk from helping the Prince of Transylvania, raise the Prince of Moldavia against him, give him two thousand Cossacks, and no peace until he is humbled or beaten. Full write-up → 15 Sept 2026 SP53/16 nos. 78 and 79, 1585 — one key for both letters, and still below threshold. Ten of the twenty commonest symbols are common to the Tempest and Barret letters against three expected by chance, so the text pools to 1151 groups; the homophonic annealer then fails planted English and French controls at that length as it did at 507. The labels are glyphs, so these are symbol ciphers of the Mary–Castelnau class. Needs the images and the SP 53/22 keys. Notes → 15 Sept 2026 Charles I and Nicholas to Boswell, 1643 — alphabet solved (R. Pitt), text read in substance. A 24-letter row repeated four times over 20–115, verified at z = 9.6 against 20,000 permuted rows. Added here: the four graphic signs are word-signs introduced inside the spelled word (good, Cousin, Master, us); the King’s letter is to the Duke of Courland’s envoy at The Hague and sends him the re-credentials Simpson printed in 1893; Nicholas asks Boswell to hinder the Dutch embassy. A dozen single-occurrence codes remain. Full write-up → 15 Sept 2026 Moray to Wood, 1568 — attempted; undetermined at 134 groups. A 5-gram Scots annealer reads five of six planted controls of the same 32-symbol profile at 93–98% and returns nothing on the letter, in Scots, English, French or Latin; no null, separator or crib survives. The catalogue says the passage is Border news, i.e. names, and 13% of genuine Scots passages score below the solver’s false optimum. Needs the page or a sibling letter. Notes → 15 Sept 2026 Feuquières to Catinat, 1691 (earlier session) — Bazeries read it in 1893 and never printed it; since read, see above. His book, read in full, confirms a 367-group petit chiffre but gives neither text nor table; the reading is in his papers at the SHD. Here the ciphertext is corrected from the 1819 pages, the two-part design fixed, and the solvers fail a matched control. Notes → 15 Sept 2026 Louis XIV to Chaulnes, 1690 — code design established, not read. 300 groups verified from the page images, a one-part Croissy table of at least 535 entries identified from its step-10 chains, and no printed plaintext found; the annealer recovers 4–12% of a matched control, so 300 groups do not fix a 116-entry nomenclator. Notes → 15 Sept 2026 Maltravers to Ormonde, 1634–35 — nomenclator confirmed; moved from partial to solved. Wentworth’s own dispatches in Knowler’s Strafforde’s Letters (1739) describe the King refusing to see Kildare and Ormonde moved for the Council “in exchange” for Crosby, clause for clause with the cipher passages. Seven of nine codes fixed. Full write-up → 15 Sept 2026 Voynich manuscript — adjudicated, not deciphered. Plain or simply enciphered European language excluded on transliteration-robust entropy; grille and free-edit self-citation disfavoured; verbose encoding against structured meaningless text left roughly even, with the tests that would separate them. Full write-up → 15 Sept 2026 Scorpion letters, 1991 — below the unicity distance. Both ciphers carry more key than the text has redundancy; matched controls produce fluent false English at 3–13% accuracy, and a claimed 2018 solution scores worse than those false solutions. Full write-up → 15 Sept 2026 Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested. Two transcriptions, ten languages, six reading conventions, 300 restarts: nothing readable, while the same solver recovers same-length controls at 96–100%. Full write-up → 15 Sept 2026 Vatican Part 5, 1542 — Meister keys verified from the scans; unit-level attack fails on segmentation. The letter is dated from its own cleartext, the historically matching key is excluded on structure, and a matched control shows why a two-stage attack cannot work. The DECODE images, now accessible, will fix the dots and uncertain digits, but the documents carry no separators between tokens, so they cannot restore a word division the manuscript never had; the key or the clear copy in Chigi M II 49 remains the route in. Full case → 15 Sept 2026 Koehler cryptograms, 1944 — skipped as intractable. Not Enigma, since the letter counts rule out machine output, and not any periodic or running-key hand cipher. What is left needs the prayer book or the FBI’s file. 15 Sept 2026 Censorship manual steganograms, WW2 — blocked on image resolution. The map’s shift direction and the exact Morse any German wording would leave are now fixed, but the pen marks are 2–5 pixels in the best public photograph. Needs a high-resolution scan of KV 2/2424. 15 Sept 2026 Debosnys, 1882–83 — attempted, not solved. The cipher poem is rhyming couplets in a French syllabary, every testable crib is excluded, and the surviving text is too short to break without one. Full write-up → 15 Sept 2026 Catokwacopa, 1875 — readings audited. Of 1,645 names, only Conington, Jowett, Shirley and Hertford fit their lines, so the Oxford reading is right in outline. Exact alternatives found for two lines, and four lines shown to be undecided by the letters. 15 Sept 2026 Vatican Part 5, 1542 — cipher family identified as Antonio Elio’s polyphonic-syllabic design, built for the chancery that sent the letter. Five measurements match it, one of them recovering a written chancery rule. Full case → 15 Sept 2026 Schmeh’s Top 50 — audited entry by entry. Nine are closed and the list does not say so; one entry is an April Fools’ joke that has sat unmarked for nine years. 15 Sept 2026 ADFGVX, 1918 — the 2017 thread consolidated: 9 solved, 3 partial, 10 open. Lasry’s unpublished sixteenth key rebuilt; Norbert’s two-block-edit method reimplemented with a German model re-derives seven pages blind; the ten open messages resist all fifteen keys and a key-free attack that fails its own control. t: Unsolved Historical Ciphers
b: The three source lists are exhausted here: everything on them that has its text online has been attempted, read, or shown to be blocked on archive access. The queue that used to sit in this place has moved to the tracker in the repository, and the open work now comes from the catalogue : twenty-five undeciphered letters from 1497 to 1610 that are on none of the lists, found by harvesting the BnF catalogue on Gallica and by reading the fine print of the cryptiana articles. Each carries its shelfmark and ark, the prior art, a difficulty class, and the check that would confirm it is genuinely open. Four of the twenty-five have since been taken to the leaf and read, partly read or closed (Lanssac, Béthune, Nevers, du Bellay) and sit at the foot of the list with their outcome; twenty-one are open, and only one of those has been viewed on the image. Open the catalogue → · Tracker with the former queue ↗ Corrections and pointers to existing decipherments are welcome — a catalogue entry marked "unsolved" is often a literature search away from "solved in 1858".

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: Ten Dutch copies of letters of the Saxon-Polish resident to Dresden, with passages in figures that DECODE says were never solved: the figures run on without separation. The digits 5 and 8 turned out to be nulls, the rest two-figure codes for letters and syllables; Kauderbach’s 1761 key in Dresden supplied the vocabulary, a one-to-one annealing search the numbers. All ten read: the Dutch quarrel over the augmentation of 1755, Yorke and the Saxon subsidy treaty, and the news of the Treaty of Versailles. The Hague → Dresden · two-figure letter-and-syllable cipher, unseparated, with nulls · December 1754 – May 1756 · read Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 201: the Dutch copies of ten letters in which the Saxon-Polish resident Johann Heinrich Kauderbach put his secret passages in figures (DECODE R1043, R1044, R1954, R1958, R1959, R2078–R2082, “never solved”). The figures were split into their codes, the key found by machine against the vocabulary of Kauderbach’s 1761 cipher in Dresden, and all ten letters read. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 19 September 2026 Kauderbach from The Hague (1754–56) — Read 93 32 13 19 22 16 63 02 11 63 14 24 69 44 72 71 94 24 il n y a pas e u de p u i s l on g te m s 5, 8 = nulls · 24 = s · 29 = t · 62 = que · 46 = qui · 66 = pour · S./. = in clear The Hague → Dresden · two-figure letter-and-syllable cipher, unseparated, with nulls · December 1754 – May 1756 · read Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 201: the Dutch copies of ten letters in which the Saxon-Polish resident Johann Heinrich Kauderbach put his secret passages in figures (DECODE R1043, R1044, R1954, R1958, R1959, R2078–R2082, “never solved”). The figures were split into their codes, the key found by machine against the vocabulary of Kauderbach’s 1761 cipher in Dresden, and all ten letters read. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 19 September 2026 Summary. The Dutch opened and copied the letters of the Saxon resident at The Hague, and ten of the copies carry passages in figures. DECODE notes that none of them was ever solved there: Kauderbach wrote the figures without any separation, so that the Stadtholder’s office could not even tell where one group ended and the next began. Here the separation was recovered first. The digits 5 and 8 never occur inside a group and are nulls; with them removed the stream falls into two-figure groups (first figure 0–4, 6, 7 or 9, second 1–4, 6, 7 or 9), about sixty of them, one key for all four years. A plain homophonic solve failed. The key to the key was Kauderbach’s own cipher of 1761, kept in Dresden and imaged on DECODE (R936): two-figure numbers for letters and syllables ( ai, de, en, que, qui, pour… ), capitals for names, and a declared null. Its numbers do not fit the 1754 letters, but its vocabulary does. An annealing search for a one-to-one assignment of the 1754 codes onto it converged twice to the same key from different starts, and reading corrected the rest (01 = oi , 12 = ai , 27 = in , 66 = pour ). The ten letters now read at 65–97%. They cover the Dutch argument over the thirty-thousand-man augmentation in 1755, Colonel Yorke and the renewal of the Saxon subsidy treaty, and the news of the Treaty of Versailles of May 1756 (“une consternation extraordinaire ici”). The names stay in clear capitals ( S./. , Q./. , P./. ), whose 1754 meanings are known only from context. DECODE R2078, the copy of Kauderbach’s letter of 23 December 1754, first page: Les Etats de Holl. se separeront enfin samedi jusqu’à nouvelle convocation , then the figures, 9332131922166302… = il n’y a pas eu depuis longtems… ; the margin note reads Details relatifs a la Commission du C te d’Affry auprès de cet Etat . Koninklijk Huisarchief, via DECODE.

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: Kauderbach (1707–1785) served the Saxon legation at The Hague from 1739 for almost thirty years; his despatches went to Count Brühl in Dresden (“Votre Excellence”). The Dutch post office copied them for the Stadtholder’s cabinet, and the copies are in the Koninklijk Huisarchief, Prins Willem V inv. 201, beside the d’Affry intercepts of inv. 192. Most are wholly in clear. DECODE catalogued the ten with figures, from photographs, and transcribed three. t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: The Hague cabinet’s note on DECODE gives the reason for their failure: “the codegroups are not separated, by blanks or dots as is usually the case.” A first count showed no preferred period of two or three figures from the start of a passage, and the copyists’ spacing is not systematic. But two figures behave differently from the rest. 5 and 8 are rare (135 and 78 in the first 6,096 digits), never follow 5 or 8, and typically stand next to the clear sigla ( …254 M./. , J./. C./. 8095… ). Deleting them as single figures restores a clean two-figure phase (index of coincidence 0.027 against 0.021 for the shifted reading; for four-figure windows 0.155 and 0.161 at offsets 0 and 2, 0.103 at 1 and 3). A short Viterbi pass over the pair frequencies then repairs the places where a copyist dropped or doubled a figure. What is left is a table of about sixty two-figure groups: first figure 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 or 9, second 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 or 9, never 0, 5 or 8. Every letter shows the same frequency profile, so one key served from 1754 to 1756 at least. That table resisted a homophonic attack. A hill-climbing solver that reads synthetic French in the same form (sixty codes, two per cent noise, nulls, realignment) at 98% produced nothing on the real stream, in French, German, Dutch or Italian, with nulls or merged look-alike figures. The statistics of the stream still looked like language (entropy, vowel alternation 0.63, long exact repeats such as 19 29 14 44 nineteen times), so the units were not single letters.

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden 10024 Loc. 08236/11 Bl. 5, the cipher for “Kauderbach in Den Haag”, 1761 (DECODE R936): pour chiffrer and pour déchiffrer , one number for each letter or syllable, the capitals A–Z for persons and states (S la Hollande , T l’Angleterre , U France ), and 6. est faux chiffre . DECODE’s transcription has “30 ni?” for 30 m . Sächsisches Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden, via DECODE. DECODE also holds the Dresden chancery’s cipher register, and one of its leaves is the key made for Kauderbach in 1761. It explains the 1754 system at once: a null figure, capitals in clear for the names, and a single number for each of about seventy letters and syllables. It is not the same key (its numbers use 5 and 8), but a successor of the same design. So the problem became an assignment: each 1754 code to a different item of the 1761 vocabulary. A simulated-annealing search over such assignments, scored by a four-letter French model built from contemporary diplomatic letters, reached the same key from two independent starts (seeds 22 and 24, −3.85 per letter, against −3.95 for true French on the same model), and it read. Reading then settled what the 1761 vocabulary lacked or the search had misplaced: 27 in (principales, provinces, interet), 91 ou , 33 qu , 79 st , 17 par , 22 pas , 46 qui , 66 pour , 23 fai , 76 ke (Yorke, Kniphausen), 77 z (treize, declarez), and the exchange of 01 oi and 12 ai , found independently by both readers (avoit, etoit, croire; raisons, mais, Pais Bas). 01 oi · 02 de · 03 re · 04 au · 06 ie · 07 le · 09 ne · 10 z? · 11 p · 12 ai · 13 y (re) · 14 i · 16 e · 17 par · 19 a · 20 fe? · 21 ce · 22 pas · 23 fai · 24 s · 26 et · 27 in · 29 t · 30 an · 31 b · 32 n · 33 qu · 34 du · 36 si · 37 en · 39 pr · 40 em? · 41 la · 42 ra · 43 c · 44 on · 46 qui · 47 f · 49 sa · 60 ent · 61 h · 62 que · 63 u/v · 64 d · 66 pour · 67 se · 69 l · 71 te · 72 g · 73 o · 74 ci · 76 ke · 77 z · 79 st · 90 k? · 91 ou · 92 r · 93 il · 94 m · 96 co · 97 x · 5, 8 nulls

b: Word division, accents and the bracketed sigla are editorial; spelling is Kauderbach’s. […] marks an unread stretch, [?] a doubtful word. The clear passages are summarised in brackets. R2078, 23 December 1754 (about 90%) [Clear: the Estates of Holland will separate on Saturday until a new convocation.] Il n’y a pas eu depuis longtems une assemblée des etats de Holl. dont les objets de deliberations aient eté plus importans et en meme tems plus embarassans pour cet etat. D’un coté l’ouverture faite par le comte d’Affry presente mille epines, et quant au fond et quant a la forme des conferences a entamer …; de l’autre coté le colonel Yorke, qui ne s’endort pas dans ces circonstances, demande dans un memoire … des explications sur ce a quoi l’on peut se tenir relativement aux engagemens … The overture is to go through commissioners, conferences auxquelles le marquis de Bonnac agira et parlera comme chef de l’ambassade ; the opponents of England font assez connaitre que le principal but est de negocier un [traité] de neutralité . R1958, 20 June 1755 (about 90%) Le colonel Yorke m’a de nouveau assuré que sa cour est tres disposée au renouvellement du [traité] de subside, et qu’il ne doutoit pas que Mr le comte de Fleming … ne s’affectionnat a cette affaire a son arrivée a Hanovre. Yorke himself, dans des momens d’impatience, se sentoit incliné pour le sisteme des anticontinentistes ; Kauderbach thinks Hanover the right place pendant qu’on y est encore dans l’incertitude des evenemens en Amerique . R2079, 6 July 1755 (about 97%) Mr Haslang mande au resident de Baviere qu’il a la parole du duc de Newcastle que son [Y./.] sera renouvellé. Les apparences pour l’augmentation des [Z./.] diminuent de jour en jour … mais j’ai de fortes raisons de croire qu’il n’en sera que mieux pour nos affaires : Amsterdam would sooner renew the subsidies than vote an augmentation, qui dans leurs principes en est une pour le pouvoir du stadhouder . R2080, 22 July 1755 (about 97%) Les principales raisons qu’on a alleguées dans les debats qu’il y a eu sur ce sujet dans l’assemblée de [S./.] se reduisent en substance aux suivantes. Primo, que si le danger dont les Pays Bas sont menacés est tel que le lord Holderness l’a fait connaitre ici, une augmentation de trente mille hommes n’est pas suffisante pour le detourner. Secundo, qu’il faut constater avant toutes choses si le danger est reel pour la republique … Tertio, Holland cannot carry the burden alone while Zeeland, Utrecht, Friesland and Groningen plead exhaustion; quarto, dans le cas de necessité … tous les bons patriotes devroient sacrifier jusqu’au dernier sol et combattre pro aris et focis; mais qu’il faudroit auparavant s’expliquer avec [Q./.] . If it must be, new taxes and encore un cinquantieme denier . R1959, 5 August 1755 (about 95%) Le bruit que [E.M.] est en negociation avec [P.] ne paroit pas etre entierement sans fondement, et l’on assure que l’on a fait reellement quelques demarches aupres de ce prince, qui auroit promis a certaines conditions de se tenir tranquile tant que la [J./. C./.] ne remueroit pas. The ambassador of [Q./.] m’a sondé plusieurs fois sur les dispositions de [J./.] pour un [traité] de subside avec la sienne, a quoi je lui ai repondu constamment que je n’etois pas instruit, et que nous avions un [ministre] a Paris auquel il etoit plus naturel de s’adresser qu’a moi. R2081, 12 August 1755 (about 93%) Les [P.] sont aussi peu contens de [J./. C./.] que des [S./.]. Il me paroit qu’ils soupconnent [U./.] de ne vouloir pas elle meme au fond embrasser ces choses … Ils disent savoir positivement que le baron de Kniphausen declame plus fortement a Compiegne contre les [P./.] que [Q./.] meme. The rumoured negotiation with [M./.] is now denied: an attempt was made three months ago mais qu’elle n’a pas pris . R2082, 15 August 1755 (about 95%) L’ambassadeur de [Q./.] assure que [E.M./.] a ecrit au roi son maitre une lettre de sa propre main … qu’il avoit une armée de cent cinquante mille hommes a son service. [P./.] says openly that if the Dutch will not arm, [P./.] abandonnera le continent, et qu’elle ne sacrifiera pas … la seule occasion decisive d’humilier [Q./.] a la pitoyable conduite de [S./.], qui apres avoir eté assez avertie se tirera d’affaire comme elle pourra. R1044, 29 September 1755 (about 85%) L’on n’entend que des plaintes des membres contre [P.I.] de ce qu’ils font tant de prises en Europe sans en donner aucune raison au public ; England had taken pour plus de vingt millions de prises sur les sujets de l’Etat in the last war, qu’on recommençoit deja ce train . [Clear: Bolza’s power useless; Kauderbach’s arrears.] R1954, 16 March 1756 (about 65%) On the demand for a secours de six mille hommes : [S./.] ne peut refuser ce secours sans rompre entierement avec [B./.], qui prendra ce refus pour une infraction … ; if the neutrality party loses, le peuple s’animera … et entrainera l’Etat malgré lui dans la querelle . Many gaps: the transcription is weak. R1043, 25 May 1756 (about 85%) On a aujourd’hui des avis certains et positifs que le [traité] dont on parle depuis si longtems a eté signé a Versailles le deux de ce mois, et selon ce qu’on m’a [fait] conter confidemment, il a pour objet primo la neutralité des Pais Bas, secundo il doit y etre stipulé qu’aucune puissance ne donnera aucun secours a l’ennemi de l’autre … et tertio … de ne pas lui etre contraire relativement a l’election d’un Roi des Romains. Cette nouvelle a causé une consternation extraordinaire ici parce qu’on croit qu’il y a des articles secrets qui vont encore plus loin. Then Bonnac and d’Affry’s visit to an ambassador’s country house, et l’on a dit aussi beaucoup de reflexions sur cette demarche . The First Treaty of Versailles was signed on 1 May 1756.

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: The sigla. The capitals with ./. (S, Q, P, U, J, C, M, E, Y, Z, W, B, G) are names written in clear, as in the 1761 key, but their 1754 meanings differ from it. S is almost certainly Holland (the Estates, the provinces), Y a subsidy treaty, Z troops; the rest are read from context only and marked as sigla in the readings. Rare codes. 10, 20, 40 and 90 occur twelve times in all and are guesses; 13 reads y and apparently also re (membres, reflexion); 66 may stand for er inside some words. R1954 (four pages in a letter-like hand) is read only at about 65%; a second transcription would lift it. Transcription slips. The DECODE transcriptions and the new ones both drop or double figures; the reading files list those met. The clear passages were transcribed quickly and are summarised, not edited. Shares read are the readers’ estimates of the cipher text given sense; 99.9% of the groups carry a key value.

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: Nine ciphered reports of the imperial vice-chancellor from Hamburg and Glückstadt, January to April 1639, in the Trauttmansdorff archive at Klášter (DECODE R3811–R4736). Mírka rebuilt the key in 2012 and read one letter but printed nothing. From the same interlinear glosses the key falls out as a regular table: 41–100 are consonant–vowel syllables, two consonants to each ten in reverse alphabetical order, and the low numbers are homophones. All nine letters decipher in a first pass: Banér in Lower Saxony, Arnim’s bid for pardon, the Danish mediation and its collapse. Hamburg & Glückstadt → Trauttmansdorff, Ferdinand III, Schwarzenberg · homophonic cipher with a syllable table · Jan–Apr 1639 · key rebuilt, all nine read in part Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt SOA Plzeň, pracoviště Klášter u Nepomuka, Rodinný archiv Trauttmansdorffů, inv. č. 200, kart. 9 · DECODE R3811–R3815, R4625, R4645, R4734, R4736 · 73 images, about 23,000 cipher signs A contemporary reader glossed one page; from it the whole table falls out. The other eight letters had never been deciphered. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 19 September 2026 Summary. Ferdinand Sigmund Kurz von Senftenau, the imperial vice-chancellor, spent the winter of 1638–39 in Hamburg, where the preliminaries of the Westphalian peace were being sounded with Sweden, France and the Danish mediator. His ciphered reports to Maximilian von Trauttmansdorff survive in the Trauttmansdorff family archive at Klášter. DECODE holds nine of them. Jakub Mírka rebuilt the key in 2012 from the interlinear decipherment on the first page of the 17 January letter and read that one letter, but he printed neither the key nor the text. Here the whole corpus was transcribed from the public DECODE images. The key was rebuilt from the same glosses, which show a regular table : numbers 41–100 stand for consonant–vowel syllables, two consonants to each ten in reverse alphabetical order, and the low numbers and signs are homophones for letters. With a German language model filling the rest, all nine letters decipher . They cover Banér’s invasion of Lower Saxony, Arnim’s bid for pardon, the Danish mediation and its collapse, and Kurz’s contempt for “universal” treaties (“ein teufflisch inventum”). The key is complete, but the reading is not: the transcription was a single pass, so 20–45 % of each letter is still garbled. A checked second transcription would close it. Status: key rebuilt; nine letters read in part.

January”, which is R3813. It is dated Hamburg 3 Feb. 1639 in its clear postscript and reports Arnim in Hamburg after his escape in late 1638. It belongs to 1639. The cipher runs inline with clear German. Kurz writes the harmless words in the clear and enciphers the names, numbers and judgments. R3811, 17 Jan 1639, first page. The small letters over the numbers are a contemporary decipherment, and they are where the key comes from. SOA Plzeň, via DECODE.

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: About 210 glossed signs on the first two pages of R3811 give the pattern straight away: 83 de, 82 di, 84 da; 43 re, 42 ri, 44 ra; 51 no, 52 ni; 72 hi, 74 ha; 93 be; 57 mi, 59 ma. Every ten is split into two halves of five. Each half has one consonant, and its first four places run o i e a : +1 +2 +3 +4 +5 41–45 ro ri re ra pu 46–50 po pi pe pa lu 51–55 no ni ne na mu 56–60 mo mi me ma hu 61–65 lo li le la ku 66–70 ko ki ke ka du 71–75 ho hi he ha gu 76–80 go gi ge ga bu 81–85 do di de da cu 86–90 co ci ce ca — 91–95 bo bi be ba us 96–100 — is es e? ru The consonants run backwards through the alphabet from 41: r p n m l k h g d c b. The fifth place of each half is a separate series of -u syllables, and each was fixed from words: Reputation and Graf von Puechheim (45), illustrissimi (50), unmüglich (55), Hunger and Churbrandenburg (60), Ankunft (65), durch (70), Herzog Augustus (75), Magdeburg, Meckelburg (80), pericula (85), Haus Österreich (95), zurück, darüber (100). The numbers 1–40 and some twenty letter and graphic signs are homophones for single letters. The commonest are 28 r, 31 n, 27 s, 26 t, 39 c, 35 h, 18/19/20 e, 17/15/16 i, 21/22/23 a, 10/11/25 u, 12/13/14 o, 36/38 g, π/α m, ψ/φ z, w /#z-tail n and 29 qu. A few stand for pairs: 9 te, 6 se, c si, n ve, d so, k ti and a looped ℓ tu. A handful of marks are nulls or flourishes. The full table, with counts, is in KEY.md . This is Mírka’s description (“homophonic substitution, bigrams, nulls, no codes”) written out as a table.

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: The readings below are word-divided and lightly normalised from the machine decipherment. Where the text is garbled, the summaries say so. 17 January (R3811) Nothing can be done with Duke Georg of Lüneburg: ohne Widerstand ist der Feindt über [the Elbe]. Recruits are going to Austria and money is short. France, Sweden and Holland im Werck sein, zum König eine ansehnliche Legation zu schicken [are about to send a considerable embassy to the King] of Denmark, to prevent a congress. Herzog Augustus von Sachsen-Lauenburg wolle sich in dennische Protection begeben [Duke August of Saxe-Lauenburg means to place himself under Danish protection]. Arnim, suspected over the Friedland affair, swears he plotted nothing against the Peace of Prague, and Kurz advises a Protectorium in optima forma . These are the points of Mírka’s summary, one by one. 27 January (R3813), a twenty-page memorandum Der Feindt gehet ganz unverwehrt hieher, zieht sich gegen Waltzwedel [the enemy comes on quite unhindered, heading for Salzwedel]. Kurz writes that it is besser ein ungeschlossener, durch den Feindt zertrennter Craistag als ein geschlossener mit einer expressen Neutralitet [better a Kreistag left unconcluded and broken up by the enemy than one concluded with an express neutrality]. He advises a defensive war to keep Austria, Bohemia and Silesia. He distrusts Salvius, who is “voller Gifft contra Domum Austriacam”, and weighs a secret particular treaty through Denmark or Brandenburg. He calls the universal treaties and safe-conducts “ein teufflisch inventum et ad exclusionem omnium tractatuum”. France wants Lorraine, Alsace and das Kaiserthumb ; mit Schweden ist umb ein leichters noch zu accordiren [Sweden is somewhat easier to come to terms with]. 3 and 6 February (R3812, R3815) Banér’s plundering will bring das ganze Stift of Halberstadt zu Grund . Between Denmark and Sweden there are grosse disgusti . Sweden wants half of Pomerania and an amnesty and will not come to a congress while it does not feel the war at home. Arnheim ist gestern Abent bei mir gewesen : Arnim describes Banér’s army as zehentausend Mann, ein ermattetes, armseliges, hungeriges Volck [ten thousand men, worn out, wretched and hungry]. To the Emperor, Kurz reports the King of Denmark ganz perplex and the Danish Reichsrat irresolut und pusillanimes . 10 and 13 February (R4625, R4645) A plan to keep the Lower Saxon Circle divided and to hold Halberstadt, Magdeburg, Hildesheim and Wolfenbüttel follows. It warns that the imperial army is gar ruinirt, et venter caret auribus . The King’s conditions for his mediation have proved empty, and wir wollen uns dannoch und auch allein wehren [we will defend ourselves nonetheless, even alone]. Count Pentz says the King must drop the mediation and denounce Sweden: ergo ruptura tractatuum hic est principium coniunctionis . 8 and 14 April (R4734, R4736) Die Interposition ist schon expirirt : the King says he has bound hands and will do nothing per force . From Glückstadt, Christian IV’s residence, Kurz writes von hinnen wolt man mich nit gern dimittiren . He reports the Danish complaint that war in Austria is paid for with peace in Lower Saxony while the Swedes sit in Mecklenburg and Pomerania: für solche Mauren geben wir unser Schweiss und Bluet [for such walls we give our sweat and blood]. A courtier ist der gescheideste in dissimuliren [is the cleverest at dissimulating]. R4736, Glückstadt, 14 April 1639: the letter is almost entirely in cipher. It opens Von hinnen wolt man mich nit gern dimittiren … . SOA Plzeň, via DECODE.

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: Agents transcribed all 73 DECODE images token by token, two at a time. Clear text went in braces and the glosses were attached to their numbers. Plain homophonic annealing with a German 5-gram model (Grimmelshausen and Gutenberg German, early spelling) collapsed into enenen… , even with a letter-frequency penalty. The glosses turned the problem into a structured one: one consonant per half-ten and one value per single sign, seeded with seventeen glossed values. That solver produced fluent German on the first run ( ich müesse die Kranckheit beschreiben, damit man sich den remediis darnach zu richten… ). The irregular signs were then fixed by reading them in context and by ranking candidate values with the language model. Of the 22,913 transcribed cipher signs, 98.3 % now have a value.

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: Transcription, not key. The images were read once. The confusions 1/7, 6/0/ c , 9/ψ/φ and “93” versus “9 3” leave 20–45 % of each letter garbled. By eye, R4645 is the best letter (about 80 % coherent) and R3814 and R4736 are the weakest (about 55 %). The Latin passages suffer most. α reads m in most places, but before l it gives Salv- ( den Salvius , salvus conductus ). Probably a second sign was merged with α in transcription (grade C). 99 is uncertain ( e ?), 90 occurs once, and 96 does not occur. The signs 3, 4, 5, 7, m , #s-loop, #dot and p are read as nulls or are unassigned (grade M). The recurring group read ml in R3812–R3814 is sometimes part of universal- and sometimes a name. It is unresolved. The clear postscripts and the two Banér copies in R4645 are not transcribed. The endorsement on R4734 (addressee) needs checking against the image.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: BnF fr. 4735 f. 124, catalogued “avec chiffre” with no decipherment. The key is a homophonic letter cipher with word signs, recovered from a sibling letter whose Court decipherment survives as gutter-cut marginal notes (“car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”) and checked against the fragments on f. 124 itself. Both passages read, and the key then opens the three election letters whose only “decipherment” was that cut gloss: the Polish nation “autant vénale … comme sont les Allemans”, the Emperor’s three hundred thousand spent for nothing, and on 9 May the election carried against the Sultan, the Emperor, the princes of the Empire, Spain, Muscovy and Sweden, “qui tous estoient bandez contre vostre Majesté”. Tomokiyo’s published table for the cipher is corrected. Warsaw → Paris · homophonic letter cipher with word signs · 1573 · read Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 BnF Français 4735, no. 51, f. 124 · 100 signs in two passages · catalogued “avec chiffre” with no decipherment · two weeks before Anjou’s election to the Polish throne Key recovered from the glossed sibling letters of 24 April (ff. 154, 156) and the decipherer’s marginal fragments on f. 124 itself; 96 of 100 signs read · the same key then reads the election letters of 1 and 9 May (ff. 160, 164, 174) Daniel Bourdeau · solved 17 September 2026 Summary. Guy de Saint-Gelais, sieur de Lanssac, joined Jean de Monluc, bishop of Valence, at Warsaw in April 1573 to help elect Henri d’Anjou king of Poland. His letter to Charles IX of 26 April is in clear except for its first three lines and a clause near the end; the BnF catalogue notes “avec chiffre” and lists no decipherment, because the decipherment that follows it in the volume (no. 52, ff. 126–127) is of the mémoire on Polish affairs that the letter announces, not of the letter. The same volume holds five more Lanssac letters in the same cipher whose Court decipherments were written in the outer margin and cut by the gutter on the microfilm; enough survives of them to fix a crib (“car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”), and f. 124 carries its own marginal fragments (“…d’Allemagne”, “qui passent”, “moins esté retenu”, “…ou oultre”). The two passages read: Sire, despuis les dangiers qu’encontrent en Allemagne les françois qui passent, et vostre ser[vice?]… and j’eusse sans doubte pour le moins esté retenu ou empesché de passer oultre . Lanssac had reached Poland only on 25 February, delayed across Thuringia, Meissen and Brandenburg, and owed his passage to the King’s Saxon pensioners Miltitz and L(u)elz, who escorted him with a strong troop of their friends. Status: read; the first word of passage one, the sign sequence for “françois” and four signs after “vostre ser” carry a query. Tomokiyo’s published table for this cipher is corrected (first row shifted by one letter from m). Section 05 carries the key into the three election letters of 1 and 9 May, whose catalogued “déchiffrement” is only the gutter-cut gloss.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: BnF fr. 4735 is the second of the volumes of “pièces originales et de copies concernant l’histoire de France, 1569–1588” and, from no. 5 to no. 80, the Court’s file of the Polish election embassy: Monluc’s letters from Konin and Warsaw, the Polish memoranda on St Bartholomew, the King’s replies, and the letters of Lanssac and Gilles de Noailles from Warsaw and Płock in April and May 1573. The catalogue marks “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” against Lanssac’s letters of 24 April (nos. 60–61), 1 May (63, 65) and 9 May (70), and “avec chiffre” alone against no. 51 of 26 April. Gallica has the whole volume as a microfilm scan (btv1b9060724s, 614 unlabelled canvases); the folio of no. 51 is 124, canvas 242, not the 126 the catalogue entry here first gave. Fr. 4735 f. 124, upper half: the ciphered opening after “Sire”, the clear itinerary, and the second passage after “j’eusse sans doubte”. The decipherer’s gloss sits in the left margin, cut by the gutter (Gallica, btv1b9060724s, canvas 242). What the catalogue calls the siblings’ decipherments turns out to be this same marginal gloss, line by line beside the cipher, on ff. 154, 154v, 156 and 157. The microfilm keeps only the last centimetre or two of each gloss line, but on f. 154v the first line of cipher stands beside “Car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”, and the cipher line is exactly long enough for it.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: Homophonic letters. Separate graphic signs (crosses, bars, figures, letter-like forms) written continuously, with points, commas and short bars as word separators. Common letters have two or three signs: e ✕ ✱ Γ Δ, a ⊤ π H, r ϕ ⊨, s 9 Lo IIII, i ⊢ ϙ, n ſ o-o, u/v o+ ff o+o, m 8 ᥙ, l 3 ⊥, o ꞔ L, t ʓ ттт, p y N, d ‡, c 7 ⋔, g ∞, f o-, h +, qu ꞗ. Syllable and word signs. et ♁, nt ꝸ, st 8 with a dot, de ᒐ, ou ᛏ, ns Λ, car Z, pour †, and Allemagne as a Z with a lower curl. Over the 741 signs transcribed from f. 124 and the first blocks of ff. 154 and 156, the merged frequencies are French: e-signs 17.6 %, then r, a, s, n, u, t, o. Tomokiyo’s table. His “Lansac’s Cipher” (cryptiana, French Ciphers during the Reigns of Charles IX and Henry III ) has the right signs but its first row is displaced by one letter from m onward (his ſ m, L n, б p, ⊨ q, 9 r, ʓ s, o+ t read n, o, qu, r, s, t, u ), his Γ = i is e , his ‡ = h is d , and the “pour” cross is the letter h in one of its two shapes. The corrected table with the evidence for each sign is lanssac/key.tsv .

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
h: The key, and how it was found
b: The glossed crib. f. 154v line 1, Z ⊢✕ | ſπϙ | y⊤9 | 7⊢ſꞗπſʓ✕, beside “Car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”, reads car ie nai pas cinquante and fixes eleven signs at once, including car = Z, qu = ꞗ and the shift in Tomokiyo’s row. Passage two by hand against its gloss “moins esté retenu … ou oultre”: † ⊥ ✕ · 8 ꞔ ⊢ o-o 9 · ✱ 8̣ Γ · ϕ ✕ ʓ ✱ ſ o+ = pour le moins esté retenu , then ᛏ Γ ᥙ y ✕ 9 7 + ✱ · ᒐ = ou empesché de , y π 9 Lo ✕ ϕ ꞔ ff 3 ттт ⊨ Γ = passer oultre , ᥙ · π ꟿ Lo = mais . Each new sign was checked in the siblings before it was kept. Annealer over the whole transcription (French 5-gram model, symbol to letter or short code, the crib letters pinned). The free signs come out the same across seeds and read words in the siblings that the cribs never touched and the glosses confirm: les dangiers , causé , l’autre , beaucoup , grant seigniur , du monde , changement , sur la teste , recommandé , doubte ou vous mettre . Lattice decode of f. 124 : each sign given its candidate values, beam search on the same model. Passage one falls out as despuis les dangiers qu’encontrent en Allemagne les françois qui passent et vostre ser… , matching the three marginal fragments “…es dangier”, “…d’Allemagne”, “qui passent”. Controls. The pinned key scores −2193 to −2198 on the real sign order and −2924 to −3009 on three shufflings of the same signs. A blind run with nothing pinned reaches a higher score (−2033) but recovers only 6 of the 21 crib letters: on a transcription this noisy the language model alone does not find the key; the cribs and the glosses do, and the model then fills the rest consistently.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: Cipher passages in brackets; sixteenth-century spelling kept; ? marks an uncertain sign, braces an unread run Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573. Sire, [despuis? les dangiers qu’encontrent en Allemagne les françois qui passent, et vostre ser{o r h e}] Les empeschementz et les plus grandes causes qui ayent esté depuis deux {ans} … toute la Turinge, Misnie et Marche de Brandebourg m’ont tellement retardé que je n’arrivay en Polongne à Mezeritz que le vingt-cinquiesme de febvrier. Et sans la faveur que j’ay receue d’aulcuns des serviteurs et pensionnaires de vostre Majesté, principalement des Sieurs Alexandre de Militiz et George Luelz(?), qui me y ont accompagné avec bonne et forte troupe de leurs amis et assisté de leurs moyens, j’eusse sans doubte [pour le moins esté retenu ou empesché de passer oultre. Mais], la grace à Dieu, je me suis rendu il y a desjà long temps avec Monsieur de Valence, lequel m’a enseigné l’estat auquel estoient les affaires qu’il a bien et dignement commencées et continuées jusques icy, et dont j’ay faict ung recueil ensemble de ce que j’ay peu juger, lequel j’envoye à vostre Majesté. Et ne sçachant à présent rien digne d’escrire oultre le contenu audict recueil, sinon que j’ay receu la lettre qu’il a pleu à vostre Majesté m’escrire du xxiii(?) de febvrier, en obéissant à laquelle je me fauldray(?) à me comporter de sorte que j’espère que le bien de vostre service et les affaires qui sont à promouvoir par deçà en demeureront advancez. Je priray le Créateur vous donner, Sire, en très parfaicte santé très contente et longue vie. De Warsauvia, le xxvi e d’avril 1573. English translation Sire, [since the dangers that the French who pass through meet in Germany, and your ser{vice?}…] The hindrances, and the greatest causes there have been these two {years} … all through Thuringia, Meissen and the Mark of Brandenburg, delayed me so much that I did not reach Poland, at Mezeritz, until the twenty-fifth of February. And without the favour I received from some of your Majesty’s servants and pensioners, chiefly the Sieurs Alexander von Miltitz and Georg Luelz(?), who accompanied me there with a good strong troop of their friends and helped me with their means, I should without doubt [at the least have been detained or prevented from passing on. But], thank God, I joined Monsieur de Valence a good while ago, who has told me the state in which the affairs stood that he has so well and worthily begun and carried on until now, and of which I have made a summary, together with what I have been able to judge, which I send to your Majesty. And knowing nothing at present worth writing beyond what that summary contains, except that I have received the letter your Majesty was pleased to write me on the 23rd(?) of February, in obedience to which I shall not fail to conduct myself so that I hope your service and the affairs to be advanced here will profit by it, I pray the Creator to give you, Sire, in most perfect health a most contented and long life. From Warsaw, the 26th of April 1573. The Miltitz were Saxon nobles in French pay; Mezeritz (Międzyrzecz) is the first Polish town on the road from Frankfurt an der Oder to Poznań. The “dangers” are the hostility to Frenchmen in Protestant Germany after St Bartholomew’s Day, which is why this passage is in cipher and the itinerary is not. Lanssac reached Monluc at Warsaw in time for the election Diet, which had opened on 5 April; Anjou was elected on 11 May. The recueil he announces is no. 52 in the volume, “Estat des affaires de Pollongne selon que le Sr de Lanssac y a peu aprendre”, in clear.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
h: The election letters, read with the same key
b: The catalogue credits Lanssac’s letters of 24 April, 1 May and 9 May with a “déchiffrement”. It is the Court decipherer’s note in the outer margin, and the microfilm keeps only the last word or two of each of its lines; the cipher passages themselves had never been readable from the scan. With the key they read in substance. Transcriptions and sign-by-sign choices are in lanssac/reading_siblings.txt ; unread runs are in braces, and words read from the gloss and the sign count rather than sign by sign carry a query. Fr. 4735 f. 174 (canvas 329): the six ciphered lines of the 9 May letter and the gloss beside them — “…la volunté et / …du Grand / …de l’Empereur / …de l’Empire / …de Spaigne / …et du / …Suède, qui tou[s] / …bandez contr[e] / …Majesté”. To Charles IX, Warsaw, 1 May 1573 (f. 160). … que pour en envoyer devant selon que les occasions des affaires premièrement surviennent. [Car je veoy que ceste nation est autant vénale et? sujette à se laisser gaigner par argent comme sont les Allemans leurs voisins.] Ce jourd’huy ilz mettent en délibération s’ilz doibvent prendre pour Roy ung Piaste ou ung prince estrangier, mais on sçait bien quelle en doibt estre la résolution. To the duc d’Anjou, Warsaw, 1 May 1573 (f. 164). … c’est de latin et d’argent, et à bonne quantité, car il y aura de quoy l’employer [à vostre désir]. … les traverses de nos contraires qui n’y espargnent rien pour nous empescher, [{5 signs} a despendu {4 signs} ensemble {7 signs}. C’est en ceste négotiation; l’Empereur en y a despendu plus de trois cens mil {3 signs}, si faict {5} {5}, riens qu’il vaille pour ser{…}. Seulement il le trouble {7 signs}, desseing faisant le pis qu’il peult contre vous.] Encores ne veulx-je faillir, Monseigneur, de vous ramentevoir … que vous fassiez donner ordre que les navires soient prestz pour l’embarquement. To Charles IX, Płock, 9 May 1573 (f. 174). … ayant esté employé en un affaire de telle importance et qui est reüssy tant heureusement [contre la volunté et menées? du Grand? Seigneur, de l’Empereur, des princes de l’Empire?, du Roy d’Espaigne, du Moscovite, {3 signs} et du Roy de Suède, qui tous estoient? bandez contre vo[st]re Majesté]. Si est-ce que j’auray encores plus d’occasion de louer Dieu si je suis tant heureux que vostre Majesté me juge digne d’estre employé en ce second … English 1 May, to the King. For I see that this nation is as venal and as ready to let itself be won by money as are the Germans, their neighbours. — 1 May, to Anjou. … has spent … together …. It is in this negotiation; the Emperor has spent more than three hundred thousand in it … and done nothing worth the name …; he can only trouble the design, doing the worst he can against you. — 9 May, to the King. … an affair of such weight, which has succeeded so happily against the will and the intrigues of the Grand Seigneur, of the Emperor, of the princes of the Empire, of the King of Spain, of the Muscovite and of the King of Sweden, who were all leagued against your Majesty. The 9 May list is the field of the 1573 election as the French embassy saw it: Archduke Ernest for the Emperor and Spain, Ivan IV, John III of Sweden, and a Habsburg-leaning party among the German princes. The “Grand Seigneur” (the Sultan) is the surprise, since the Porte was generally reckoned to favour the French candidate, and that group is read from the gloss (“du Grand”) and the sign count rather than sign by sign. The 300,000 of f. 164 is the Habsburg outlay as Lanssac reckoned it; the unit sits in an unread group. New sign values from these leaves — 4 = b, three strokes = z as well as t, the tailed 4 = p, Λ = ns, the hooked C = qu, the 6-like sign = o, Δ = g, the o with cross below = et — are listed in the notes; the last makes f. 124’s “retenu ou empesché” rather “retenu et empesché”.

b: Despuis rests on two signs read once each (ꝛ as de , N as p ); the gloss fragment “…es dangier” is compatible with “…uis les dangiers” but the gutter takes the start of the line. François : the signs give fran-c-o-r-s ; the seventh sign must be the i sign ϙ, which this hand writes close to the r sign ϕ, or the word is another. Qui rests on the gloss; the cipher has ꟿ Γ, and ꟿ reads i in mais . Et vostre ser is followed by four signs that read o r h e under the key; service with one misread sign is the likely word and is left in braces. Two forms of the et sign ( et and nt ) and of the cross ( h and pour ) are told apart by context, not by shape, in the present transcription. The sibling readings of section 05 are first readings from the microfilm: f. 160 is sign by sign, f. 164 has four unread runs and one word-sign ( l’Empereur ) fixed only by the f. 174 gloss, and in f. 174 “Grand”, “de l’Empire”, “estoient” and “vostre” rest on the gloss and the sign count. t: Erving at Madrid (1807) and Adams at St Petersburg (1812) — two legation codes
b: Two American diplomatic-code results from the State Department’s microfilmed despatch books. Erving’s private letter of 24 March 1807, printed from Madison’s own decode with the key “not found”: every hole closes from both received copies and Pinckney’s decoded despatches, and the holes turn out to be Madison’s slips. John Quincy Adams’s despatches are not in Armstrong’s code; his own (the = 1385) is rebuilt from the clerk’s decodes on NARA M35 reel 3, and the nine lines of No. 88 that Ford printed as not decyphered read, 124 of 134 groups: Count Rumyantsev’s strokes at Wilna.
