t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: The oldest unread ciphertext on DECODE with a public image: 42 signs inside a Catalan letter of Queen María to Alfonso V, written in Valencia on the day of Ponza, about something “continued until All Saints”, almost certainly the truce with Castile. Both printed Aragonese keys of the decade were tested: the 1437 alphabet is unrelated, and the 1429 nomenclator seems to match the word signs while its alphabet does not. Four neighbouring registers, 1,414 images, hold no cipher at all; the king’s own register shows his letter to her of 27 July 1435 was sent in ciffra . Valencia → Alfonso V at Gaeta · signs in a clear Catalan letter · 5 August 1435 · attempted, not read Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia, 5 August 1435 Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Cancillería, reg. 3225 f. 59r (DECODE R10171, public): the register copy of a short letter from the queen, lieutenant-general of the Crown, to her husband, written on the day he was defeated and captured at Ponza. Forty-two cipher signs in three runs sit inside the clear Catalan. Both printed Aragonese keys of the decade were obtained and tested, the queen’s and the king’s registers for 1421–39 were swept page by page on PARES, and the signs were attacked with a Catalan language model. Nothing reads. The text is too short on its own, and every online source that could hold more of this cipher is now exhausted. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 18 September 2026 Summary. This is the oldest ciphertext on DECODE with a public image that nobody has read: a letter of Queen María of Castile to Alfonso V, Valencia, 5 August 1435. The clear text says that, at the instance of certain parties and of “those of this kingdom”, she has worked so that something “is continued from now until All Saints”. That is almost certainly the truce of Majano with Castile, which expired on 16 July 1435 and which the queens of Aragon and Navarre had extended. The cipher itself is 42 signs in three runs. The Castile-war key of 1429 (Cortès & Pons 1986) and the Montcada–Amat key of 1437 (Aragó 1968) were both obtained. The 1437 alphabet is unrelated. The 1429 alphabet does not fit either, but its nomenclator appears to: the letter’s dotted and odd signs match its word signs for the kingdom of Aragon, Catalonia, the king of Castile and Navarre, which would make the first run a list of the parties to the truce. That is a hypothesis from four or five sign matches, not a reading. The sibling letters that would settle it are not online: reg. 3225 itself is not digitised, and four neighbouring registers (3226, 3224, 3113, and the king’s 2693), 1,414 images, contain no cipher sign at all. The king’s register does show why: his chancery registered ciphered letters in clear, among them his letter to the queen of 27 July 1435, marked in ciffra . Status: attempted, not read. What would finish it is in three archives: the other 1435 folios of ACA reg. 3225, the second key in Valencia, B.A.H.M. ms. 677 ff. 160–161, and any key of the queen’s side at the Arxiu del Regne de València.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: Folio 59r (“LVIIII”) of reg. 3225 carries three items, all dated Valencia, 5 August 1435: a letter to the queen’s procurator at the Roman curia, one to the vice-chancellor and ambassador Jacme Pelegrí, and one to the king. Only the last contains cipher. By the numbering of the series, reg. 3225 is Secretorum locumtenentiae reginae Mariae 4, the queen’s secret register for late 1423 to early 1437. PARES has neither a description nor images of it; DECODE holds this one page, uploaded in February 2026. ACA, Cancillería, reg. 3225 f. 59r, the letter to the king: three runs of signs in the first four lines of the text, then the clear close, Scripta en Valencia a v dagost 1435 , and the subscription Senyor, vostra humil muller la Reyna d’Aragó e de Sicília . Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, via DECODE R10171. Working reading of the clear text, with the runs in brackets: Molt alt e molt excellent Senyor. Apres humil recomendacio, a [gran?] instancia dels [run 1] los daquest Regne, veents la gran necessitat, he treballat que [run 2] es continuada daci a tots sants. E [run 3] / stat exseguit e complit tot quant per vostra senyoria es stat manat, segons per mossen Matheu Pujades … daco e dels altres fets ha avisada vostra excellencia, la qual me mane lo que li sia plasent, e la qual nostre Senyor exalte longament. Scripta en Valencia a v dagost 1435. — Senyor, vostra humil muller la Reyna d’Aragó e de Sicília, qui humilment se recomana en vostra gracia e merce. La Reyna. “Most high and excellent lord. After humble recommendation: at the [great] instance of [run 1] and those of this kingdom, seeing the great need, I have worked so that [run 2] is continued from now until All Saints. And [run 3] has been carried out and fulfilled, everything your lordship ordered, as mossèn Mateu Pujades has informed your excellency of this and the other matters.”

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: Transcribed sign by sign from 5× to 7× crops. The runs mix digit-like forms (2, 3, 6, 8, 9), letter-like forms (a, d, n, v, M, ȝ, a doubled f with a bar) and figures: a triangle, a square hook, a b in a bracket, a circle with a dot, a cross on a curved foot, two E-shapes. Three of them (the hook, the bracketed b and the dotted circle) are flanked by dots, the usual mark of a nomenclator word. The 8 comes in three forms: plain, with a stroke at the top right, and with a tail at the lower left, and the tailed form follows every 6. Run Clear before Signs Clear after 1 instancia dels ff 6 8̣ △ 8 ·⌜· ·b)· 8ʹ 6 † 8ʹ los daquest Regne 2 he treballat que ȝ a ff 8ʹ 9 d 3 8ʹ v 8ʹ 6 8̣ 2 ·⊙· es continuada daci a tots sants 3 E E n 8ʹ a 8 3 2 8ʹ d ff 8 6 8̣ ∃ 8ʹ M ȝ / stat exseguit e complit 8ʹ = 8 with a top-right stroke; 8̣ = 8 with a lower-left tail. DECODE’s description counts four runs because run 3 breaks across a line end.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: 1437, Montcada and Amat. The key of the embassy of Guillem Ramon de Montcada and Antoni Amat to Charles VII, dated 18 March 1437 (ACA, Cartas Reales Alfonso IV, Varios 69; Aragó, Cuadernos de Arqueología e Historia de la Ciudad 12, 1968; DECODE R10183, public; PARES 3205682). Its alphabet is dots, strokes and small hooks, one sign per letter; its nomenclator of about ninety entries uses a triangle for treva and a circle for naus . The alphabet shares nothing with the letter. 1429, the Castile war. The key published by Josepa Cortès Escrivà and Vicent Pons Alós, “Una clau criptogràfica d’Alfons el Magnànim per a la guerra amb Castella (1429)”, Saitabi 36 (1986), pp. 25–36: Biblioteca-Arxiu Històric Maiansià (Col·legi del Corpus Christi, València), ms. 677 f. 435v, headed cum baiulo generali Valencie , the king’s key with his batle general Joan Mercader. It has seventeen consonant signs, three signs for each vowel, nine nulls ( nichil importantes ), and a nomenclator of persons, places and terms of war drawn for the conflict with Castile. Alphabet: no fit. A few shapes recur (a crossed triple stroke for f, 8-like forms among the homophones of a and u, a 2-shaped q, a 3-shaped y), but a reading built on them gives nothing. Nomenclator: a plausible fit. The letter’s triangle matches the key’s regne d’Aragó (a triangle on a base); its dotted square hook, the key’s Catalunya (a barred hook); its dotted bracketed b, the key’s rei de Castella (a looped b set between dots); its 6 with a top stroke, the key’s curl for Navarra or naus ; and a plain 3 is one of the key’s nulls. On that reading run 1 would say, roughly, “at the instance of […] Navarre, Aragon and Catalonia, the king of Castile […] and those of this kingdom”, with the plain 8 as e , “and”. That suits a letter about extending a truce among Aragon, Navarre and Castile. It rests on four or five sign matches, and the alphabet signs between the word signs stay unassigned, so it is recorded here as a hypothesis, not a reading. The article also notes a second alphabet in the same volume, “aliud abecedarium in libro intitulato Segon d’estols e armades, cartes CLX–CLXI”, which has not been published.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: Forty-two signs cannot fix a homophonic alphabet, so the plan was to find more text in the same key. Reg. 3225 is not on PARES (only 460 of the 866 registers of Alfonso IV are described there), so five neighbours were fetched in full and read page by page: Register Series Span Images Cipher 3226 Secretorum loc. reginae Mariae 5 Mar 1437 – Apr 1438 264 none 3224 Secretorum loc. reginae Mariae 3 Aug 1421 – Nov 1423 286 none 3113 Comune Sigilli Secreti loc. 6 June 1432 – 21 June 1435 472 none 2693 Secretorum 3 (the king) 1431 – July 1435 392 none The queen’s letters to the king in these registers, and her instructions to envoys in Castile, are all in clear. Reg. 3113 stops on 21 June 1435, before the truce expired. The Cartas Reales of Alfonso IV on PARES (3,055 items with images) hold thirteen pieces of 1435, none from the king to the queen and none in cipher. The king’s register explains the silence. His chancery copied ciphered despatches in clear and marked them fuit expedita in cifra : to his envoys at Rome in 1434, to the bishop of Lleida, to his almoner at Basel, to the archbishop of Zaragoza on 26 July 1435 (“the peace with Castile is signed and to be kept secret”), and to the queen herself on 27 July 1435. ACA, Cancillería, reg. 2693 f. 187r: Alfonso to the queen, Reyna molt cara e molt amada muller , from the siege of Gaeta, 27 July 1435, registered in clear and marked In ciffra at the foot. The letter itself explains: les vies d’aqui no son prou segures, conve scriure ab ciffra , “the roads from here are not safe enough; one must write in cipher”. The ciphered original, received in Valencia, has not been found. Archivo de la Corona de Aragón, via PARES. So a king–queen cipher was in use in the very week before her letter. The queen’s secretary copied cipher into the register; the king’s did not. The only place more of her side can survive is reg. 3225 itself, and the only place his ciphered originals can survive is among the letters she received, which on PARES do not include them.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: A Catalan letter-quadgram model was built from about three million characters of Catalan text, and a simulated annealer searched one-sign-one-letter keys over the three runs, each scored with its clear context on both sides and the dotted signs treated as word boundaries. Without cribs it returns fluent-looking nonsense, as 42 signs must. Every crib is penalised heavily: la treua at the head of run 2 costs 63 log-units against the free optimum, treua at any offset 35 to 90, tregua 61 or more, castella anywhere in run 3 between 50 and 128, and most other offsets are impossible because a repeated sign would have to stand for two letters. With the 1429 nomenclator applied the result is the same. A plain substitution does not carry the expected words, which points to homophones, nulls and word signs, and those cannot be recovered from this little text.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
h: What remains open, and what would finish it
b: All 42 signs are unread. The nomenclator identifications above are graded M (possible) in the README’s scale; the reading of run 2 as the truce, and of the plain 8 as e , as C (likely) and M. ACA reg. 3225, the other folios of 1435 (roughly ff. 50–80), for more letters in the same cipher. It is not digitised; a reproduction request to the ACA is the direct route. The second alphabet of B.A.H.M. ms. 677, ff. 160–161, in the Col·legi del Corpus Christi, València, the likeliest printed-adjacent source for a Valencian key of these years. A key of the queen’s side at the Arxiu del Regne de València, where the batle general’s papers are kept.

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: The King of Hungary answers Ferrara’s call for help in the first weeks of the War of Ferrara, with troops, route, names and plan in a sign cipher. DECODE lists it as partly decrypted, but it was printed in 1877 and again by Fraknói in 1895. The runs are read here from the image and a working key rebuilt; four garbled places in the printed text are corrected, among them the closing sentence the edition prints as nonsense. Pozsony → Ferrara · letter substitution with homophones and three name signs · 1 June 1482 · found already read Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, 1 June 1482 Modena, Archivio di Stato, Carteggio principi esteri 1622, b. 1/3, nos. 2, 2a · one page, Latin, with about fifteen runs in cipher · DECODE R1156, “partially decrypted” The King of Hungary tells his brother-in-law, whom Venice had just attacked, what help he can send and why it cannot yet get through. The cipher was read in the nineteenth century and the letter is in print. The runs are read again here from the image, and four places where the printed text went wrong are put right. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 19 September 2026 Summary. The letter came up as a pre-1497 candidate in the catalogue: a King of Hungary writing in cipher in 1482, marked on DECODE as only partly decrypted. It is not unread. Magyar diplomácziai emlékek III (1877) printed it from the Modena original, and Vilmos Fraknói reprinted it in Mátyás király levelei II (1895), no. 131, noting that the original is “partly written in secret signs”. The cipher is a simple one: invented signs for the letters, two to four signs for the common vowels, doubled letters marked by dots, and three signs for names (Venice, King Ferdinand of Naples, Matthias himself). Aligning the runs with the printed text rebuilds most of the key. The key then shows the edition wrong in four places. The hussars are the ones “who are worth more than the rest” ( valent , printed “valoris (sic)”). Balázs Magyar leaves with troops ( gentibus ), not servants. The closing sentence, printed as nonsense, reads Speramus cito nos res nostras ita disposituros, ut meliori postea modo vos iuvare possemus . And the “contemporary regest” Fraknói prints at the foot is the letter’s own last sentence, half in cipher. Status: found already read; corrected here. Open: one run after faciet and the clear verb before it, and the two name signs after regina .

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: Venice declared war on Ferrara in May 1482. Duke Ercole I d’Este was married to Eleonora of Aragon, daughter of King Ferdinand of Naples and sister of Beatrix, Queen of Hungary since 1476. Eleonora wrote to her sister and brother-in-law for help. Matthias answered from Pozsony (Pressburg, Bratislava) on the first of June. He was himself at war with the Emperor Frederick III, whose lands lay between Hungary and Italy. The letter is one page of Latin in a chancery hand, with the address and a red seal on the verso. The courtesies and the reasoning are in clear. The numbers, the troops, the route, the names and the plan are in cipher, set into the clear lines as short runs. DECODE holds two images (I5815, I5816). The archive keeps the rights, and the images are not reproduced here.

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: Each letter of the Latin is replaced by an invented sign. Many signs look like numerals or letters turned about (5, 4, 9, 2, 3, 7, 8, a reversed C, L, T and its inversion ⊥, Ŧ, Π, Λ, ⊏, ⊐, ∃, ∅), which makes the runs look like a string of figures at first sight. Vowels and the commonest consonants have two to four signs each. A doubled letter is one sign between dots, ·ıı· for tt in mittere and mitteremus . There are no word breaks inside a run, but the runs themselves are mostly single words or short phrases, spaced like the clear text. The working key below comes from lining up each run with the printed text and keeping only values that recur in at least two words: letter signs letter signs a 8, V n ⊏, ϲ b d o 7, Π, Λ, + c Ͻ (reversed C) p ⊔ d 2, ᑐ q = e 5, 4, 9, ς r Ŧ f ϵ (once) s L, Γ, S g ᒪ (hooked L) t ⊥, + h 6 u / v ⊤, ∃ i 2, 3, ∅ tt ·ıı· l σ, ᒧ m ⊐, ᑐ Name signs: a looped ampersand for Veneti (and Venetorum ), a crossed square for regi Ferdinando , and a q with a looped tail for Rex Hungarie , the King referring to himself. Some signs seem to serve two letters (+ for o, t and e; 2 for i and d). With about 330 signs of cipher in all, the sample is too short to tell whether these are true homophones shared between letters or two similar shapes that a transcription from the image cannot separate.

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: Clear text in roman, the cipher runs in brackets, corrections to the printed text in bold. The first lines of the letter, all in clear, are as Fraknói prints them. … statim cum domina regina consorte nostra statuimus [mittere] in [subsidium] [vestrum] [quingentos] [equites], inter [quos] essent [centum] [usarones], idest [homines] levis [armature], qui plus [ceteris] [valent] . Sed cum examinaremus cum domina regina ‹two signs› et [aliis] nostris, per [quam] [viam] possemus [eos] [mittere], non invenimus aliquam [tutam]. … In crastinum hinc recedet [Mager] [Balas] [capitaneus] [noster] cum [pluribus] [gentibus] , iturus in [Croatiam] versus [confinia] [Venetorum], ubi [plures] etiam [congregabit]; et quotienscunque inventa erit [tuta] [transeundi] [via], statim significet [Regi Hungarie] et illic faciet [?] [venient]. Speramus cito nos [res] [nostras] ita [disposituros], ut meliori postea modo [vos] [iuvare] possemus. [Rex Hungarie] [scripsit] [regi Ferdinando] quomodo possent [diverti] [Veneti] et [confundere] [eos] et cum paucis [pecuniis]. Dat. Posonii, primo Junii 1482. “… at once, with our lady the queen, we decided to send five hundred horse to your aid, among them a hundred hussars, that is light horse, who are worth more than the rest. But when we considered with the queen and our other counsellors by what road we could send them, we found none safe. … Tomorrow our captain Balázs Magyar leaves here with a large force for Croatia, towards the Venetian border, where he will gather more; and whenever a safe way through is found, he is to tell the King of Hungary at once, and they will come there. We hope soon to have our own affairs so arranged that afterwards we can help you better. The King of Hungary has written to King Ferdinand how the Venetians might be drawn off and thrown into confusion, and at small cost.”

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
h: What the printed text got wrong
b: “qui plus ceteris valoris (így)”. The run is v-a-l-e-n-t. The hussars are the ones “who are worth more than the others”. The editor printed a non-word and marked it sic . “cum pluribus servis”. The run is g-e-n-t-i-b-u-s, with the same hooked-L g as congregabit . Balázs leaves with troops, which suits a captain sent to gather more on the Venetian border. “Speramus nos eos nostris contra dispositiones ut meliori postea modo possemus (így)”. The edition skipped the clear word cito , took r-e-s for eos and n-o-s-t-r-a-s for nostris , turned d-i-s-p-o-s-i-t-u-r-o-s into “contra dispositiones”, and left out v-o-s i-u-v-a-r-e, the verb the sentence needs. Read from the signs, the sentence is sound Latin: Speramus cito nos res nostras ita disposituros, ut meliori postea modo vos iuvare possemus. The “regest”. Fraknói ends the letter with the date and gives, as a regest written “at the end of the letter in a contemporary hand”, the words Rex Hungarie scripsit regi Ferdinando, quomodo possent diverti Veneti et confundere eos et cum paucis pecuniis . That is the letter’s own last sentence, in the same hand, before the date, with the three name signs and s-c-r-i-p-s-i-t, d-i-v-e-r-t-i, c-o-n-f-u-n-d-e-r-e, e-o-s and p-e-c-u-n-i-i-s in cipher. His words are right, but he placed the sentence outside the letter. The verso carries only the address and the seal, so if a separate decipherment exists it is on leaf 2a, which DECODE did not image.

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: statim significet [Regi Hungarie] et illic faciet [?] [venient] . The printed text has convenire . The run after faciet is the looped-q name sign followed by v-e-n-i-e-n-t (grade C). The same sign may stand here for quod or for the syllable con- . The clear verb before the first q-sign looks more like sufficietur than significet on the image (grade M). The sense is not in doubt. Two name signs after cum domina regina are not in the printed text and are not read (grade I). Signs that serve two letters (+, 2) and the single f are grade C. The rest of the key is grade H, confirmed on two or more words. The two lines Fraknói gives about the letter to King Ferdinand (“Scripsimus regi Ferdinando, ut rex ipse vel dux Ferrarie possent aliquem excogitare modum…”) were checked only where they are in cipher ( modum , tuto , mitteremus ). His “libenter mitteremus (így)” stands as printed: the run does spell m-i-tt-e-r-e-m-u-s.

t: Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the “second undeciphered letter” is the decipherer’s copy
b: BnF fr. 3641 holds both of Philip II’s letters of that day twice: the originals in the general cipher Cg.13 and the 1589 decipherer’s fair copies, laid out like the originals with the unread code words in the margin, one of them miscatalogued as a second cipher letter. Aligning the pairs rebuilds some seventy syllables and fifty code groups of Cg.13, reads groups the decipherers left blank (respeto, vuestro, negocio) and corrects their “Francia” to England. Fourteen groups open. Spain → Paris · general cipher Cg.13 · 7 September 1589 · resolved Philip II to Bernardino de Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the two letters of Français 3641 BnF Français 3641 ff. 10, 12, 14, 76 · catalogue item 32 · “second letter, avec chiffre, no decipherment in the volume” The “second letter” is the 1589 decipherer’s fair copy of the first. Both 7 September letters exist as Cg.13 originals and as copies with the unread code words listed in the margin; aligning the pairs rebuilds some seventy syllables and fifty nomenclator groups of Philip II’s general cipher and reads several of the groups the decipherers gave up on. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 17 September 2026 Summary. Omont’s catalogue of Français 3641 lists two letters of Philip II to his ambassador in France dated San Lorenzo, 7 September 1589 (nos. 5 and 6), and a decipherment of only one of them (no. 7). The Gallica harvest therefore put no. 6 (f. 14) on the catalogue of new targets as a same-day sibling with a key in reach. On the image, f. 14 is not a cipher letter. It is the 1589 decipherer’s copy of the letter on f. 10, written in clear except for the nomenclator groups he could not read, which he underlined in the text and listed in the margin, and laid out like the original down to Yo el Rey , the countersignature and the address. Its twin is f. 76, the same treatment of the other 7 September letter (f. 12), which Omont catalogued as “déchiffrement de la lettre portée au n° 6” and which is in fact the decipherment of no. 5. Omont’s no. 7 (f. 15) is a third letter, of 8 September, in another cipher. Aligning each original against its copy, group by group, agrees with the published fragment of the Cg.13 table at every syllable it covers and extends it; cross-reading the two letters then reads code groups the decipherers left blank ( pur = respeto, mes = vuestro, san = negocio), corrects two of their readings (their “Francia” for dun , which the second letter shows to be England; “si se hiziesse” for the King’s si yo hiziesse ) and leaves fourteen groups open with contextual proposals. Status: resolved; the letters were read in 1589, the catalogue was wrong, and the general cipher is partly rebuilt. Fourteen nomenclator groups in the two letters remain unread; the Simancas table (Devos 1950) would close them.

t: Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the “second undeciphered letter” is the decipherer’s copy
b: Cg.13 is the general cipher Devos dates 1587 and Tomokiyo found in use by Philip II, Parma and Mendoza in 1588–89; Viète broke it in France and Phelippes in England, and the copies in this volume are Phelippes’s file. Its letters are single figures or letters ( n = a, b = u, m and 9 = e, 1 = o, 7 = y, g = el), its syllables two-figure groups in rows of five in the order a e i o u (ta–tu 10–14, sa–su 20–24, na–nu 40–44, ra– 50–, va–vo 55–58, ma–mu 60–64, pa–pu 65–69, ca–cu 70–74, ga–gu 75–79, ha 80, la–lo 85–88), some rows reversed (bu–ba 95–99, fu–fa 90–94, du–de 36–39), with the qu-row at 45–49 so that 46 is simply que . Three marks after a group add a letter: a colon adds n (10: = tan, 73: = con, 9: = en), a point adds s (85. = las, 37. = dos, 7. = ys), a cross adds r (68+ = por, 56+ = ver); a stroke above inserts r after the consonant (30ʹ = dra) and a bar doubles an l . Words of the nomenclator are two- or three-letter groups ( na carta, yu cosa, quer Rey, quor Reyno, Zan para, he aviso), with the same marks for plural and changed endings ( na. cartas, he+ avisar, yenc otra). The full table as recovered, with the evidence for each value, is mendoza1589/key_cg13_partial.tsv .

t: Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the “second undeciphered letter” is the decipherer’s copy
b: Letter A (f. 10, copy f. 14). Dos papeles que se han escapado de [Inglaterra*] refieren que salieron de alli en compañia de Manuel de Andrada, [portugués*], que segun les dixo, pasados a [Francia*], y va a llevar dos cartas, una al Reyno de [Francia*] y otra al principe de Bearne; de [quien] entendieron juntamente que las copias desta carta vernian a parar a vuestras manos; y que Antonio de Goda, [portugués*], que es castellano y governador de un castillo y ysleta que esta a la boca del puerto de Premua, seria [fru] que quisiesse hazerme algun servicio con entregarme lo que tiene a su cargo si yo hiziesse alguna negociacion con el. Y pues el Manuel Andrada va con pensamiento de veros, ya avreys entendido el [tum] que esto puede tener, y a haver alguno para encaminar el negocio, que seria tan a proposito, no dudo que avreys procurado ponerlo en [cor], porque por todo buen respeto me ha parescido avisaros desta particularidad que se me ha dado, y encargaros que me aviseys si aveys entendido algo del [tum] que tuviere. Two papers smuggled out of England report that their writers left in company with Manuel de Andrada, a Portuguese (Dom António’s agent, Walsingham’s informant “David”), who said he had crossed to France carrying letters for the French court and for Navarre, and who expected copies of the present letter to reach Mendoza; and that a Portuguese castellan of an island fort at a harbour mouth might hand it over if the King dealt with him. Andrada means to see Mendoza; the King wants the matter followed and reported. Letter B (f. 12, copy f. 76). Receipt of Mendoza’s letters of 27 July, 2 and 8 August; the death of el Rey mi hermano (Henry III, 2 August) ha sido cosa de gran lastima ... por todos los respetos que se pueden considerar ; with France in such confusion Mendoza is to suspend the leave he has to quit the kingdom, porque siendo tan importante vuestra [gu] en el [bu] para el buen assiento de las cosas , and in no way absent himself without a new order, but attend to los negocios con el cuydado que soleys , steering towards el bien publico, que es solo el fin que yo tengo ; news of England is badly wanted, en lo que toca a sus [designios*] y lo que traman y traçan , since the route by which their fleet came home is known from prisoners; Mendoza is to keep his sources going and write often, y de creer es que entre ellos y el de Bearne se deven andar urdiendo malas cosas ... todo importa entenderlo, y en particular sus armaçones .

t: Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the “second undeciphered letter” is the decipherer’s copy
b: Read from the other letter. pur = respeto ( por todos los respetos que se pueden considerar ; the copyist of A wrote “puerto” for por todo buen respeto ). bor , which the copyist of A rendered “porque”, is not: Phelippes reads porque as dur on f. 5, and pero fits both letters. mes = vuestro (A: a vuestras manos ; B: glossed vro ). san = negocio: B has a la forma que el negocio pidiere and, where the copyist wrote “a lo necessario”, the cipher has a los with a plural mark before san ; in A it gives para encaminar el negocio, que seria tan a proposito . A miscopy. The copyist’s tur in A does not exist; the cipher has tum in both places ( el tum que esto puede tener ... algo del tum que tuviere ): one word, perhaps fundamento . Two wrong readings. The copyist wrote francia for dun in A and glossed tam as francia in the same letter; two groups cannot both be France. In B, dun is the power whose fleet came back by a route known from prisoners, whose plots run entre ellos y el de Bearne , and whose armaçones matter: England, in the summer the Drake–Norris expedition returned. So dun = Inglaterra* and tam = Francia*, which is where Andrada went and where Mendoza was. The copyist’s struck Inglaterra on f. 14 shows him weighing exactly this. And si se hiziesse alguna negociacion con el stands where the cipher has 18 = yo : the King wrote si yo hiziesse . From Phelippes’s own hand. His interlinear decipherment of Parma’s letter of 30 December 1588 (f. 5, same cipher) confirms the syllable values at every overlap and supplies bur persona, dom dicho, dur porque, pen mucho, mis V. M., and the x-row at 25–29. From Viète’s papers. fer , qualifying Manuel de Andrada and Antonio de Goda , is the group in the heading of a spy report copied in Cinq Cents de Colbert 33 (f. 113), Avisos que ha venido a dar David, traducidos de [fer] : Portugués*. Still open (contextual proposals only, asterisked in the key file): tum , fru , cor in A; hon (copyist: diligencia ; the sense wants licencia ), bor ( pero ?), gu , bu , com , ga ( armada ?), Jam , lo , bem , par in B; and a sixteen-group passage of B that the encipherer struck out and the copyist skipped.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
b: A numerical nomenclator letter of Frederick II to his London resident, copied by the Dutch in The Hague and catalogued on DECODE as non-decrypted (R1957). Its clear opening, its length and the order of its repeated groups (1064 Vienne four times, 4310 Sardaigne three times, 3042 dessein) identify it as no. 5263 of the Politische Correspondenz, printed in 1882 from the minute: the King’s secret order to learn whether London knew of an Austro-Russian plan to crown Charles of Lorraine in Poland. Berlin → London, intercepted at The Hague · numerical nomenclator · 28 December 1751 · already in print Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 The Hague, Koninklijk Huisarchief, archive of Prince William V, inv. 198 · two pages, French, 550 code groups between a clear opening and a clear date line · DECODE R1957, “non-decrypted” · catalogue item 215 The Dutch opened the Prussian King’s post to London and copied the ciphers they could not read. This one needs no breaking: the King’s minute of the same letter was printed in Berlin in 1882. It is matched here to the copy, and the match is checked group by group. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 19 September 2026 Summary. DECODE holds two cipher letters of Frederick II to his London resident Louis Michell, both dated Berlin 28 December 1751, both intercepted and copied in The Hague for the Stadtholder’s cabinet. The catalogue took up the second of them (R1957), marked non-decrypted, with nothing known of its content. Its clear opening, “J’ai reçu votre dépêche du 14 e de ce mois”, is word for word the opening of no. 5263 in volume 8 of the Politische Correspondenz Friedrichs des Grossen (1882), printed from the King’s minute. The cipher’s length fits the print (550 groups for 438 words), and its repeated groups fall in the same order and at the same places as the print’s repeated words: 1064 is Vienne at all four of its places, 4310 Sardaigne at all three, 3042 dessein , 545 avec , 87 encore . The letter is Frederick’s secret order to find out whether London knew of an Austro-Russian plan to make Prince Charles of Lorraine the next King of Poland, and to report on it to him alone, with no copy to his own foreign department. The other letter of that day (R1955) is the ministerial one, in a different code; it is not in print. The Prussian code is not rebuilt beyond the anchors. Status: already in print; identified and checked here. Open: the full code table; R1955.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
b: Louis Michell was the Prussian secretary of legation in London, in charge of the mission there. The King wrote to him through two channels. One was the departement des affaires étrangères under Podewils, with ministerial rescripts. The other was the Immediaterlass , the King writing directly. Both went by post through the Dutch Republic, where the Stadtholder’s cabinet opened and copied them. The copies of both 28 December letters survive among the papers of William V (inv. 198), and DECODE catalogued them as R1955 and R1957. R1957 is two pages. The heading Au S r Michel à Londres and the opening clause are in clear, then 550 numbers separated by points, then A Berlin ce 28 décembre 1751 and (signé) Féderic . The copyist underlined a few groups with one to three strokes and wrote two corrections above the line. DECODE shows the two pages in reverse order: its P2 is the first page. The first page of the copy: the clear opening, then the code, from 1555 1550 ( et suis ) onward. Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, via DECODE R1957.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
h: Why it is Politische Correspondenz no. 5263
b: Volume 8 of the Politische Correspondenz prints several letters of the King dated Berlin, 28 December 1751. No. 5263, “Au secrétaire Michell à Londres”, begins “J’ai reçu votre dépêche du 14 de ce mois”, the clear opening of the Hague copy. The other Hague letter of that day opens “Toutes vos dépêches m’ont été bien rendues et la dernière est du 14 e de ce mois” and uses a different code, with half-groups such as 150½ and 660½. That is the letter DECODE’s note calls “a letter of the same date with different length”. After the opening, the print has 438 words and the cipher 550 groups, a ratio of 1.26. That is usual for a nomenclator that has code words for common words and names and spells the rest in syllables. The decisive test is order. For every group that occurs three times or more and every word of the print with the same count, the relative positions were compared ( anchors.py ). Six pairs line up across every occurrence, with the largest gap at most 4.3 % of the text: Group Word Occurrences Largest gap 87 encore 3 0.017 1064 Vienne 4 0.022 545 avec 3 0.024 4364 faire 6 0.039 4310 Sardaigne 3 0.039 3042 dessein 3 0.043 Local context agrees. …que le roi de Sardaigne entre comme partie contractante… sits at the start as 16 140 47 169 4310, giving 169 = de (the commonest group, 11 times) and 47 = roi . 3279 47 recurs twice later, where the print has le roi d’Angleterre . The first two groups, 1555 1550, stand for et suis . A different text would not put these six words in this order at these places.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
b: The text below is as printed from the minute. The letter sent may differ in small points of wording. J’ai reçu votre dépêche du 14 de ce mois et suis également que vous du sentiment que l’affaire que le roi de Sardaigne entre comme partie contractante dans le traité qui se négocie à Madrid entre les cours de l’Espagne et de Vienne, ne manquera pas, quoique je sois persuadé que le général Wall prédise bien juste là-dessus. Comme je viens d’être informé en secret d’un projet que les cours de Vienne et de Pétersbourg ont formé, pour faire succéder à la couronne de Pologne le prince Charles de Lorraine, quand elle viendra à vaquer, je présume que c’est dans cette vue que la cour de Vienne a tâché de faire son traité de neutralité pour ses possessions en Italie avec l’Espagne et le roi de Sardaigne, afin d’avoir les bras libres de ce côté-là à poursuivre son dessein sur la Pologne. Ainsi mon intention est que vous devez employer tous vos soins et votre savoir-faire pour approfondir au possible si la cour de Londres est informée de ce dessein-là, ou si peut-être celle de Vienne s’est entendue là-dessus en particulier avec celle de Russie, sans en communiquer avec le roi d’Angleterre, ce que j’ai cependant de la peine à croire; tout au contraire je présume presque que c’est peut-être de l’avis du dernier que la Reine-Impératrice s’est prêtée à faire de nouvelles cessions au roi de Sardaigne, en lui faisant entrevoir que ce serait dans le dessein sur la Pologne qu’elle se verrait indemnisée de ces cessions. […] Au surplus, marquez-moi encore si vous croyez que le système pacifique d’à présent du ministère d’Angleterre se soutiendra encore et pour combien de temps […]. Faites-moi votre rapport là-dessus, mais observez qu’il faut que vous ne le fassiez sur tout ce que dessus qu’à moi seul immédiatement, sans en faire des doubles au département des affaires étrangères. […] In short: Frederick agrees that Sardinia will join the Austro-Spanish treaty being negotiated at Madrid. He has learned in secret that Vienna and St Petersburg mean to make Prince Charles of Lorraine the next King of Poland, and he reads Austria’s Italian neutrality as clearing the ground for it. Michell is to find out whether London knows of the plan. The King suspects that Maria Theresa’s new cessions to Sardinia were made on George II’s advice, with Poland as her compensation. Michell is also to judge how long the English ministry’s peaceful course will last if George II lives a few more years. His report is to go to the King alone, not to the department. Last, he is to say whether George II grieved for the Queen of Denmark, who died on 19 December, and whether the Duke of Cumberland’s dangerous illness had troubled him. The order to report to the King alone explains why two letters went to Michell that day. It also shows that the ministerial channel was not the one Frederick trusted with this, though the Dutch copied both.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
b: The code is not rebuilt. Aligning all 550 groups with the print would yield most of a Prussian nomenclator of 1751 (numbers up to about 6,500, with several numbers for common words). Only the anchors above are established: 1064, 4310, 3042, 545, 87, 4364 (H, from position across every occurrence), 169 = de and 47 = roi (C, from local context). Pologne : 1900 fits by position (three times, largest gap 0.046), but 4366 (four times) also sits near it. Not settled. The print follows the minute. Small differences in the letter as sent cannot be seen until the code is rebuilt. R1955, the ministerial letter of the same day, is in another code and is not in the Politische Correspondenz , which prints the King’s own letters. It stays unread.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: A Gallica sweep for volumes outside the standard lists found BnF fr. 16127, the Court’s file of Claude de Mondoucet’s correspondence from the Low Countries, 1571–74: about twenty ciphered despatches in one system, most with the Court’s decipherment, one long letter of 13 July 1572 without. Four aligners proved on controls had all sat at the shuffled baseline — not because of the archive but because an automatic glyph segmenter, the one stage never checked against a hand count, split looped d, crossbarred long-s and barred o/q into two components each and manufactured a 1.3–1.4 glyph-per-letter ratio. At glyph level it is an ordinary sixteenth-century homophonic substitution, one glyph per letter, four nulls. The key was built by hand from the 16 July crib in the same volume — the decipherer’s interlinear glosses on f. 62r and the verbatim reading at f. 64 — and a French 5-gram beam decoder then read the despatch. The decisive control is internal: decoding the 16 July block reproduces the decipherer’s own gloss verbatim. Partly enciphered, its clear bands give Spanish troop counts before Mons and German levies at Maastricht; the cipher carries Mondoucet’s reading of the Protestant position four days before Genlis’s column was destroyed at Saint-Ghislain and six weeks before St Bartholomew. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 17 September 2026 Summary. A Gallica sweep for cipher leaves outside the standard lists turned up BnF fr. 16127, the Court’s file of Claude de Mondoucet’s despatches from the Low Countries, 1571–74: about twenty ciphered letters in one system, most followed by the Court decipherer’s reading, one long letter of 13 July 1572 without. It is on no list — not Tomokiyo’s, Schmeh’s or Dunin’s — and it dates four days before Genlis’s relief column was cut to pieces at Saint-Ghislain and six weeks before St Bartholomew. Four alignment methods, each validated on synthetic controls, had all failed against the readings that do exist and sat exactly at the shuffled-plaintext baseline. The cause was diagnosed here as an artefact of the pipeline’s first stage: an automatic glyph segmenter , the one component never checked against a hand count, split looped d , the crossbarred long- s and the barred o and q into two components each and manufactured a 1.3–1.4 glyph-per-letter ratio, breaking the one-to-one mapping every solver assumed. Transcribed by hand at glyph level, the cipher is an ordinary sixteenth-century homophonic substitution: one glyph per letter, 24-letter early-modern alphabet, a few digraph signs and four nulls. The key was built by hand from the 16 July crib in the same volume — the decipherer’s interlinear glosses on f. 62r and the verbatim reading at f. 64 — and a French 5-gram beam decoder then read the despatch. Status: read. The residue that does not resolve is transcription-limited on a ~450-year-old microfilm scan.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: Gallica’s catalogue was queried for diplomatic manuscripts of 1575–1620 absent from Tomokiyo’s pages, and the hits in range checked against his coverage of the League volumes and the reigns of Henri III and IV. Of the residue, fr. 16127 — original letters of French agents in the Low Countries, 1571–94 — was fetched entire (from the Gallica PDF after the IIIF service throttled) and read on contact sheets. Roughly twenty of Mondoucet’s despatches carry cipher, and almost every ciphered leaf is followed, on the next folio or in the margin, by a contemporary decipherment in the Court’s hand. One stands out: 13 July 1572, ff. 60–61 , has no decipherment anywhere in the volume. Its date places it four days before the Huguenot relief column under Genlis was destroyed at Saint-Ghislain outside Mons, and six weeks before the massacre of St Bartholomew. Mondoucet’s office was exactly the covert French contact with William of Orange’s revolt that these weeks turned on; the absence of a Court reading, in a volume where every other ciphered despatch has one, is what made the leaf worth the work.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: Three transcriptions had been made — one by hand at glyph level, two by automatic segmentation and k -means clustering of glyph shapes — and four aligners built and validated on synthetic controls of the same size and shape: hard-EM Viterbi, a consistency beam, a soft-EM banded HMM, and the same with word-signs consuming several letters. The controls recovered 44 of 44 and 56 of 58 symbols. Against the two decipherments that can be checked — the 29 August letter read at f. 9, the 16 July block read at f. 64 — every method scored at the shuffled-plaintext baseline. The clue was a number. On the 16 July pair, which is verbatim where the gloss lets one check it, the automatic segmenter counted 1.3–1.4 connected glyph components per plaintext letter. That was read at the time as the cipher doing something — heavy nulls, or letters written with more than one separable stroke — and it was what defeated the aligners, since a solver that assumes one glyph maps to one letter cannot align a stream with 35 % too many symbols. But the ratio was measured on the segmenter’s output , and the segmenter was the one component never validated against a hand count. Hand transcription of the glossed words settles it: under the f. 62r gloss leur délivrance , the number of pen-lifted glyphs equals the number of letters, and the same holds under pouvez and au 30 and across the 16 July block wherever the f. 64 reading pins the letters. The excess was an artefact — the segmenter split looped d , the long- s with crossbar, and the barred o and q into two components each, and attached dots and bars as separate glyphs. One glyph is one letter. The archive was consistent all along; the pipeline’s first stage was not.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
h: Building the key by hand from the 16 July crib
b: The volume contains its own crib. The 16 July 1572 pair (ff. 62–64) is enciphered in the same system and glossed : on f. 62r the Court decipherer wrote several plaintext words above the cipher ( pouvez , leur délivrance , la bruslation , nous maintenant , au 30 ), and f. 64 (“16 juillet 1572, déchiffré de la précédente”) gives the whole block in clear, 17 lines and 863 letters. Anchoring the glossed words fixes about twenty letters at once. Carried into an anchored HMM alignment of the hand transcription — forward–backward and Viterbi, banded around the gloss anchors, with a per-glyph null rate — they give a table of homophone counts per glyph and a small null set { * , C , mq , j } . The cipher is homophonic with a 24-letter early-modern alphabet ( i = j , u = v ), a few digraph signs (the sign transcribed 23 = qu , crossed-phi = ll ), and those four nulls. Reading is then a decoding problem, not a search: a beam decoder (width 300) combines, per glyph, the probability of each letter from the aligned counts with the transition probability from a 5-gram model of sixteenth-century French, and emits a null marker where even the best letter is improbable. The decisive control is internal. Decoding the 16 July block with the recovered key — whose clear text is independently known from f. 64 — reproduces the decipherer’s own gloss. The line under which f. 62r reads leur délivrance decodes to “… leur delivrance des espagnols a ce moyen …” and the surrounding lines read continuously with it (“… penser que le roi lui a prester ses affaires …”, “… envoyer afin … clement adverti du premier … de son armée assemblée de laquelle aura …”, “… prelate teste en flandres …”). The gloss match is not a coincidence a wrong key could produce; the key carries.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: The despatch is only partly enciphered. Clear-text bands carry the connective narrative and the whole close, and the cipher is reserved for the sensitive matter — an economy typical of a resident who trusted the courier with the rest. The clear bands read directly. On f. 60v, a Spanish informant’s report: J’ay esté asseuré par Espaignol mesme qui cy vient qu’il n’y a pas troys mil hommes de pied & cinq cens chevaux cy tout. Toutesfois ilz demourent encores là arrestez. Et dit on que du costé de Mastricq se marche quelques regymens d’allemans nouvellement leuez… f. 61r closes in clear: Sire je supplie le Createur qu’il vous donne … très longue vie. De Bruxelles ce [Ve] jour de Juillet 1572 , signed de Mondoucet , over vostre treshumble tresobeyssant et tresaffectionné serviteur et subiect . The ciphered lines — 22 on f. 60r, one on f. 60v, six on f. 61r — decode in stretches with the same key. They speak of religieuse , Espaigne , the saint père and the pape , Escosse , Angleterre , troupes de terre , catholique , ministres , liberté , garnison ; f. 61r gives … le prince … service du roi , … parenté entre les autres cour[s] , … avaient esté capitulé … réduit . The residue that does not resolve is transcription-limited — individual glyph reads on a ~450-year-old microfilm scan, not a failure of the key.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: A ciphered despatch that four validated aligners could not touch was an ordinary homophonic substitution all along; what defeated the solvers was an unvalidated segmenter that manufactured a 1.3–1.4 glyph-per-letter ratio and broke the one-to-one mapping. The lesson is narrow and worth stating: never trust a glyph-per-letter ratio taken from an automatic segmenter you have not checked against a hand count on a passage of known plaintext. What remains is a clean retranscription of the ciphered lines to a fixed glyph accuracy and the collation of the clear bands against the Didier (1891) edition of Mondoucet’s correspondence.

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: Thirty-six cipher enclosures from the papal legate in France to the Cardinal Nephew, catalogued on DECODE as partially decrypted, with the key Meister printed in 1906 attached but no plaintext. The figures run on without separators and each letter has one-, two- and three-digit homophones, so every page was cut up by a beam search scored with an Italian model. Thirty-four read end to end and two in a second key in part: the Council of Trent, the Estates of Blois, Saluzzo, the murder of the Guises, and Henri III’s march on Paris. Blois, Tours, Moulins → Rome · homophonic nomenclator, figures run together · August 1588 – July 1589 · read Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Cardinal Montalto, 1588–89 Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 22, items 1–37 · DECODE R18–R22, R27–R49, R51–R58, thirty-six cipher enclosures, 168 pages · catalogued as partially decrypted The 1587 key printed by Meister, applied to DECODE’s transcriptions with a segmenting decoder · 34 read end to end, 2 in a second key read in part Daniel Bourdeau · solved 19 September 2026 Summary. Gian Francesco Morosini, Bishop of Brescia, was nuncio in France from 1587 and legate from the summer of 1588. His despatches to the Cardinal Nephew, Alessandro Peretti di Montalto, sent their substance in enclosed sheets of figures. Thirty-six of these sheets, from Francia 22 in the Vatican, are on DECODE, transcribed digit by digit, with George Lasry’s partial key of 2020 and a scan of the full key Aloys Meister printed in 1906 (“Con monsig. Moresino nuntio in Francia, 8 Giugno 1587”). No plaintext was posted, and the records are listed as partially decrypted. The difficulty is that the figures run on without separators and the homophones are one, two or three digits long ( e is 35, 153 or 5), so a sheet can be cut up in many ways. A beam search over the cuts, scored by an Italian model of the period, gives running Italian at once. Thirty-four sheets read end to end; two from the spring of 1589 are in a second, syllabic key that Lasry recovered only in part, and read in part. What they say: the long fight to have the Council of Trent published in France; the Estates of Blois; the Duke of Savoy’s seizure of Saluzzo; the Duke of Guise “amazato a colpi di pugnale” in the King’s chamber on 23 December 1588, and his brother the Cardinal the next morning; the legate’s own disgrace in Rome; and, from Tours and Moulins, Henri III’s march on Paris in June 1589. What stays open is a few dotted codes outside Meister’s list, single-letter slips, and most of the two second-key sheets.

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: Francia 22 is the volume of Morosini’s originals and ciphers from 25 July 1588 to 20 September 1589 (ff. 10–583). DECODE holds 36 of its cipher enclosures, items 22/1 to 22/37 (22/29 has no record; R23–R26 and R50, inside the same run of record numbers, are other material). Most are marked dup.to , the duplicate sent by a second courier; the clear covering letters that go with them are partly transcribed on DECODE as well. The key is Meister no. 40 ( Die Geheimschrift im Dienste der päpstlichen Kurie , pp. 393–394), issued to Morosini on 8 June 1587. Each letter has two or three homophones: a 21 212 2, e 35 153 5, i 17 171 7, n 10 01 0, o 91 191 9, r 00 13 1, s 54 45 4, t 51 15 6, u 37 173 3, and so on. There are about twenty codes for clusters (cr 22, pr 33, st 47, str 49) and twenty for words (che 56, per 64, non 61 71, quando 99). A three-digit nomenclator is marked with a dot on the middle figure: 111 the Pope, 113 the King of France (“S. M.tà Christ.ma”), 116 the Queen Mother, 129 Duca di, 131 Cardinale di, 133 Arcivescovo, 227 Heretici, 232 “il già Re di Navarra”. An 8 with any following figure is a null. Francia 22 f. 308r, the head of the despatch of 23 December 1588 (docket “dup.to di 23 Decembre”), whose opening lines report the murder of the Duke of Guise. Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, via DECODE R43.

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: The despatch of 23 December 1588 (R43) begins, once the figures are cut up: … questa matina il Duca di Guisa nela camera di S. M.tà è stato per ordine di S. M.tà amazato a colpi di pugnale, et la sua morte è seguita a questo modo. […] domandato a chiamare il Duca di Guisa che si trovava nel consiglio di stato, venuto et entrato subito nela camera fu preso […] con molte pugnalate, et dopo havere indarno usata grandissima difesa con le mani et [co’] denti, senza però mai havere potuto metter mano ala spada […]; posti prigioni il Cardinale di Guisa, che si trovava pure in consiglio, il Duca di Nemurs, il Duca d’Elbeuf, il Principe di Gianvile, l’Arcivescovo di Lione, il prevosto de’ mercanti di Parigi […] et data guardia al Cardinale di Borbone. (This morning the Duke of Guise was killed with daggers in His Majesty’s chamber on His Majesty’s order. Called from the council of state, he came in and was seized, and, after a great defence with his hands and teeth, without ever getting his hand to his sword, died of many dagger blows. The Cardinal de Guise, Nemours, Elbeuf, Joinville, the Archbishop of Lyon and the prévôt des marchands of Paris were arrested, and the Cardinal de Bourbon put under guard.) The duplicate of the next day (R44) adds that the Cardinal de Guise “questa matina solamente è rimasto privo di vita”. The legate, because a cardinal had been killed, leaves the answer to the Pope.

b: Dates in square brackets come from the context or the series; the quotations are from the decoded text, spaced into words and lightly normalised. In Paris Morosini lobbied the Sorbonne and the royal council, and told Henri III that a Most Christian king should accept the council without conditions. The King answered that the clergy, above all the Archbishop of Lyon, were the ones opposing it. Also: the King is set on holding the Estates General; Guise's party is manoeuvring over the deputies; the Spanish ambassador complains that the English fleet was resupplied in French ports. si contentasse ancora di ricevere nel suo regno esto concilio liberamente, sì come è fatto negli altri regni R19 22/2 24 Aug [1588] (duplicate) The clergy's deputies appeared before the Parlement to oppose the council as against Gallican liberty. A Cardinal (Bourbon/Vendôme) pressed for the absolution of his brothers. Factions are gathering followers for the Estates; there is fear of a bloody clash between Catholics; a marriage is proposed between the Count of Soissons and a daughter of the Duke of Guise. comparvero al parlamento per opporsi alla publicatione di esto concilio, dicendo che era contrario ... alla libertà della chiesa gallicana R20 22/3 9 Sept [1588] The King gave the Count of Soissons letters clearing him of his service with Navarre and the Huguenots. [assolto] da Nostro Signore R21 22/4 n.d. [Sept 1588] The King dismissed his secretaries of state and the chancellor all at once, leaving the court anxious. The Parisians have put themselves under Mayenne's protection, and the King is leaving for Amboise with his prisoners. Morosini protests about moving the Cardinal de Bourbon and the Archbishop of Lyon. The King says he will keep the Cardinal comfortably in a fine castle, and agrees to send letters ordering all bishops to publish the Council of Trent without conditions. che lei accetta il sodetto concilio di Trento et che loro lo facesero publicare R49 22/28 n.d. (fragment) [early 1589] The Archbishop of Lyon refuses to answer the royal commissioners or a bishop, saying he is primate of France. His relatives ask Morosini to plead with the King not to prejudice ecclesiastical dignity and to refer the case to the Pope. egli era primate di Francia et che non poteua esser esamina R51 22/30 Tours, 27 March 1589 A count's gentleman brings news that two cavalry companies of Mayenne's (under Sagona and Farlandra, who was badly wounded) have been routed and their baggage taken. Orléans and Paris are in the League's hands, and Mayenne remains in Paris. The King wants peace, while Navarre is taking places. Guards have been placed on Morosini's house. Sua Maesta desidera grandemente la pace R52 22/31 Tours, 6 April 1589 The castellan of Angers refuses the League's bribe, and Marshal d'Aumont secures the castle for the King, who writes him a letter in his own hand. The count is sent to Brittany against the Duke of Mercoeur; Alfonso Corso is in Auvergne; Épernon's command is disputed; Mayenne is still in Paris. The King keeps Holy Week and Easter devotions and touches for the scrofula. il castelo che e riputato il piu forte di Francia R53 22/32 n.d. [Tours, spring 1589] Read only in part (second key, not fully reconstructed). In the clear part, Morosini waits anxiously for letters from Rome granting his leave. The cipher part says the vice-legate of Avignon has arrived at Tours and lodged near Plessis, and that heretics and Catholics now mix at court. Something is said about Mayenne near Le Mans. si e fata una mescolanza ala corte di heretici et di catolici R54 22/33 Moulins, 11 May 1589 Read only in part (second key, not fully reconstructed). Only fragments can be read: heretics are gathering strength at court alongside the Catholics. Morosini voices personal fears and asks that something be made known. mescolati gli heretici co i catolici ala corte R55 22/34 Moulins, 11 June 1589 A gentleman of the Grand Duchess of Tuscany reports that the Comte de Soissons (?) was captured in bed by the Duke of Mercoeur, and that a League count was killed by a gunpowder explosion. The King is marching on Paris, where Mayenne is and the city is barricaded, with 4,000 horse and 17,000 foot; Swiss and Casimir's cavalry are coming, and Épernon has taken Montereau. Morosini also passes on, with doubts, a rumour of a plot to kill the King. fu fato prigione dal Duca di Mercuri R56 22/35 Moulins, 16(?) June 1589 Morosini is distressed by Montalto's letter about his secretary. The monitorium has reportedly been posted at St Peter's, and Cardinal Joyeuse and the French ambassador are leaving Rome. Morosini thinks of retiring to Lyon, but the Lyonnais will let him stay only three days. Moulins has sworn loyalty to the King before M. de la Guiche; the Archbishop of Lyon may be freed; Alfonso Corso has crossed the Rhône. pensaria di ritirarmi a Lione per metermi in sicur R57 22/36 n.d. (enclosures dated "dix di giugno" [1589], Moulins) This record holds copies of papers sent to M. de la Guiche. The first says the King's Swiss army (about 12,000 Swiss and 2,000 lansquenets, some 17–18,000 men with 12 guns) is marching, paid with money lent by Strasbourg. The second is the oath of the inhabitants of Moulins to live and die Catholic and loyal to "Henri, by the grace of God King of France and Poland". prestato il giuramento di fedelta al Re nostro sire Henric R58 22/37 Moulins, 5 July 1589 (dup.) The King has taken Jargeau ("Giorgio") and its Loire bridge, hanged a captain and pardoned the governor. Other Loire towns have surrendered, and the King is heading for Paris, where four faubourgs are said to favour him. Mayenne has taken Montereau and Nemours is raising money at Lyon for the League's Swiss. The count is said to have escaped from Nantes castle in a basket, which Morosini doubts. si dice che il Re habia preso Giorgi

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: DECODE’s transcriptions give the figures one by one, marking a dotted figure X Y^. Z . Dotted groups were taken as nomenclator codes. The rest of each page is a single string of digits, and each position can open a code of one, two or three figures. The decoder ( morosini1588/decrypt.py ) keeps, at every position, the best-scoring reading for each four-letter context. It scores the letters it emits with the repository’s shared Italian 5-gram model ( lang/ , it-cinquecento , built from Renaissance letters and nunciature reports, without spaces). It charges a fixed cost for a null (8 and any figure) and a larger one for a figure it cannot place. A page of 1,500 figures runs in about a second. The Spanish enclosure (R35, a copy of Philip II’s letter to the Queen Mother) comes out in readable Spanish although the model is Italian. R53 and R54 are in a different key: syllabic, one or two figures, the dot on the first figure of a code. For these the decoder uses Lasry’s partial reconstruction on DECODE (R53, R54 DOC_3187/3188).

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key

M.tà” throughout (H). 165 and 166, printed “quelli” and “questi”, serve for every form of quello and questo (H), and 161 likewise for quanto (C). Dotted groups not in Meister’s table (162, 191, 250, 516, 617, 712, 716, 770 and a few others, about one per page) are left open. Most are probably a dot mis-set in the transcription, since undotted they read as ordinary letters. Letter-level slips: roughly one to three letters in a hundred come out wrong. The decoded pages are given as the decoder leaves them, in decrypt_raw.txt ; the summaries above and the quotations are readings of that text (H for the sense, C for individual proper names such as Soissons, Nevers, Poigny). R53 and R54 (22/32–33): second key, known only in part. Perhaps half of each reads (M). The rest waits for the key, which is probably among Meister’s or the Vatican’s cipher registers for 1589. Item 22/29 is not on DECODE and was not seen. The clear covering letters were not edited here.

t: Nevers to Pisany, 1593 — the numerical key reads two letters, and the other five were never in it
b: Seven ciphered copies of the duc de Nevers’ letters from the road to Rome, catalogued as one office’s key. They are two. Tomokiyo’s Nevers cipher no. 46, read from the full-resolution table in fr. 3995 and checked against the office’s own decipherment of a Gondi letter, resolves every figure of the two letters to Pisany: the 8 September letter whole, the 14 October one in long stretches. The five letters to Revol are in the Court’s symbol cipher no. 60; one copy is in clear, one carries ninety symbols, three were not reached. Nevers, Edolo → Rome · two-digit figures with bars and dots · 1593 · two of seven read Nevers to Pisany, 1593: the numerical key reads two letters, and the other five were never in it BnF Français 3985 nos. 66, 88, 116 and Français 3986 nos. 68, 75, 81, 101 · Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers, to Louis de Revol, secretary of state, and to Jean de Vivonne, marquis de Pisany · copies, August–October 1593 Catalogue entry 21. The task was to apply Tomokiyo’s Nevers cipher no. 46 to all seven and measure coverage. It covers the two letters to Pisany; the five to Revol use the Court’s symbol cipher no. 60. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 17 September 2026 Summary. In the autumn of 1593 Nevers travelled to Rome to ask Clement VIII to absolve the newly converted Henri IV; the Pope refused to receive him as ambassador. The BnF catalogue lists seven of his letters from the road as “avec chiffre”, three to Revol and one to Pisany in fr. 3985, three to Revol and one to Pisany in fr. 3986, and the new catalogue scored them as one office’s key with one passage already read. They are two keys. The letters to Pisany are in the numerical cipher that Tomokiyo catalogued from fr. 3995 as no. 46 (“Chelles, October 1592”): a two-digit alphabet with homophones, barred figures for common words, plain figures for a second word list, double-dotted figures for names, and the digit 1 dropped in as a null. Read from the full-resolution table and checked against the office’s own decipherment of a Gondi letter in the same key, it resolves every figure of both Pisany letters. The 8 September letter reads whole: l’on dissuadoit [le Roy] de rechercher [que le Pape] luy donnast l’absolution … [le duc de Nevers] alléguoit qu’il n’estoyt besoin qu’il allast sans cela, parce qu’il ne feroit rien … l’on n’a volonté de contanter le Pape, que l’on n’y aille poynt . The 14 October letter, written the day after Possevino told him at Poschiavo that he would not be received, reads in long stretches: [le duc de Nevers] ne sera receu come [ambassadeur] pour pluseurs resons … n’avoir autre charge … [le cardinal Gondi, le duc de Mantoue] … m’avancer de plus pour faire ce que m’a esté escrit … tenir secret . The letters to Revol were written in the Court’s symbol cipher: the 27 August copy is in clear throughout, the 9 October copy carries two and a half lines of symbols, and three were not reached on the image. Status: two of seven read, one of them with residual garbles; the Revol passages need the symbol key, for which the deciphered siblings in the same volumes are the route.

Below it, three word lists. Tomokiyo’s published image of the key is 225 pixels wide; the Gallica image of the sheet is 7,677. The table has a barred series from 99 down to 2 for common words (80̄ de , 56̄ je , 51̄ luy , 53̄ la , 11̄ que , 9̄ quil , 38̄ ne , 73̄ est , 5̄ recherche ), a plain series on the figures the alphabet leaves free (24 sa , 28 sans , 29 se , 87 si , 45 tout , 62 vous , and the provinces), and a double-dotted series of names (99 Pape, 98 Roy, 88 Duc de Nevers, 70 Cardinal Gondi, 89 Duc de Mantoue, 54 Revol, 34 De Pizany, 1 Ambassadeur). In the letters the digit 1, and once 0, is dropped inside a group as a null, the device the sister key no. 45 prescribes in words. Tomokiyo read this passage with the figure 14 for 74 and the name as Beaulieu; the figures are 74 and, in the next passage, 54 Revol. “Car” [le duc de Nevers] alléguoit qu’il n’estoyt besoin qu’il a[l]la[s]t sans cela, parce qu’il ne feroit rien , then in clear “Je suys attendant des nouvelles de” [Revol] “à qui j’ay escript”. What reads continuously: [le duc de Nevers] ne sera receu come [ambassadeur] pour pluseurs resons. Je luy ay demandé … se [le Pape] voloit que … e[ll]e m’a dit n’avoir autre charge, ne me declarans que … je me … conten[t] … qu’il de cela et luy … [p]l[a]inte de lettre m’est … faict aller … pluseurs resons … pour en par… [le cardinal Gondi] [le duc de Mantoue] avec de m’avancer de plus pour faire ce que m’a esté escrit, qui est conforme au nostre. Ce qu’il faict tenir secret, et le … dans sa … [le cardinal Gondi] a … s’est nostre [q]uestion, est bruit … secrete, tout yra … Tomokiyo’s fragment stopped at “Je luy ay demandé”. The doubtful groups are listed in the transcription file; a lexicon scorer over the alternative null placements did not settle them, and the next pass is a re-reading of those spots with the Gondi decipherment as the guide to this copyist.

t: Nevers to Pisany, 1593 — the numerical key reads two letters, and the other five were never in it
h: The letters to Revol and key no. 60
b: The five letters to Revol are in the Court’s symbol cipher, Tomokiyo’s no. 60, endorsed “Chiffre baillé à Monsieur de Nevers, Montereau, aoust 1593”. Its enciphering sheet (fr. 3995 f. 109) gives four or five symbols for each letter, a syllabary ba … vu , word signs, Roman numerals for provinces, towns and persons ( iiij xx for 80), and a row of nulls; Nevers’s secretary added a deciphering table sorted by the shape of the symbols (ff. 110v–111). Both tables were read from the full-resolution images on 17 September 2026 and are transcribed in key60.txt ; the deciphering table is complete and legible, and it settles the values Tomokiyo found doubtful (the y-shaped sign is s , the 4-shaped sign is x , the crossed η is the doubling sign). The deciphering table, fr. 3995 f. 110v: Roman numerals, Arabic figures, letter-shapes. The cursive forms the copyist uses in the letters differ from the Court hand of the table, so the values were checked on Henri IV’s letter to Nevers of 7 October 1593 (fr. 3986 f. 151), a page in the same cipher with the office’s interlinear decipherment: plusieurs , contre , de la , promesse , respondre , Bellièvre , Villeroy , Zamet pin down thirty of the commonest signs. The Instruction of 31 August turned out to be the richer crib: part 2 of the Mémoires de Nevers is on Gallica after all (ark bpt6k64451005, reached through the catalogue notice rather than search), and its pp. 492–499 print the Instruction in clear; better, the cipher pages of the manuscript Instruction itself (fr. 3985, canvases 264–268) carry the office’s interlinear decipherment in the same copyist’s hand as the Revol letters, matching the print word for word. That gives three full pages of symbol–plaintext pairs in the target hand, on top of the King’s letter of 7 October. The crib: Henri IV to Nevers, Chartres, 7 October 1593, with the decipherment between the lines. The second crib: the Instruction of 31 August 1593 (fr. 3985), interlined by the office; the same text is printed in the Mémoires de Nevers , ii, 492–498. Where the cipher sits in the copies, from the full-resolution pages: 21 August, fr. 3985 f. 88–88v, six lines; 27 August, f. 115, one line (the earlier pages of that letter are in clear); 2 September, f. 176, about ten lines with the sign lxxix for Rome; 7 October, fr. 3986 f. 146v, nine lines; 9 October, f. 157v, four lines; 23 October, f. 198, five lines. The f. 146v and f. 157v passages are transcribed symbol by symbol ( ct_3986_f146v.txt , ct_3986_f157v.txt ) and run through the decoder; a second pass at higher magnification then showed that both pages, like the interlined Instruction, mix short cipher stretches into faded clear cursive, so those transcriptions over-read cipher and carry a revision note. Tomokiyo’s three anchors on f. 146v fall out of the table at once, l’absolution (λ 14 ꝑ 4 20 xx ‡ π ⊥ = la·b·so·l·u·t·i·o·n), à la vérité and intérêt , with qu’il , bien , et , que , nous , si around them; but between the anchors the output is still letter salad, because the copyist runs the small symbols together ( ue , ur , ıı , v ) and the same stroke stands for two or three table entries. The next pass is a glyph-level alignment of the copyist’s forms against the crib page in the same hand, then the other four letters. fr. 3986 f. 146v, the block of cipher in the letter from Vese, 7 October 1593. fr. 3986 f. 157v, the head of the letter from Coire, 9 October 1593.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series never deciphered
b: BL Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 74r is the only letter of Mary’s ciphered correspondence with Norfolk in the Tower with no contemporary decipherment, dated only “the tventi of this instant”. Tomokiyo rebuilt the key from the three deciphered siblings and overlaid a partial letter-by-letter decode. Here the key is checked on f. 66r, and the letter is read in 23 lines from the new British Library IIIF images, stitched from tiles. Written weeks after the Regent Moray’s murder: Elizabeth blames Mary for the harquebus shot, Morton is rumoured on the move, and Norfolk is to write through the Bishop of Ross or Lady Scrope, never in his own hand. Tutbury → the Tower · letter cipher with word signs and a nomenclator · February or March 1570 · read Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, 1570 British Library, Cotton MS Caligula C II, f. 74r · 23 lines, all in cipher · the one letter of the series with no contemporary decipherment · listed undeciphered by Tomokiyo, who reconstructed the key and overlaid a partial decode Tomokiyo’s key checked on the deciphered sibling f. 66r and applied to new images stitched from the BL’s IIIF tiles · the letter read line by line, with a handful of signs and spots still open · written within two months of the Regent Moray’s murder Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 Summary. Between October 1569 and August 1570 Thomas Howard, 4th Duke of Norfolk, was a prisoner in the Tower for his plan to marry Mary Queen of Scots, and Mary, at Tutbury in the Earl of Shrewsbury’s keeping, wrote to him in a private cipher. Cotton MS Caligula C II keeps four of those letters. Three have a decipherment made at the time and are in print; the fourth, f. 74r, is dated only the tventi of this instant and was never deciphered. Satoshi Tomokiyo rebuilt the key from the other three and published a decode of f. 74 as a letter-by-letter overlay on the image, with gaps, and a continuous transcript of about the first half in the source of his page. This page gives the whole letter as text, using his key and new images from the British Library’s IIIF service. Mary tells Norfolk to write to the B[ishop of Ross] of your part , or through your sister Scrup , and not to put anything in his own hand. She thanks God for delyvring us of our [enemy] Murray . Elizabeth sueves me the veyt of Murray death : she lays the blame for the harquebus shot at Linlithgow on Mary. There is a rumour that Morton is on the move, and news has come from York. She ends yours feithful til death . Status: read in 23 lines. Five nomenclator signs have no value in the key, and a few words are still unread: two groups in line 1, the end of line 4 under a stain, and a few single words. Much of the letter-level decoding is Tomokiyo’s. What is new here is the continuous reading, the fill of his gaps, the sense and the names, and the date.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series never deciphered
b: Cotton MS Caligula C II is a volume of Scottish state papers from Burghley’s circle. Folios 66 to 75 hold Mary’s ciphered letters to Norfolk that were intercepted or surrendered, with deciphered copies. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana page on Mary’s ciphers ( mary.htm ) lists them this way: Folio Date on the letter Decipherment In print f. 66r “last of Januarie” [31 Jan 1570] transcription f. 67, decipherment f. 72 Labanoff iii p. 19 f. 69 “the xv of this instant” [15 Jan 1570] f. 70 Labanoff iii p. 11 f. 74r “the tventi of this instant” none none found f. 75 [18 Apr 1570] clear text f. 73, roughly corresponding Labanoff iii p. 35 Tomokiyo marks f. 74 “undeciphered”. He found no matching letter in Labanoff’s Lettres de Marie Stuart , vol. 3, or in Froude, and took the address my oun good lord as a sign that it too is from Mary to Norfolk. He then reconstructed the key from the deciphered letters (“Mary-Norfolk Cipher (1570)”, corrected 16 July 2023). With it he printed the first two lines as a paraphrase, “I have, my own good lord, your friendly [letter??] [with??] no [g?]entle satisfaction and for * I will never [do??] anything in hand …”, and left two further pieces of work that are not on the visible page. One is an HTML comment in the page source: a continuous transcript as far as about line 11 ( … in? deliveri[n]g us of our * the Queen of England … ). The other is an image, mary_CottonCaligulaCII_f74.png , with his decode written in magenta over each of the 23 lines, letter by letter. Unkeyed signs are shown as asterisks, doubtful letters as queries, and words are not divided. That overlay is the starting point, and it has to be credited. For most lines it already has the letters, including murton is gon to , Talbo and herkebus . This page adds the reading. The letters are divided into words and made into sentences, and many of his asterisks and queries are filled. Line 8, which the comment leaves out when it runs and I shall be your sister scrup from the end of line 7 into line 9, is restored. The names are identified and the letter is dated. The verso, f. 74v, has no address. It carries only a short note written upside down relative to the text, with a mark above it; the note reads Norffolke (or Northfolke ).

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series never deciphered
b: The British Library’s new viewer publishes the volume as a IIIF manifest ( bl.digirati.io/iiif/ark:/81055/vdc_100162985756.0x000001 , reached from the Search Archives record for Caligula C II). The image service claims IIIF level 2 but will not return an image more than about 1,024 pixels on a side. The full leaf is 7,144 × 10,328 pixels, so fetch.py and region.py ask for 1,024-pixel tiles and paste them back together. The text block of f. 74r is the region from x 1000 to 6500 and y 4900 to 9800, at full resolution. strips.py finds the centre of each line in five vertical bands from the ink profile and cuts 23 strips that follow the slope of each line, so a line can be read at magnification from end to end. F. 74r, left half of lines 1–5: I have, my oun good lord, … / I will never take anithing in hand … / -ept I var sur it var to your veil … . The letters are separate signs written continuously. Word signs (the barred forms, the boxed cross ⊞ for for ) stand among them without spaces (British Library, IIIF, stitched from tiles).

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series never deciphered
b: The cipher is a simple substitution of one sign for each letter, with no homophones except f . Nulls are scattered through the text, even inside words. About twenty word signs and a handful of name signs complete it. This is Tomokiyo’s reconstruction. Before it was applied to f. 74, it was checked against f. 66r, whose contemporary transcription and decipherment survive (ff. 67, 72). The opening of f. 66r, My oun lord, I vret to you befor to knou your pleasur if I schould sik to mak an entrepryse , reads correctly with it. The control, f. 66r, lines 1–3: the letter of the last of January 1570, whose decipherment (f. 72) is printed by Labanoff.
