t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series never deciphered
b: The letter gives only the day, the tventi of this instant , without a month or place. The content fixes it closely enough: After Moray’s murder. The Regent was shot with a harquebus at Linlithgow on 23 January 1570 by James Hamilton of Bothwellhaugh and died the same night. The letter thanks God for delyvring us of our {o—} Murray , speaks of Murray death , and has Elizabeth talking as if I would caus schut her friend a harkebus-schut . So the 20th is not 20 January. Elizabeth already knows, and blames Mary. Labanoff’s chronology puts Elizabeth’s receipt of the news, and her placing of the Bishop of Ross in the Bishop of London’s custody, on 10 February. Norfolk in the Tower. He was there from October 1569 to August 1570, which fits the warnings about writing and the talk of forces and meanes . Mary’s letters of January to April 1570 printed by Labanoff are dated from Tutbury. That leaves 20 February or 20 March 1570. One point leans towards February without settling it. Labanoff prints (iii, pp. 31–33) a decipherment of Mary to Norfolk dated the 19th of march which opens I have forborn this long time to write to you, in respect of the dangers of writing and grieves for Pembroke, who died on 17 March. A letter written the next day that says nothing of Pembroke would be odd. So would one written a day after she said she had not written for a long time. F. 74 says neither.

b: Five unkeyed signs. ⊕ in line 2 (read from the sense as unless ), a circle with a b inside (⊘) in line 8 (a person, perhaps a nomenclator for a name), ø after Murray death in line 13, ⊗ in line 17 (someone Norfolk might have write for him), and the two dash signs in lines 5 and 11 ({a—}, {o—}). The {o—} before Murray is read as enemy in the paraphrase only from the sense. None of these occurs on the three deciphered leaves often enough to fix it. Unread spots. In line 1, the two groups after your friendl[y] and the group ∠ s 3 ɹ after lord ; the end of line 4 under a stain; single words in lines 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17, marked [..] above. Line 16 is the weakest line: [ane?] this: nicht to me Lord Talbot is read letter by letter, but how it hangs together is a guess. Word division and sense. The signs run on without spaces and nulls stand inside words, so the division into words is an editorial choice. In lines 5–6 and 9–10 the sentences are read as closely as the words allow, and the paraphrase should be taken as one reading of them. The month. February or March 1570, as set out above. Nothing on the leaf decides between them. The hand. Tomokiyo remarks that the hand of the Norfolk ciphers looks like Mary’s own but differs in the h and in spelling from her autograph letters, and suggests comparing it with her secretary Raulet’s. That was not attempted here.

t: The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 — already read by George Lasry, and 61 more nomenclator groups recovered
b: Twenty-four ciphered despatches of Clement XI’s Secretariat to the nuncio at Madrid (ASV Segr. Stato Spagna 364D, DECODE R154–R177), catalogued here as an unread transcription job behind a login. They were neither. George Lasry reconstructed the key in October 2020 and filed his segmented decipherment of the whole Spagna 364 corpus on every one of the records; measured token by token it reads 97.6 per cent of the 34,243 cipher groups. The gap was the nomenclator, where 189 of the 399 four-digit groups in use carried no value. Because the key is alphabetical in runs, 61 of them are recovered from the brackets and the corpus contexts — promozione, aggiustamento, giurisdizione, tribunale, vascelli, Vicerè, corriere — and the calendar block resolves into two parallel Gennaio–Dicembre runs, with 4538 Luglio confirmed by the date of Alberoni’s promotion. Rome → the nuncio at Madrid · homophonic cipher with a nomenclator · 1718–1720 · already solved; key extended The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 Archivio Segreto Vaticano, i. 1025, Segretario di Stato, Spagna, dossier 364D · twenty-four ciphered despatches, 4 January 1718 to 6 January 1720 · DECODE R154–R177, 90 pages · catalogue item 249, rated “noted”: a transcription job behind a login Not a transcription job and not unread · George Lasry reconstructed the key in October 2020 and his decipherment of the whole corpus sits on every record · measured here at 97.6 % read · the real gap was the nomenclator, and 61 of its 189 valueless groups are recovered Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue listed this dossier as a job of transcription: DECODE calls the records “partially decrypted” and notes a contemporary decipherment written into the letters, so the text was presumed read at the time and merely unpublished. Both halves of that were wrong. The contemporary marginal decipherment is a few words a page and several of them are mistakes. What is actually on the records is much better: each of the twenty-four carries, as an attachment, a reconstructed key signed George Lasry, 24 October 2020 , and an 800 KB file holding his segmented decipherment of the whole Spagna 364 corpus — volume 364C items 1–32 and 364D items 1–24, the digit stream cut into groups with the plaintext aligned underneath. The cipher was solved six years ago and the letters have been readable ever since. Measured token by token, Lasry’s reading gives a value to 33,408 of the 34,243 cipher tokens in 364D, 97.6 per cent . The one real gap is in the nomenclator: his filed key lists 268 four-digit groups, the corpus uses 399, so 189 groups — 11.0 per cent of all nomenclator tokens — stood without a value . Those do not need cryptanalysis, because the key is alphabetical in runs and the corpus is 85,000 tokens long: each unvalued group has a bracket from its lettered neighbours and a dozen contexts to read it in. Sixty-one groups are recovered here , among them promozione , aggiustamento , giurisdizione , tribunale , vascelli , Vicerè , corriere , cifra and negoziato , together with the entire calendar block, which resolves into two parallel Gennaio–Dicembre runs. Unknown nomenclator usage falls from 11.0 to 3.4 per cent across the corpus. Status: already solved by others; nothing about the system was open. What is new is the measurement and the key extension.

b: From Lasry’s key sheet, whose editorial notes state the design outright: The despatch is an undivided stream of digits, with no word division and no group separation. Ordinary elements are two digits ; nomenclator elements are four digits beginning with 4 . Reading is therefore deterministic: a 4 opens a four-digit group, anything else is a pair. The single digit 3 is a null — except when it falls among the three digits after a 4 prefix, where it belongs to the nomenclator group and is not a null. This is the one place the scheme is not context-free, and Lasry flags it. Homophony is modest for letters and heavy for punctuation: 50 alone for a , 17|71 for i , 12|21 for c , but six variants for the full stop ( 303|323|343|363|373|393 ). A few two-digit groups are syllables or short words rather than letters — 91|94 = che , 55 = con , 78|88 = del , 01 = al . The nomenclator is where the design shows. It is not one alphabet but a series of runs, each ordered alphabetically within itself, and this is what makes the missing values recoverable: range contents 4001–4078 particles, pronouns and word endings, loosely alphabetical ( ancora, ben, come, essere, fare, molto, quando, quanto, questo, tutto, -zione ) 4079–4296 nouns, titles and names, A–R ( Arcivescovo, Armi, Auditore, Camera, Capitolo, Chiesa, Concistoro, Corte, Ecclesiastica, Guerra, Imperatore, Italia, Napoli, Pace, Regni, Religione ) 4401–4479 the same alphabet continued, S–V ( risoluzione, Roma, S. Sede, scrittura, sempre, Sig.re, Spagna, spedizione, subito, tempo, troppo, Turco, Ungheria, Vienna ) 4485–4531 calendar words and the day numbers, 4501–4531 = 01–31 in plain order 4532–4543, 4552–4563 two parallel month runs, Gennaio to Dicembre (see below) 4564–4619 a second alphabetical run, A–T ( aggiustamento, alcun, altro, attenzione, Breve, conforme, costì, dispaccio, giustizia, parola, possibile, pubblico, riflessione, stesso, tempi ) 4681, 4706, 4870+ scattered later blocks ( Cristian-, contro, espulsione, present- )

b: No cryptanalysis was needed and none was done. The method has two halves, and a value was only accepted when both agreed, or when one of them was overwhelming on its own. The bracket. Because each run is alphabetical, an unvalued group is pinned between its nearest valued neighbours. 4467 sits between 4466 troppo and 4468 Turco , so it begins tr… to tu… . 4198 sits between 4197 maggior and 4200 necessari . 4233 sits between 4231 occasione and the opportun­ recovered at 4236, so it is of… . The contexts. The corpus is 84,961 tokens with everything else already read, so each unvalued group comes with its sentences. 4467 appears in “far retrocedere le numerose — che si dicono già incamminate” and “presi nelle proprie case con — di fanteria”. Both halves give truppe . The agreement of the two is the check. 4469 lies between Turco and Vescovo , so it is va–ve ; its contexts are “li — di Spagna hanno preso camino”, “il soccorso de’ — da mandarsi in Levante” and a list of “due palandre et undici barche”. Vascelli satisfies both and nothing else does. The calendar block, and the control it supplies. The month codes fell out as a structure rather than one at a time. Lasry’s sheet has only three of them: 4535 “Apte” , 4539 Agosto , 4562 Novembre . The corpus uses 4533 to 4539 contiguously and 4560 to 4562, always after a day number and before passato or corrente . Two parallel Gennaio–Dicembre runs at 4532–4543 and 4552–4563 place Agosto at 4539 and Novembre at 4562 exactly, and make Lasry’s puzzling “Apte” simply Aprile , the fourth slot. That scheme puts Luglio at 4538, and 4538 then supplies its own proof. The corpus has “in data delli 4499 4538 passato, qual appunto fu il giorno della promozione del Sig. Card.” Giulio Alberoni was created cardinal by Clement XI on 12 July 1717 . The month run, derived from an offset, lands on Luglio; the day code beside it is 12; and the sentence names the day of the promotion. Three independent things agree, and 4499 = 12 comes free.

t: The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 — already read by George Lasry, and 61 more nomenclator groups recovered
b: These are Clement XI’s Secretariat writing to the nuncio at Madrid in the two years when relations with Philip V collapsed: Alberoni’s Sardinian and Sicilian expeditions, the Quadruple Alliance, and Spain’s retaliation against the Roman jurisdiction. Two words run through everything and both of them were among the unvalued groups, which is a fair measure of what the gap in the key was costing. The first is promozione , the 45-token group: whether Rome would make the promotion Alberoni wanted, and whether it should be held back as leverage. The second is aggiustamento , the settlement of the “note pendenze” — the giurisdizione , the tribunale of the nunciature in Spain, the abolition of the Nunziatura at Naples, the espulsione of the nuncio. Around them run the vascelli of Spain taking their course for the Levante, the Emperor’s truppe in the Ferrarese, the Turco , and the Trattato of the neutrality of Italy. A specimen of the text as it now reads, from 364D/3, where the transcription is clean and no group in the span is unvalued — the Secretariat on the Spanish ambassador at Rome, Cardinal Acquaviva: … Card. e Acquaviva, a cui non solo per mezzo mio ma da sé stesso ha procurato N.S. di fare conoscere l’indispensabile necessità di tal sospensione. Non mostrando d’appagarsene, pretese di rimuoverne N.S. con dedurre le sue ragioni compilate nella scrittura, di cui, non con altra mira, se le manda copia che per fare vedere costì la loro insussistenza et la stranezza delle [ragioni] con le quali si sostengono…

t: The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 — already read by George Lasry, and 61 more nomenclator groups recovered
b: 135 nomenclator groups still without a value , in 221 tokens — 3.4 per cent of nomenclator usage across the corpus. Almost all occur once to four times, which is why they resisted: a single context, often in a badly transcribed line, does not settle a value against a bracket several letters wide. The frequent ones among them are 4434 (13 tokens, somewhere in the S run), 4130 (10, a person named “il Sig. e —” who carries news to N.S., bracketed D–E), 4795, 4340, 4213 and 4063, all in passages the transcribers left half-legible. 722 tokens unvalued in 364D overall (2.1 per cent), the great majority of them two-digit groups the 2016–17 transcribers could not read. These are an image problem, not a cipher problem, and the images are behind the DECODE login. Volume 364C (items 1–32) is covered by the same key and the same corpus file and was used here only as context for the key extension. It has not been read through on its own account. Three of the twenty-four items (R172, R174, R176) are dated 1717 and fall outside the dossier’s stated span; they are in the same cipher and were measured with the rest.

t: A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 — the three keys bound with it do not fit
b: BnF fr. 3413 no. 62 was catalogued with three cipher keys bound in the same volume that might read it. None does. The letter, from a secretary of Cardinal Pellevé in Rome to Jean de Piles of the League’s council in Paris, is almost all in clear and carries the news of Henri III’s murder as it reached Rome. Its ninety-odd signs of cipher are in the Nevers–Piles alphabet that Tomokiyo identified. His partial table was filled out from a deciphered letter of 1586 in fr. 4715 in the same cipher. Rome → the League council in Paris · symbol cipher inside a clear letter · 23 August 1589 · read in part A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 BnF fr. 3413 no. 62 · a secretary of Cardinal Pellevé writes to Jean de Piles, of the League’s council in Paris, as the news of Henri III’s murder reaches Rome · catalogued with three cipher keys bound in the same volume None of the three keys fits · the cipher is the Nevers–Piles alphabet, filled out from a deciphered letter of 1586 · most of the ciphered words now read, about thirty signs are still open Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 18 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue entry supposed that one of three keys bound in BnF fr. 3413, nos. 53, 61 and 69, might read the letter at no. 62. None of them does. No. 53 is a numerical key and the letter has no figures. No. 61 is an Italian key with a different set of signs. No. 69 is a League key in which the square sign is e , where the letter needs n . The letter is almost all in clear . It comes from a secretary of Cardinal Pellevé in Rome, dated 23 August [1589], and carries the news of Henri III’s death. About ninety signs are in cipher, in short groups. Satoshi Tomokiyo identified the cipher as the Nevers–Piles alphabet and read one name in it. His table comes from BnF fr. 3612, which is not digitised, and it is partial. It was filled out here from BnF fr. 4715 f. 2 , a letter of 1586 in the same cipher whose decipherer wrote the plaintext above each line. The readings: Mons. Cassin , la protection , vostre regne , depeschera , mon maitre a esté retiré , and the signature, probably Baron . Status: read in part. The bound keys were tested and none fits. About thirty signs, most of them code signs, are still open.

t: A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 — the three keys bound with it do not fit
b: Fr. 3413 is a Nevers-collection volume of League papers, on Gallica as btv1b52510705j . No. 62 is ff. 126r–127r (views 259–261), and the address is on f. 127v: A Monsieur, Monsieur l’Abbé d’Orbais, Con er au Conseil estably a Paris pour la S te Union, A Paris . The abbé d’Orbais is Jean de Piles. He was the League’s envoy to Rome earlier in 1589 and later a deputy of the clergy at the Estates of 1593. The letter is dated only “du lieu que vous sçavez ce xxiij e d’Aoust”, but its content fixes the year. It reports how the news of the King’s death came to Rome. A courier from Spain had passed through Lyon on the 12th. The Grand Duke of Tuscany sent an express, which reached Rome on the 20th. It carried the Duke of Lorraine’s copy of a letter of 8 August from his agent in Paris, the s r Bardin: le Roy a esté tué, et c’est le Roy de Navarre qui l’a faict faire, l’on a proclamé Roy a Paris Mons. le Cardinal de Bourbon, et au mesme temps le Roy de Navarre s’est aussi faict appeller Roy par ceux de sa secte The writer apologises that his senior colleague, “son aisné de mesme charge”, has been kept from writing by a fever for a fortnight. He asks Piles to keep him in mind, and he signs in cipher.

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Doubled letters written with consecutive figures betray a regular key (consonants three figures each from 7, vowels from 64, nulls 91–111). Every spelled word reads, and the nomenclator is then confirmed clause for clause against Wentworth’s own dispatches in Knowler’s Strafforde’s Letters (1739): the King refusing Kildare, and Ormonde moved for the Council “in exchange” for Sir Piers Crosby. Ireland / England · nomenclator · 1634–35 · solved Lord Maltravers to the Earl of Ormonde Dorking, 13 September 1634 and Whitehall, 22 January 1634/5 · HMC, Calendar of the Manuscripts of the Marquess of Ormonde , i (1895), pp. 28–29 The letter alphabet, its nulls and the layout of the key recovered from 59 printed figures; the nomenclator then confirmed clause for clause against Wentworth’s own dispatches Daniel Bourdeau · solved 15 September 2026 Summary. Two letters from Henry Frederick Howard, Lord Maltravers, to James Butler, Earl (later Duke) of Ormonde, contain 59 figures of a numerical cipher, printed undeciphered by the Historical Manuscripts Commission in 1895 and listed as unsolved by S. Tomokiyo. The figures divide cleanly into letters (below 91), nulls (91–111) and a small nomenclator (112 and above). The doubled letters in letters and councellor are written with consecutive figures, which betrays a regular key: consonants in alphabetical order, three figures each from 7, vowels from 64. With it every spelled word reads — angry , letters , Crosby , a councellor — and the nomenclator falls into place from the history of the 1634 Irish Parliament: Kildare came to England "because he was angry [with] the Lord Deputy, [and the King] refused to see him because he brought no letters from the Lord Deputy"; and in January 1635 "the Lord Deputy hath written … much in praise of Ormonde … for his good carriage in Parliament, and upon his motion Ormonde is to be a councellor" — Ormonde was sworn of the Irish Privy Council that month. Wentworth’s own dispatches, printed by Knowler in 1739, describe both events in the same terms: the King “refuseth to admit” Kildare, and Ormonde is moved for the Council “in exchange” for Sir Piers Crosby, with the warrant to swear him sent back in the margin. Status: solved. Seven of the nine nomenclator codes are fixed by the documents; the two parties in one clause about Crosby (185, 149) are not.

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Maltravers (1608–1652), heir of the Earl of Arundel, sat in the Irish Parliament of 1634 and was a friend and correspondent of the young Earl of Ormonde. His letters from England report court news; the sensitive parts — the quarrel between the Earl of Kildare and the Lord Deputy, Wentworth, and what was being written about Ormonde himself — are in figures. The originals are in the Ormonde papers (now National Library of Ireland); the only witness online is the HMC calendar, whose figures were checked against the page scans. HMC Ormonde MSS, old series i (1895), p. 28 — the letter of 13 September 1634 (Internet Archive, calmarqormonde01greauoft ). 13 Sept 1634: ...he came over because he was 65, 35, 21, 26, 59, 98, 113, 186, 108, 143, refused to see him because he brought no 28, 69, 49, 50, 70, 44, 89, from 186, 99. 22 Jan 1634/5: You desire to know what 93, 185, 95, hath written unto 99, 149, concerning 98, 10, 44, 79, 47, 8, 59, for whom 270 thus hereafter ... 95, 186, 98 hath written unto 98, 218, 97 much in praise of 100, 174, 103 in general, and particularly for his good carriage in 111, 95, 221, and upon his motion 93, 31, 174 99 is to be 64, 99, 11, 79, 85, 35, 12, 69, 28, 29, 79, 44, in which courses 174 shall do well to continue.

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Red = spelled in cipher · blue = nomenclator code, value from the documents in §05 · nulls dropped 13 September 1634. My lord of Kildare is long ago in England though I have not seen him; it is said he came over because he was angry [113 = with] [186 = the Lord Deputy] ; [143 = the King] refused to see him because he brought no letters from [186 = the Lord Deputy] . 22 January 1634/5. You desire to know what [185] hath written unto [149] concerning Crosby , for whom 270 thus hereafter; of which I can give you no account at all, only by what I hear it is like to go worser with him rather than better. [186 = the Lord Deputy] hath written unto [218 = Secretary Coke] much in praise of [174 = Ormonde] in general, and particularly for his good carriage in [221 = Parliament] , and upon his motion [174 = Ormonde] is to be a councellor , in which courses [174 = Ormonde] shall do well to continue. The history confirms the reading. George FitzGerald, 16th Earl of Kildare, fell out with Wentworth over the Kildare estates during the 1634 Parliament and crossed to England that summer; Sir Piers Crosby, having opposed the Lord Deputy in the same Parliament, was removed from the Irish Council early in 1635; and Ormonde, who had backed Wentworth in the Commons debates, was sworn of the Irish Privy Council in January 1635 — the very month of the second letter. 186 as the Lord Deputy is used three times consistently; 174 as Ormonde ("your lordship") three times; 221 as Parliament follows "his good carriage in". The next section fixes 143, 218 and 113 from Wentworth’s own letters; 185 and 149 remain open.

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Wentworth’s dispatches were printed in 1739 by William Knowler as The Earl of Strafforde’s Letters and Dispatches . Volume I covers 1634–35, and the events behind both cipher passages are in it, in Wentworth’s own words, with Secretary Coke’s answers in the margin. Wentworth to Coke, October 1634 (i. 309). “The Earl of Kildare went away from hence without the privity of this State, and in seeming displeasure against me … within an hour after, he put to sea for England. Indeed I should not have mentioned thus much, but that I hear his Majesty refuseth to admit him to kiss his hand , which I acknowledge as a respect to me.” Margin: “The Earl of Kildare shall be sent back as is advised.” That is Maltravers’s sentence of 13 September: Kildare angry [113] the Lord Deputy ; the King refused to see him because he brought no letters from the Lord Deputy. So 143 = the King , and 113 is the connective between “angry” and the Lord Deputy (“with”; Wentworth’s word is “against”). Wentworth to Coke, Dublin 22 December 1634 (i. 352–3). “In the Higher House, there is my Lord of Ormond, that hath as much advantage of the rest in judgment and parts, as he hath in estate and blood; and one, who upon my observation since I came hither, expresseth very good affections to the Crown and Government; so as I hold him a person of consequence, and fit to receive some mark of his Majesty’s favour, and humbly offer it to his Majesty’s wisdom, whether it were not seasonable to make him a Counsellor … so as I should think we had got much the better by the exchange of the Earl of Ormond for Sir Piers Crosby .” Margin: “for the Earl of Ormond, your Lordship shall receive herewith his Majesty’s warrant to swear him Counsellor, according to your advice.” Maltravers, a month later: the Lord Deputy hath written unto [218] much in praise of [Ormonde] in general, and particularly for his good carriage in [Parliament], and upon his motion [Ormonde] is to be a councellor . The match is clause for clause: 186 = the Lord Deputy , 174 = Ormonde , 221 = Parliament (Wentworth’s “Higher House”), and 218 = Mr Secretary Coke , the addressee of the dispatch. The dispatch was for the King and Coke’s marginalia are the King’s answers, so “the King” is the alternative for 218, but the King already has 143. 270 is the code Maltravers assigns to Crosby after spelling the name once. James Howell, writing to Wentworth from Westminster on 1 January 1635, has Crosby in England and “in a bravery resolved never to see Ireland while your Lordship governs”: the court gossip behind “like to go worser with him”. code value evidence 186 the Lord Deputy (Wentworth) three consistent uses; Knowler i. 309, 352–3 174 the Earl of Ormonde three uses; Knowler i. 352–3 and Coke’s marginal 221 the Parliament “good carriage in” ↔ “in the Higher House” 143 the King “refused to see him” ↔ “his Majesty refuseth to admit him to kiss his hand” 218 Mr Secretary Coke (or the King, through Coke) addressee of the 22 December dispatch 270 Sir Piers Crosby assigned in the text 113 with / against connective between “angry” and the Lord Deputy 185 unidentified party “what 185 hath written unto 149 concerning Crosby”; not the Lord Deputy 149 unidentified party same clause; not the King or the Lord Deputy

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: 185 and 149. Ormonde had asked what one party had written to another about Crosby, and Maltravers “can give you no account at all”. Since the Lord Deputy and the King have their own codes in the same letters, these are other parties unless the key carried homophones: the adjacent numbering of 185 and 186 suggests a grouped list of officers (Lord Treasurer beside Lord Deputy), and 149 beside 143 the royal or Council group. Only the key sheet, or Ormonde’s letter asking the question, would settle it. The fourth figure of angry is printed 26 , which the grid makes k ; r is 43–45. The scan confirms the print, so either Maltravers slipped or the 1895 transcriber misread 44/45. "Angry" is the only word that fits a n g ? y . 89 at the end of letter is either u (a slip for s , if the vowel blocks are six wide) or a null/plural sign (if they are five wide). 31 (= m ) before 174 in "upon his motion 31 174 is to be" is unexplained — perhaps "m[y lord]" begun and abandoned. A key sheet, if one survives, would be among the Ormonde papers (NLI) or the Arundel papers; neither is online. t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
b: Six Ordnungspolizei radio messages from the Eastern Front in the Army’s double-box cipher, published by Frode Weierud and posted by Klaus Schmeh in 2020 as unsolved. One has a Bletchley decrypt: sixteen police killed on the Bobruisk–Mogilev road and the village of Borki razed. The five of 27 February 1942 turn out to share one key, 970 letters. Every ciphertext-only attack fails, on the real text and on a synthetic control of the same size, because the second pass through the same boxes leaves no gradient. A known-plaintext solver needs about 80 pairs, and the Borki decrypt does not align with its ciphertext. Mogilev, Rovno, Proskurov → Berlin · Doppelkastenschlüssel, two boxes, two passes · February and June 1942 · not solved German police double-box radiograms, 1942 Six radio messages of the Ordnungspolizei on the Eastern Front, intercepted at Beaumanor, kept in NSA’s Historic Cryptographic Collection at NARA, and published by Frode Weierud (CryptoCellar, 5 August 2020); Klaus Schmeh posted them as unsolved on 30 August 2020. One of them has a Bletchley decrypt; the other five do not. The five messages of 27 February 1942 are one key, 970 letters. No ciphertext-only attack tried here breaks them, and none breaks synthetic text of the same size either. A known-plaintext solver would, from about 80 pairs. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 18 September 2026 Summary. In 1942 the German Order Police enciphered their radio traffic in the Army’s double-box system: two 5×5 boxes, each letter pair enciphered twice through the same boxes. Weierud published six intercepts. The message of 16 June 1942 from Mogilev has a plaintext, the Bletchley decrypt reproduced by Hanyok in Eavesdropping on Hell : sixteen men of Police Battalion 51 killed on the Bobruisk–Mogilev road, and the village of Borki razed and its inhabitants “liquidated”. The five messages of 27 February 1942 have none. Their discriminator groups show that all five, seven parts and 970 letters, are enciphered in one daily key. Every ciphertext-only attack tried here fails on them: single encipherment is excluded outright, and for the double encipherment annealing, staged scoring, tempering, relaxation and EM all fail on a synthetic 970-letter text with a known key as well, so the failure on the real text says nothing about the plaintext. The failure is measured: the true key sits in a basin eight to ten swaps wide, and the second pass leaves the search nothing to climb outside it. A known-plaintext solver recovers the boxes from about 80 plaintext–ciphertext pairs. The obvious source of pairs, Bletchley’s text of the June message, does not align with its ciphertext under any spelling, layout or length tried, so the words enciphered were not the words in the decrypt. Status: not solved. What would finish it is about 80 known pairs for one key: Bletchley’s decrypts of the 27 February traffic (TNA HW 16/17, not online), or the exact German wording of the June message.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
b: A115 is Nr. 14 from Mogilev, callsign SQF, the station at the headquarters of the Higher SS and Police Leader Russia Centre, handed in at 2325 on 16 June 1942 by its preamble and taken down at Beaumanor on 3742 kHz; stations 51 and 43 both copied it. Hanyok’s Eavesdropping on Hell (NSA, 2005) follows this one message from intercept to decrypt, and reproduces Bletchley’s decrypt as entry 21 of that day’s German police decrypts: Bletchley’s decrypt of A115, entry 21. NARA, RG 457, HCC, Box 1386, as reproduced in Hanyok, Eavesdropping on Hell (NSA, 2005). An Rf SS und Chef Orpo. An Strasse BOBRUISK–MOGILEW, Partisanenkampf: 16 Mann von Pol. Batl. 51 gefallen. Das Dorf BORKI, in dem Waffen und Munition gefunden wurden, wurde dem Erdboden gleichgemacht. Die Einwohnerschaft liquidiert. Von Höheren SS und Pol.führer Russland Mitte. To the Reichsführer SS and the Chief of the Order Police: in a fight with partisans on the Bobruisk–Mogilev road, sixteen men of Police Battalion 51 were killed; the village of Borki, where weapons and ammunition had been found, was levelled; the inhabitants were liquidated. From the Higher SS and Police Leader Russia Centre. Hanyok notes that several villages named Borki exist in present-day Belarus and does not locate this one. The decrypt is what makes this group of messages “partially solved” in Schmeh’s 2021 list of unsolved Second World War ciphers. An odd count The message is 228 letters in both intercepts and in the German preamble. Without the discriminator that leaves 223, but the cipher works on pairs and every enciphered text has an even length. The German clerk therefore added or dropped a letter, or a letter was lost in transmission. Where it went can be measured. A double-box cipher is deterministic on pairs, so a repeated plaintext pair in the same position of the layout gives a repeated cipher pair, and the pairs only show their repeats when they are counted from the right starting point. Counted from the end, A115 has 25 repeated digraphs of 19 types. Counted from the start it has 8, which is chance level. So the stray letter lies among the first nine or so, and the rest of the text pairs up normally.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
b: Weierud reads the discriminator as the last three letters of the group, in any order, and cites the Bletchley note that four discriminators were issued with each daily key. Read that way, with the O/Q confusion allowed for in one group, the seven parts of 27 February use exactly four: discriminator parts WOJ D33 ( KFWOJ ); D67 part 1 ( OWQWJ , read OWOWJ ) OSX D34 part 1 ( DNOSX ); D67 part 2 ( WNSXO ) ANR D34 part 2 ( DRANR ); E72 part 2 ( LENRA ) WYY E72 part 1 ( SBWYY ) Two parts of one message carry different discriminators, and the Mogilev and Proskurov traffic shares them. The four are therefore four names for one key, and all seven parts, 970 letters, can be attacked together. C43’s XOS is also OSX , which suggests either that it is misdated by a year or that a key ran for more than one day; Weierud already noticed the shared indicator. C43 was kept out of the pooled text.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
b: Two manuals survive and both were read here: the OKH draft Schlüsselanleitung zum Doppelkastenschlüssel of 2 December 1940 and the OKW issue of December 1941. They agree. There are two 5×5 boxes. The plaintext is written in double lines of 17 letters, and the pairs are the letters that stand one under the other; a remainder too short for a double line is split in half. Each pair is enciphered twice with the same boxes. When the two letters of a pair fall in the same row, each cipher letter is taken from the right. The spelling rules are CH → Q, ß → SZ, and the hyphen written STRIQ. The reference implementation, dk.py , enciphers both manuals’ worked examples letter for letter (the 1941 manual prints tylhu on p. 5 for the tvlhu it has correctly on p. 6). The Army’s “NI” field cipher, as NSA’s Cryptologic Quarterly describes it, is the same scheme with 21 -letter lines and the left neighbour for same-row pairs; its worked examples (EU → VR → QZ, en → FL → NC, ea → HK → TT) also reproduce exactly. Which variant the police used is not documented, so every attack here was run under both. That February 1942 is the double-box period at all rests on Hanyok: the police changed from double transposition to double Playfair between September and early November 1941, and Bletchley found the new system easier to read. The cross-row identity The double pass is what matters. After the first pass the first letter of a pair has been taken from box B, but the second pass looks it up in box A. So each letter is used by its position in both boxes. Write each letter as four coordinates: its row and column in A and its row and column in B. Deciphering a cipher pair (c1, c2) in the cross-row case gives the intermediate pair v1 = A[ B-row of c1 ][ A-col of c2 ] v2 = B[ A-row of c2 ][ B-col of c1 ] and the plaintext pair p1 = A[ B-row of v1 ][ A-col of v2 ] p2 = B[ A-row of v2 ][ B-col of v1 ] Every step mixes an A-coordinate with a B-coordinate. Between the two passes sits the map from each letter’s cell in box A to its cell in box B, a random permutation of the 25 cells. Section 06 shows why that permutation, rather than the size of the key, is what stops the attacks.

b: A failed search proves nothing without a control, so each attack on the double encipherment was first run on synthetic text: 970 letters of German text enciphered twice with random boxes by mksyn.py and dk.py , in parts of the same lengths as the real ones. Scores are quadgram log-probabilities per letter from 25-letter German tables ( build_lm.py ); German text scores about −3.9 and random letters about −6. hypothesis or method result verdict Single encipherment, all seven parts pooled, line length 1–30, pairs in written and reversed order best −5.91 per letter against about −3.9 for German excluded Single encipherment per part and per discriminator group, line lengths 1, 17 and 21, both pair orders −5.0 to −5.6, the level at which short texts overfit noise excluded Double encipherment, simulated annealing on quadgrams ( dksolve2.cs ) on the synthetic 970-letter text it never leaves noise (−6.0); started four swaps from the true key, it does not climb back fails on its control Staged unigram → bigram → quadgram scoring; steepest-ascent iterated local search; parallel tempering; relabelling moves; a row/column product score; Sinkhorn relaxation on GPU ( relax.py ); hard EM with the plaintext as a variable ( emsolve.cs ) all fail on the synthetic text. Random starts stall at unigram score −1.39 to −1.42, where the true key scores −1.221 fails on its control The same, with the true A-cell → B-cell permutation given and only the letter labelling searched still stalls at −1.42 fails on its control SAT solving (z3) with 20 to 37 known pairs no answer within 15 minutes for any case inconclusive Known plaintext, meet-in-the-middle score ( kpsolve.cs ): encipher the plaintext pair once, decipher the cipher pair once, and score row-by-row and column-by-column agreement of the two intermediates from random starts, recovers the boxes from 111 synthetic pairs in about a minute (111 of 111 consistent); 80 pairs nearly (68 of 80); fails at 60 or fewer, or with 10% of the pairs wrong works on its control Key-free alignment of Bletchley’s A115 text to its ciphertext ( align115c.py , align115h.py ): repeated cipher pairs must match repeated plaintext pairs; exact backtracking over spellings, X separators, numbers written out, address and signature placement, Borki / Mohilew / Bobruiisk variants, 222 or 224 letters, line lengths 1–24 no consistent alignment. The same search recovers a synthetic spelling in 35 seconds no alignment The single-encipherment results exclude that hypothesis: the pooled text is 970 letters, far more than a single-pass double box needs, and the best key found is nowhere near German. The double-encipherment results exclude nothing about the plaintext, because the same methods fail on text where the answer is known. They measure the attacks, not the messages. The alignment result does say something. A115’s repeated cipher pairs are real (section 02), and the aligner, given a synthetic text spelled in one of the ways it tries, finds it. On A115 no combination of spellings, separators, numbers, layout and length makes every repeated cipher pair fall on a repeated plaintext pair. Either the words enciphered differ from Bletchley’s rendering, through abbreviation, order or extra matter such as a longer address, or the police layout differs from both manuals.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
h: Why the second pass defeats local search
b: This matches the public record. Hill-climbing solvers by Lasry, Norbert and others break single-pass double-box texts of 100 to 150 letters, and the Army’s Truppenschlüssel, a simplified one-pass relative, has been broken ciphertext-only from surviving messages. No published attack breaks a double pass through the same boxes. The synthetic runs here show where the difficulty lies. The true key is the optimum, but a narrow one. Under the unigram score the true key is the best key (−1.221). Its basin is only about eight to ten swaps wide. Under the quadgram score it is narrower still: annealing started four swaps from the true key does not climb back. Outside the basin there is nothing to climb. Random starts stall at −1.39 to −1.42. The local optima they reach share no row or column structure with the true boxes: measured as the precision of their row and column groupings against the key, they score about one in six, which is chance. Size is not the problem. Giving the solver the true permutation of cells between box A and box B, which leaves only the labelling of the letters to find, does not help: it still stalls at −1.42. The difficulty is the conjugation through a random cell permutation (section 04). The likely mechanism: a key that is partly right gives intermediate letters that are wrong, and the second pass sends those to unrelated cells, so partial correctness earns no score. Known plaintext changes this, because it removes the second pass from the scoring. kpsolve.cs enciphers each known plaintext pair once forward, deciphers its cipher pair once backward, and asks the two intermediates to agree row by row and column by column. Each half is a single pass, which gives the local search a gradient; on the synthetic controls about 80 pairs are enough.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897
b: Twenty-eight ciphered sheets in the register of the nuncio to the Emperor, catalogued as undeciphered with their contents unknown. Their contents have been published since 1897: Kiewning’s volume of the Nuntiaturberichte prints these despatches from the Roman office’s own decipherments, headed dechiffr. The identification is confirmed against the register’s clear pages, which run straight through the cipher sheets and carry the edition’s wording, and against the enclosure on p. 13. The cipher itself is not broken here, and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table an aligner learns predicts unseen text no better than the same table shuffled. The failure is measured instead. On synthetic ciphertext the identical pipeline recovers a random key in full from a clean transcription, 87 codes of 100 at a 0.5 per cent digit error rate and 7 of 100 at 1.7 per cent, and a run-length control then went further: the longest provably consistent alignment between cipher and plaintext is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36 to 39, where the synthetic cipher at the same noise reaches 207. The sheet is not a two-digit encipherment of the text Kiewning prints, and the twenty-seven-letter opening match is below chance. Vienna → Rome · numeric cipher, code width undetermined · August–November 1629 · contents already in print Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 Twenty-eight ciphered passages in the register of Monsignor Giovanni Battista Pallotto, archbishop of Thessalonica and nuncio to the Emperor: Vatican City, BAV, Barb.lat. 6960, digitised in full on DigiVatLib. DECODE carries them as R286–R313, all “Non-decrypted”, and the catalogue entry said that what the cipher hides is not known. It is known. Hans Kiewning printed these despatches in 1897 from the Roman office’s own decipherments, and the register’s clear pages confirm the identification word for word. The cipher itself is a separate question, and it is not answered here. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 — already in print 55 70 83 65 03 29 00 69 38 73 · 11 36 50 23 22 07 92 20 86 H O R I C E V U T A · L A R I S P O S T A … the opening of the despatch of 4 August 1629, and where the alignment stops Vienna → Rome · numeric cipher, code width undetermined · August–November 1629 · contents already in print Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 Twenty-eight ciphered passages in the register of Monsignor Giovanni Battista Pallotto, archbishop of Thessalonica and nuncio to the Emperor: Vatican City, BAV, Barb.lat. 6960, digitised in full on DigiVatLib. DECODE carries them as R286–R313, all “Non-decrypted”, and the catalogue entry said that what the cipher hides is not known. It is known. Hans Kiewning printed these despatches in 1897 from the Roman office’s own decipherments, and the register’s clear pages confirm the identification word for word. The cipher itself is a separate question, and it is not answered here. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 Summary. Barb.lat. 6960 is the Barberini register of Pallotto’s nunciature at the imperial court in the second half of 1629, the months when the Mantuan succession was pushing the Emperor and France towards war. Its 194 pages interleave sheets written entirely in figures with pages of clear Italian. DECODE catalogued twenty-eight of the ciphered sheets as undeciphered, with no indication of their contents. Their contents have been published since 1897: Hans Kiewning’s volume of the Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland for 1629 prints some forty of Pallotto’s despatches under the heading dechiffr. , taken from the copies received and deciphered in Rome, now ASV, Nunz. di Germania 119. The first ciphered sheet, pp. 5–6, is headed in clear Di Vienna 4 di Agosto and is Kiewning’s Nr. 153; the register’s clear pages on either side of it run straight through the cipher sheet and carry that document’s wording exactly, and p. 13 is its second enclosure, again verbatim. So the historical question the catalogue asked is closed. The cryptanalytic one is not. The cipher is numeric and written without separation, and its code width could not be established: there is no phase preference for two-digit or three-digit codes anywhere in the 112,805 digits. The opening twenty-seven letters of the 4 August despatch do align as two-digit codes, and then the alignment breaks and never recovers — but a control shows twenty-seven is below the chance baseline for this material, so that match is not evidence of anything. No partial key is claimed : a held-out test shows that the table learned from one part of the despatch predicts the rest no better than the same table with its letters shuffled (0.355 confirmations per letter against a control mean of 0.359), so the 55 per cent consistency an aligner reports is the aligner fitting the crib. What the failure does have is a measured cause. On synthetic ciphertext — the same plaintext under a random two-digit key — the identical pipeline recovers the whole key from a clean transcription, 87 codes of 100 at a 0.5 per cent digit error rate, and 7 of 100 at 1.7 per cent, because each inserted or dropped digit flips the code phase for everything after it. So the method is sound. A third test then went further: the longest provably consistent two-digit alignment between the cipher and the known plaintext is 39 letters, and controls that shuffle the plaintext or reverse the cipher give 36 to 39 — while the synthetic cipher at the same noise gives 207. The real material sits exactly on its chance baseline. Transcription noise is therefore not a sufficient explanation, and on this evidence the sheet is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of the text Kiewning prints . Status: contents already in print; key not recovered, no partial key claimed, and the obvious hypothesis ruled out. What stays open is which hypothesis replaces it: a different code width, a sheet that encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or a nomenclator-heavy or variable-length system that no fixed-width alignment can match.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897
h: The volume and the twenty-eight ciphertexts
b: Barb.lat. 6960 is on DigiVatLib at digi.vatlib.it/view/MSS_Barb.lat.6960 , 194 pages, with an IIIF manifest. It is an old bitonal microfilm scan and the image service’s own info.json gives a maximum of 748 × 1088 pixels per page; anything larger the server returns is an upscale of that. At that size a figure is about ten pixels wide. DECODE, however, holds its own scans of the same leaves at 1491 × 2066 — four times the pixel area — behind its login. Anyone transcribing this manuscript should work from those, not from DigiVatLib’s. DECODE’s records R286–R313 are the twenty-eight ciphered passages; R315 is the volume as a whole, described there as “mixed ciphertext and cleartext”. Each record’s note gives its page range in the same DigiVatLib pagination, so DECODE page n is canvas n . The ranges run from pp. 5–6 to pp. 192–193, and the volume’s own title describes the ciphers of Pallotto dal 4 agosto al 29 settembre 1629 , though the records carry dates as late as 29 November. The cipher sheets are written across the full width of the page in a dense unbroken stream of figures, about thirty lines to the page and some sixty-six figures to the line. The clear pages are written quite differently, in a narrow column on the right of the leaf with a wide margin. The two alternate through the volume. Barb.lat. 6960, p. 5: the first ciphered sheet, headed in clear Di Vienna 4 di Agosto · Ill. mo et R. mo Sig. r Card. le P. rone , with a struck-out opening line of plaintext above the figures. © Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana. Transcriptions of all twenty-eight were made for DECODE by volunteers in 2019 and 2020 and are downloadable as DOC_R*.txt . They record the figures one digit at a time, so the manuscript’s (decorative and irregular) grouping is lost. Measured, they come to 112,805 digits; the shortest is R308 at 854, the longest R306 at 9,332, and R286 — the one worked in detail here — has 3,573.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897
b: The relevant edition is Hans Kiewning (ed.), Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland nebst ergänzenden Aktenstücken. Vierte Abteilung: 17. Jahrhundert , Band 2: Nuntiatur des Pallotto 1628–1630 , 2: 1629 (Berlin 1897). It is on archive.org as item 4-2_20200807 , in full text. Kiewning works from the copies received in Rome, ASV, Nunz. di Germania 119, and heads each ciphered despatch dechiffr. with the date the Roman office deciphered it — Nr. 153 is “Pallotto an Barberini, 1629 August 4, dechiffr. 22. August”. What he prints is therefore the contemporary decipherment. He gives the substantive passages in Italian verbatim and summarises the rest in German regesta, so the coverage is close to complete but not literally complete. Two checks tie the register to the edition. The 4 August despatch. The cipher on pp. 5–6 is headed Di Vienna 4 di Agosto , which is Nr. 153. The clear pages around it are not a decipherment written against the cipher but the register’s own fair copy, and they run straight through the cipher sheet: p. 4 ends … non haver facoltà di accettar altro partito, che’l proposto in and p. 7 resumes nome del suo Rè . That sentence is Kiewning’s Nr. 153 word for word. The enclosure. Page 13 is the paper Kiewning prints as Nr. 153, Beilage II, Propositione P. Valeriano per Sabran (his source: Bibl. Barber. LXIX 60 fol. 122). The manuscript reads, and the edition prints: … il quale aggiunse di più, che fatta la pace, quando S. S. tà , come padre comune, proponga una lega et unione di questi eserciti, affine di abbatter il Turco commune nemico del nome christiano, che S. M. tà mandaria plenipotentiarii in Italia, acciò N. S. re potesse concludere così gran negotio, con che il demonio resteria ingannato e burlato. Barb.lat. 6960, p. 13: the enclosure to the despatch of 4 August 1629, printed by Kiewning as Nr. 153 Beilage II — P. Valeriano Magno’s proposal for Sabran, ending con che il demonio resteria ingannato e burlato . © Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana. What the ciphers hide, then, is the business of the Mantuan succession crisis in the second half of 1629: Pallotto’s attempts, working through the Capuchin P. Valeriano Magno and the imperial minister Eggenberg ( Echembergh in the despatches), to mediate between the Emperor and the French envoy Sabran over Casale and Monferrato, the civil rather than armed possession of the duchies, the withdrawal of the French from Susa and the imperial troops from the Grisons, and, behind it, the fear that the real object was to humble Venice and restore imperial authority in Italy.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897
h: The cipher, and why it is not broken here
b: The figures are numeric only, written without separators. Across all twenty-eight ciphertexts the digit frequencies are markedly uneven — 0 at 16.1 per cent, 4 at 4.8 per cent — and adjacent digits carry about 0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured rather than random. Beyond that the structure would not resolve. The code width does not show. For a fixed-width numeric code one phase should stand out from the others. None does. Taking the twenty-eight ciphertexts together, the index of coincidence of two-digit codes is 0.01462 at phase 0 and 0.01466 at phase 1, and the digit distributions at even and odd positions agree to within 0.2 per cent at every digit. Three-digit codes behave the same way at all three phases. The crib takes hold and then lets go. With the plaintext of Nr. 153 in hand, the opening of R286 aligns exactly, as two-digit codes, for twenty-seven letters: 55 70 83 65 03 29 00 69 38 73 11 36 50 23 22 07 92 20 86 72 52 06 38 97 12 33 23 H O R I C E V U T A L A R I S P O S T A D A T A M I I That is not merely a fresh assignment at every step: 38 occurs twice and is T both times, 23 occurs twice and is I both times, which by chance would happen about once in 180 tries. The twenty-eighth code conflicts, and from there nothing is consistent. A banded dynamic-programming aligner over the whole despatch, allowing two-digit codes plus one- and three-digit resynchronisation for transcription slips, and iterating the code table to convergence against a hand-corrected 3,359-letter crib, reached about 55 per cent code-to-letter consistency — well above the 20 per cent a wrong alignment gives, well below what a recovered key looks like. Ciphertext-only search fails. Fixed-multiset simulated annealing over the hundred two-digit codes, on 5,000 codes of text, scored by a space-free Italian five-gram model built for this from the repository’s clean Italian corpora (12.0 million characters), settles at −3.54 log-probability per character where real Italian of the period scores about −1.5. A syllabic reading of the same codes — each two-digit group standing for one to four letters — was tested against the known plaintext and collapsed back to single letters for every well-attested code, so there is no syllable table to find. The 55 per cent is not a partial key. A held-out test settles it. Learn the table on the first 55 per cent of R286 against the crib, freeze it, then align the remaining digits to the remaining crib and count confirmations — cases where the code was already in the table and agrees. Against eight controls that keep the table but shuffle the letters among the codes: confirmations per letter DP score key learned from the first half 0.355 −3266 shuffled controls (mean of eight) 0.359 −3313 No separation at all. The same test on a “two-digit codes plus nulls, no digit slips” model gives 0.440 against a control mean of 0.431 — again nothing. The consistency figure is the aligner fitting the crib, and any partial key read off it would have been an artefact. The positive control, which is where the useful number is. Encipher the same crib with a random two-digit homophonic key, damage the digit stream with single-digit insertions and deletions at a chosen rate, and run the identical learner. The fraction of the true key it recovers: digit error rate key recovered 0 % 100 / 100 0.5 % 87 / 100 1.7 % 7 / 100 4 % 19 / 100 The method is sound; it simply needs a transcription accurate to better than about half a per cent of digits. Above roughly one per cent a two-digit key cannot be recovered from this much text even with the plaintext in hand, because every inserted or dropped digit flips the code phase for everything after it. That also explains why no phase preference shows in the statistics above: slips scattered through thirty lines randomise the phase across the corpus. The run-length test, which settles it. A crib aligner can fake a fit, because a fresh code may always be given a fresh letter. What cannot be faked is a long consistent run: inside one window a repeated code must carry the same letter and the mapping must stay a function, so a false run dies at its first repeat conflict. Scanning every pairing of digit offset against crib offset and extending each run while it stays consistent: longest consistent run real cipher against the plaintext of Nr. 153 39 letters control: plaintext letters shuffled (five runs) 39, 39, 36, 38, 36 control: cipher reversed 39 synthetic two-digit cipher, same text, 1.7 % digit noise 207 letters synthetic two-digit cipher, clean transcription 2705 letters The real material sits exactly on its own chance baseline, while a genuine two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise runs five times further. The tool is not the weak point either: on that noisy synthetic text this method recovers 81 of 100 key codes, where the dynamic-programming learner managed 7. And because chance runs here reach 36 to 39 letters, the twenty-seven-letter opening match quoted at the top of this page is below the baseline — it is not evidence, and I was wrong to present it as a one-in-180 coincidence. So transcription noise is no longer a sufficient explanation. On this evidence the cipher sheet is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of the text Kiewning prints as Nr. 153 . Which of the remaining possibilities is true — another code width, a different despatch or wording on the sheet, or a nomenclator-heavy or variable-length system — this material does not decide. How good is the transcription, then? Re-read on DECODE’s larger scan, line 1 of p. 5 differs from DECODE’s transcription in two digits out of seventy-four — both substitutions, with no length difference (they read 93 where the scan shows 73, and 30 where it shows 38). Line 2 differs by a digit or two and possibly in length. So the transcription is close, no length error is demonstrated at the point where the alignment breaks, and the break there is not a transcription artefact. Two explanations therefore remain open and cannot be separated from this material: the transcription carries enough length errors elsewhere to defeat recovery, or the cipher is not a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext at all.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897
b: The key is not recovered, the code width is undetermined, and no partial key is claimed — the held-out test above rules the apparent one out. Nothing in this write-up should be read as a decipherment made here: every Italian word quoted above comes from Kiewning’s edition or from the register’s own clear pages. The twenty-seven-letter alignment at the head of R286 is not suggestive: the chance baseline for consistent runs on this material is 36 to 39 letters, so it is a run of luck shorter than average. Kiewning’s coverage is close to complete but not literal: where he gives a German regest rather than the Italian, the exact wording of that passage is still only in the cipher. The sibling volume is the obvious next step: catalogue entry 236, BAV Barb.lat. 6956 — seventy ciphered sheets of the same nunciature for 1628, DECODE R215–R318 — is still open, and Kiewning’s Band 1 (1628, Berlin 1895) covers exactly those months. That has not been checked here. What would move it now is not a better transcription but a better hypothesis, since the two-digit one is dead: test the other Kiewning despatches of the same dates against the same sheet, test three- and four-digit and variable-length codes with the run-length tool, and check whether the Barberini register’s wording departs from the Rome-received copy Kiewning printed. A cleaner transcription from DECODE’s 1491 × 2066 scans, by glyph segmentation and clustering, would still help, but it is no longer the blocking step.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: Nine pages, mostly in cipher, that Tomokiyo lists as only partially deciphered: the League’s agent in Spain reporting to Mayenne’s councillor four months before the Estates of 1593. Tomokiyo’s key for Pelissier’s later letters fits; calibrated on 1,764 signs of those letters aligned with their clear text, it reads 94 % of the ciphered words, every gap marked. Philip grants 500 ducats, Pelissier argues against holding the Estates now and for two armies at 300,000 écus a month, and reports the case being made in France for Navarre. Burgos → France · homophonic letter cipher with nulls and code groups · 1592 · read, gaps marked A. Pelissier to Pierre Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 BnF Français 3982 no. 22, ff. 46r–50r · nine pages, 377 cipher runs, about 18,400 signs · listed by Tomokiyo as “mostly in cipher, only partially deciphered” · the League’s agent at Philip II’s court, four months before the Estates of 1593 Tomokiyo’s key for Pelissier’s cipher fits. It was calibrated sign by sign on 1,764 signs of Pelissier’s October letters aligned with their clear decipherment, and the whole letter was then re-read with the split sign classes: 94 % of the ciphered words now read (90 % firmly), and every gap is listed Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 Summary. Pelissier was the Catholic League’s agent in Spain, and this is his long report of September 1592 to Pierre Jeannin, the duc de Mayenne’s councillor. The clear-text passages had been legible all along. The ciphered ones, most of the letter, carry the negotiation itself, and the letter survives with only a few scattered interlinear glosses by a contemporary decipherer. Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed Pelissier’s key from two later letters in the same volume that have a clean decipherment (nos. 45 and 46, 27 October 1592), but he did not read no. 22. His key reads it. What the cipher says: Philip grants Pelissier 500 ducats to stay and wait for news. Pelissier argues against holding the Estates now and for two armies in the field, one to push Henri IV back from the Seine to the Loire, the other to free Paris and Rouen, at about 300,000 écus a month . He reports what people in France were saying for recognising Navarre, and the suspicion that Philip wanted France kept divided. He warns that Mayenne’s authority is being undermined, and he is still waiting on the 50,000 écus the Idiáquez keep promising. A first reading got about half to two-thirds of the cipher. The residue was not in the key but in look-alike signs merged in transcription, so the key was then calibrated on Pelissier’s own October letters , 1,764 signs aligned with their clear decipherment, and every page re-read with the split sign classes. 94 % of the ciphered words now read , 90 % firmly; the 256 remaining gaps are single hard signs, holes in the paper and a few names, and they are marked as unread rather than guessed. Two new code groups are identified from context: 310, probably the Duke of Savoy, and 441, probably France.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: BnF fr. 3982 is one of the Mémoires de la Ligue volumes (fr. 3974–3995), which gather League correspondence, much of it ciphered, from the 1580s and 1590s. No. 22 runs from f. 46r to f. 50r with the address on f. 50v: nine close-written pages, about fifty lines each, dated “A Burgos le xiij septembre 1592”, signed “Vre bien humble et obeissant serviteur Pelissier”, and marked Tripta (the third copy sent). Clear French and cipher alternate within the same lines, and the cipher is written with a small repertory of letter-like signs, figures and marks. f. 46r: “Monsieur J’entreprins mon voyage de la court si a contre temps que arrivant a Valladolid ou le Roy avoit sejourné deulx moys…”, and then the first cipher. The small writing between the cipher rows is the contemporary decipherer’s. His glosses are few and scattered, and they are the letter’s whole “partial decipherment”.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: Tomokiyo’s League page reconstructs the cipher Pelissier used in nos. 45 and 46 (Madrid, 27 October 1592) from their clean decipherment on f. 115. It is a homophonic alphabet with one to seven signs per letter. Some signs are two-digit numbers (24, 26, 28, 30, 33, 36, 44, 56, 60, 80). There is a sign for et , signs for the doubled letters rr , ss and uu , and six nulls. His table is not reproduced here; it is on his page. No. 22 is six weeks older and on the same key, with two additions: Code group 315 is the Béarnais , Henri IV: “le [315] ayant incontinant tourné la teste et s’estant campé pres l’armée catholique”, “les forces d’Allemaigne … iointes au [315]”. It occurs on four of the nine pages. Code group 310 occurs once, on f. 50r: “ne correspondront pas a ce que pretend [310], et l’ambassadeur … a esté renvoyé sans aultre esclaircissement sur ses demandes”, next to a passage on the governor of Milan. A claimant with an ambassador at Philip’s court and a Milanese connection is most likely the Duke of Savoy , Philip’s son-in-law, who had his own pretensions in France; the Duke of Lorraine is the alternative. Context only. Code group 441 occurs once, on f. 49v: “non seulement en [441] mais en toutes aultres regions de la Chrestienté”, which asks for France . Context only. The decipherer’s glosses check the key wherever they are legible. They agree on de , auisa , meschans , roy , les tirer , Noyon , a la main qu , n’auoit , en atendant , quar la bataille , mais le retour , de crainte , langaiges , Valentia , a gens matez des and (qu’ay)ant pleu a Dieu , among others. One gloss disagrees in an instructive way. Over “nos forces” the glosser wrote os a orc : he applied the table’s ϝ = a literally where the sense needs f . The hand that deciphered this letter in 1592 was working from the same table, and it slipped on the same sign. Calibration. Tomokiyo’s table gives each sign a letter; it does not say how to tell apart signs that look alike on a fast page, and that is where the first reading stalled. The two letters he built the key from were therefore aligned with their clear text on f. 115, sign by sign: 835 signs of no. 45 (f. 111r) and 929 of no. 46 (ff. 113r–v). That settles the look-alikes with known plaintext: 4 : the plain closed 4 is n (and often m ), never t ; t is the 4 with a hooked lead-in off the crossbar, or with a curl. The first transcription had written both as 4, and a decode that let every sign take any letter wanted that 4 to be t 355 times. ⊤ : flat-topped is a ; with a hooked top and a descender, p ; with a tail, s . The lone hooked τ is g . δ : with a straight ascender o ; curling over into a long hook, c ; with a big open loop over a closed bowl, r . 56 : compact, y ; with the long hooked 5 and the 6 set high, c . 8 : plain, n ; crossed at the waist, q . + is h and ∐ is l , never e ; π is i , never s (the tailed ϖ is s ); the barred ӿ is u and the large plain ✗ a null; 7 is b , or h . The October letters and no. 22 were written by the same hand six weeks apart, and the page readers found a few further habits in no. 22 alone: an alpha-shaped sign and a barred 5 for g , a small box-shaped ∐ for e , the tall double long-s for rr , and a looped ℓ that stands for u or e by context. The whole guide, with exemplar crops of every form, is pelissier1592/GLYPHS.md and cal/atlas/ . f. 46v. Clear text (“a l’arrivee du Roy en ce dict lieu de Burgos Je retornay treuver le seigneur Don Joan, lequel m’ayant donné une heure particulliere”) runs straight into cipher. The cipher opens “i’exposay pour fondement de mon discours qu’il n’est rien plus requis en un estat que la conservation de la reputation”.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: Deciphered words are in the reading as written, with the letter’s spelling. The page summaries below are in English. The full text, page by page, with gaps marked, is in pelissier1592/READING.md . f. 46r. Pelissier reached Valladolid just as the court was leaving, and Don Juan de Idiáquez put business off to Palencia. In cipher, he says his credit is gone, “le credit m’est[oit] failly pour n’avoir satisfaict au payement des sommes qui m’ont esté prestées a Madrid”. He takes the King’s long silence for a refusal and asks leave to go home. He is told Philip has his own ministers in France. Philip’s answer to the rest is “yo lo creo”. Then comes the grant: “elle m’avoit ordonné cinq cens ducats, qui valent environ quatre cens cinquante escus, ou plus”, payable in Madrid, “ou je me pouvois retirer avec les ambassadeurs et aultres estans par deça de la part de princes estrangiers”, so that he can wait for news. f. 46v. At Burgos, Don Juan gives him a private hour. Pelissier’s theme is reputation, and his example is Parma’s army of 1592. While it flourished, “la plus part de la noblesse catholique qui suit ce party se retira chacun en sa maison” and towns began to treat. If it had wintered in France, the Béarnais would have been brought to “une ruine tres certaine”, and the Germans “n’eussent eu l’audace de sortir de leur pays pour l’assister”. Its return to the Low Countries undid everything: League towns afraid of being exposed if the enemy returned began their own dealings, and La Fère, Soissons and the places of Picardy, perhaps Corbie “pres d’Amiens” (a doubtful reading), were left in danger. ff. 47r–47v. The French “aymeroient mieux mourir touts l’un après l’aultre” than be forced, as the rising against “le dernier Roy” showed; mildness and benefits would win them to anything. The King asks whether Pelissier speaks on Mayenne’s orders. He has had no word since the armies faced each other at Caudebec. The Spanish answer is that no king had ever given such help, and any failure lay with those who received it. Pelissier’s reasons for putting off the Estates are taken for a trick. The minister recalls that Mayenne, in the time of the Cardinal de Bourbon, had pressed for everything else to be set aside for the Cardinal’s “deliurance”, and Pelissier is heard to say it would be “necessaire que l’on mist sus deux armées”. Yet the minister concedes that the League’s French would take it very badly if Spain delayed “la nomination d’un roy legitime pour l’opposer a l’heretique et tyran”. Of the Spanish ministers, Pelissier writes: “ilz ont les oreilles delicates”. f. 48r. He calls for a “troisiesme moyen”. This is the wrong time to hold the Estates: the people are exhausted, the clergy intimidated, and the nobility held only by its interests, and they would sooner accept “un accord qui creera un Roy pour l’opposer a celuy qui se pretend”. He foresees a war that may end only “par l’extermination de la race de l’un desditz deux Roys”. His remedy is the plan already put to Philip “de tenir deux armees en pied”. One army would drive the enemy from the Seine to the Loire. The other would take the Seine towns and free Paris and Rouen. He answers the cost, “pres de trois cens mil escus par mois”, by saying the effort need last only a few months. A war left to drag on would be “si sanglante” that, driven to despair, it would spare neither age nor sex: “ne pardonnant a aage ni sexe”. f. 48v. The army should be mostly French, “tant a pied qu’a cheval”, stiffened by “un corps de sept ou huit mil Alemans” and some Spaniards and Walloons “assistés de bons capitaines”. A victory would ruin the enemy. After a defeat, an army of Philip’s own nations “seroit preste pour recueillir les reliques de ceste deffaicte”. Piecemeal aid only ruins the provinces. And if Philip showed “quelque affection particuliere en la nomination du roy”, everyone would follow. f. 49r. The campaigns of 1591–92: Chartres, Noyon, the Prince of Ascoli’s relief, Caudebec, Henri’s daily offer of battle, and the retreat towards Château-Thierry. The clear text blames Parma for letting chances go by, which gave the enemy room to spread the rumour that Philip fights only to keep the French busy while he subdues his Low Countries rebels. f. 49v. What Frenchmen were saying: that Philip wanted France kept “en telle balance” so that he could take his share of a divided crown. Then the case for Navarre. God called him “comme par miracle a la succession”. He has lived “en perpetuelle peine et travail, pauvre et miserable”, and so he will want peace. If he turned on the Catholics, they would be “libres du serment de fidelite”. Such talk works on “gens matez des maux soufferts et plains de desespoir de mieux”. Philip alone can cure the malady, and would add to “Catholique” the names “tres chrestien” and “liberateur de la Chrestienté”. f. 50r. “Ilz vont minant l’authorité” of Mayenne: finances first, then command, then credit: “ilz luy diminuent le credit … l’abaisser le plus qu’ilz pourront. Dieu veulle que je me trompe”. Whatever [310] pretends to, its ambassador has been sent home without an answer, and Pelissier pleads for a union among the League so close that an offence to one would be felt by all. In clear, Pelissier stays “pour essayer de tirer une derniere resolution sur la partie de cinquante mil escutz”. A postscript describes a visitor sent to Palencia, whom the King received well enough to send him horses for his audiences.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: Transcription by sign. Each page was cut into third-width bands at 1.5× from the full-resolution Gallica scan. Every sign was written as a token (a name for its shape) and every clear passage in full. Seven parallel agents did ff. 47r–50r; ff. 46r–46v were done here and served as the worked example. A beam decoder, not a solver. Each token carries the letter the key gives it, plus cheap alternatives where two signs look alike. A beam search over a conditional quadgram model of period French picks the reading, and word breaks come out of the model. Second pass. For every row that did not decode to French, the signs were re-read at 2.5× and genuine misreadings were corrected on every page. A change was made only when the sign was visibly different on the leaf, never just because French would then appear. Each page’s reading lists the glosses and whether they agree. Calibration and third pass. The key’s own source letters were aligned with their clear text (section 02), the look-alike families were split into separate tokens, and every row of all nine pages was re-read against the scans with them. Unread words fell from 413 to 256 and doubtful ones from 278 to 158. What went wrong, usefully. Twice, once per page and once over the whole letter, the sign-to-letter map was hill-climbed against the language model from the key as a start. Both times it drifted to the degenerate “every frequent sign is e ” attractor, which a noisy transcription always rewards. The key was right. The errors were in the tokens, which had merged signs the key keeps apart: 56 with a flourish is c , and plain 56 is y . The plain δ is o , the δ with a long curling hook is c , and the closed-loop ∂ with a curled top is r . The flat-topped ⊤ is a , the hooked τ is p , and the small curled “Tz” is g . Among the barred I forms, the plain one is l , the bold-footed one is o , and the double-barred one is o as well (Ƒ). vv is et , and also ff . ϝ is a in the table and f in dozens of words. That diagnosis was right, and the calibration in section 02 is the remedy: most of these splits are now tokens in their own right, confirmed on known plaintext.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: 256 words unread , marked [?] , against 3,734 read inside the ciphered stretches (94 %), and 158 more read but doubtful, marked (?) . Every page’s reading lists its open rows with their tokens. They are single signs the eye cannot settle, a hole in f. 50r, and names. Nothing is supplied by conjecture. Grades. The key is H (in print, and confirmed on 1,764 signs of known plaintext and by the glosses). The reading of the firm stretches is H; the (?) words are C. 315 = the Béarnais is H (it recurs, and “appeler [315] comme par miracle a la succession” fixes it); 310 = Savoy and 441 = France are M, one occurrence each; Corbie and Amiens on f. 46v are I. Names. The Dominican confessor on f. 50r reads c-o-r-n-e | n-t-(u/e) across a line break, “Cornente” or “Cornete” if a heavily inked 4 is cancelled; not identified. A “don …” beside the governor of Milan, the visitor of the postscript, and a place in the 1592 campaign (f. 49r) are unread. Everything is in the repository under pelissier1592/ : the account in NOTES.md , the reading in READING.md and reading_46r.md … reading_50r.md , the token transcriptions t46r.txt … t50r.txt , the decoder beam.py with cands.txt , the sign vocabulary in TOKENS.md , the calibrated guide in GLYPHS.md , and the alignments of nos. 45 and 46 with their exemplar crops in cal/ .

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: BnF Français 3982, Gallica ark btv1b9060543f : no. 22 at views 100–108; nos. 45 and 46 at views 230 and 234–235, with their decipherment on f. 115 at views 238–239. S.
