t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: The Ministry of Communications copied every telegram to or from Sun Yat-sen’s people for the Japanese Foreign Ministry, which filed them unread. Fifty-six condenser telegrams of March–May 1916 read under five more keys of the Swatow telegram’s family, each accepted only when it read telegrams it was not fitted to, with rhyme-day dates as an independent check. They cover the monarchy cancelled, money wired via Taiwan, the price of a Wuhan rising, Chen Qimei’s murder, and the Foreign Ministry’s own advice relayed back to Sun. Also a Hankow +111 telegram and Sun ↔ Dai Jitao, March 1917. Shanghai ↔ Tokyo · telegraph code + code condensers · March 1916 – March 1917 · read Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 The copies the Ministry of Communications made for the Japanese Foreign Ministry of every telegram to or from Sun’s people · JACAR, Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, 特定人ノ発受郵便物取調, vols 2–4 · no decodes in the files Fifty-six condenser telegrams of March–May 1916 read in whole or in part under five further keys of the Swatow telegram’s family and two tentative ones; a Hankow digit telegram; and Sun ↔ Dai Jitao, March 1917, in another key of the family Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 Summary. The Swatow telegram of 3 April 1916 ( read here earlier ) turned out to be one sheet from a much larger intercept. Through 1916 and 1917 the Communications Bureau of the Japanese Ministry of Communications sent the Foreign Ministry a copy of every telegram and letter to or from Sun Yat-sen’s circle. The Foreign Ministry filed them and could not read the ciphered ones: there are no decodes in the files, and the analysts’ kana worksheets on one stream break off with pencilled guesses. Almost every condenser telegram of March–May 1916 in the files decodes under a key of the same systematic family as the Swatow telegram, with one key for each pair of correspondents. A key was accepted only when it stood at z ≥ 6 on one long telegram and then read others that played no part in finding it. Rhyme-day date codes in the signatures agree with the dates on the forms. Read in date order, the telegrams follow Sun’s party through the end of Yuan Shikai’s monarchy: 帝制取消 on 25 March, money raised in Manila and wired by way of Taiwan, a Shanghai rising that needs two weeks more, the price of a rising at Wuhan, and then, on 19 May, 英士昨下午在山田家被兇[轟?]斃 (“Yingshi was shot dead by assassins yesterday afternoon in the Yamada house”). A week later Tokyo tells Sun that Huang Xing reports the Foreign Ministry’s view that he should put off going to Qingdao. The Foreign Ministry was sent a copy of that telegram too, and could not read it. Status: read. Most long telegrams keep a few unread groups, marked [?]. Sun’s own six-vowel 文密 code of July 1916 onward, and the June 1917 telegrams, are not in the family and are not read.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: The series is 各国内政関係雑纂／支那ノ部／革命党関係（亡命者ヲ含ム）／特定人ノ発受郵便物取調, Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, volumes 2 to 4, on JACAR as B03050088300, B03050088400, B03050089100, B03050090000, B03050090100 and B03050090200. Each batch comes under a covering note headed 特定人發着郵便物等取調ノ件 (“inquiry into mail etc. sent and received by specified persons”), from the Director of the Communications Bureau (逓信省通信局長 田中) to the Director of the Foreign Ministry’s Political Affairs Bureau (政務局長 小池, Koike Chōzō). A typical note, 秘第八?之一號 of 25 May 1916, received the next day, reads 別紙寫電報及左記郵便物有之候: “attached are copied telegrams and the postal item noted below”. The telegrams are copied onto the Imperial Telegraphs’ own forms. Outgoing messages from Tokyo are on “Forwarded” forms, signed 中山 (Nakayama, Sun’s Japanese alias) or, in May, with the handler’s name 林蔚陸 (“Linwailuk”). Incoming messages are on “Received” forms addressed to “Rosamonde Tokio” (Soong Ching-ling), to “Linwailuk Tokio”, or to Nakayama at 109 Harajuku, Aoyama. The correspondents are Yamada Junzaburō in Shanghai (“Junzaburo Shanghai”), “Konglipo” in Manila, Kayano Nagatomo and Ju Zheng’s men at Qingdao (Seitō), “Youngchina” at San Francisco, Honolulu, Hankow, and the Shanghai leadership: Chen Qimei, Xu Chongzhi and the rest. Some of the traffic is in clear English (“2000 through Shokinginko”), and some is in plain telegraph code. Most of it is in ten-letter condenser words. The files hold no decodes. The Foreign Ministry did try. In B03050089100, frames 0076–0078 are a notebook copy of a long romanised kana stream (126 ten-letter groups, ending owari ), and frames 0079–0081 are the analysts’ worksheets on it. They copy the stream into katakana, divide it with slashes into groups of two or three, and pencil kanji guesses beside the groups, often with a question mark: 事, 先生, 國, 電, 軍, 謀. No continuous sense comes out of them, and the stream is not read here either.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: The system is the one described on the Swatow page . Twenty consonants (no w ) and five vowels give a hundred syllables numbered 01…99, 00, and two syllables make one four-figure group of the standard Chinese telegraph code. The syllables run on across ten-letter words without regard to the word breaks, and there is no additive. Every table in the family is a rule: the alphabet rotated or reversed, the vowels in some order, the numbers filled vowel by vowel. What changes between correspondents is the rotation and the vowel order: key row for 01 vowel order used on swatow1916 l e a i o u “Tanaka”, Swatow → Rosamonde, 3 April 1916 ( the Swatow telegram ) shanghai1916 z (alphabet reversed) i o a e u Sun ↔ Yamada Junzaburō, Shanghai; Shanghai (Chen Qimei, Xu Chongzhi …) → Rosamonde, March–April 1916 manila1916 g o e u a i Sun ↔ Konglipo, Manila; one Shanghai telegram signed by Xu Chongzhi seito1916 m u i e o a Qingdao (Ju Zheng; Kayano Nagatomo) ↔ Tokyo, March–April 1916 sanfran1916 x o e u a i Tokyo → “Youngchina”, San Francisco yamada1916 q e u i o a Tokyo (Xie Chi, “Linwailuk”) ↔ Junzaburo, Shanghai, May 1916 shanghai1917 k a e u o i Sun ↔ Dai Jitao, March 1917 ( below ) “Row for 01” is the consonant that takes 01 with the first vowel; the next consonant in the alphabet takes 02, and so on. The key names are those in famtest.py . Two more keys are tentative, each resting on one short telegram: Honolulu (alphabet reversed, filled consonant by consonant, vowels e a o u i ; z 4.9) and Manila in May (row for 01 d , vowels e u a o i ; z 4.4). Finding and accepting a key. The whole family, 57,600 tables counting the fill orders, origins and the ±111 additive, was run on each telegram, and each table was scored with a Chinese character model. The z figures on this page are that score measured against the whole family. A short telegram can put a wrong key on top by chance, so a key was accepted only when it reached z ≥ 6 on at least one long telegram and then read other telegrams it had not been fitted to. For example, shanghai1916 was found on a long Shanghai → Rosamonde telegram and then read Sun’s own outgoing telegrams to Yamada at z 7–10. The May key yamada1916 reads every telegram that carries the clear prefix word “Thirtyseventh”. Some short telegrams read under their pair’s key although another table scores slightly higher on them alone. They are counted as read because the text makes sense and the key is fixed elsewhere, not because of their own score. The dates check themselves. Chinese telegrams give the day of the month by a rhyme-category character (韻目代日). Where a signature carries one, it agrees with the date on the Japanese form: 支 4, 元 13, 篠 17, 皓 19, 號 20, 箇 21, 漾 23, 有 25, 宥 26, 豔 29. The one exception is a Shanghai telegram handed in on 22 May that ends 馬, the 21st. The date characters come out of the decryption and the key search never looked at them, so the agreement is an independent check. The clerks. These are copies made by Japanese telegraph clerks, copying letter strings that meant nothing to them, and they make the same mistakes throughout: g ↔ q by far the most often, then x written like d or s , h ↔ k ↔ n , e ↔ c , a ↔ o , and a dropped pair of letters now and then. Every emendation is a single letter of one of these kinds, justified by the sense and usually by a clean occurrence of the same group elsewhere. Examples are gequ → qequ 款 (“funds”), which recurs across the Manila traffic, and dunu → xunu 東. The transcriptions give the letters as written and list each change. A telegram with a pair dropped reads as noise until the pair is restored. The 25 May telegram from Tokyo scores z 4.1 as written and 6.8 once the missing ge of its first word is put back.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
h: March–April 1916: the monarchy cancelled, the money, the Shanghai rising
b: Conventions: [?] = group read as written but doubtful; a character in brackets = the reading after a one-letter emendation, where the notes mark it; □ = unread. Frame numbers are JACAR frames of B03050088300 unless stated. Yuan Shikai announced the end of his monarchy on 22 March 1916. At that point Sun Yat-sen was in Tokyo and his party was planning a rising in Shanghai. 25 March, Shanghai → Rosamonde (fr. 0468; z 6.7) 帝制取消，馮、朱等當漸觀望。滬異派力弱，於我略可從容佈置。海軍[?]發策較萬全，然猶急備未懈… “The monarchy is cancelled. Feng [Guozhang], Zhu [Rui] and the others will now wait and see. The opposing faction in Shanghai is weak, so we can make our dispositions at some leisure. A plan launched by the Navy … is safer, but we are still preparing urgently without slackening …” There is no signature. 26 March, Sun → Yamada (fr. 0465; z 7.4) 京信□□□策：袁暫退，使黎代；俟歐戰終，乃借英力[復]出。故滬事當發於袁退之前乃可。文 “The Peking letter … plan: Yuan to step down for now, with Li [Yuanhong] acting; when the European war ends, he comes back with British support. So the Shanghai action must be launched before Yuan withdraws. — Wen.” The same evening a 38-word telegram from Shanghai signed 美 (Chen Qimei; z 9.2) asked for arms to be shipped and a handover procedure, and closed: 穆日當局允暗濟械，已有接洽否？ (“The authorities have agreed to supply arms secretly: has contact been made?”). 穆 occurs twice with the same letters and is probably a cover word. 27 March, Sun → Konglipo, Manila (fr. 0462; manila1916) 滬電乃崇智所發，勿疑。文 “The Shanghai telegram was sent by [Xu] Chongzhi. Do not doubt it.” Earlier that day Manila had asked who was using the code to send telegrams from Shanghai, calling it 萬可疑, “most suspicious”. Xu Chongzhi’s own telegram of the 26th, signed in clear Shuichunchee , is in the Manila key, not the Shanghai one. 30 March – 4 April: money Much of the traffic is fund-raising. Tokyo asks the Fujian merchants in Manila to 盡力向閩幫籌[款?] (“do their utmost to raise funds from the Fujian guild”); Qingdao asks for fifty thousand, 惟需五萬元，懇速電匯 (“only we need 50,000 yuan; wire it urgently”); Manila reports what seems to be four thousand sent through the Hongkong Bank (a four-word telegram, weakly scored), and Tokyo acknowledges [四?]千圓. From Shanghai on 31 March (z 8.2): 田在滬交五千，到漢匯八千。近[又?]索三萬，無力應之 (“田 [a person] handed over 5,000 in Shanghai, 8,000 to be remitted on reaching Hankow. Lately another 30,000 is demanded; we have no means to meet it”). On the same day Sun warns Yamada (fr. 0485; z 7.9): 北方來電，帝制取消，軍心益振。而[滬?]反[?]觀望。恐前聯絡之人皆多不實，故托此爲辭，[?]得款耳。望兄詳察，勿受其欺。孫文 “Telegrams from the north: the monarchy is cancelled and the army’s spirit rises. But [Shanghai?] is … waiting to see. I fear the people we contacted earlier are mostly not genuine and use this as an excuse to get money. Look into it carefully and do not be taken in. — Sun Wen.” 4 April, Sun → Yamada (fr. 0494; z 9.8, no emendation) 由臺灣電六百金，請交寶昌路寶康里一八三號張宗海，往甘費。聞西林赴南寧組政府，定設法破之。文 “600 gold wired by way of Taiwan: please give it to Zhang Zonghai, 183 Baokang-li, Baochang Road, for the journey to Gansu. I hear Xilin [Cen Chunxuan] is going to Nanning to form a government: I will find a way to break it. — Wen.” This is the cleanest telegram in the files: forty characters and not one letter to change. Two more went out that afternoon. One ends 山東消息甚佳，月內當動。孫文。支 (“news from Shandong is very good; it will move within the month. — Sun Wen, the 4th”). The other, to Kayano at Qingdao (fr. 0492; seito1916, z 7.4), reports fifty thousand sent through the Yokohama Specie Bank, and arms to be shipped under the name of the Qingdao military administration (以寄青島軍政官名義). 13 April, Hankow → Sun (B03050088400 fr. 0517) This telegram is in digits, not condenser letters. It uses the +111 code that Consul Segawa described to the Foreign Ministry that May: each four-figure code group has 111 added, here without the digit reversal. A search over every additive and both digit orders puts −111 175 log-points clear of the next candidate, and the telegram then reads with no emendation: 武漢發動事，日人謂非念五萬不辦。迭電陸參兩部，桐以軍械運輸困難且爲時久。刻人心已熟，海陸均有七分以上把握，三萬可行。機不可[失]，望速決電示。元 “On the Wuhan rising: the Japanese say it cannot be done for under 250,000. [We] have wired the Army Ministry and the General Staff again and again; 桐 says the arms and their transport are difficult and would take a long time. Opinion here is ripe; army and navy are both more than seventy per cent sure; 30,000 would do it. The moment must not be missed. Decide quickly and wire. — the 13th.”

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: By May, Sun was in Shanghai, where he arrived at the start of the month, and the Tokyo end was run by Xie Chi (謝持), who signs 持 and dates with rhyme characters. Every Tokyo–Shanghai condenser telegram of that month that reads at all reads under one key, yamada1916 (frames of B03050089100). 19 May, Shanghai → Linwailuk, Tokyo (fr. 0066; z 6.0) 英士昨下午在山田家被兇[轟?]斃，捕兇[一?]人，關係者數人。 “Yingshi was shot dead by assassins yesterday afternoon in the Yamada house; one assassin and several accomplices arrested.” Chen Qimei (陳其美, courtesy name Yingshi) was murdered in Shanghai on 18 May 1916 in the house of Yamada Junzaburō, the addressee of most of the Tokyo traffic. Tokyo replied the same day in two telegrams (both signed 持皓, the 19th): 英士被刺，傷[勢?]如何？盼覆 (“Yingshi stabbed: how are the wounds? Please reply”), and then 電悉。英士捐軀，極堪慟悼。主使爲誰？盼覆。先生[?]在滬[?]，務處處戒備。持皓 “Telegram received. Yingshi has given his life; we mourn him deeply. Who was behind it? Please reply. The Master … in Shanghai … must take every precaution. — Chi, the 19th.” Others asked the same question in other ways. From Kobe, 英士君遭難確否乞覆 came in plain code. From Manila, received on 23 May, 聞陳英士死確否？請覆 came to Tōyama Mitsuru in a key of its own. The Shanghai answer of 22 May (z 8.2) gives the instigator as 遣之暗殺主謀爲[政?]府, “the government”, and says that the pistols have been entrusted to Miyazaki to bring back. 23–25 May: arms and the students Tokyo on 23 May (z 8.2): Wu Feiji, back in Shanghai at 26 Rue Joffre, has ordered 300 Type-30 rifles and 100 Browning pistols through the Ōkura company at Dalian, with 2,000 taels already paid as deposit. Tokyo and Shanghai also wire back and forth about 席、趙兩處學生事, the business of Xi Zhengming’s and Zhao’s students at Tianjin, which had been demanding money for a rising. On 22 May Shanghai orders it stopped; on 24 May it says 學生事暫擱 (“shelve the students affair”); on 25 May Tokyo asks which of the two it means. 26 May, Tokyo → Yamada (fr. 0092–93; z 9.6) 克強言外務省意先生宜緩赴青島。又軍械事能得青木一電參謀本部較更有力云云… 宥 “Keqiang [Huang Xing] says the Foreign Ministry’s view is that the Master should put off going to Qingdao. Also, on the arms, a telegram from Aoki [probably Lt-Gen. Aoki Nobuzumi] to the General Staff would carry more weight … — the 26th.” Here Sun’s Tokyo office passes the Japanese Foreign Ministry’s own advice to Sun, and the Foreign Ministry was being sent a copy of the telegram. It had no means of reading it. Earlier that morning Tokyo had asked 報載先生昨[潛?]離滬，確否？ (“the papers report that the Master secretly left Shanghai yesterday; is it true?”). 29 May, Tokyo → Yamada (fr. 0113–14; z 6.6) 據譚根云，岑有軍[火]船四艘由神戸回粤，今遣彼來東運機[?]二臺，交該船載[?]…謝持 豔 “According to Tan Gen, Cen [Chunxuan] has four military steamers going from Kobe back to Guangdong, and has sent him to Japan to ship two machine[-guns?] on them … — Xie Chi, the 29th.” Cen Chunxuan is the “Xilin” whose government at Nanning Sun had promised on 4 April to break.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
h: After the condensers: Cai E and Huang Xing
b: From July the ciphered traffic changes to a code that is not in the family ( below ), but some telegrams in the later volumes are in plain telegraph code. Two of them belong to the same story. 10 July, Luzhou → “Ilchang Tokio” (B03050090000 fr. 0417) 宥電敬悉。承念甚感。久罹喉病，軍中失調，醫治漸痊，幸釋綺注。鍔叩。蒸 “Your telegram of the 26th received with respect. I am most grateful for your concern. I have long suffered from a throat illness, made worse by life with the army; treatment is gradually curing it; please set your mind at rest. — E, the 10th.” This is Cai E (蔡鍔), who led the Yunnan rising against the monarchy. The throat illness killed him in Fukuoka on 8 November 1916. 13 September, Tokyo (中田) → Huang Xing, Shanghai (B03050090100 fr. 0471) 閱報憂悚。接[?]電，母[恙?]稍安。請靜養。現如何？ “Alarmed to read the papers. […] telegram received; your mother is a little better. Please rest. How are you now?” Huang Xing was already ill, and he died on 31 October 1916, eight days before Cai E. The Japanese clerk’s own kanji glosses on this form differ from the codebook at two groups (4443 and 3225).

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: B03050090200 (vol. 4, item 5, frames 0503–0513) holds three condenser telegrams of late March 1917. Two are from Sun in Shanghai, signed Sunwen in clear, to “Toi c/o Kikuchi Rioichi” in Tokyo. The third is the reply to “Sun yatsen Shanghai”, signed Tenkiutai (天仇, Dai Jitao). “Toi” is therefore Dai Jitao (戴季陶), staying with Kikuchi Ryōichi (菊池良一). The key is a seventh member of the family: row for 01 k , vowels a e u o i , no additive. It was found by running the family on the 23 March telegram alone, where it scores −321.6 against a population mean of −556.4 and s.d. 25.8, about nine standard deviations up; the next unrelated key is 124 points behind. The Swatow key gives nonsense. The 25 and 26 March telegrams played no part in finding the key, and both read in it at once. Dai Jitao to Sun, 26 March 1917 (JACAR B03050090200, frame 0506). The last word, written zimucuzaku , ends in zahu = 1359 宥 with the clerk’s h → k slip. 宥 is the rhyme code for the 26th, the date on the form. 23 March, Sun → Dai (fr. 0504) 前電云三日後商妥□□□□□後音。此間必俟前約取消，始可致電北京照辦。各約已取消否？速覆。公司抄件瑞士尚未辦妥。文 “My previous telegram said that after three days [the matter] would be settled by agreement … [further] word. Here we must wait until the former contract is cancelled before we can wire Peking to act accordingly. Have the contracts all been cancelled? Reply at once. The company copy … [瑞士?] not yet settled. — Wen.” Words 4 and 5 as copied, pixaqaqe eianakerele , have 19 letters where 20 are needed, and ei is not a syllable. The clerk misplaced the word break and lost or misread at least two letters. pi completes 妥, and the last code of the damaged run, lebe 接, reads as written, so “…接後音” (“received further word”) is likely. The five codes between cannot be recovered with confidence. A search allowing one insertion and up to two substitutions finds nothing clean. 瑞士 needs an x / m change and is the least certain emendation. The telegram’s last word, qixapfete , has nine letters; read qixa pi ne te it gives 辦妥 and 文, Sun’s signature character, which also closes the 25 March telegram. 25 March, Sun → Dai (fr. 0507) 函悉。約取消後，當□□□能否。取消卽覆。文 “Letter received. After the contract is cancelled, [whether] … is possible. Reply as soon as it is cancelled. — Wen.” 能 needs zubo → xubo ; three codes do not read, and no one-letter variant makes sense of them. 26 March, Dai → Sun (fr. 0506) 本定今日赴熱海。□□來云：彼等須先□定，約三日回。□公司事如何？電示。宥 “I was to have gone to Atami today. … came and said that they must first settle …; [I shall be] back in about three days. How stands the company matter? Wire me. — the 26th.” 公司 has the same qabo for 司 that reads cleanly on 23 March. The two characters before 來云 do not read. 小池 (Koike Chōzō, who had left the Foreign Ministry’s Political Bureau in 1916) is two letters away and is no more than a guess. Together the three telegrams show Sun, in the last week of March 1917, waiting for “the former contract” to be cancelled before he can wire Peking, pressing Dai for news, and Dai asking after “the company matter”. They do not say what the contract or the company was. That needs the Chinese record for March 1917, which has not been consulted.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: Sun’s 文密 code. From July 1916 (B03050090000 fr. 0416: Tokyo → 中華新報 Shanghai, and Tokyo → 軍務院 Zhaoqing with the prefix 文密 ) to June 1917, some of Sun’s traffic uses ten-letter words with y as a sixth vowel and w as a consonant. It is not in the five-vowel family. A six-vowel version of the family, about 200,000 tables, finds nothing above z 4.1. The prefix names it as a separate code, probably one built on a table that is not a rule. The June 1917 telegrams between Sun and Dai (B03050090200 fr. 0509, 0511) are in that system, and they also contain clusters that are not consonant–vowel pairs ( myzoasdoke , liriopen ). Transcribed, not read. Late May 1916. Five Tokyo → Junzaburo telegrams have no “Thirtyseventh” prefix. Three are eight words long, and one survives as a typed copy, so misreading is ruled out. The pair statistics say the text is structured, but no key in the family reads them, and yamada1916 fails with every additive from 0 to 9999. Two Shanghai → “Ylchang Tokio” telegrams of 29–30 May use w as a consonant. These are probably early 文密. The kana stream of B03050089100 fr. 0076–0078, which the Foreign Ministry’s analysts worked on, is not read here either. The Swatow original. Every Latin-letter form in B03050088300 and B03050088400 was read, and none is from Swatow. The copy in B03050738800 is still the only one found, and its three garbled tail groups stay lost. Unread groups. Most long telegrams keep a few groups marked [?]: names that are not in the model, codes one letter from several readings, and supplementary-code characters. The two tentative keys (Honolulu; Manila in May) rest on one short telegram each. The March 1917 lacuna and the identity of the contract and the company are open.

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: Twenty consonants, five vowels, ten-letter words: a code condenser over the standard Chinese telegraph code. The family of systematic tables is small enough to brute-force, and one key reads 41 characters: Mo Qingyu’s independence at Chaozhou and Sun’s men ordered out of the Swatow garrison headquarters, 3 April 1916. China / Japan · telegraph code + code condenser · 1916 · solved "Tanaka" at Swatow to Sun Yat-sen Swatow, 3 April 1916, 6.05 pm, to "Rosamonde Tokio" · intercepted by the Japanese Foreign Ministry · JACAR B03050738800 (Gaimushō 680682) The condenser table recovered from 177 letters by brute force over the family of systematic tables; 41 of about 44 characters read Daniel Bourdeau · solved 15 September 2026 · updated 18 September 2026 Summary. In April 1916 the Japanese Foreign Ministry secretly obtained a 22-word telegram from a "Tanaka" at Swatow to "Rosamonde Tokio" — Soong Ching-ling's English name, so Sun Yat-sen's household — and could not read it. S. Tomokiyo listed it as unsolved in 2021 after trying the two code condensers known from Sun's Japanese supporter Yamada Junzaburō. The letters are the 20 consonants and 5 vowels of exactly such a condenser, and both known tables are systematic (alphabetical consonants, permuted vowels, filled row- or column-wise). That family is small — 57 600 keys with additives — and one of them, scored against a Chinese character model, stands eight standard deviations above the rest. The plaintext, in the standard telegraph codebook, is a field report from the revolutionaries' side at Swatow: 潮城由莫擎宇獨立。我軍亦光復汕頭。後莫率大隊來，令我退出鎮守府。我軍力薄，暫由翼□支持。文慧返…… "Chaozhou city has been declared independent by Mo Qingyu. Our force too has recovered Swatow. Then Mo came with a large body and ordered us out of the garrison headquarters. Our force is weak; for now we are supported by 翼□. 文慧 is returning …" — which is precisely what happened between 27 and 30 March 1916. Status: solved; three codes at the end are garbled in the received copy, and one name is unresolved. Sequel: the same family of keys reads some sixty more telegrams of Sun’s circle from the Ministry of Communications’ intercept files, 1916–17 — Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire .

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: JACAR B03050738800 is a Foreign Ministry file of 29 April – 11 May 1916 on Sun Yat-sen's cipher telegrams. It contains (i) five telegrams from Sun in Tokyo to a policeman of the Hankow consulate, in four-figure groups — the "+111" code that Tomokiyo has already read; (ii) a despatch, 機密送第一號, from Foreign Minister Ishii to the acting consul at Swatow, himself named Tanaka, asking who this "Tanaka" was, why he wired Sun, whether he was misusing the consul's name, and "if at all possible" to decode the telegram; (iii) the telegram; and (iv) the Hankow consul-general's report of 11 May on Sun's next scheme (five-figure groups, digits reversed, 111 subtracted). Nothing in the file reads the Swatow telegram. The first sheet of the telegram (JACAR B03050738800, frame 680682; crop by S. Tomokiyo). Station from Swatow, No. 1507, 22 words, 3/4/16 6.05 pm; address "Rosamonde Tokio". Twelve baxuxupeja qicijinati bemigasiqi jakebiqoye kufohemige tuxaboboba gedocijiga poyevayoxa leyoleveke biromapesa vorobenife xikebiqoye qekufiyaqa tijaqixiqo xitonatula xopavajejo ropezpo ngobunibai tanaka As read from the form. Tomokiyo's transcription has gedoeijiga and xitohatula ; the handwriting is c and n , and the decipherment requires exactly that. "Twelve" is the table indicator (Yamada's telegrams begin "Sixtyfour" for his 六十四號 table).

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: Alphabet. Consonants b c d f g h j k l m n p q r s t v x y z (twenty, no w) and vowels a e i o u — the 20 × 5 = 100 syllables of a two-digit code condenser: each syllable stands for a pair of digits, two syllables for one four-figure codebook group, and the syllables are run together and cut into ten-letter "words" to be charged as one word each. 177 letters → 88 syllables → 44 groups, one letter lost. Vowel u is rare (7 of 89 syllables against ~20 each for the others). In a column-major table each vowel owns a block of twenty numbers; the block 81–99, 00 is almost never a page number in the codebook (which stops in the 80s), so u is the high block. That already fixes the layout type. Known condensers. Yamada's Guoshiguan table runs x y z b c … v across rows and u o i e a down, numbered 01–99, 00 row by row; his Michigan table runs b … z alphabetically and o u a e i, numbered column by column from 00. Both are pure rule tables. The natural hypothesis for "table twelve" is another member of the same family: a rotation (or reversal) of the alphabetical consonants, a permutation of the vowels, either fill order, either origin, perhaps an additive as in Sun's own telegrams.

b: Codebook = 電報新編 / 明密碼電報書 numbering (identical to the modern standard telegraph code for these characters). Dotted = emended letter · red = unresolved ba xu · xe pe · ja qi · ci ji · na ti · be mi · ga si · qi ja · ke bi · qo ye · ku fo · ne mi · ge tu · xa bo · bo ba · ge do 3390 1004 3945 5459 2348 1342 3747 4539 2053 6511 0076 0342 1788 3073 7333 1775 潮 城 由 莫 擎 宇 獨 立 我 軍 亦 光 復 汕 頭 後 ci ji · ga po · ye va · yo xa · le yo · le ve · ke bi · ro ma · pe sa · vo ro · be ni · fe xi · ke bi · qo ye · qe ku · fi ya 5459 3764 1129 7130 0171 0109 2053 6622 0427 6966 1343 1650 2053 6511 0500 5631 莫 率 大 隊 來 令 我 退 出 鎮 守 府 我 軍 力 薄 qa ti · ja qi · xi qo · xi to · na tu · la xo · pa va · je jo · ro pe · [zpo ngobunibai] 2548 3945 5065 5068 2388 2170 2429 1979 6604 暫 由 翼 □ 支 持 文 慧 返 … 潮 城 由莫擎宇獨立。我軍亦 光 復汕頭。後 莫 率大隊來，令我退出鎮守府。我軍力薄，暫由 翼□ 支 持。 文慧 返 …… The events. On 26 March 1916 Mo Qingyu (莫擎宇), a regimental commander at Chaozhou under Long Jiguang's Chao-Mei garrison, was won over by Chen Jiongming, Lin Hu, He Haiming and the local revolutionaries; on the 27th he occupied Chaozhou city and wired the provincial authorities "率師占領潮城，宣布獨立" — 潮城 , the very word of the telegram. On the 30th the Swatow guard troops declared for him and he formally proclaimed independence with his headquarters at Swatow. Sun's own Chinese Revolutionary Party men had meanwhile taken the town's garrison headquarters (鎮守使署); "Tanaka", one of the Japanese adventurers serving with them, reports on 3 April that Mo, arriving in force, has ordered them out, that they are too weak to resist, and that someone is returning — presumably to Tokyo to report. The Ministry's suspicion that the sender was trading on the Swatow consul's name is a nice irony: the consul was also a Tanaka.

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: 城. The form reads baxuxupeja → 90 04 , and no codebook has page 90. One vowel-stroke away is xe pe = 1004 城, which the history all but dictates (潮州 1558, 潮梅 2734 and 潮汕 3073 are unreachable from the letters). The second u is probably an e. 翼□ (5065 5068). Both syllables of 翼 are confirmed elsewhere; the second group's to is not, and 5068 (翿) is not a word. A name or a unit that "supported" the revolutionaries once Mo displaced them — the Swatow guard? a ship of Tang Tingguang's squadron? — is expected here. 文慧 (2429 1979). Sent as read; presumably a person who "returns". 文 is also Sun Wen's signature character. The tail. After 返 the form has zpo ngobunibai : a seven-letter "word" cannot occur in this system, and ng , ai are not syllables. An exhaustive search of all strings within three plausible edits (h/n, u/n, c/e confusions, dropped letters) yields no decoding into valid codes. Roughly three characters — a place or a request — are lost unless the second sheet of frame 680682 can be read at higher resolution. The two h syllables of the transcription ( he , ha ) both decode as nonsense and both read as n on the form (光, 支). The h row of the table is therefore unattested, but the layout leaves it no other place.

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: The JACAR file was read page by page (the archive's image server refuses automated access; the PDF was supplied by hand) for context and to check the letters. Syllable statistics: the 20 + 5 alphabet and the deficit of u pointed to a systematic, column-major condenser. Brute force over the whole systematic family (57 600 keys) with a character-unigram score over the standard codebook (Unihan telegraph tables; the 1916 numbering verified on Tomokiyo's decoded Sun telegrams). Four doubtful groups examined by one-letter alternatives; the readings 光復, 支持, 莫, 潮城 chosen by sense and then found in the handwriting. Edit-distance search over the garbled tail (negative). Historical check against the 26–30 March chronology of Mo Qingyu's rising.

t: Throckmorton — archived key and published plaintext
b: Twenty DECODE records in BL Add MS 4136 lead to Forbes and CSP. The archived third cipher reads two short samples, 42 tokens in all. A record-to-edition concordance separates the published counterparts from full token verification; composite material remains to be checked. France → Cecil, Elizabeth I and the Council · Homophones and nomenclator · 1560–63 · Prior solution verified Throckmorton: the key survives, and the text was printed Twenty records catalogued as non-decrypted in BL Add MS 4136 lead to surviving keys, Forbes's eighteenth-century edition and the Calendar of State Papers. Two samples verify the connection. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 Summary. The proposed target was a group of twenty DECODE records, R9220–R9234, R9242–R9245 and R9255. All 54 image references were obtained; they represent 39 distinct photographs because adjacent records share leaves. Four nearby key records add 17 photographs. R9262 supplies the archived “Third Cipher” and reads a complete numbered extract on R9220, matching Forbes I, p.355. A second, shorter check on R9230 matches Forbes II, p.12. A twenty-record concordance identifies published counterparts, most by date and addressee. These are 42 verified tokens, not twenty complete decryptions . Tomokiyo had already identified the printed texts and surviving keys; this result confirms that route and corrects the target description.

t: Throckmorton — archived key and published plaintext
h: A key test on the first leaf
b: R9220, f.110, begins in the middle of a letter. Its first complete numbered extract, (6), reads: all be it i be revoked or the warr breake In modern English: “albeit I be recalled, or war break out.” Throckmorton is asking Cecil to obtain permission for Mr Jones to remain abroad and gain experience, even if the ambassador is recalled or war begins. Forbes prints the phrase in volume I (1740), p.355, within the 7 March 1559/60 despatch. The same leaf includes the 8 March continuation and the separate letter to the Queen of 9 March. The 27 transcribed cipher tokens include two nulls. The alphabet on R9262 image P1 supplies the letters: dotted 4, 5 and 6 all represent r ; plain 4 represents o ; colon-marked 6 represents u/v . P3 gives the marked A for all and marked b for be . P4 gives the suffix -ed , and P9 gives the curved T for the/to . Thus the reading tests the alphabet, word signs, suffixes and nulls together. The final word before breake is warr , with two different r homophones, not wars . R9230, f.133, offers a second check at the opening of extract (1): orleans or burges These fifteen alphabet tokens agree with Forbes II (1741), p.12. CSP Foreign V, no.425, paragraph 11 summarizes the surrounding warning: the apparent preparations against Orleans or Bourges may conceal an attack on Rouen, Newhaven (Le Havre), and Dieppe. No.426 describes a separate decipher of the ciphered passages. The rest of that sentence has not been transcribed token by token here. Both checks have grade H : values read from the archived key. Spacing and capitalization are editorial. The printed counterparts were available during verification, so these are known-plaintext checks, not blind decipherments. The token labels and values are preserved in control.json and control_9230.json , with a replay script. The script verifies substitution of those labels; inspection of the images establishes the glyph identifications.

h: Prior work and the misleading target description
b: Satoshi Tomokiyo's Elizabethan cipher study already identifies the Add MS 4136 ciphertexts as largely extracts, cites Forbes, reconstructs three Throckmorton ciphers, and records the archive keys in a November 2024 note. This is not a newly discovered key or first publication of the plaintext. DECODE's “Non-decrypted” status describes the record and cannot by itself establish that the text is unread. t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: The duplicate of the viceroy of Sicily’s ciphered despatch from Messina, two months into the Great Siege, AGS Estado leg. 1394 no. 247: clear Spanish with every sensitive word in two-digit figures, and no decipherment on the leaf or in PARES. Two runs beside clear words, seiscientos soldados and en tiera , gave eleven letters; the figures 12–43 run through the alphabet in order, so the rest was predicted and confirmed, and all 1,930 groups read. The Piccolo Soccorso got into the Borgo; a second run of galleys turned back four miles out on La Valette’s signals, as Mosiur de Lenni reported; and Sicily cannot pay for the war. Messina → Philip II · homophonic figure cipher in alphabetical order · 16 July 1565 · solved García de Toledo to Philip II, Messina, 16 July 1565 AGS Estado leg. 1394 no. 247, the duplicado of a ciphered despatch from the viceroy of Sicily two months into the Great Siege of Malta · four pages of Spanish with every sensitive word in two-digit figures · no decipherment on the leaf or in the catalogue Broken from two runs beside clear words; the key is the alphabet in order on the figures 12–43, so the rest was predicted and then confirmed · 1,930 groups read end to end Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 Summary. On 16 July 1565 Don García de Toledo, viceroy of Sicily, wrote to Philip II from Messina with news from besieged Malta. The copy at Simancas is the duplicado : clear Spanish with the names, numbers and intelligence replaced by runs of two-digit figures, and nothing on the leaf or in the PARES record to say what they mean. The cipher is a homophonic substitution in which the figures 12 to 43 run through the alphabet in order, three figures for each vowel and one for each consonant, with no nulls and no code words. Two runs standing beside clear words, seiscientos soldados after los and en tiera after puso , gave eleven letters; the order of the table predicted the rest. The letter reports that the 600 soldiers Don Juan de Cardona landed entraron en el burgo a saluamento ; that the Grand Master wept for joy; and that a second run of galleys toward the harbour turned back when La Valette made them las sennales del fuego clarissimas para que no entrassen . The rest is money and fortification: El estar sin galeras me destruye , and in the kingdom there is nothing si no infinitas deudas . Status: read end to end; a handful of words are doubtful in sense, none in their figures. The original despatch, which could carry a contemporary decipherment, has not been found.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: The Archivo General de Simancas, Estado, legajo 1394, no. 247, is catalogued on PARES as Duplicado de carta cifrada de García de Toledo, capitán general del Mar, a Felipe II, rey de España , 16 July 1565. It is two leaves: four pages of text (ff. 1r–2v) and an address leaf, sealed and inscribed En manos del señor Franco de Erasso , for the King’s secretary Francisco de Eraso. The first page is docketed Dupp.do in the upper left. A duplicate was a second copy sent by another route in case the first was lost, and this one is a clerk’s copy: it carries copying slips that the original presumably does not ( quesido for querido , puddo for puedo , lonze for onze ). PARES serves the six images (four text pages and the address leaf twice) as plain JPEGs about 915 pixels wide. That is the largest size the viewer gives; asking for any zoom other than the default returns a smaller image. At that size the figures are legible when a line is cropped and enlarged two and a half to five times, which is how every figure here was read. F. 1r, lines 1–3: Llevo tan [ ruyn ] . [ nueua ] a V. Mag. el correo passado que no me ha parescido detener este para que [ en parte ] la mejore. los [ seiscientos / soldados ] que don Juan de Cardona puso [ en tiera ] fue . The run after los and the run after puso are the two cribs that broke the cipher (AGS, PARES, image 1). The letter is written in running Spanish, and the figures stand in the line wherever a word was thought sensitive: the relief, the Grand Master, the galleys, the signals, sums of money, place names, the enemy. Figure runs are written without word breaks, so a run such as 3618243616241829 is one or several words run together.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: A homophonic substitution on two-digit figures, in which the values 12 to 43 are assigned to the letters in alphabetical order. The five vowels and u/v have three figures each, every consonant one: letter figures letter figures letter figures a 12 13 14 i 24 25 26 r 35 b 15 l 27 s 36 c 16 m 28 t 37 d 17 n 29 u / v 38 39 40 e 18 19 20 o 30 31 32 x 41 f 21 p 33 y 42 g 22 q 34 z 43 h 23 The alphabet has no j , k or w , and u and v are one letter, as in the clear hand. The table uses exactly the thirty-two values from 12 to 43, and no figure outside that range occurs in the letter: no nulls, and no code groups for names or words. Names are spelt out letter by letter, Caragoca (Syracuse), Augusta , Cabo Bono , Argel , Maltta , Mecina , Mosiur de Lenni . The homophones are not used evenly. Of the three a figures, 13 occurs about 140 times, 14 about 95 and 12 about 50; of the e figures, 19 is used twice as often as 18 and nearly four times as often as 20; of the o figures, 31 about a hundred times against 40 for 30 and 13 for 32. The clerk had favourites. The overall letter frequencies are ordinary Spanish: a and e first, then s , r and o . Four things about the hand need to be known before the decode reads cleanly. ñ is written nn ( sennales , Espanna , campanna ). Double letters are sometimes written single ( en tiera ) and sometimes doubled where the word has one ( spantaado , quinta[a]les ). The duplicado has its own copying slips, listed above. And the confusable pairs in this hand are 17/19 , 35/36 , 35/38 (a long-tailed 3 against a dotted 8) and 13/14 .

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: Two cribs from the clear text. The second line of f. 1r has los followed by the run 36 18 24 36 16 24 18 29 37 30 36 and, on the next line, 36 30 27 17 13 17 31 36 . Eleven figures with the first repeated at the fourth and eleventh places, standing after an article, fit seiscientos , and the next run then reads soldados . A few words on, the run after don Juan de Cardona puso is 19 29 37 25 19 35 14 , en tiera , “put ashore”, spelt with one r . Together these fix a c d e i l n o r s t , with two figures each for a , e , i and o . The table closes itself. Set out by value, the recovered figures were already in alphabetical order: 13 14 a , 16 c , 17 d , 18 19 e , 24 25 i , 27 l , 29 n , 30 31 o , 35 r , 36 s , 37 t . Once that was seen the gaps did not need solving. Each could be predicted from its position and then checked on a word: 21 f , 41 x , 42 y and 43 z were filled that way and confirmed on 18212118373136 effetos , 15124119271836 baxeles , 42151329 yban and 332712431935 plazer . Transcribe, decode, correct. The whole letter was then transcribed digit for digit with the clear text around the runs, and decoded by script. Nonsense in the output points to a misread figure, almost always one of the confusable pairs above, and every correction to the transcription was found that way rather than by re-reading at random. The audit. All 1,930 figure groups fall inside 12–43; all thirty-two values occur; no run has an odd number of digits. An out-of-range value or an odd run would be the mark of a transcription error, and none is left.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: A key built from the clear text could in principle only reproduce what the clear text already implies. The check is a name the clear text does not contain. On f. 1v, after the Grand Master’s signal not to enter, the clear hand writes y ansi lo dize and then the run 2830362539 35 1719 271929 2925 , which decodes to Mosiur de Lenni : Monsieur de Leinì, that is Andrea Provana di Leinì, the Savoyard commander whose galleys sailed in the relief squadron, and exactly the man who would report whether the signals were made. Nothing in the clear text points to him. F. 1v: millas del [ puerto ]. el [ maestre ] les hizo [ las senna / les ] del [ fuego clarissimas ] para que no [ entrassen ] / y ansi lo dize [ Mosiur de Lenni ] y todos los demas y dentro de . The run after dize is the check on the key (AGS, PARES, image 2). The rest of the ciphered matter is consistent in the same way: Don Juan de Cardona’s 600 soldiers, the pilot Don Juan Çanoguera , the Conde de Módica serving at his own cost, Gian Andrea Doria’s claim on the viceroy’s funds, and the fortification of Syracuse and Augusta.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: Clear text roman, figures in italic ; spelling of the leaf kept ( nn = ñ, u / v as written); word division inside a figure run is editorial, since the cipher writes none; square brackets are editorial f. 1r Llevo tan ruyn nueua a V. Mag. el correo passado que no me ha parescido detener este para que en parte la mejore. Los seiscientos soldados que don Juan de Cardona puso en tiera fue Dios servido de guiallos tanbien que todos entraron en el burgo a saluamento . Dizeme este que ha salido que fue tan grande la alegria del maestre , abracando la gente sin podello hablar, que lloraua de plazer ; y tanbien dize que otro dia salio la misma gente a dar en los Turcos y que mataron mas de dozientos, aunque estas salidas en ningun caso queria que las hiziese , y por muchas letras se lo tengo scripto con mucho encarescimiento. Del maestre no tengo carta , que estoy spantado [ms. spantaado ] dello, pero no tengo por mala seña olvidarse de mi, aunque no creo que tardara a dos o tres dias a venir; y conforme a lo que scriuiere uere de proueer lo mas que por el se pudiere . El estar sin galeras me destruye , porque se po- f. 1v -drian hazer algunos effetos en baxeles suyos que van y vienen, pero trayendo las que aca ay ocupadas en iuntar la gente no se puede proueer a todo . Si [u]iniessen las de Spanna me darian mucha ayuda . Las galeras que yban a entrar por el puerto llegaron a quatro millas del, con muy buena orden y gran determinacion , y aquella noche , que sera lunes , vna hora antes que amaneciesse , viniendo el martes , entro a saluamento la uarqueta que yo hauia embiado para auisar al maestre de las sennales , con la qual tuuo auiso de lo que hauia de hazer ; y tornando las galeras el martes en la noche a otras quatro millas del puerto , el maestre les hizo las sennales del fuego clarissimas para que no entrassen , y ansi lo dize Mosiur de Lenni y todos los demas; y dentro de la hora sennalada las continuo la segunda vez, y las galeras se tornaron a meter a la mar por no ser descubiertas , y han llegado aqui esta mannana . El don Juan Çanoguera, que es el que las guiaua , lo hizo muy bien , y todos los demas. Y este no sabe que[r]ido [ms. quesido ] el maestre aceptar estas galeras ; aunque podria ser por parescelle la entrada muy dificultosa , no dexo de tenella por buena senal . Dizen todos los nuestros que, en acabando de hazer el maestre las sennales , vieron y oyeron vna gran cantidad de arcabuzeria, y que juzgauan ellos que sera salua para mostrarnos que nuestra gente sera dentro . Este ombre que es venido salio del burgo el mismo lunes a los diez y nueue, y no trae nueua de la uarqueta que entro , porque no sera aun llegada ; la qual puso el que yo embie a do le mande, y de alli f. 2r hauia de yr a nado hasta el burgo , y ansi llego saluo , como a la clara se ve por las sennales ; y la ciudad hizo el mismo fuego , que tanbien es indicio que llego el que por aquella parte embie con el duplicado . Los tiempos son tales y las necessidades tan grandes, que aunque se tuuiesse mucho dinero no osaria deshazerme de vn rreal para pagar deudas ; y aunque es justissimo lo que V. Mag. manda de Juan Andrea, se podra hazer poco con el, pero lo que se pudiera no se dexara de hazer como V. Mag. lo manda, que cierto yo desseo dalle toda satisfacion, y el solo sera en este tiempo el que de mi cobrara alguna quantidad. Es necessario poner luego mano en comencar a fortificar , por todo lo que podria suceder , la fruente que Caragoca tiene en tierra firme , y en leuantar vn cavallero en la mar que corresponde —çierto es secanos donde podria ser assaltada . Tanbien es necessario comencar al fin de octubre la fortificacion de Augusta , por que la ocasion no mostrasse a los enemigos el segundo salto. Para estas casas es menester dinero , y en este reyno no ay si no infinitas deudas . V. Mag. mande echar quenta de los ytalianos que se han de leuantar , y de los spannoles que se han de pagar, y del sueldo de las naues, que cada mes importa quarenta mil escudos sin dos mesadas que se les deuen; y vease tanbien el uizcocho que de nueuo es menester hazer, que aunque despues se desquente a las galeras su parte, todavia este dinero sale del que V. Mag. me ha embiado. Hanse comprado quinientos quintales de artilleria de peso f. 2v de Espanna , mucha xarcia y madera para las yaretas [jaretas]; y aunque esta xarcia y madera puede seruir para las galeras que se huuieren de hazer, y lo del metal es dinero que no se pierde , todavia cuesta buen pedaço. Tanbien se haze armamento para las ocho galeras que vienen de Espanna , y otros gastos de botas, barriles, murriones y coracinas que no se pueden escusar. Y si se quenta esto, y se añade el sueldo de la ynfanteria , contando tanbien el gasto de [l]onze galeras que se arman de nueuo, vera V. Mag. que la prouision echa no basta para tantas casas, ni yo pu[e]do [ms. puddo ] sustentar con ella los gastos que V. Mag. apunta en su carta , tanto mas si esto se fuesse nada alargando . Y los quarenta y ocho mil ducados que venieron para las galeras ya estaua comido la mitad , y otra buena parte se deue a la gente. Y considerado esto, suplico a V. Mag. mande proueer como mas se paresciere que conuiene a su seruicio, y en el gastallos se terna el miramiento que V. Mag. manda. Dize este que ha salido que todos los turcos que estan en tierra , demas de los bastiones a do tienen sus baterias , estan todos circundados de trincheas siete, ocho y diez palmos altas , assi a la parte de los nuestros como a la parte de la campanna ; y que quando el partio no hauia otros que no las tuuiessen si no mil y quinientos turcos que estauan al agua . Confirma que hauian perdido mucha gente , y que en el campo corrian dolencias de que morian . Por essos auisos vera V. Mag. los nauios que hallo sobre Cabo Bono el baxel que yua con uino a la Goleta . Tengo por cierto que son los de Argel que se uienen a iuntar con la armada ; y esto creo por no saber que de Maltta aya salido cantidad dellos , porque dize este que del armada no se hauia desmandado nauio ninguno quando el partio , ni tan poco lo escriue el gouernador de la ciudad , como vera V. Mag. por su carta original que yra con esta. Cuya vida guarde Nuestro Señor por tan largos años como sus criados y vassallos desseamos y la christiandad ha menester. De Mecina , a XVJ. de Julio 1565. Postscript (entirely in the clear) Ya tengo scripto a V. Mag. por otras quan bien le sirue el conde de Modica, y a su costa; y hauiendole agora scripto el almirante su padre la muerte de la duquesa su madre, y llamandole que vaya a España, no obstante que esto le ymporte mucho, no ha querido hazello ni yrse deste reyno hasta ver el sucesso de las cosas de aca. Hame parescido muy justo auisar dello a V. Mag., para que tenga entendido su voluntad y el seruicio que haze en ello a V. Mag. English García writes from Messina on 16 July 1565, about two months into the siege and some days after the relief known as the Piccolo Soccorso reached the Borgo (Birgu) at the start of July. Everything below that is in italics in the Spanish was in figures. The relief got in. He had sent the King bad news by the last courier and writes now to soften it: the six hundred soldiers Don Juan de Cardona put ashore all entered the Borgo safely. A man just out of the Borgo says the Grand Master embraced them, unable to speak, and wept for joy; and that the next day the same men sortied against the Turks and killed more than two hundred, though García had written many times that there were to be no sorties. He has no letter from the Grand Master himself and expects one within two or three days. A second run turned back. The galleys meant to enter the harbour came within four miles of it, in good order. That night, an hour before dawn on Tuesday, the barqueta he had sent ahead to arrange the signals with the Grand Master got in. On Tuesday night the galleys came again to four miles off, and the Grand Master made the fire-signals, very clear, that they were not to enter, and repeated them within the appointed hour, as Monsieur de Leinì and all the others report. The galleys put back out to sea so as not to be seen, and reached Messina this morning. Çanoguera, who guided them, did it very well. Nobody knows why the Grand Master would not take the galleys in; perhaps the entry looked too hard, but García takes it for a good sign. As the signals ended the galleys heard a great volley of arquebus fire, which they judged a salute to show that the men were inside. The messengers. The man who left the Borgo that Monday has no news of the barqueta , which had not arrived when he left. The barqueta landed García’s messenger where it was ordered, and from there he was to swim to the Borgo; the signals show he arrived. La ciudad , Mdina, made the same fire, a sign that the man sent by that route with the duplicate had arrived too. Money. Even with money in hand he would not dare part with a real to pay debts. He will do what he can for Gian Andrea Doria, as ordered, and Doria will be the only one paid anything. He asks the King to reckon the Italians to be raised, the Spaniards to be paid, and the ships, which cost forty thousand escudos a month with two months’ pay already owed; biscuit to be baked; five hundred quintals of artillery by Spanish weight, cordage and timber for the jaretas ; fitting out the eight galleys coming from Spain and eleven more being armed; casks, barrels, morions and cuirasses; and the infantry’s pay. The provision sent does not cover it: half the 48,000 ducados sent for the galleys is already spent and much of the rest is owed to the men. “Being without galleys ruins me.” Fortification. Work should begin at once on the landward front of Syracuse and on a cavalier facing the sea, where the ground would let it be stormed; and on the fortification of Augusta at the end of October, so that the occasion should not show the enemy “the second leap”. For this money is needed, and in this kingdom there is nothing but infinite debts. The besiegers. The man from the Borgo says all the Turks ashore, besides the bastions where they have their batteries, are ringed with trenches seven, eight and ten palms high, facing both the Christians and the open country; when he left, only fifteen hundred Turks at the water were without them. The Turks have lost many men, and sickness is killing men in their camp. At sea. The ships that a vessel carrying wine to La Goleta found off Cape Bon, García is sure, are the Algiers squadron coming to join the fleet. No ship had left the fleet at Malta when his man came away, and the governor of la ciudad says none either, as his original letter, sent with this one, will show. Postscript, in clear. The Conde de Módica serves well and at his own cost; summoned to Spain by his father the Admiral after his mother’s death, he will not leave Sicily until he sees how things end here. The letter was written during the worst of the siege, while García was still gathering the force that landed on Malta as the Gran Soccorso on 7 September; the siege was raised days later. In July he had few galleys to spare, and this letter shows what they could do: put small parties into the Borgo by night and watch for the Grand Master’s fires.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: yaretas (f. 2v, line 1): the figures are unambiguous, 42 12 35 20 37 14 36 . It is read as jaretas , the netting rigged over a galley’s deck; with the 41/42 confusion it could be xaretas , the same word. secanos (f. 2r): “çierto es secanos donde podria ser assaltada ” is taken as shoals or dry ground that would let the sea-facing cavalier be stormed. The figures read; the sense is a guess. “salio del burgo el mismo lunes a los diez y nueue”: taken as the hour, not the day of the month, since 19 July is after the letter’s date. Which duplicate went by way of Mdina (f. 2r, el que por aquella parte embie con el duplicado ) is not said; it is presumably a second copy of García’s own message to the Grand Master. The original despatch, which this is the duplicate of, and the Mdina governor’s letter that went with it have not been found on PARES; a search for the ciphered Toledo letters of 1565 returns only this item. The original could carry a contemporary decipherment in the secretariat’s hand, and that would be the independent check on this reading. Until it is found, the check is internal: the self-consistency of the table, the audit, and the names. No published text of the letter was found in web searches for the document and for editions of the Simancas Malta correspondence (18 September 2026). That is not the same as a search of the printed literature on the siege, and an edition may exist that the searches missed.

t: Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich — a book cipher on his own Jewel, read without the plaintext
b: Eight lines and a “Decagram” of numbers on the last leaf of The Jewel (1652), Schmeh’s Top 50 no. 28. Number k indexes a word on physical page k of the book, and Urquhart took the first word of the initial he needed: a habit checkable without any plaintext. The public transcription was thirteen numbers short; the 1983 edition’s photographs on the HCPortal give 285, which decode straight with 238 of 284 first-occurrence hits against 0.43 for shuffled and random-page controls, into a royalist prayer for Charles II. Vals AI published the rule in August 2026 as a Claude Fable 5.1 result; the companion distich claim does not reproduce. London · book cipher on the author's own printed book · 1652–53 · octastich read Thomas Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich and Distich The Jewel (1652), final leaf · eight lines and a “Decagram”, 285 numbers to 201 · Logopandecteision (1653), “The Cyphral Distich”, 64 numbers to 70 · Schmeh’s Top 50, no. 28 The octastich is read in full from the EEBO-TCP text of The Jewel and a fresh transcription of its 285 numbers from the 1983 edition, without using the plaintext published by Vals AI on 31 August 2026; 238 of 284 numbers are first-occurrence hits against 0.43 for both controls. The distich rule does not reproduce. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 16 September 2026 Summary. Urquhart printed a verse under the octastich saying the key was “gather’d out of my Exskybalorum” and that he loved “an aphaeresified treason”: the cipher takes word-initials from the book it is printed in. The k -th number, counting straight through the poem, is a word index into physical page k of the 1652 Jewel , and Urquhart took the first word on the page that began with the letter he wanted. That habit makes the rule testable without any plaintext: whether number n on page k is the first word of its own initial is a fact about the page. The public transcription (Schmeh, 2015) turned out to be short by thirteen numbers; the 1983 Jack and Lyall edition, photographed on the HCPortal record, gives 285. Decoded one number per page against the TCP text, 238 of 284 are first-occurrence hits, against 0.43 for the same numbers shuffled and 0.44 for random pages, and the poem reads: Great Lord, mantaine that regal familie, / Whereof King Charls the second is the head, / And grant that he may beare the supreme sweigh / Where English, Scots and Irsh are borne and bred; / And […] this usurp’d authoritie / Reigne in his royal predecessors stead: / Let him be our sole Cesar, Artur, Hector, / Our Emperour, King, Monarch and Protector. / Amen, so be it. Vals AI published this rule and plaintext on 31 August 2026 as a Claude Fable 5.1 result; here it is reached from the text and the numbers alone, and their two caveats are traced to defects of the digitised copy. The distich claim, i -th number into the i -th Proquiritation, gives 34 of 64 first-occurrence hits, chance for texts that short, and no English. Status: octastich read, ten letters of line 5 excepted; distich open.

t: Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich — a book cipher on his own Jewel, read without the plaintext
b: The distich stands under the heading “THE CYPHRAL DISTICH” after the thirty-two Proquiritations that close Logopandecteision , followed by six lines promising that “an honest skilful man” will find in it “his own heart’s wishes, and the Author’s minde”. Reticuli Labs showed on 1 September 2026, and the 1834 Maitland Club reprint confirms, that this page is in the 1834 Works (p. 417) and not in the British Library’s 1653 copy. The octastich stands on the last leaf of The Jewel (1652), a leaf missing from every digitised copy; its public transcription is Klaus Schmeh’s, from a scan sent him in 2014, and the HCPortal record holds a scan with the verse beneath it, which a reader quoted in 2019: To this Octastick if you will subjoyn / A Decagram of this same stuff of mine, / All gather’d out of my Exskybalorum, / You’ll find a Rule by which, with great decorum, / You may most comfortably regulate / Your actions, thoughts and speeches; and know that / I love an aphaeresified treason / Better then any prosthesized reason. Aphaeresis is the loss of a word’s first letter. Urquhart says, in his way, that the cipher is made of initials taken out of his own book.

t: Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich — a book cipher on his own Jewel, read without the plaintext
h: A test that never sees the plaintext
b: A book cipher of this kind is normally judged by whether the letters it yields make sense, which invites the objection that a determined reader can make sense of anything. Urquhart’s habit removes that objection. If he scanned each page from the top and stopped at the first word beginning with the letter he needed, then for the right page the number he wrote is the index of the first word of its own initial. That is a property of the number and the page alone. For a wrong page, or a wrong rule, it holds at the base rate, which in this book is about 43 % for a random page and index because small indices are common and the first few words of any page are first occurrences by construction. The EEBO-TCP transcription of The Jewel was parsed into word lists per page. The 1652 printer numbered pages 34–35, 38–39, 42–43 and 46–47 twice and skipped 60 and 110, so pages are counted physically from p. 1, and three duplicated page breaks that the TCP carries for re-shot images are removed. Schmeh’s 272-number transcription, the only one in circulation since 2015, omits the run-over lines of stanzas 2 and 6, one figure, and misreads one; a dynamic-programme alignment that may skip pages still placed it at 231 first-occurrence hits in 267 and read five lines. The photographs of the 1983 edition on the HCPortal record give the full 285, which then decode straight, one number per page. Run First-occurrence rate The 285 numbers, one per physical page 0.838 (238/284) Same numbers shuffled, 200 trials mean 0.434, max 0.491 Numbers in order, pages randomly permuted, 200 trials mean 0.436, max 0.509 Schmeh’s 272 numbers, aligned with page skips 0.865 (231/267), vs 0.686 shuffled and re-aligned Distich, i -th number into i -th Proquiritation 0.53 (34/64), no English Distich, shuffled, against pages of The Jewel , 100 trials mean 0.50, max 0.62 Line 1 alone makes the case: 28 of its 33 numbers are exactly the first word of the needed initial on physical page k , and the other five are one word off (25 for 26, 18 for 17, 23 for 22, 75 for 74) or a TCP variant, which is the size of difference one expects between a modern tokenisation and a 1652 page.

t: Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich — a book cipher on his own Jewel, read without the plaintext
b: The same test applied to the distich under Vals’ Proquiritation rule, using Reticuli’s tokenised Proquiritations, yields 34 first-occurrence hits in 64 and the string NTMAMNDN_OHTISEABRPTTSGSNTAATVTD , not O God uphold King Charls the second . Texts of thirty to a hundred words give high base rates, so 34 of 64 is chance. Page-index variants on either book, with either numbering, with the second line restarting at page 1, all sit inside the shuffled control. Reticuli’s ten infeasible positions stand. The distich is a different construction, or the same construction on a text not yet tried, and it remains unread.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one found solved, one read, one without its key
b: Three imperial ciphers in BnF fr. 3022, listed with no decipherment. Del Vasto’s letter from Ischia of 27 September 1527 had been solved by George Lasry and Satoshi Tomokiyo. The anonymous “report” is del Vasto’s own letter of December 1527: Lasry had its letters, and about forty of its code groups are identified here, which makes it readable as his plan to march on Siena, Perugia and Urbino. The Madrid letter to “Garbino” is in Hieronimo Ranzo’s initial-letter code. Its numbering is not alphabetical, and without the table only its function words come out. Ischia, Rome and Madrid → Charles V and “Garbino” · letter cipher with code groups; initial-letter code · September 1527 – April 1528 · partly read Del Vasto to Charles V, and a letter to “Garbino” from Madrid, 1527–28 Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 3022 nos. 6, 10 and 20 · imperial papers that reached French hands during Lautrec’s campaign in Italy · catalogued with “no decipherment noted” One of the three was already solved elsewhere. One is read here except for about fifteen code groups. The third is in a code whose key does not survive, and it stays unread. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 18 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue grouped three pieces as one target: a letter of the Marquis del Vasto to Charles V from “Ysola” (Ischia), 27 September 1527 (no. 10); an anonymous “Rapport … à l’empereur” (no. 6); and an Italian memoir from Madrid, 11 April 1528 (no. 20). The first thing to check was whether anyone had read them already. No. 10 had been solved : George Lasry in 2023, text edited by Satoshi Tomokiyo in 2026. No. 6 is del Vasto’s own letter of early December 1527. Lasry had its letter layer but not its code groups; about forty of those are identified here from context, and the letter reads as del Vasto’s plan for moving the army out of Rome. No. 20 is a letter to “Garbino” in the code of Hieronimo Ranzo, a kinsman of the Chancellor Gattinara. All 1,315 of its groups were transcribed, with about 2,600 more from Ranzo’s own letters. Without the key, only its function words can be recovered. Status: partly read. No. 10 found solved by others; no. 6 read except about fifteen code groups; no. 20 not read. It needs Ranzo’s code table or a clear copy of one of his letters.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one found solved, one read, one without its key
b: Français 3022 is a sixteenth-century recueil of originals and copies, mostly imperial correspondence of 1527–28 that came into French hands. There are about twenty letters of Juan Pérez, the imperial secretary in Rome, several of them in clear. There are three letters of the Marquis del Vasto (Alfonso d’Ávalos), who commanded the imperial infantry after the Sack of Rome. There are Spanish “avertimientos” of 1528 from Fuenterrabía and Bayonne, and a small bundle of Italian espionage papers. The notice’s folio numbers run about three higher than the ink foliation. Below, folios are the ink numbers and “views” are Gallica’s (ark btv1b90601558). No. Folios (views) What it is Outcome 10 ff. 26–28 and loose f. 39 (51–55, 76–77) Del Vasto to Charles V, “de Ysola”, 27 September 1527 Already solved (Lasry 2023, Tomokiyo 2026) 6 ff. 16v–17v (32–34) Catalogued as an anonymous report; actually del Vasto to Charles V, Rome, early December 1527 Read, about fifteen code groups open 19 ff. 40–43 (78–85) Del Vasto to Charles V, Rome, 6 November 1527 (not in the target, same key as no. 6) Lasry’s letter layer, partial; content summarised in CSP Spain 20 ff. 44–46v (86–91) Italian letter to “Garbino”, Madrid, 11 April 1528 Transcribed; not read 20bis, 21 ff. 48–50v (94–98) A jargon, a code-name list and an “Aditione nel zifra” Read; they explain the design of no. 20’s code

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one found solved, one read, one without its key
h: Checked first: who had read them
b: The catalogue says “no decipherment noted”, and the obvious place for a French decipherment was checked first. The eighteenth-century Clairambault copies were searched. Clairambault 327 ff. 279–280 copies no. 20 as “Lettre non signée écrite au seigneur Garbino du 11 d’avril 1528 … partie en chiffre, partie non”, with the cipher copied and nothing deciphered. Clairambault 314 f. 337 copies the addition sheet. Neither carries a decipherment, and none turned up in the neighbouring français volumes. The decipherments are modern. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana pages record that George Lasry sent him a solution of no. 10 in 2023. In 2026 Tomokiyo edited it into a Spanish text and published it as “Gasto–Charles V Cipher 1”. He also published Lasry’s preliminary letter-level decryption of a second cipher, used in no. 6 and in no. 19, asking for someone who knows Spanish to finish it. No. 10 is therefore counted here as found, not read. Its text was checked against the ciphertext and not redone. BnF fr. 3022 f. 26r, no. 10: del Vasto from Ischia, 27 September 1527. The cipher letters are disguised Latin letters with word divisions kept, which is why it fell to Lasry’s solver. Bibliothèque nationale de France.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one found solved, one read, one without its key
b: The piece catalogued as an anonymous report opens in clear: “A seis de noviembre escrivi a V. M. muy largo y tanbien a xxvij de setiembre, cuyos duplicados van con esta”. The clear first page reports the agreement with the Pope for “la libertad suya y de los cardenales” (the capitulation of 26 November) and says that del Vasto is still in Rome only because the Prince of Orange, “el qual se espera que verna de aqui a tres dias”, has not yet arrived to take the command. That puts it in the first days of December 1527. f. 16v: “y por otros se sabe como han buelto sobre Mylan”, then cipher. The first cipher words, dʃfp nnbt qʃftxp , read creo mas presto . Bibliothèque nationale de France. The cipher is a Caesar shift of one place over a 21-letter alphabet, with homophones, plus a nomenclator of three-letter groups beginning with b , c or d . Lasry’s decryption has the letter layer right; it checks against the f. 16v ciphertext word for word. It leaves the groups as [doz] , [deh] and so on, and some of its short homophone labels are consistently off: “con” is como , some “al” are el , some “fin” are mas . Taking every occurrence of each group across nos. 6 and 19 and reading the Spanish around it fixes about forty of them. Group Reading Deciding context doz Lautreque “piénsase que [doz] será para ir sobre el reino” deh la Marca “su camino es por la [deh], porque traen su artillería por agua hasta Ravena” bog buelta “camina la [bog] del reino”; “la [bog] de Perosa” ceg hombre “no quieren ser más [ceg]s d’armas” daf quiere “para caminar un exército se re[daf]n” (requieren) dor para “[dor] ir sobre el reino”, “[dor] caminar” baf primero “mi parecer es [baf] que salga el exército” dnd qual “Siena, la [dnd] es muy devota de V. M.” dnb dinero “alguna manera de [dnb] o de hazelles la guerra” biq , boq duque, estado “al [biq] de Urbino”; “el [boq] de Urbino y tomallo” cef gente “esta [cef] ha venido en un número tan poco” dod , don , dum , cez , raq quando, si, su, ni, mi “por vía de [dum] Santidad”; “no se puede mover [cez] dar un paso” The full table, with confidence marks and the twenty or so probable readings (Milán, Florencia, poco/poca, mil, Roma, liga), is in n6_reading.md . With them the cipher of ff. 16v–17v reads as a strategic proposal. Del Vasto wants the army out of Rome and moving north before Lautrec settles the matter in Lombardy. His plan: secure Siena, “la qual es muy devota de V. M.”; threaten Florence so that the League must come to its aid; take Perugia, “una tierra del Patrimonio muy rica y muy gruesa”, and the state of Urbino, “en el qual se hallará poca resistencia”; and pass into the Marche, “donde no pueden faltar vituallas”. It ends with a warning that runs through all his letters of that winter: “que el exército por lo de advenir no se puede sostener desta manera”, and that with so many shortages “es imposible que el servicio de V. M. se haga como sus fieles vasallos deseamos”. About fifteen groups stay open, each with a single context that could support two or three words. A third letter in the same key would settle them. No. 19 is one, but only its first leaf has a decryption, and CSP Spain III.2 no. 233 summarises its content from a copy in the Salazar collection, not its words.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one found solved, one read, one without its key
h: No. 20: the Garbino letter and Ranzo’s code
b: f. 44r, no. 20: “R. de […] S. r da poi de haverni scripto per piu l[ette]re”, the dates of letters received (23 November, 3 and 28 December, 4 February), then the code. Every group is a small letter with a number above it. Bibliothèque nationale de France. No. 20 is an Italian letter, dated at Madrid on 11 April 1528, endorsed on the back to “Garbino”. It alternates clear and code. The clear passages report that the Chancellor was ill with gout, that fifty galleys were being fitted out, that a million ducats had been raised in Castile and 500,000 more were expected from the Cortes of Aragon, and that the Empress was in the seventh month and the prince would be sworn heir. The coded passages, about two thirds of the letter, are what it was sent for. The design is explained by the sheets bound after it. On f. 48 is a jargon, with more on f. 49: cover letters signed “Antonio de Cosenza” to “Andrea Romano in Valencia”, news disguised as the price of grain, and a list of cover names. On f. 49v the Emperor is “Joan Jacobo”, del Vasto “portolano de Gergenti”, Garbino himself “antonio petra”. On f. 50 is an “Aditione nel zifra” that shows how the code works. f. 50, the “Aditione nel zifra”: apresso a 327 , al garbino a 330 , Defensione d 308 , havendo h 106 , perilche p 400 . Syllables ( ar , are , an , exne ) have groups too. Bibliothèque nationale de France. Each code group is the initial of the word with a number: apresso is a 327 , Cartagenia c 327 , Garbino g 215 , soa santità s 395 , and common syllables get groups of their own. The addition continues each letter’s list from where the base table stopped (a1–326, b1–156, c1–326 …). The same code is used in the signed letters of Hieronimo Ranzo in BnF fr. 2988 ff. 2 and 9–10 and fr. 3019 f. 73. Ranzo was a Vercelli nobleman at Charles V’s court, of the family of Gattinara’s mother. Norbert Biermann had already tied the addition sheet to Ranzo’s code in a 2017 Cipherbrain thread. The Garbino letter is very likely Ranzo’s.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one found solved, one read, one without its key
b: An initial-letter code is usually weak for one reason: if each letter’s list is in alphabetical order, the number tells you roughly where in the dictionary the word sits. That was the first thing tested. The distribution of the numbers within each initial was compared with where frequent Italian words fall in an alphabetical list, against shuffled orders. No. 20 scores z = −0.5. The same test run on Castiglione’s letters encoded with a genuinely alphabetical code scores about +6.5. Ranzo’s numbering is not alphabetical , so a number says nothing about its word beyond the initial. What is left is a word substitution under one constraint, the initial letter, with about 550 group types in no. 20 and 730 in Ranzo’s own letters. All 1,315 groups of no. 20 were transcribed from full-resolution scans, and about 2,600 more from the six Ranzo pages. The two share 316 group types, which confirms the key is one table. An annealer then assigned each group a word with the right initial, treating the z groups as nulls, and scored the result with a word-bigram model built from Castiglione’s Lettere (diplomatic Italian written from Spain in these same years) and Guicciardini. It was first run on a control: 3,900 words of Castiglione held out of the model and encoded the same way. Test Tokens right Group types right Control, 3,900 encoded words of Castiglione about 46 % about 9 % No. 20 and Ranzo, 3,900 groups Same function words on every restart; content words vary from run to run That is the limit of the method, and the control shows it. Frequent words come out, because their contexts pin them: c170 che , i100 il , p149 per , n38 non , r41 re , s233 sua , m170 mi , p246 più . The words that carry the news occur once or twice each and do not. Nor was there a crib to be had. No Ranzo page repeats a passage of no. 20 (the longest shared run is a stock three-group phrase), the copy marked “dup.ª” duplicates another Ranzo letter rather than this one, and the Clairambault copy is undeciphered. The other “pièces en chiffre” of fr. 2988 are a different, French, symbol cipher.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one found solved, one read, one without its key
b: Only new evidence will finish no. 20: Ranzo’s base table, or any of his letters that was deciphered at the time or survives in clear. The places to look are Gattinara’s papers in the Archivio di Stato di Vercelli, the imperial correspondence in Simancas and Vienna, and the other side of the Garbino network. The transcriptions and the solver are ready for a key or a crib; with even a few hundred words of known plaintext the substitution would close quickly. For no. 6, a clear copy or a full decryption of no. 19 would settle the remaining groups.

t: The Farnese letter — Simon Klee’s solution reviewed
b: Farnese to the nuncio Poggio, four folios of unseparated digits, set by George Lasry as Vatican Challenge Part 5 in 2019. Simon Klee recovered the mixed one-/two-digit key and a candidate plaintext in September 2026; MysteryTwister accepted the submission. Independent half-text recovery, controls, manuscript checks and historical corroboration support the key and the substance of the reading. The earlier Antonio Elio classification on this site is retracted. Solution review · September 2026 The Farnese letter, solved by Simon Klee Cardinal Alessandro Farnese to the nuncio Giovanni Poggio at the court of Charles V, Rome, April 1542.
